IMPORTANT NOTICE: The objective of this publication is to share with the public and have come alive the wonders of the Uintas, making everybody’s experiences life enhancing, and SAFE. The last item is crucial as it deals with SURVIVAL and avoiding the unnecessary loss of life that occurs each summer three or four times in the Uintas. There will be a modest charge for the eBook--strictly for the purpose of recovering a portion of the considerable expenses had over the 16 years dedicated to producing this work, and also make possible continual updating of the book. So, in reality this is a project of PUBLIC SERVICE. COVER by Cordell M. Andersen PHOTOGRAPHS: 1,738 of the 1,774 photographs* & maps, including photo art and creation of maps with routes and distances by Cordell M. Andersen.

Aerial photographs--by Jonathan Jaussi. Other photographs by Jake Hirschi, Matt McKell, Elisabeth Johanson, Doug Perry, Albert Richens, Mike Ward, & the Utah DWR—Division of Wildlife Resources, all used gratefully with their permission and given credit given in the footnotes. National Geographic TOPO! Outdoor Recreation Mapping Software CD/ROM

was the basic source of topographic maps. For permission for their use I contacted the Managing Editor of the NGS Image Collection Dept. resulting in her saying, “I doubt we ….. have rights to most of them….sorry we could not assist you with this.” This prompted me to research deeper and I learned that the National Geographic Society sponsored the software, but the copyright was held by, and I quote, “TOPO! Is a registered trademark of 2006 NIGHT, Inc., copyright 2005 Tele Atlas, North America, Inc. – www.teleatlas.com.” Said, website, and NIGHT, Inc. are now non-existent. A search of the entity that succeeded them list no connection to TOPO! Additionally I discovered that the TOPO! software is no longer commercially available. So I go forward under the fair use doctrine as a PUBLIC SERVICE, using the license I purchased along with the software in 2006. The logo on the software, as seen below, is embedded in each topographical map, giving proper and grateful credit to the original sponsor and producer of the software. The maps with routes, distances and labels were created by the author of this book, who holds rights to their use. Permission for copying them for personal use is given to all those who purchase this eBook. Earth images, and others converted into maps are used in accordance with Google Guidelines and the fair use doctrine, and, as explained in the box above--this book is produced as a Public Service, and each image I use is given clear and visible attribution to Google, with the Guidelines, under these circumstances stating: “Feel free to move forward with your project.” Some earth views are converted into maps with routes highlighted; Others routes are created and labels added by the author all in accordance with the guidelines.. Several photographs, articles and inserts from websites, like, Wikipedia, are used in accordance with the fair use doctrine, and all are properly given attribution in the footnotes, and in the Reference section.

Printing of the entire eBook, or portions of it, can be made for personal, non-commercial purposes, such as guidance for auto-tour, hikes, backpacks, horse & goat packing, but only by those who have purchased the e-book, as long as credit for what is reproduced be given the author. Other uses of the eBook, portions thereof, and photographs cannot be reproduced or transmitted in any form or by any means, electronic, photocopying, or otherwise without prior written permission from the author—unless with the clear objective of promoting the availability and distribution of this book for the public good. front matter (9)

FORWARD by Dr. Ralph "Ted" Packard & Charlie Peterson

NOTE BY THE AUTHOR: I feel honored and blessed to have my original two High Uinta Friends be the ones to introduce this book--which is the culmination of what’s working out to be a 67 year long effort to meet my 1952 vow to:

“Explore, photograph and report on all of the High Uintas”

Above you see us at the end of our 1954 two week backpack crossing the Primitive Area. We were 18 and 19 years old. ********************************* On the right you see us 54 years later in 2008--when 72 and 73 years old, on our GOLDEN ANNIVERSARY BACKPACK to the Red Castle area. It had been 50 years since our last backpack together. Now, 11 years later in 2019, we are together again -- them helping me meet the VOW I made 67 years ago on my first backpack, described in my PREFACE. I deeply appreciate them having years ago led me to the Uintas, still be my TRAIL BUDDIES, and for announcing this book to the world. ********************************** All three of us began our university studies majoring in Geology and planning on thereafter organizing a geologic exploration company and getting rich during the then ongoing uranium boom in Utah. In the following letters from Ted, and then Charlie, and in my PREFACE, you’ll notice our interesting divergent paths, but with one constant:

OUR LOVE OF THE HIGH UINTAS. Cordell M. Andersen *****************************************

front matter (10)

Pictures from 2008 GOLDEN ANNIVERSARY BACKPACK

By Ted Packard

Forward to the High Uinta’s Guidebook Cordell Andersen is unique, one of a kind, a true friend, and someone who likely knows more about Utah’s iconic High Uinta Mountain range than anyone on the planet. It started early, getting close to 7 decades ago, with a major early highlight being when three fast friends, Charlie Peterson, Cordell and myself, set out on a 15-day trek from the West to the East end of the then “High Uinta’s Primitive Area.” Quitting our 1954 summer jobs right after Labor Day, we returned to our homes in Provo and made hasty preparations. Charlie and I had been inspired by a wonderful scoutmaster, Les Leichty, early on, and the three of us had been on shorter Uinta mountain backpacks in the immediately preceding years to lakes with exotic names like Pinto, Granddaddy, Lodgepole, and Mohawk. But this was the “big one” all the way from the West entry point at Defa’s Dude Ranch (then 8 hiking miles from Granddaddy Lake) to the Eastern terminus at the old U-Bar Ranch far down the Uinta River. Available maps were primitive, even including the two USGS quadrangles with copyright dates of 1905 or 1906 that we had found. Our gear was equally primitive by today’s standards and included a surplus Army rucksack and homemade pack boards, a 2-man floorless pup tent, surplus rain ponchos, a leather jacket (worn by Cordell), midcentury fishing gear and topping it all off, specially purchased Alpine hiking hats, including jaunty feathers, on each of our heads. Many adventures followed still vividly encoded in our memories--sleeping the first night in the middle of the narrow trail after a late afternoon start; meeting a herder on the trail heading home after a summer of grazing sheep in high mountain meadows and the only other person encountered the entire trip; getting briefly lost trying to find Squaw Basin; sleeping 3 in the 2-man tent when it rained; catching 2-pound “brookies” at North Star Lake in a snow storm; using copper wire and small pliers to sew the sole back on Cordell’s boots while perched atop King’s Peak; and me surviving the treacherous mud bog on the NW shore of one of the Chain Lakes while my laughing buddies pitched mudballs directly at me. It

front matter (11)

was a life changing experience for three adolescent boys as they transitioned into adulthood and in the process stored up indelible memories that would last at least into old age. Many more High Uinta backpacking trips followed, never quite as long or as devoid of other humans (contrasted with the many happy hikers of later decades), sometimes with one or both of our threesome, often with family members or young boy scouts or other friends, and even into our dotage years with considerably less taxing goals and plans. After undergraduate college, I earned a PhD in counseling psychology from the University of Minnesota and spent 40+ great years as a faculty member at the University of Utah and never too far away from the life changing High Uinta’s. Charlie completed an MBA at Harvard, a later law degree from the University of Utah, established several businesses over the years, was an early environmental advocate as an elected member of the County Council in Moab, UT, and in recent years has lived on Vashon Island across the Bay from Seattle, WA. Always involved in the mountains and great outdoors, the imprint of those earlier High Uinta’s grand adventures has affected him with equal impact. Cordell has led an exotic life but one no less influenced by our shared Uinta Mountain experiences. After a few years building Andersen Samplers in a business established by his father, Cordell moved his family to Central America and for well over three decades developed altruistic programs and agricultural businesses amongst the indigenous Mayan people living in the Guatemalan highlands. The culmination of his humanitarian efforts was the Guatemalan Foundation and, especially, the implementation of various educational and service programs that have long influenced the lives, for the better, of many of these neglected peoples. The second and more recent great goal of Cordell’s life has been both to experience and to chronicle the mountain landscape that influenced the three of us so deeply during those early formative years. Over the past 16 years since returning to Utah, while hiking literally over two thousand miles, Cordell has backpacked to most lakes, hiked most trails, and driven almost every jeep trail and paved road that relate to this wonderful mountainous area. And, incredibly, he has chronicled this with almost 1,800 color photos, scores of detailed topographic maps, and reams of notes and related documents. The result is The High Uinta Mountains: A Complete Guide to High Adventure that follows. I’ve long been a collector of High Uinta’s guidebooks that, while more helpful than what was not available in the 1950s, are without exception relatively brief, cover limited topics and possibilities, are black and white, lack the brilliant colors and pictures that distinguish the High Uinta’s, and aside from brief descriptions of entry roadways, say little about the surrounding countryside. Cordell’s tome does it all! At close to 700 pages this is not designed for relaxing read-it-fromcover-to-cover in a couple of settings, but as an encyclopedic reference covering the High Uinta’s from all angles. It is unique and in a class by itself. The gorgeous photos alone, most taken by Cordell with his single lens reflex camera, add immeasurably to the experience. The brief Introduction section includes several relevant but little-known stories about High Uinta’s happenings (e.g., Jedediah Smith’s early connection, the Tie Hackers later involvement, etc.).

front matter (12)

Chapter 1 details for the first-time 856 miles of the many roads, paved as well as dirt, that surround this massive mountain range and provide entry to innumerable lakes, short hikes, longer backpacks, historical sights, and gorgeous scenery. All points of the compass are covered. Chapter 2, the veritable heart of the book, deals with the official High Uinta’s Wilderness Area so designated in a 1984 legislative act by the US Congress. In about 250 pages, Cordell covers in considerable detail all access trails, major trail systems (e.g., the Highline trail), and less well and even unknown trails. All named lakes are described comprehensively, usually supplemented with gorgeous color photos, and several unnamed bodies of water, some containing fish populations, also are included. The chapter is organized into North Slope and South Slope sections, and the commentary proceeds systematically drainage by drainage facilitating reader comprehension. Chapter 3 introduces a new dimension and covers the Western portion of the mountain range that was not included in the 1984 wilderness act. Many lakes, trail systems, and scenic features that drain into the Provo, Weber, and Bear Rivers are discussed in 60+ pages of detailed printed and pictorial information. Though smaller in size, this western portage of the Uinta range is comparable in many ways to the designated wilderness area described in Chapter 2 and presents additional opportunities for meaningful mountain experiences. Chapter 4 continues in this vein by describing in about 40 pages many less frequented landscapes in the Eastern end of the High Uinta’s. Lakes, trail systems, and access roads are described clearly and represent topography less frequently visited than popular official wilderness locations. Chapter 5 becomes highly personal and in about 70 pages Cordell shares insights, recommendations, and experiences from an unusual life, much of it lived in mountainous, exhilarating, and sometimes remote outdoor environments. His sage advice is unique in many ways and shares food for thought gleaned from an independent, unusual and well-lived life. An informative and lengthy Appendix follows that includes more than a dozen articles, some authored by Cordell, on various topics and experiences related to his lifelong involvement with the High Uinta’s. He even provides highly personalized recommendations not only for backpacking but also for dealing with life’s bumps and bruises. The eBook ends with a brief section citing References and a 14-page Index that lists page numbers organized alphabetically for all lakes, trails, geographic features, names, topics, etc., and facilitates readers access to specific information. As with the life, so with the man. As I said in the beginning, “Cordell Andersen is unique, one of a kind, a true friend, and someone who likely knows more about Utah’s iconic High Uinta Mountain range than anyone on the planet.” This one of a kind eBook is recommended heartily to all who love the great outdoors and who venture, in real time or in their mind’s eye, into the known and the unknown.

Ted

front matter (13)

Pictures from 2008 GOLDEN ANNIVERSARY BACKPACK

CHARLIE PETERSON

Author’s note: Charlie didn’t want to mention his university degrees or other accomplishments, but, as you’ve noticed, Ted does say a needed brief word about both of them--for me they are both among the most unique individuals I’ve ever known for whom I’m profoundly grateful. In 2019, 83 years old. Charlie preferred describing himself and wife, in an email to me, saying: “We are still engaging in outdoor physical activities. We’re both active cross-country skiers in winter and backpackers and cyclists in summer. I still run to stay in shape and my best claim to physical ability is probably that I still participate in cross-country ski races. I also enter an occasional running race (not to exceed 10k), Politically I’m a diehard environmentalist and believe that we need to do more to preserve this planet for our grandkids. We live frugally, we walk and bike and take public transportation; we recycle whatever we can. I’m very fortunate to be able to follow the lifestyle I do and realize I won’t forever. I spoke this morning with a friend who’s suffering terrible back problems and there are certainly more like him than not, so I try to live by enjoying what I can right now. I do hope you—Andy, will be able to get on a trail this coming summer.”

Charlie

THE LEGACY OF THE UINTAS I would be remiss if I didn’t describe my own introduction to the Uintas--one that includes memories of hikes into the wilderness that even predate Cordell’s first efforts. I do this, not to describe myself, but to describe a person who first took Ted Packard and me on an overnight backpack into the Uintas--a person I’ll never forget and who deserves all the praise Ted, and I can extend. He was the person who introduced me to the Uintas, “got it in my blood” as he used to say, and with whom I shared many miles of trail. Les Liechty was a youthful Boy Scout leader when I first met him in 1949. I was 13, had visited the Uintas a couple of times with family, but never overnight in the backcountry. In the summer of 1950, Les led a group of us, including Ted Packard, on a weeklong hike from the Mirror Lake trailhead into the Pinto/Governor Lake area. The following winter at Boy Scout meetings, Les

front matter (14)

helped us build our own backpacks out of thin, wooden boards and long, triangular, “mothersewn” pockets on either side of the lashed-on sleeping bag/tent. The next summer, he led a similar group of us teenage Boy Scouts up Rock Creek and into Grandaddy Basin for my first visit to that particular set of lakes. Around this period of time, Ted and I had met Cordell, and as Cordell has written, thus began many trips from Defas Dude Ranch up Lightning Ridge and into the Grandaddies--culminating in our two week super backpack adventure of 1954 as described by Cordell and Ted. The rest, as someone once said, is history. History as well described by Cordell in these writings, but history that always reminds me of the legacy left us by Les Liechty. Les was a lifelong schoolteacher, father, and leader, but to me he will always be much more--the person who inspired so many of us to follow him up those wonderful Uinta trails. I have been privileged for some 70 years to hike into the Uintas, not only with Ted, Cordell, and many others, but at the very beginning under Les’ able leadership. Les died in 2006 at age 80. Cordell has had a varied and challenging life. He has fought through multiple physical challenges, but he has maintained that stubborn perseverance characterized by his determination to hike throughout his wonderful Uintas. And not only to hike the hike, but to document his achievements, his struggles, and his (sometimes) disappointments. I seriously doubt that anyone has matched his efforts to hike to every lake and walk every trail in the Uinta range and to then describe just what he’s accomplished, and describe it he does. Cordell’s writings span many years and include more than just his own personal experiences. He has included descriptions of just about every trail; how to drive to and around the mountains; and descriptions of the various trailheads. He has researched history; wildflowers and other flora; animals; maps; and more. And he includes reminiscing and even photos of the many hikers and other folks he has met up with in his research, travels, and hikes. I could say more about Cordell’s ambitious project to describe in detail the High Uintas--its description, its history, its memories, but what strikes me as most significant is the lifelong attraction so many of us feel that keeps pulling us back time after time again. It’s been over 70 years since I first visited and experienced the lakes, the sky, the forests, and the mountains that we call the High Uintas and even though I now live in the Northwest, I still keep traveling back and hiking in to our beloved “Grandaddies.” As you read Cordell’s book, you will get a feel for that magnetic attraction that still tugs at me. Cordell’s lifelong High Uintas explorations and efforts dwarf my own, but even though I’ve continued to backpack throughout the western United States, I still find myself longing to always go back one more time to the Uintas.

Charlie

front matter (15)

Charlie, Ted & Little Andy on THE GOLDEN ANNIVERSARY BACKPACK in 2008 ***************************

So, FORWARD, exploring the….

…..“hypnotic” allure & wonderment of the UINTAS.

p. 1

PREFACE

"Hey, Cordell…let's head for the GRANDADDIES for the fish opener on Saturday." My new friend, Charlie Peterson, went on,

"Tomorrow is the 4th and we don't work so we can prepare our packs, drive up over Wolf Creek Pass and be at the Hades Canyon Trailhead by nightfall. We can hike up the canyon during the night and be in the Grandaddies by first light."

This is what Charlie was talking about-- Grandaddy Lake, the largest in the Uintas and the Grandaddy Basin

I was new in the area and among the neighborhood kids was the only one who had an old family car I could use for such a trip……so I was one popular kid! I didn't know what he was talking about, but soon learned that the Grandaddies was what those in the know called an alpine basin in the High Uinta Mountains--that stretched along Utah's northern border south of Wyoming, to the northeast of the Wasatch Front where we lived in Provo, Utah. That had me so excited, that Charlie wondered what the heck was happening to me. Why was I almost not able to contain myself?

p. 2

It was summer 1952 in Provo. Our family had just moved to Utah a month before from Albany, California where I grew up. For some reason--maybe my Mormon pioneer heritage, I had grown up intensely interested in the outdoors, but living in the San Francisco Bay area I had never really been able to experience it much, so I had lived it vicariously through books and outdoor magazines. When around 8 years old I was making a little money delivering a weekly newspaper--and doubling my earnings with sympathetic tips--as it was said that my load of 200 newspapers to begin the route weighed more than me. I soon had the whole set of 8 Tarzan books. From them I graduated to books about the mountain men and fur trappers of the old West, Alaska and Canada, and soon had subscriptions to the outdoor magazines. In that phase of expanding my horizons I replaced Tarzan as my "first hero" with unmatched explorer and mountain man, Jedediah Smith. You'll see later the impact this great man had on my life and his connection to the Uintas.

At 16, with the Wasatch Mountains almost literally in our backyard, I was beginning to live my dream roaming the hills with my dad's Browning .22 rifle, but hadn't heard about the High Uintas until Charlie hatched the Grandaddies plan. I was excited! For the first time I would be able to use my Army surplus rucksack, mummy sleeping bag, and Army issue poncho--all of which had seen service in World War II in the Pacific against the Japanese. I had bought them cheap in California at the then very common ARMY & NAVY SURPLUS stores, with money from my last job there--working 7 days a week from 5-7 AM cleaning up Ted's Bar--mopping up disgusting slop and debris after what looked like pretty wild nights. Then in Utah we passed on the celebration of Independence Day and prepared our trip, loaded the family's 2nd car I was permitted to drive, a 1939 Plymouth, and headed up Provo Canyon to Heber and from there made our way to Francis and soon we were on a dirt road grinding our way over the 9,485 foot Wolf Creek Pass, and then dropped down to the North Fork of the Duchesne River near Hanna.

p. 3

Note: That road is now the paved Utah Highway 35…..I don't remember what it was called back then.

Six miles up the Duchesne River canyon, with night coming on, we passed Defa's Dude Ranch, seen at twilight above, and just a little beyond parked at the Hades Canyon Trailhead. It was near dark as Ted Packard, Charlie Peterson, and 2 or 3 others shouldered our packs and started up the trail. My on-the-job training in backpacking was beginning-the hard way. Ted and Charlie, having grown up in Utah, already had some experience backpacking, had pretty good gear, and knew the steep trail up Hades Canyon. It must have been me and the other guys who didn't know what we were doing as I recall one of us carrying a watermelon, and I was lugging several quarts of Hires Root Beer--of course in glass bottles--no plastic or aluminum yet, plus Baby Ruth candy bars, and cans of Pork & Beans. Somehow in my years of feasting on outdoor magazines I hadn't ever noticed the phrase, "lightweight backpacking," which likely didn't exist yet, and it would be 40 years before Ray Jardine would come up with books, like, BEYOND BACKPACKING: Guide to Lightweight Hiking.

Author’s labeling of Wilderness map to fit 1952 Primitive Area designation Soon we were struggling up Hades Canyon's Lightning Ridge. Ahead of us were 10 tough miles, and 3,000 feet of elevation gain to the pass. There was only one flashlight in the group and we began having trouble keeping on the trail along the raging waters of Hades Creek that literally cascaded down the canyon. Once I recall hearing blood-curdling screams behind us from one of the guys who had fallen behind. We rushed back with the flashlight and got there just in time to help pull our buddy out of the ice cold creek. Luckily he had kept on his feet and was just in up to his knees.

p. 4

About half way up we passed SPLASH DAM and the lake that formed behind it. Many years later I came to know "splash dams" on the North Slope that were connected to "tie hackers" and logging efforts that were part of the Transcontinental Railway construction in 1867 creeping across Wyoming to the north. NOTE: In the INTRODUCTION I'll get into telling

the story of this tough bunch of lumbermen--the tie hackers, which most Utahans and others know nothing about--as they are not even mentioned in the history books about the Transcontinental Railroad, which was key to conquering and developing the West. But, what these temporary log dams were on the north, didn't make sense in Hades Canyon….until now in the new century—my research revealing it was a senseless effort, which story I'll tell when we get to the details of "The Grandaddies."

That night became one of the most unforgettable hiking experiences of my life. Quite a few hours later in the faint light of dawn we waded through a snow drift, and finally made it to 10,700 foot high Hades Pass. In the dim light we made out a large rustic Forest Service sign announcing that we were in the High Uintas Primitive Area. I've inserted above the dimly lit sign describing what in 1984 would become designated by the U.S. Congress as the High Uintas Wilderness Area, almost doubling its size to 456,705 acres making it Utah's largest Wilderness, and by far the most diverse. With the eastern sky beginning to glow we maneuvered our way through more snow drifts and began our descent to the basin making out in the dim light the reflections of several of the 26 fishable lakes that dotted the basin. Eventually I would learn that this was just the beginning of more than 1,000 lakes of the High Uinta Mountains that stretched nearly 150 miles to the east ending at Flaming Gorge and Brown's Hole, now Brown's Park, famous for being a hideout of Butch Cassidy and his gang, the "Wild Bunch." The Green River flowing through those areas becomes sort of the eastern edge of the Uintas, a good portion of its water coming from the Uinta's North Slope streams, and then downstream added to by the streams of the South Slope. Of course back then I was oblivious to all of that and much, much more.

p. 5

Soon we made it down to Grandaddy Lake, and then others--Betsy, Mohawk, Lodgepole, and were revived in spirits casting our red & white Daredevil spoons into the crystal clear waters, and catching mostly eastern brook trout--so many that we soon lost count, keeping only--of course--our legal limit to take home, but releasing literally hundreds. I don't remember much more about that trip, except that, in spite of the extreme difficulty doing that 10+ mile hike in the dark, I became hooked on the High Uintas, and joined Ted and Charlie who had already experienced the mysterious, almost hypnotic allure that many fall prey to. I don't even remember who the others were, except that after making it back to the car and heading home, they swore they would never go backpacking again! Backpacking wasn't for the faint hearted! For me it was just the beginning, and other backpack trips were made that summer to places that became our favorites, like remote and off-trail Fern Lake, seen at sunrise in the precious photo panel on the previous page. The next summer--1953, there was more backpacking, and learning how to do it more effectively opening up the way to explore deeper into the Primitive Area. By the end of that second year we hatched a big plan for the end of the 1954 summer season to traverse the entire Primitive Area from Hades Canyon, through the Grandaddy Basin to the Highline Trail and following it along the spine of the Uinta Mountains all the way to the Uinta River. Ted had graduated from high school a year ahead of Charlie and me--we graduating in 1954. That summer we all had summer jobs. Mine was as a trapper and hunter in a Wildlife Research Project for the University of Utah at the Army's Dugway Proving Grounds in the West Utah Desert. We all worked through August, and then launched ourselves into the Uintas for our super-backpack, returning just before school started at BYU in midSeptember.

By then we had learned a bit more about backpacking, but I still used my Army surplus rucksack, and Army poncho that also served as my lean-to shelter every night. I had 55 lbs. on my back as we began the daytime hike up Hades Canyon and at the pass Ted took a picture--seen above on the left of me and Charlie with the Primitive Area sign.

p. 6

We worked our way east for two weeks, logging 150 miles to the Uinta River Trailhead--seen in the previous photos. We had sort of thought that by then we "would have seen it all," but for me it was just a small beginning.

Above is seen a Google Earth view of the High Uinta Mountains—with the author’s labels, more than 100 miles long, the majority in 1984 becoming the WILDERNESS AREA --the lightly colored area above timberline--11,000 ft. in Uintas. MAP: ©2018 Google LLC, used with permission. Google and the Google logo are registered trademarks of Google LLC.

I realized we had basically just seen "the spine" of the Uintas to the Uinta River Drainage where the Primitive Area ended, but there were all the drainages that started at the "spine," with major streams forming the South Slope, and many others forming the North Slope. I vowed that before my life was over I would explore, photograph and report on all of the High Uintas Primitive Area, later the vow expanded to the larger Wilderness Area. Eventually my life would lead me away from Utah for nearly 3 years as a missionary for the LDS Church in Central America. On my return I married and started a family, while at the same time fulfilling my military obligation becoming a Medical Specialist in the Army, and eventually a graduate from BYU. Below I'm seen at a remote grass landing field in Guatemala. The other photo is of some of our Explorers in the Uintas, explained next.

For a couple of years, back in Utah, there was some fairly intense High Uintas activity, with

p. 7

In that period Ted was an Explorer leader--I being his assistant. We worked with a group of 23 young men who didn't seem to be the type interested in wearing uniforms and getting Merit badges, so we got them interested in manly adventure involving the High Uintas with the big summer project being a two week backpack including climbing Utah's highest mountain--Kings Peak. The winter was spent helping them make their backpacks, acquiring the equipment they needed, and learning how to enjoyably and safely backpack. Separate from that, Ted and me had our high adventures together in the Uintas--trips we could have never risked with the boys. Those were great experiences catching record arctic grayling and native cutthroat trout seen below.

The arctic grayling on the left was caught by Ted in Lake Atwood in 1962 when huge grayling began hitting our spinning lures--a rarity as usually flies are used for grayling that have small mouths. The camera used was later dropped into the water and transparencies saved were badly damaged resultant in the poor quality photos, the upper one improved after creating the one with titles. The heavy bodied native cutthroat, seen on the right, I caught in upper Red Castle lake, was saved in a snow bank to take home un-cleaned for weighing, but animals got to it, leaving only the lighter tail half that weighed 3-1/2 lbs. with which we determined the whole live weight at over 8 lbs.

Eventually Ted headed east for higher education, and I headed south to work among the Mayan Indians in Guatemala--a quixotic adventure that began in 1967, and was predicted,

"At 6 months you’ll come running home with your tail between your legs!"

p. 8

But, after going through a 30 year long Guerrilla War, and almost every other kind of scary and incredibly rewarding experience known to man, I finally came "running home with my tail between my legs," after 35 years of high adventure among the Mayans. As the years in Guatemala were coming to an end, I recalled my vow to:

"Explore, photograph, and report on all of the High Uintas Primitive Area." I knew that it had become the much larger Wilderness Area, and began making my plans which developed into what I began calling an "expedition" that would be 27 days of noresupply backpacking 206+ miles crossing the Wilderness area, with zigs and zags from the spine south, and then north as I followed the Highline Trail east to the Uinta River. I calculated I would begin with a load a bit over 80 lbs. on my back and around my waist, including a new Nikon camera and needed lenses, a whole bag of 35mm. transparency film, plus emergency equipment, like a satellite phone, and my Colt .45 Defender. Especially because of my small stature and advancing age--by that time in my 67th year, I was going to have to be tough and strong. Making that possible, during my years in Guatemala, we not only actually lived among the Indians, but I personally worked along with my Indian employees, including always helping them unload from trucks the 100 lb. bags of feed and fertilizer. This broke with the tradition of rich landowners which was to live in a city and not do manual labor, rather prance around finely dressed with highly polished shoes, and just give orders. Most such wealthy types—called there Ladinos, hated me for it, with one exception with whom the major business deal of my life was to depend--he trusting me totally to be an honest man because of my work ethic and treatment of the Indians as my brothers and sisters. First, it was on a large 600 acre plantation that I developed into a dairy, eventually with the largest producing cow--12 gallons/day, and the Champion Jersey cows in all of Central America. Then, after establishing the resident Indians into their own community, I moved on to a smaller farm growing coffee. Towards the end I also began to run each year in an

p. 9

International Half Marathon and doing it for 14 consecutive years…..so I had maintained myself in good condition. But, with the upcoming "expedition" I had to do more, and so I began hefting to my shoulders a 100 lb. bag of fertilizer, and hiking around the rolling hills of my farm. I did half a mile the first day, and stretched it out finally to 1 mile, then 2, and eventually to 4 miles 2-3 times a week. Often it was after our frequent rains on slippery trails that taught me better balance, agility, and sometimes how to struggle back onto my feet after a fall with a 100 lb. load on my shoulders. I also began doing every other day a video exercise program called TAE' BO, all in addition to actually working on our farm. Additionally of great importance I discovered key supplements that made my bones hard as rock, and held back the aging process. Then in 2000 I experienced the acid test when in Guatemala City with 2 of my boys, Jesse and Nephi. We were downtown on 6th Avenue in front of a Taco Bell when I was jumped by 3-4 gangbangers, one had me in a strangle hold trying to pull me to the ground. The others were ripping my pants to shreds in an effort to get at my pockets. I had vowed as a young kid, working out with a punching bag, to never hit anyone with a doubled up fist as I had the impression I would kill someone. But, all of a sudden the chips were down and I went to work hitting as fast and as hard as I could with the full intention of hurting real bad all of my attackers. This gang was well known for being armed and for having actually killed victims, but they apparently had never expected that a 64 year old gringo would fight back. My 13-1/2 year old son, Jesse--a future Marine, wadded into the fray to help, hitting the one who was strangling me. All of a sudden they gave up and fled, likely afraid that the armed guard in Taco Bell, or police, would come to my rescue. You can read about that fight in COMBAT HANDGUNS, March, 2001. See the entire article in Appendix 9.

p. 10

The point being that my body was able to resist and withstand 3-4 youthful attackers and win with basically no injury, and no loss of valuables, except for my shredded pants that left me almost naked surrounded by onlookers. Without working and exercising as I was doing, I don't think that would have been possible. By the way it all happened so fast in a blur of furious action that we were never sure whether there were 3 or 4 attackers. By 2002, after 35 years of living and working in Guatemala, I returned to Utah "with my tail between my legs," while at the same time being in a situation where I had to be a Mr. Mom to 5 children in the beginning from 3 to 11 years old--three boys, and two adopted girls. I was also the "eternal" volunteer director of the Foundation for Indian Development that had been organized in 1970 to help with the altruistic aspects of my life among the Mayans-work which I continued doing after returning to the U.S. through two volunteer Guatemalan representatives until completing our GOLDEN ANNIVERSARY in 2017. Note: At the end the

foundation's name was the GUATEMALAN FOUNDATION which, if you are interested, you can learn about, as the website will be maintained forever at: http://www.guatemalanfoundation.org/ Once back in Utah I began making plans to begin fulfilling my "vow" beginning with the summer of 2003. My Army surplus equipment was replaced by fairly lightweight gear. I made a couple of warm-up backpacks into the Grandaddy Basin and then launched the "expedition" with 83 lbs. of load to do my solo 27 day, no resupply backpack. I coined the name of what I was doing, The HIGH UINTAS WILDERNESS PROJECT. I innocently assumed that my "expedition" would pretty well get the entire job done.

I rather learned--again, that I was still just scratching the surface of the Uintas, so kept backpacking and by the end of the 2017 summer season completed 15 years of effort in my 82nd year with around 2,000 miles of backpacking. and can at least say that I have been to all the basins and drainages in the Wilderness Area. Remaining are a few little nooks and crannies not explored and photographed which I'll have to admit I might not get to, even though I'll keep pecking away at it as long as I can.

p. 11

During most of these 15 years I have always had with me a satellite phone, provided by Russ Smith of SKYCALL SATELLITE, and have been a "scout," or correspondent, for KSL Outdoors Radio from Salt Lake City calling into the program each Saturday morning from wherever I was in the mountains. During the 2014 season Russ and Tim Hughes, who runs the program, suggested, perhaps jokingly, that a lake be given my name, but I'm a simple man and took it seriously and chose a no-name, no-number lake nobody would care about located at 12,302 feet in the eastern shadow of South Kings Peak, and named it "Little Andy Lake," using my nickname as a youth. I tried twice during the summer of 2015 in my 80th year to get to it and came up short--due to experiencing high altitude sickness, but learned important lessons I have shared freely on my website, and explained clearly in this book. But, my constant theme being, "NEVER, NEVER GIVE IN……EASILY," I finally learned to manage my High Altitude Sickness, and in 2016 did a 6 day backpack through the Henry's Fork Basin, over Gunsight Pass and made it to Little Andy Lake you see below in a photo taken from South Kings Peak.1 It happens to be the highest lake in Utah, 550 ft. higher than Mt. Timpanogos that looms over Utah Valley.

Over those 2,000 miles I have experienced and survived about everything imaginable, all of which will be shared at the appropriate places throughout this work, including "my most amazing experience in the outdoors" when I deal with Jackson Park and the Crow Basin; and of most importance my survival experiences and what I did to get through them. I want to get into circulation the key principles that will save lives--not only in the High Uintas, but in any wilderness.

1

Photograph taken by Elisabeth Johanson, and used with her permission.

p. 12

Part of this "life saving" effort will be to furnish information about those sad tragedies where survival principles were ignored and lives were lost…needlessly. All of that will be inserted in the appropriate places throughout this guidebook, and listed clearly in the Index. During all these years I have also delved into the history, the mysteries, the legends and the tall tales of our Uintas, along with many miles of related exploration and discovery--all of which have multiplied many times the enjoyment I want to share--like the first white men in the Uintas--even as early as 1540, and the legends of GOLD IN THE UINTAS --with whole mountains of gold. Then comes the story of unmatched legendary explorer & fur trapper, Jedediah Smith and his team, plus on the North Slope the story of the unknown and "unsung heroes without whom the West might not have been won," called tie hackers, including President Eisenhower's hero, Tom “Bear River” Smith, and his involvement in the Beartown ghost town on the High Uinta's Bear River described as, "the liveliest if not the most wicked town in America." And, I will not neglect including my "vision in a dream" of BIG FOOT & SON up Little East Fork of Blacks Fork--and much more. So, I will sprinkle throughout my book this wonderment, along with what I call VISIONS OF NATURE, to enrich the reader, and have come alive your hikes and backpacks into the mountains. Above all I believe my own personal smidgen of experience in the Uintas can be a guiding blessing for your outdoor experience which can inspire each to also share with others and multiply the safety, enjoyment and inspiration of God's great swath of beauty we call the HIGH UINTA MOUNTAINS.

Above is a hodgepodge of some of the places, institutions, people and sources where I have done extensive research to share a wealth of information about our magnificent High Uinta Mountains There will be many references in the footnotes, and at the end of the book there will be a complete list of the References used, and the many YouTube videos I have produced, including what the Salt Lake Tribune called, “The Grandfather of all Utah hiking slide shows.”

p. 13

INTRODUCTION: UTAH’S ALPINE WONDERLANDTHE HIGH UINTA MOUNTAINS Its Mysterious Past & Present “The largest alpine area in the Intermountain West" 2

I was struggling up the boulder fields towards the summit of Utah’s highest mountain, Kings Peak (13,528 feet)—“struggling” as I was slowed by my backpack. Most climbers do the peak as a day hike from Henrys Fork Basin's Dollar Lake, a 16 mile roundtrip. Others leave their packs back on nearby 12,600 foot Anderson Pass. I was a rarity as I was planning on bivouacking that night on the peak to get some unique full moon photographs, as well as sunset and sunrise shots. In my 68th year (2003), and being alone, I had to be cautious as I couldn’t afford a miss-step and stopped frequently to rest. Notable was the gathering storm all around the mountain. A couple working their way towards the peak paused to say hello.

“I’m Kristian, and this is Dorina, my wife. We are from Belgium.” My immediate response was, “What are you doing here rather than in your famous Alps ?” I got a wonderfully unexpected reply.

“WE PREFER THE UINTAS TO THE ALPS,” replied Kristian. 2

See Ashley National Forest website: www.fs.fed.us/r4/ashley/recreation/highuintas/index.shlml

p. 14

I beamed with pride, and asked them why our High Uintas had won out. Kristian continued, “The Uintas are more remote, more pristine, more diverse and less commercial—

for us, a true wilderness.” I was always ready to promote Utah’s largest Wilderness, that in my opinion not even Utah’s National Parks could compete with, but my new Belgian friends didn’t need to hear my sales pitch, although a few readers might--which you probably guessed I’ll get to in a minute. Kristian and Dorina had left their packs back on 12,600 foot Anderson pass. They soon left me behind as they disappeared in a swirling cloud that enveloped the mountain. A bit later I noticed Kristian and Dorina coming down from the summit, and Dorina shouted over the howling wind, “Why is the weather so terrible?” Kristian smiled and yelled something I couldn’t understand and soon they were gone. They had hitched a ride to the High Uintas’ Henrys Fork Trailhead from Fort Bridger, Wyoming 36 miles to the north. They then hiked the 16 miles up into the High Uintas Wilderness through the Henrys Fork basin, over 11,850 foot Gunsight Pass and on to the peak. They were to go down to the west across the upper reaches of Yellowstone Creek, then to the north over Smiths Fork Pass into the spectacular Red Castle Peak area and follow the Smiths Fork Trail down to the China Meadows Trailhead and hitch a ride back to civilization. I told them to check out Red Castle Peak that I suggested many feel is the most beautiful mountain scene in Utah. I added they would be treading hallowed ground for some of us along East Fork of Smiths Fork, named in honor of arguably one of the greatest mountain men and explorers of the old West—Jedediah Smith. The Email address Kristian gave me never worked, so I haven’t heard from them again, but will never forget the chance encounter.

I went on to the peak, removed my backpack and was entranced photographing all the wonderful storms and alpine basins around me, and then found the ammo box with notes from climbers and photographed a half dozen. I'll insert one of them below.

p. 15

I should have rather immediately looked for a spot for my bivouac bag and set it all up, ready to take refuge, and I should have put on my rain gear, but all of a sudden I was engulfed by those ominous looking clouds dumping rain and hail on me. There wasn’t time for me to set up and lash myself to the boulders on the one little 3 foot wide ledge just under one side of the peak with a several hundred foot drop off to the west. So I decided it best to achieve my goal another day. I shouldered my backpack and carefully started down. The quartzite rocks gave me good traction, but the pack weight increased the downward pressure on each boulder I used as a foothold--moving some without warning, and I always had to have chosen a secondary boulder to move to fast. Then I came to a layer of slate that was extremely slippery with the rain and hail. I prayed for help with each step. It seemed to have a calming effect having me more alert and time after time I was able to react quickly and keep in control. It was late when I arrived at Anderson Pass, but I paused briefly for a prayer of gratitude, quickly put on drier and better gear, then headed down east for my base camp off-trail in the Painter Basin. It was dark soon but luckily the weather cleared and with a full moon guiding me I was able to find my base camp in a little cluster of scrub alpine firs.

I was wet and quite fatigued and I knew I had to get dry and warm fast before hypothermia and sickness took me down. Luckily I had covered the firewood left over from the night before, and I was able to quickly get a good fire going. You see me in the photo entertaining myself with a special issue of the National Geographic I had taken with to keep alive what then was the "impossible dream" of one day becoming enough of an expert, without a PhD, to get something into print. Soon I downed a hot meal and drink, took some recovery supplements used by marathoners to which I add a couple of items, and with dried clothing, and a warm body was soon snug in my sleeping bag, determined to one day go back to the peak and do everything right to achieve my goals. My heart was warmed by my new world traveling Belgian friends, Kristian and Dorina, recognizing the incredible beauty and uniqueness of our High Uintas Wilderness.

p. 16

NOW A BIT OF GOOD INFORMATION It's logical to begin understanding what the word UINTA means. From the Museum in Vernal, we learn, along with a correction of a common misconception:

Knowing that the word UINTA means, "PINE FOREST," I recall on one backpack meeting a group on horseback, their leader saying one of them was from the eastern U.S. and was surprised to see that "Utah had trees!" Some apparently think of Utah as a treeless desert, but our UINTAS dispel that mistaken understanding--the Native Americans recognizing the Uintas with tons of trees: Engelmann spruce, Douglas fir, lodge pole pine, quaking aspen-Utah's State Tree, and more. To widen our understanding and appreciation of the Uintas, let's also look at what a Forest Service display--at the beginning of the RED CLOUD LOOP, says about our mountains:

You'll recall from the PREFACE that in 1952, when 16 years old and a new resident of Utah, I was introduced to the Uintas. Then it was the 252,000 acre High Uintas Primitive Area and I soon learned that the Uinta Mountains were much more than that—actually being nearly 150 miles long, and around 40 miles wide. Then, while I was off on my 35 years of working with the Mayans in Guatemala, the Primitive Area was expanded by Congress, on September 28, 1984, to the 456,705 acre High Uintas Wilderness Area. This will be my main focus in this writing for adventurers in CHAPTER 2. It is Utah’s largest Wilderness, supervised by the Uinta-Wasatch-Cache National Forest (North Slope) and the Ashley National Forest (South Slope). 3

THE UNITAS: UNIQUE LIKE NONE OTHER Many have heard that the Uinta Mountains are unique as the most prominent range in the lower 48 states with an east-west orientation. 4 But, even more impressive is the fact that,

next to the San Juan Mountains of Colorado, the Uintas have the greatest amount of contiguous above timberline area in the Continental U.S.5 3 4

See: www.fs.fed.us/r4/ashley/recreation/highuintas/index.shtml From the Ashley National Forest website & in all the descriptions of the Uintas.

p. 17

That fact is very noticeable on seeing a Google Earth view of the Uintas below. The light coloration being the above timberline area that is continuous from east to west, and from north to south (Note: Timberline in the Uintas is at 11,000 ft. ).

MAP: ©2018 Google LLC, used with permission. Google and the Google logo are registered trademarks of Google LLC But, perhaps even more impressive, according to INTERMOUNTAIN FLORA "….the Uintas' area above timberline in a true alpine flora surpasses all of the alpine areas in the Intermountain West combined.” 6

For one aspect of the flora—see on my website my collection of more than 316+ varieties of wildflowers--from the foothills to Kings Peak. Many of them will be inserted throughout this book, including the mushrooms, and also the bird and mammal life. You might have guessed already that all of what has been described also makes the High Uintas the most biologically diverse region in Utah with around 500 species of fish, amphibians, birds, and mammals.7 The sum total is an unbelievable swath of fascination and beauty with few equals—actually with no equals in the U.S.

THE MAKING OF THE UINTA MOUNTAINS Once again a glance at a Google Earth image, or a good map, shows an east-west backbone kind of image with alpine ridges radiating out north and south. Geologically the Uinta Range was born over 25 million years ago by an east-west fracture of the earth’s crust and a massive uplift that pushed the area above sea level. This was a stroke of very good luck without which the face of modern Utah would be incredibly different. 8

Glaciers began sculpting the basins, canyons, and valleys leaving in their wake majestic mountains and peaks. These glacially carved canyons extend to the south about 20 miles, and to the north between 10-15 miles. This gives nature lovers an idea of the distance you will have to hike to get into the real high country.

Above we see on the North Slope, Middle Basin and Ryder Lake where Stillwater Fork of the Bear River is born, all watched over on the west by 12,479 ft. high Hayden Peak--prominently viewed to the east of the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway.

All the canyons lead to alpine basins along the spine of the Uintas, one example seen in the above photo. This guide book will be organized by those drainages, after first introducing the famous Highline Trail, then with the first drainage on the west of the North Slope that reaches up into the Wilderness Area at Hells Hole Basin. From there we will work our way east, drainage by drainage each with their trailhead and details of the backpacks possible from each, and then swing around to do the same on the South Slope drainages. Down these glacially created canyons flow all the important rivers of Utah beginning on the northwest with the 4 important tributaries of the Bear River, then tributaries of the Green River: Blacks Forks, Smiths Forks, and Henrys Fork, and many creeks. From the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway as it drops down to the north towards Wyoming you come to the gravel North Slope Road and 12 miles east on it you come to 10,235 ft. Elizabeth Ridge (Pass), which is a divide—to the East the Green River Drainage that swings south around the eastern end of the Uintas to join the Colorado River that flows southwest into the Gulf of California and the Pacific Ocean.

p. 19

On the west side of the divide are various branches of the Bear River which eventually flow into the Great Salt Lake which will be described in depth when the guide book describes that drainage, but it’s worth mentioning right here that the Bear River is one of a kind in our hemisphere--it being the largest and longest river in North America that doesn’t empty into an ocean.9 Further west is the Weber River Drainage, flowing northwest into the Great Salt Lake. THE NORTH SLOPE, is the area just south of the Wyoming border. In addition to it being of key geographical importance for its important rivers and creeks, it is rich in key aspects of Western U.S. history and culture as we will see in the next paragraphs. The streams, lakes, peaks and Forests bear the names of famous mountain men, explorers, surveyors and naturalists of the West—Smith, Henry, Ashley, Powell, King, Hayden, Agassiz, and more. Key aspects of the first explorations of the west by the mountain men and fur trappers will be mentioned, especially by one I talked about in the PREFACE who became one of the heroes of my youth--Jedediah Smith--and is even more so now as I have learned more about this incredible man who accomplished so much in his short life of 32 years. For you fishing enthusiasts, Blacks Fork, near Ft. Bridger is where fly fishing was first introduced into the Intermountain West by Wilford Woodruff who was with the 1 st company of Mormon pioneers in 1847.10

THE UNSUNG HEROES OF THE WEST--TIED TO THE UINTAS Regarding the key aspects of Western U.S. history the North Slope is dotted with ruins of what I call “The Tie Hacker Culture.” "Tie hacks" originally were very tough--mostly Irish--lumbermen, sent in 1867 to live and work 12 months a year in the North Slope drainages with their broad axes to make millions of railroad ties for the Transcontinental Railroad.

There are ghost towns, and hundreds of tie hack cabin ruins, and remains of their “splash dams” in all of the tributaries of the Bear River, West, Middle and East Forks of Blacks Fork, West and East Smith Forks, Henry's Fork and many creeks throughout the North Slope. 9

From Mirror Lake Scenic Byway sign—Evanston, Uinta Country, Wyoming

10

SAGEBRUSH COUNTRY, by Philip L. Fradkin, page 97

p. 20

The early Tie Hacker period was from 1867 to 1880, their stumps now mostly rotted away, their cabins identified by their small size, no windows, use of square nails, and rocks for fireplaces--all seen in the next photographs. Most of the cabins from the early period have rotted away as are the stumps seen on the left below, with a notable exception or two, like at The Old Blacks Fork Commissary. 11

In the later period from 1912 to 1936, stoves were used, cabins were larger and had windows, round nails--invented in 1910--used rather than square, and even sometimes signs of outhouses, and garbage dumps--all a sure way to identify ruins from the latter period.

NOTE: In the introduction to the Tie Hackers on the previous page, the tie hacker cabin is from the later period, 1912-1930. It is found in Mt. View, Wyoming. It was dismantled from the Steel Creek Commissary ghost town on the North Slope and assembled at the Forest Service Ranger Station in Mt. View. A similar one is found at the Bear River Ranger Station on the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway. Most of their work was done in the winter when they used sleds to transport the ties and accumulate them behind temporary "splash dams." When the run-off came in the spring they would blow the dams with dynamite and the resultant "SPLASH" would wash the ties down into Wyoming where they were picked up by the railroad.

On the left we see the remains of a splash dam on the West Fork of Smith's Fork (North Slope) a few miles up the trail from the Hewinta Guard Station. On the right is an old photograph of the ties behind a splash dam, ready to be blown and washed down into Wyoming.

11

The list of references for the TIE HACKER CULTURE are numerous and will be listed in the REFERENCE SECTION. One report, considered by many as the best, was made by me in a YouTube video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gwO3sB59hvg ): TIE HACK TOUR, Part 1 & then 2.

p. 21

Another unique system of transporting the ties and other wood products was the construction of the 30 mile long Hilliard Flume in 1870 beginning at the Mill City ghost town on the slopes of Gold Hill, just west of the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway. The Hilliard Flume, was called "Sloan's Folly," but it worked and was even considered an engineering marvel, ending at Hilliard, Wyoming, 12 miles north of the Utah border where there was a series of kilns used to make charcoal, as seen below in Forest Service displays.

The flume crossed the Highway just above the turn-off road to the west marked "Mill City Creek - Gold Hill" and on the east side of the highway, as shown in the Google Earth view in the middle below where a short road turns east to what I call in this book the "HELL'S HOLE TRAILHEAD," where in the 3rd photo my car is seen in the distance parked in the pathway of the flume--we are looking south up the pathway that had a slope of 15 degrees carrying the products 30 miles north to Hilliard in about two hours. Middle image12

A mile or so downstream from this point the Howe Feeder Flume came from the east bringing additional water for the flume from Main Fork that comes out of Hell’s Hole Basin which will be our first basin visited on the NORTH SLOPE in Chapter 2, Section 2. I’ll insert there a few of the only published pictures of the Howe Feeder Flume remnants and artifacts. As we tour around the North Slope I will add little tidbits of history and pictures from each area concerning the tie hacks and their ghost towns. One town, Bear Town, or Bear River City, located just north of Hilliard, Wyoming, grew quickly to 2,000 railroad workers, tie hacks and accompanying business people with their traveling newspaper, general store, saloons and brothels, described as “the liveliest, if not the most wicked town in America,” story told next in Chapter 1, entitled: “Merrily We Roll Along” In Our Cars Doing an 856 Mile Loop Tour of the Uintas13 12

This tour includes doing the Wyoming portion of the loop, the complete Piedmont Tour through Mt.View, then the entire North Fork Scenic Backway, and the complete South Slope Scenic Backway, plus the Weber & Coalville loops.

p. 22

We will visit the area 13.5 miles north of the Utah border, and 10 miles south of Evanston where we will see displays that explain this fascinating history, a summary of which follows:

On the upper-right we see a photo of Bear Town or Bear River City in its heyday around 1868, and below is the exact spot today—the two photos matching as can be observed in the skyline.

Bear Town was out of control, and a teamster for the railroad, Tom Smith, soon earned a reputation as a tough guy and was asked to be marshal of the town. He had been a policeman in New York, and a professional middleweight boxer, but in New York was involved in the accidental death of a 14 year old that had him deciding for a time to not carry a gun anymore—rather subdue the bad guys with his fists. He soon headed west taking a job with the railroad as a teamster, ending in Bear Town as the marshal.

But violence erupted when vigilantes among the businessmen hanged a couple of murderers and arrested others who worked for the railroad. The bad guys, as many as 100 or more, came after the vigilantes holed up in the General Store, armed with a new shipment of Henry Rifles, and as the mob came into view, 15 of the railroad mob were killed in the first volley from the store. Tom, once again carried a revolver—reportedly two, and tried to stop the violence, but was badly wounded. But the fight was out of control, the mob trying to burn down the jail and government buildings, and not stopped until soldiers arrived from Fort Bridger. It became the bloodiest fight between white people in Wyoming’s history—with various histories reporting from 16 to 58 dead.

p. 23

Tom, there acquired the name, Tom “Bear River” Smith, by which he would be known until his death in Abilene, Kansas where he was also known as “The Bare Knuckle Marshal,” and finally killed in a shootout with criminals. Years later he became President Dwight Eisenhower’s hero. Ike reportedly, on visiting his home town, Abilene, would go to the cemetery to place flowers on Tom “Bear River” Smith’s grave.14 As a result of the conflict in Bear Town, the railroad decided to not run a spur to the town, which spelled its doom and everyone moved on to Evanston. Bear Town became a ghost town—seemingly wiped from the face of the earth like Sodom & Gomorrah, with reportedly not even any relics or artifacts left—but I have found some as reported on my website.15 Some have told me this history I retell very briefly here—would make a great Western movie, which, if I could live long enough, maybe will be worked on.

Note: Beartown is one of the many towns, and perhaps the most notorious, of those shown on the TV series HELL ON WHEELS. Other ghost towns and historic sites, connected to the High Uintas, such as The Old Blacks Fork commissary, Suicide Park, and more will be pinpointed on the “Adventurous North Slope Scenic Backway tour.” But, for many more details and photographs, see my website to learn the story of these “unsung American heroes, without whom the West might not

have been won!” LEGENDARY APPEARANCES OF BIG FOOT If it wasn’t enough to know about “unsung American heroes,” and a western version of “Sodom & Gomorrah,” be advised that there have been more alleged sightings of Big Foot in the Uintas than any other place in Utah, and having heard that Little East Fork of Blacks Fork was where most reports have come from…..I made it a point to keep an open mind and make several backpacks up there to give Big foot a chance to find me to take a family portrait. I had my camera at ready every waking moment—lens cap off…even when I dozed off once. In so doing something really was witnessed that I’ll tell you about when we get to Little East Fork of Blacks Fork, in Chapter 2: Section 8 in the guide book even with a photograph of a hairy guy, or thing!
