FASCINATING FACTS & HISTORIC GEMS FROM THE SOUTH SLOPE As exciting and scandalous as some of the history of the North Slope is, the South Slope refuses to take a back seat as you will see.

THE FIRST WHITE MEN TO VIEW THE UINTAS: Aztecs, Spaniards, Gold, Lost Rhoades Mine, Butch Cassidy and more! I’ve said in some of my writings that even before Michel Bourdon discovered and named the Bear River in 1818 (Note: You’ll read about that in the Preface to the BEAR RIVER DRAINAGE, Chapter 2, Section 4), Fathers Escalante and Dominguez were the first white men to view the Uinta Mountains from the south in 1776. In researching their exploration I learned they had come north from Santa Fe, New Mexico following what history calls “the old Spanish Trail.” It was a trail that obviously was already there coming up from the south, crossing the Green River and reaching the Uintah Basin. Where did it originate? A little more research opened up a vast new historic horizon that I’m still working on, but the way the story goes makes the history of the South Slope even more fascinating than that of the North. 16 The legend goes something like this: In 1521 when the Spanish Conquest of the Aztec Empire was going on directed by Hernando Cortez in Mexico, Montezuma, the Aztec Emperor, allegedly loaded up 1,500 slaves with most of the riches of his empire and sent them north to hide them out of reach of Cortez and the Spaniards. And, as the story goes, they came way north to the Uintah Basin and to the High Uinta Mountains where the treasure was, and is, hidden — the Utes allegedly today being the guardians of the treasure. Thereafter, Cortez sent his men north to find the treasure, creating “the old Spanish Trail” all the way to the Uintah Basin and beyond. Thus the first to view the Uintas, other than the Native Americans and Aztecs, were the Spaniards in 1540, 178 years before Michel Bourdon discovered the Bear River, and 184 years before my revered Jedediah Smith began trapping beaver with his team on the North Slope of the Uintas. From that springs the legends of 7 Spanish mines, and caves with unbelievable riches, and interwoven into it all are the legends of the Lost Rhodes Mine, John Rhoades caretaker of the mine for Brigham Young, and the LDS Church, and Caleb, John Rhoades’ son who ended up with the secrets. The histories eventually even come to involve two opposing factions trying to find the mines, with Butch Cassidy and his gang being employed as bodyguards in the affair for one of the factions. Then a shootout with one of the Wild Bunch, Matt Warner, captured and put in the Vernal jail, but to avoid a lynching, or rescue by Butch and gang, the Sheriff from Vernal moved Warner in the dark of night, using the Old Carter Military Road that crossed the Uinta Mountains following one of the two ancient Indian routes, to the railway and then on to Ogden, Utah.

16

GOLD OF CARRE-SHINOB: The Final Chapter in the Mystery of the Lost Rhoades Mine & Lost Cities and Montezuma's Treasure, by Kerry Ross Boren and Lisa Lee Boren. DISCLAIMER: Author, Kerry Ross Boren, is today (2018) in the Utah State Prison, and some question some of his writings, yet he is a celebrated historical author in Europe and elsewhere, whose books were published by a friend. Do your homework for greater understanding.

p. 25

Butch and his gang followed that same route and stayed one night in one of the tie hacker connected towns--today the Piedmont Ghost Town, Wyoming, which I hope all will decide to include in your auto-tour, whether The Pavement, or The Adventurous North Slope one. They were on their way to rob the bank in Montpelier, Idaho to have the money needed to hire a lawyer and get their buddy, Matt Warner, out of jail in Ogden. 17 I’ll mention more details in Chapter 1.

Some of these legendary historical gems will be inserted into our guide book at the appropriate places to help your hikes come alive—including me actually finding and photographing a whole mountain of gold—several times! You’ll see my photographs of it further along. One of said “historical gems” involves legendary folk hero in the Hanna area, Frank Defa, and a fascinating real life story of what I call a “fake gold rush” on the North Fork of the Duchesne River in the area where today is located the Stockmore Ranger Station—at the junction where you come down from Wolf Creek Pass on your way to Hanna and Tabiona. More on that later when we describe the South Slope. Now let’s get back to what we do know for sure. On the South are born the other major rivers of Utah, beginning on the western end with the Provo River that flows southwest to Utah Lake and on to the Great Salt Lake. The next major streams are all born in the Wilderness Area being the Duchesne River, Rock Creek, Lake Fork River, Swift Creek, the Yellowstone, Uinta and Whiterocks Rivers, and many creeks. All of these flow into the Green River and then into the Colorado and on to the Pacific. Just think for a moment how crucial the High Uinta Mountain streams are for giant life giving hydroelectric & water conservation projects like The Central Utah Project (that gives life to the Wasatch Front), Flaming Gorge, Lake Powell and Lake Meade Reservoirs and more. These are Utah’s major rivers born in the Uintas which provide 90% of Utah’s water. Without the Uintas, Utah would be a true desert wilderness.18 These streams add up to over 400 miles of trout streams, more than half of which are relatively untouched and untested by fishing enthusiasts. Backpackers, goat packers, and horsemen are all usually hurrying along the streams on their way up to the alpine lakes in the high country and rarely stop to fish. Most of the streams are off-trail, and some of the 17

The above sign is part of the historical display at the Piedmont ghost town and kilns.

18

UTAH WILDLANDS, by Stewart Aitcheson

p. 26

best are in deep gorges that put them out of reach of all but the most adventurous fishermen, with some stretches never touched by man. Of greatest interest to many are the lakes, more than 1,200 of them, many of which in pioneer days were barren of fish as the native trout couldn’t get to them from the streams below, such as Grandaddy Lake seen below—the largest in the Uintas. Below I’ve inserted my life-long buddy Ted Packard into the scene—picture taken from the East Grandaddy Mountain saddle. He was with me hiking to this choice spot on my 3rd hike.

The lake was named in 1906 when famous pioneer artist-photographer, George Beard, was asked by a government surveyor which was the largest lake in the Uintas? George replied, pointing on the map and saying, “it is the Granddaddy of them all .” The surveyor accepted the phrase and since it has been the Grandaddy Lake and Basin. Stocking began of brook and cutthroat fingerlings into approximately 427 lakes initially carried in milk cans on mule back, but since 1955 done by the Division of Wildlife Resources (DWR) using airplanes following 3-6 year cycles.

DWR airplane seen above on the left loading fingerlings at the Heber City Airport, and then aerial stocking the High Uinta lakes, done since 1955, replacing mules & milk cans. Another airplane flys out of the Roosevelt Airport in the Uintah Basin19

Now 149 lakes have natural reproduction—Grandaddy being one of them where the amazing spawn can be witnessed early each summer in the 3 small streams entering its western shore. 19

Photographs provided by the DWR and used with their permission.

p. 27

Note: UPDATING THE LAKES—On February 4, 2019 I met with personnel from the Division of Wildlife Resources and we worked for about 3 hours to update the old pamphlets, LAKES OF THE UINTAS—that date from 1986-1999, as explained in the References on page 779. Since, with continual help from the DWR, I have done my best to incorporate into the book the most current information. Thirty-five High Uinta lakes now have Arctic grayling, and 82 have Tiger trout—a cross between brown and brook trout. Years ago even Golden trout were stocked in the South Slope’s Atwood Drainage, and in recent years Golden trout have been stocked in 6 lakes which will be identified in the Guide chapters. During the 2019 season Splake—a cross between brook and lake trout—potentially a trout that will develop good size, the Utah record at 17 lbs., will be stocked in Crater Lake, along with Brook and Tiger trout, already there. In the Guide chapters I describe 630 lakes listed and supervised by the DWR. Fishing in remote, off-trail lakes can sometimes be spectacular such as those seen below. First below is seen on the left a heavy bodied native cutthroat trout 19-1/2” long, then two unofficial State records: One in the middle an Arctic grayling, 19” long, caught by my buddy Ted Packard in Lake Atwood in 1962, mentioned in the Preface. Then on the right a heavy bodied, hook jawed Eastern brook trout, conservatively estimated at 28” long, likely around 10 lbs. and easily a Utah State record. 20,21

The exact length of the brook trout on the right wasn’t possible to determine as I let him swim around while getting out my tripod to get historic photographs, but when I was ready, he was gone! Luckily I had already taken the shot we see here his long, very heavy body stretching down into the clear water.

ACCESSIBILITY TO HIGH ADVENTURE Access to the High Uintas is exceptional with 24 maintained Forest Service Trailheads, and others I call “unofficial,” with trails that lead to the high country, and sometimes faint paths that leave from the end of logging and jeep roads. Official sources say there are around 600 miles of maintained trails, and many more of trails the Forest Service purposely doesn’t maintain anymore—to preserve the “wilderness” flavor of our mountains. I so far have backpacked around 2,000 miles over the last 15 years, some of those miles were on 20

For other good information about High Uintas Fishing, go to: http://www.redrockadventure.com/fishing/uintas/fishing_overview.htm 21

https://wildlife.utah.gov/record-fish.html

p. 28

trails nearly invisible. Other miles were off-trail going across arctic tundra, boulder hopping, or bushwhacking through trail-less forest—which, by the way I’ve now sworn off of as deadfall—downed timber, makes it very difficult for this 83+ year old. The High Uintas are uniquely adapted to doing this safely. Just make sure you have a good map, and compass, know the lay of the land, and leave word with family and friends where you are heading. I have to add that it’s good to also have in a group a satellite phone, and a SPOT Satellite Personal Tracker or similar device—which you have to use EVERY DAY. This is especially crucial if you are going alone—which I don’t recommend anybody doing, UNLESS YOU TAKE ALL THE PRECAUTIONS I ALWAYS TAKE. As you will notice throughout the book, SURVIVAL will be a major theme, inserting in the right places the stories of those who didn’t survive, and why, and then my SURVIVAL STORIES and what I did to make it safely to civilization each time, and still be backpacking after 83. The most famous trail is the HIGHLINE TRAIL. In Chapter 2, Section I will give more detail including photographs and maps of this famous trail, but for now, briefly: The Trailhead is at an elevation of 10,382 ft. near Hayden Pass on the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway (Utah Highway 150 from Kamas, Utah to Evanston, Wyoming). From there the trail follows the backbone of the Uintas 102 trail miles to the East where it actually ends near Flaming Gorge, on U.S. Highway 191 north of Vernal. It takes you through more than 10 drainages, over 6 of the Wilderness Area’s 22 passes, plus 3 more to the east of the Wilderness, and through the shadows of the 9 named 13,000+ foot peaks. I’ll insert below a photo of the Trailhead entrance with Hayden Peak in the background.

I wasn’t kidding….here’s one of the MOUNTAINS OF GOLD!

Additionally this famous trail takes us by many other no-name 13,000+ foot peaks, including 13,387 foot Mt. Jedediah, Utah’s 5th highest peak seen on page 242, which I have un-officially named in honor of Jedediah Smith who was unique among unbelievably tough mountain men and explorers, he being famous for carrying his Bible, “…didn’t use tobacco, liquor,

never swore, and stayed away from loose women…” 22 22

From, UTAH, 5th edition, p. 54 by Tom & Gayen Wharton

p. 29

If a backpack of 102 miles, following the spine of the Uintas all the way to near Flaming Gorge, doesn’t get you excited, you can easily stretch it to 200 miles or more by zigzagging back and forth—to the North Slope, and then back to the South Slope, as you gradually move eastward. I did this in 2003 on my 27 day no re-supply expedition for a total of 206 miles mentioned in the PREFACE. Last of all I must say that I’m not so naïve as to believe that our High Uintas Wilderness can actually compete with the Himalayas’ “world’s highest trail,” Nepal’s “heaven-high Annapurna range,” South America’s Andes, or Africa’s Mt Kilimanjaro, but let’s get real— for us average Joe’s with families to support, or old guys living on Social Security—and not quite as nimble as we once were, those are places most of us can only read about. On the other hand the High Uintas Wilderness and Mountain Range is within reach of all. In 2003 on my “expedition” on the Highline Trail climbing Rocky Sea Pass near Pigeon Milk Springs I met Will and his brother-in-law, Charlie, from Virginia and Maryland, who explained why they had come so far and do it every year:

“It is the only Wilderness area in the U.S. where you can fly in, rent a car at the airport and in 2 hours be on the trail to the high country and incredible wilderness adventure!”

p. 30

If you haven’t experienced the High Uintas, I encourage you to come and have a wonderful wilderness experience, and, if you already have, do it again, and again where I hope we meet on the trail soon…….maybe at magnificent Red Castle Peak and Lake, seen below —that some consider the most beautiful mountain scene in Utah.

Visit the Red Castle area, or come exploring and find your own

“Most beautiful mountain scene in Utah!”

NOW WE PLUNGE INTO THE IMPRESSIVE DETAILS Including throughout the colorful history, legends, & survival stories with information that can save your life.  CHAPTER 1: A detailed guide for an exciting AUTO-LOOP TOUR of the UINTA MOUNTAINS, following the paved highways—the SCENIC BYWAYS, and importantly the SCENIC BACKWAYS that get you up close to the mountains following well graded gravel/dirt roads, along with a few more adventurous/rougher ones—but, not to worry, you will be warned in plenty of time to take safer routes.  Three Guide Chapters with 2019 updated DWR information on all the fishable and potentially fishable lakes for hikers, backpackers, horse and goat packers, including topographical maps with routes and distances for all areas: Chapter 2—THE WILDERNESS AREA; Chapter 3—THE WESTERN UINTAS; and Chapter 4—THE

EASTERN UINTAS.  Chapter 5: WHY WE EXPLORE & HOW TO DO IT ENJOYABLY and SAFELY.  APPENDIX with exciting and colorful extra information for your enjoyment.  REFERENCE SECTION including a list to all YouTube videos produced by the author, including a link to what the Salt Lake Tribune calls: “The Grandaddy of all Utah hiking slide shows.”  A detailed INDEX including a listing of all named High Uinta lakes.

p. 31

CHAPTER 1: An Auto-Loop Tour of the Uinta Mountains PREFACE THE VERY FIRST AUTO LOOP TOUR OF THE UINTAS

Yes, it was way back with a Model-T Ford—not the pickup model on the left that the tie hackers wore out up the West Fork of Smiths Fork, but rather a four door model pulling a wood trailer. It was in June 1926 with a BYU graduate student, Clarence Cotton, driving with Dr. Vasco M. Tanner up front directing the scientific adventure. In the back seat were two other graduate students, Claudius Brown, and C. Lynn Hayward. Brown would go on to become a well known Entomologist. Hayward would become an authority on the area, and authored several books on the ecology of the Uinta Mountains, and was a long-time professor at BYU (and his wife, Libby, my English teacher at Provo High School in 1954). He authored the book from which I learned of this adventure: THE HIGH UINTAS: Utah’s Land of Lake & Forest, by C. Lynn Hayward, published by the Monte L. Bean Life Science Museum, Provo, Utah, June 1983. The picture above is taken from said book. Their purpose was to collect and preserve specimens of the ecology of the Uintas: Birds, mammals, insects, and other objects of the natural history of the area. From Provo, Utah they drove to Fort Bridger, and Mt. View, Wyoming, then southeast through the badlands to Lonetree. They continued along the Henry’s Fork that flowed out of the Uintas, and camped a couple of days in the lush ranch country near where the 1st Mountain Man Rendezvous had been held in 1825. They struggled on to the Green River and even saw rusted machinery of a time when a dam had been thought of for the area—of course 50 years later the Flaming Gorge Dam was built there. The journey became interesting as often what was supposed to be a road, was actually just a trail, and they had to push and pull up steep grades, and out of impossible muddy stretches, even calling themselves the “handcart company.” They struggled on to Greendale which they hoped was a town as they were low on gas and supplies, but it was rather a ranch and only an old sheepherder was in the vicinity. They asked him about the prospect of getting food and gasoline. He looked at them and their equipment with "an expression of disbelief," then began to laugh. The road ahead was just a trail and he told them it would be impossible to get to Vernal. He did feed them and the next morning sent them on their way.

p. 32

The road ahead was under construction and they had to wind their way in and out around hundreds of stumps. Eventually they met a Forest Service crew working on the road and got some gasoline, but were told that the road ahead was nothing but a steep trail. Eventually they came to a divide and from there on it was downhill and they finally saw ahead the lights of Vernal. From there they circled back to Provo, making complete the first loop tour of the Uinta Mountains. I couldn't quite glean how many days it had taken them, but it was such an adventure that Dr. Hayward wrote: "Such was my introduction to the Uinta Mountains, and at that time I

might have had no inclination to ever see them again. But in the years since that time I have climbed their peaks, explored their innumerable lakes, and followed the trails through the eternal forests. I have harkened to the bleat of the pika from the deep crevices of the rocks, heard the sharp whistle of the marmot, and listened to the songs of the robin, hermit thrush, and white-crowned sparrow. I have hauled glistening trout from deep, cool lakes. I have learned to love these primitive lands of the High Uintas, and would like to tell more about them." GO TO DR. HAYWARD'S BOOK FOR DETAILS 23

Here we basically see the loop tour of the Uintas donde in 1926. I will now show you how we can today do a tour that would have Hayward and crew be green with envy!

CHAPTER 1

"Merrily We Roll Along"

In Our Cars Doing an 85624 Mile Loop Tour of the UINTA MOUNTAINS I promise you that this tour will make the Uintas equal to or better than many National Parks "Hey outdoor lover, FORGET YOUR BACKPACK and all the sweat, and see the Uinta Mountains as part of your 'love affair with your car!' I promise you it will be surprisingly adventurous, colorful and inspiring. That "love" phrase was coined in 1961 in a TV show entitled "Merrily We Roll Along," promoting General Motors. Our love affair has multiplied many times and become an essential part of our lives, so…..just for those of you who for whatever reasons would like to roll around the Uintas in the comfort of your shinny new SUV, or RV I will begin our exploration of the High Uintas with a ROAD TOUR GUIDE. It would even be fascinating for you died-in-the-wool backpacker/horse packer/goat packer--to do it first in your car and fill you in on all your options before you plan your trip --what undoubtedly will be trips as your adventurous self will want to explore often--enough for a lifetime.

It could be done in a couple of three days, but you'd be like the marathon backpacker who brags about doing 20 and 30 miles in a day--then criticizes me saying things I take pictures of in the same areas don't exist--the vast inconsistency because they go so fast they miss 24

This includes doing the Wyoming portion of the loop, the complete Piedmont Tour through Mt.View, then the entire North Fork Scenic Backway, and the complete South Slope Scenic Backway, plus the Weber & Coalville loops.

p. 34

much of the beauty, fascination and what I call "VISIONS OF NATURE." Best take several days--or even a week or more, going slow to not miss anything--and explore all of the scenic BYWAYS--paved roads, and BACKWAYS--usually well graded dirt/gravel roads, and others I will point out that don't have names--except those I will unofficially give them, and where you will see the real Uintas missed by those whose objective is to just rush to get to some imagined destination, rather than enhancing their lives by taking it slow and easy. I will insert here a general map that shows the various routes--roughed in, that will be described. As we move along we will zoom in on specific areas and for the North Slope Scenic Backway we will use topographical maps.

Highlighted routes, new routes and labels by the author.

The red line represents the present paved U.S. Interstates, and State highways that circle the Uinta Mountains, and basically shows the route taken by Dr. Hayward and group in 1926. The other highways and roads highlighted will be those we will explore in the loop(s) tour(s), I add the plural "s" as while looping around the Uintas we will also take lesser loops and short side trips on secondary roads--with clear instructions. When we get into the details I'll include the names of places that I'll take you to. You can even do some GLAMPING, a relatively new term meaning "glamorous camping," like with your RV, or more luxurious camping gear--too heavy for backpackers, using the many Forest Service campgrounds, or just pick your spot that is permissible in many parts of

p. 35

the two National Forests that manage the Uintas. I will also guide you to some down-toearth State Parks, Historical Sites & Monuments, Forest Service displays, plus--importantly, colorful western resorts, dude ranches, saloons, country stores and unique informal and home-made museums very different than the stuffy, formal ones, even though we end with a really professional quality one--all showing real historical treasures. Some of the resorts offer cabins and rooms for rent and all kinds of enjoyment surrounded by what I call "the visions and textures of nature," -- all part of the Uinta Mountain's wonderment. Oh, and by the way, on this tour you will also see most of the wonderful creeks and rivers that come out of the Uintas--that easily add up to 400 miles of wonderful fisheries, many stretches of which have seldom if ever been fished, plus lakes and reservoirs at every turn. So, if you're a fisherman or fisherwoman, bring along your fishing gear and make sure you are properly licensed to fish, catching rainbow, native cutthroat, German brown, Eastern brook, golden and tiger trout, as well as even arctic grayling.

From the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway, we look down upon the Provo River, in a section very seldom fished, where you'll have to bushwhack to for some great fishing -- like for trout for years I have speculated was a golden/cutthroat hybrid, caught in a remote section of the Uinta River, but likely is just a very colorful native cutthroat trout .25

LOTS OF PROGRESS SINCE 1926 Unlike Dr. Hayward in 1926, we've got the Freeways to take us up to Wyoming's Evanston and Fort Bridger, then on to Mountain View, Lonetree, Manila and Flaming Gorge, with wonderful U.S. Highway 191 to get us through the Hayward pioneering ordeal from Flaming Gorge to Vernal, then smooth U.S. Highway 40 to get us from Vernal back to the Wasatch Front. But, for the first leg of our tour, let's focus on another highway Dr. Hayward and crew didn't have--the “highest paved highway in the State of Utah: THE MIRROR LAKE SCENIC BYWAY--UT-150.” So, with this breathtaking drive we begin our road tour.

THE 856 MILE AUTO LOOP TOUR NOTE: This guide will be sort of like the photo/essays I do on my website, or my YouTube videos with many photos, yet not so many as to make doing the tour unnecessary--rather it will include enough as teasers to hopefully get you excited about actually doing the tour and seeing for yourselves all the amazing details of the magnificent High Uinta Mountains. 25

http://wildlife.utah.gov/blog/2014/theres-gold-in-the-uintas/

p. 36

THE GATEWAY(S) TO THE UINTAS. ODOMETER: 0 miles, KAMAS to Bald Mountain Pass = 29.5 miles, TOTAL=29.5 miles. Around the Uinta Mountain Range there are a number of communities that rightly claim to be "THE GATEWAY TO THE UINTAS." Each of them lead to great portions of the Uintas and we will get to each of them on our tour.

But, most of us will come from Salt Lake City and the Wasatch Front, so we will begin at the closest, westernmost Gateway in Kamas, 40 miles from Salt Lake City. It is in Summit County that covers almost the entire North Slope of the Uintas. The population in 2012 of Kamas was 1899, but don't let that fool you--it has everything you will need for your tour.

This Scenic Byway is easily the most important paved road that takes you right into the heart of the Uinta Mountains, and along the western edge of the Utah's largest and greatest Wilderness Area. It gives access to many of the Trailheads that are starting points for hiking into the high country. On the previous map, it is the bright green highway. In 1933 the state legislature approved SR-150 ("SR" means "State Road"-- but we'll usually use UT- or WY- ) running east from Kamas to the Wasatch-Cache National Forest boundary. In 1953 it was extended to the east and north going over 10,759 foot Bald Mountain Pass, then past Mirror Lake, up to Hayden Pass and from there down to the Wyoming state line, and on to Evanston. I quote below: Mirror Lake Highway Scenic Drive | Utah.com 26 [U-150] Heading east from Kamas into the Uinta Mountains, through the Wasatch-Cache National Forest In addition to scenic viewpoints and picnic areas, numerous lakes and campgrounds line this highmountain byway. Much of the journey parallels the Provo River. 26

https://utah.com/scenic-drive/mirror-lake

p. 37

The byway climbs to an elevation of 10,687 [mistake] feet at Bald Mountain Pass before descending past Mirror Lake, then to Bear River Ranger Station with its Historical Tie Hack Cabin. From here the route parallels the Bear River and on to Evanston. Recreational activities along the byway include camping, fishing, cross-country skiing, hiking, riding ATVs and snowmobiling. Visitors must purchase a recreation pass to use facilities in this area [to just drive through you don't need a pass]. A $6 [pass] is available and good for 3 days; a $12 pass is good for 7 days; there is also a $45 annual pass available. [a lifetime pass--I think they call it a "passport"-- for seniors is available for $10 and valid in National Forests all over the U.S.]. **Highway is maintained by UDOT (Utah Dept. Of Transportation). Highway is open until the snow is too deep to plow. To check road conditions go to http://511.commuterlink.utah.gov/tats.web.report/

To check accessibility, snow depths/temperatures on Bald Mountain Pass, Wolf Creek Pass & others, go to: http://udottraffic.utah.gov/CLALertViewer.aspx?CLType=3

FOR YOUR ENJOYMENT: ADDITIONAL INFORMATION Before leaving Kamas, you might want to make several stops. First at the FOREST SERVICE RANGER STATION, 50 E. Center St. where you can get information, maps, free literature, and books related to the great outdoors and the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway.

Then there is a wonderful old hall that has been converted into the magnificent NEW WEST COUNTRY STORE: (95 S. Main St.), www.newwestcountry store.com

Here you can find a wonderful variety of western/country items. Of course also in Kamas there is a supermarket, banks, restaurants, etc., lodging for the night, a great little library and much more. As you head east out of town, if for whatever reason you're hungry already, there is on the left DICK'S BURGER SHACK for some great food, where our tradition has always been to stop when coming back from a tough backpack.

p. 38

THE MIRROR LAKE SCENIC BYWAY (UT-150) This is the highest paved highway in Utah, and in my opinion a "must drive" road trip to introduce one to the High Uintas. From Kamas to Evanston it is 80 miles, but one of our options will be 47 miles ahead where the North Slope Road leaves the pavement and heads east--which will be the "Adventurous Loop" version--we'll decide which later.

We stop briefly a few miles out of town at the SAMAK COUNTRY STORE to pick up a few more things we'll need.

I couldn't resist spending .27 cents on a postcard.

I had to have it to remind me how things might be for me in a few years --and how I've got to keep fighting old-age like the stubborn guy some say I am.

p. 39

DRIVE CAREFULLY AS DEER, MOOSE & BLACK ANGUS CATTLE OFTEN CROSS THE HIGHWAY -- ESPECIALLY AT TWILIGHT AND AT NIGHT

Note: At night a very dark moose will blend into the black of the night--so BE CAUTIOUS!

I recommend stopping to see all the historical markers, and Forest Service displays which will greatly enhance your appreciation of all the wonders we will see. There are also signs indicating Trailheads and I highly suggest you drive in to each one and see the information about the alpine areas the trails take you to, and the Rules all must observe religiously to maintain pristine the Uintas--above all: TRED LIGHTLY - LEAVE NO TRACE! Four or 5 of the trailheads offer lakes with just short hikes of a mile or so for better fishing like the Crystal Lake, Bald Mountain, Fehr, Pass Lake & Ruth Lake Trailheads. I won't list all of them in this chapter, nor include photos, except for a few special ones for which I can't resist saying something with a photo or two, but all will be included in the three guide chapters: Chapter 2; THE HIGH UINTAS WILDERNESS AREA; Chapter 3: THE WESTERN UINTAS; and, Chapter 4: THE EASTERN UINTAS. Some of these Trailheads lead to lakes just 1 or 2 miles from the highway, hikes you might want to take as the fishing will be much better than in the lakes along the road. A few miles up the canyon there is a Forest Service pull-out where there used to be a booth, but now gone, replaced by Self-service-- where you can pay a Forest Service Recreation fee, only $6.00 per vehicle for a 3 day pass, $12.00 for 7 days that should be displayed on the dashboard. For those of us over 65, Golden Age Passports are valid, which you can get at Forest Service offices anywhere. If you will just be driving through, only using a restroom, there is no need to pay the fee, unless you want to make a contribution--WHICH I HIGHLY RECOMMEND. As you will see there are Forest Service campgrounds with restrooms that are found all along the highway with necessary fees posted for camping. There are also many places along the highway where you can park your RV, or car and camp out without the fees charged at the campgrounds, such as we see "glampers" doing below. GLAMPING, mentioned before, is a combination of two words: Glamorous and camping, = "glam-ping." which for the Uintas is a way to experience the outdoors—without having to sacrifice creature comforts, such as is common nowadays with travel trailers and R.Vs.

p. 40

Don't miss the beautiful Provo River Falls, and there are lakes and streams along the Highway where you can wet a line for feisty native, brook, rainbow, and tiger trout, and even lakes that have arctic grayling. NOTE: specific details about each lake will be provided in the

Guide chapters, 2, 3 and 4, including lakes just a mile away. You then come to 10,759 ft. BALD MOUNTAIN PASS & TRAILHEAD. If you are taking it slow and easy, and want to get some exercise you can park in the Trailhead parking lot and do the 1-2 hour hike to the top. Below we see several of my friends who did this and are on the crest of Mt. Baldy (11,943 ft.), from which we see the panoramic view of the High Uintas looking east over the basin where the Duchesne River is born--with 12,479 ft. Hayden Peak in the dead center, and Mirror Lake far below in the right bottom corner. The Mirror Lake Scenic Byway can be seen in the middle of the picture switch-backing up to Hayden Pass.

From the crest of Mt. Baldy, as some of us affectionately call it, you can view in the opposite direction--to the west (below), the peaks of the once proposed Mt. Watson Wilderness Area which will be described in Chapter 3 on the WESTERN HIGH UINTAS.

ODOMETER: 29.5 mles -BALD MT. PASS to HAYDEN PASS/HIGHLINE TRAILHEAD = 4.6 miles, TOTAL=34 miles. Just after the pass, and dropping down a bit, we see on the right this interesting DIVIDE SIGN--which many miss.

p. 41

The Basin we are viewing is where the Duchesne River begins and flows onto the South Slope, joined by many other streams that flow into the Green River, and eventually the Colorado that flows into the Gulf of California and the Pacific Ocean. On the west side of the pass, from where we have just come, is the drainage of the Provo River that flows into the Great Salt Lake (the Great Basin). From the sign, where you also get a great panoramic view of the area, we drop down into the MIRROR LAKE AREA and from there climb up to Hayden Pass (10,382 ft.), that has no sign, but at that point we see to the east Hayden Peak and the sign to the Highline Trailhead.

HIGHLINE TRAILHEAD.

This is the Uinta's most famous trail, which from here follows the spine of the Uintas--we see below, east for 102 miles to near Flaming Gorge

In the INTRODUCTION I described somewhat this famous trail, and it will be mentioned further along in our tour when we visit the eastern end, and also drive up into the heart of the Uintas to visit the rarely visited Leidy Peak & Hacking Lake Trailhead, mistakenly thought by many to be the end of the trail--or beginning. It is so important for the Uintas that a lot more will be said about it in Chapter 2, Section 1 when we begin to describe in detail the HIGH UINTAS WILDERNESS AREA, the Preface to which will introduce the important story of Survival of an Australian 64 year old backpacker who launched himself from the Chepeta Lake Trailhead to backpack the 60 miles to UT-150, and then disappeared for 5 years. His final discovery, and what was the reason for this mysterious loss is explained, along with how each of us can avoid the same.

ODOMETER: 34 miles HAYDEN PASS & HIGHLINE TRAILHEAD on to the BEAR RIVER RANGER STATION = 13 miles, TOTAL=47 miles.

p. 42

WE CONTINUE TO THE NORTH SLOPE & MEET THE TIE HACKERS

"Unsung American heroes without whom the west might not have been won!" From the Highline Trailhead we begin to drop down to the north towards Wyoming. Along the way there are fascinating displays and historical markers, and more trailheads. At 15 miles from Bald Mt. Pass we come to the first display that introduces us to THE TIE HACKER CULTURE. The tie hackers, described some in the INTRODUCTION, were tough lumbermen, mostly Irish immigrants, sent into the North Slope of the Uintas in 1867 with their broad axes to work 12 months a year making millions of railroad ties for the construction of the Transcontinental Railroad.

The display is 44 miles from Kamas, or about 15 miles from the Bald Mt. Pass--the display is about 100 yards from the highway to the west on the WHITNEY ROAD. It refers to one aspect of the tie hackers--THE HILLIARD FLUME, but display now totally worn out in 2018, so I've inserted it above for your information--picture taken a few years before time and weather obliterated it. It deals with the tie hacker period carrying wood products from Mill City at Gold Hill north 30 miles to Hilliard, Wyoming.27 It was called "Sloan's Folley," yet it worked and many considered it an engineering marvel that was constructed using 80 tons of square nails. The tour will take you north to the Bear River Ranger Station, and then into Wyoming and near Hilliard where there are displays that explain more of this interesting chapter of our Western history that many know nothing about. A couple of miles further, from the Whitney Rd., we come to the bridge that crosses the Bear River and a little further an important gravel road leading to CHRISTMAS MEADOWS/STILLWATER TRAILHEAD where important trails take one to three important alpine areas including the Ostler Peak area, which imposing mountain is seen below as we look to the east across Christmas Meadows--the mountain to the right is 27

From the revised edition of The Historical Guide to UTAH GHOST TOWNS, Mill City--Summit County page 59, by Stephan L. Carr

p. 43

Spread Eagle Peak. This view is near the Trailhead, 4 miles from the junction on the highway--at which point we have come 47 miles from Kamas, with Evanston 33 miles further to the north.

THE BEAR RIVER RANGER STATION, a mile further north, is our next point of interest with a pay phone, clean rest rooms, cold water, and free literature as well as good books and maps on the Wilderness, it's natural wonders, the Mountain Men and more.

Out back you shouldn't miss the Tie Hack Cabin dismantled from the Steele Creek Commissary ghost town--26 miles to the east on the North Slope Road, and reconstructed here. Inside there are tie hack tools and fascinating displays that explain the tie hacks work and heroic efforts from 1867 to 1880, and again from 1912 to 1936. Without these tough outdoorsmen there wouldn't have been a Transcontinental Railroad, but strangely the "tie hacks" are not even mentioned in the history books that document the railroad crucial in the development of the West, nor are they mentioned in the TV series Hell on Wheels—even though a few times wagons full of hand-hewn ties are seen--coming from somewhere. The drainages of the North Slope are sprinkled liberally with ruins of their cabins, splash dams, burial sites, and ghost towns--many will be seen by those who take the "Adventurous North Slope Scenic Backway Tour." In that section I will insert a map of the sites pinpointed by the Forest Service, plus others I have discovered and report on publicly for the first time. A DUMP STATION can also be accessed between the Ranger Station and the North Slope Road, located east a short distance up a paved road to Lily Lake. The North Slope Road, a dirt/gravel road, continues in one way or another 138 miles east all the way to UT-44 and US Highway 191 near Flaming Gorge. We'll describe that road in a moment--in fact that will be the main focus of our auto tour of the High Uinta Mountains seeing the Uintas up close rather than from afar which you do from the "paved" version of the tour--but it will best be done by adventurers with a 4WD vehicle. We'll get back to it in a moment.

p. 44

ODOMETER 50 miles, - NORTH SLOPE ROAD & BEAR RIVER LODGE, then to the Wyo. Border, 6 miles, TOTAL=56 miles. We just passed the North Slope Road turnoff and we come to the BEAR RIVER LODGE, where you can stay a night or two, swim in their pool, and have your kids fish in their pond. They also rent ATV's with many roads and pathways in the area where such are permitted.

Those who know me might recall me saying about ATV's, "I hate those suckers!" Yet as I grow older I've had to soften a bit realizing that one day I might just have to use one to continue enjoying the outdoors--BUT, NOT UNTIL I'M OLD, WORN OUT AND INCAPABLE OF HIKING ANYMORE! Nothing can compare to going slow on foot and seeing up-close, at every turn, the VISIONS & WONDERS OF NATURE--which you miss roaring around on an ATV. At the Lodge Resort28 there is a nice store where you can get your snacks, your Mountain Dew, replenish your fishing equipment or get that insect repellant, or cap you forgot. The Lodge is also open in the winter and rents snowmobiles with which you can have a unique experience, even making your way back up to Mirror Lake and the Bald Mountain Pass. But, remember, in the winter you'll have to get to the lodge through Evanston, as the Scenic Byway closes as soon as the snow gets too deep to plow.

FOR THOSE WHO WANT TO DO THE LOOP ON PAVED HIGHWAYS & ALSO THOSE OF THE "ADVENTUROUS LOOP TOUR" NOTE: For those who want to do what I'm calling the "Adventurous Loop Tour'' on the gravel North Slope Road, we'll get back to it, but even for you adventurous souls, it would be really worthwhile to stick with the pavement as described below, swinging through Evanston, and then do the extra Piedmont Ghost Town Scenic Backway segment, and even visit Ft. Bridger and the Wyo. State Park there, then back to the North Slope Road. BUT, IF FOR WHATEVER REASONS YOU WANT TO GO DIRECTLY TO THE NORTH SLOPE SCENIC BACKWAY, JUMP AHEAD TO PAGE 57. YOU'LL SAVE 127 MILES. ******************************** So, from the NORTH SLOPE ROAD/BEAR RIVER LODGE MIRROR LAKE SCENIC BYWAY junction, 50 miles from Kamas, we drive 6 miles north to the WYOMING BORDER, then continue 12 miles north into Wyoming and as you approach some high hills to the north there are some very worthwhile displays on the left that you shouldn't miss. 28

http://bearriverlodge.com

p. 45

Just past the displays on the right is the turn-off road CR-173 to the Sulfur Creek Reservoir and the Hilliard ranching community. There, and all the way from the Utah border, if you look carefully, you will see some ranch/animal structures a few of which were built with materials cannibalized from the Hilliard Flume that ended here at the kilns.

ODOMETER: 50 miles at NORTH SLOPE ROAD & BEAR RIVER LODGE to Wyoming border = 6 miles, then 12 miles north to Displays & HILLIARD TURNOFF, TOTAL=68 miles.

I suggest that after you see the displays--to understand the history, you make a couple of mile loop on the pavement and see a few kiln ruins. It is not part of the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway, but is the Hilliard road (County Road) CR-173--paved as it passes the site of Hilliard where the Flume ended with the kilns, several ruins of which can be seen mixed in with the ranches that now cover the area south of the Sulfur Creek Reservoir. That road soon turns into the dirt/gravel Piedmont Scenic Backway, and from there you should return to WY-150.

p. 46

Back on WY-150, a little further north, before the highway swings to the west, there is another pull-out with some fascinating displays, and one you can't miss with a description of BEAR TOWN or BEAR RIVER CITY which is described as "….the liveliest if not the most

wicked town in America."

In the INTRODUCTION I've already discussed some the tie hackers and this Hells On Wheels town, along with some photos. Below I'll enlarge the sign that explains details.

Also in the INTRODUCTION I've shown the exact location and talked about President Eisenhower's hero, Tom "Bear River" Smith, and suggested this story will, or could, become a great Hollywood movie…..one day. See pages 22, 23.

p. 47

From there it is 10 miles to Evanston, where most of the survivors of Bear Town migrated once the "wicked town" disappeared from the map like Sodom and Gomorrah.

EVANSTON, UINTAH COUNTY, WYOMING & POINTS OF INTEREST ODOMETER: Bear River City display to Evanston, Wyoming =10 miles, TOTAL=80 miles. Evanston is the seat of Uintah County, Wyoming, that actively promotes the High Uinta Mountains along with other attractions from the area. The Uinta COUNTY MUSEUM is found at 1020 Front St. in downtown Evanston and is a very worthwhile stop for your tour with great historical displays, information and artifacts about this important railroad town, and area on the High Uinta's North Slope.

In pioneer times the area was inhabited by the Shoshoni Tribe, led by famous Chief Washakie who was of key influence in seeking peace and was given a full U.S. Military funeral when he passed away in 1900 at 102 years old. You will be given a warm and free welcome by Kay Rossiter, Director, we see to the left above. You will also meet one of the huge animals that roamed the Uintas many, many years ago.

The Uinta's Bear River flows right through the city. You should have noticed from the displays 10 miles to the south, and repeated in my historical comments, that it is the longest river in the hemisphere that doesn't empty into an ocean. It is born in the High Uintas, flows north into Wyoming, then swings northwest into Idaho where it makes a U-turn around the north end of the Wasatch Mountains, and returns to Utah emptying into the Great Salt Lake--500 miles long, and worthy of a WYOMING STATE PARK found on the south side of the freeway as it heads east.

p. 48

The visitor's center is more than worthwhile with wildlife displays, information about the important Bear River, and in a side room has a display on the tie hackers and the Hilliard Flume with an award winning model of the flume--seen to the right above, made years ago by a Junior High School student from Evanston. There is also a large outdoor area where you can see American bison (buffalo).

NOTE: If you're on the Adventurous Loop Tour, and will take the turn-off to Piedmont and from there return to the Uintas-- you should fill up with gas before leaving Evanston, as from Piedmont back to the North Slope Road, and then the 148 miles to the pavement near Manila, there is no gas station. MORE ABOUT THE TIE HACKERS: You can learn more about them by driving 277 miles north to Dubois where there is a special outdoor TIE HACKER MUSEUM & monument. See pictures in Appendix 8.

OPTION FOR THE "PAVEMENT LOOP TOUR" and THE "NORTH SLOPE ADVENTUROUS TOUR"-- You can see the fascinating PIEDMONT GHOST TOWN, by leaving I-80 about 20 miles east of Evanston at Exit #24 and head south 7.5 miles to Piedmont on a good gravel road. Along the way you can stop and see a display of the MORMON PIONEER MUDDY CREEK CAMP & CROSSING, and then continue on to the Piedmont ghost town.

THE PIEDMONT GHOST TOWN Piedmont once had a general store, a couple of saloons and a two story hotel where Butch Cassidy and gang stayed one night on their way to rob the bank in Montpelier, Idaho. Piedmont, in its hay day, not only hosted Butch Cassidy and gang, but also was where Calamity Jane, famed frontierswoman and professional scout lived as a young girl.

p. 49

The ghost town is on private property--easily observable from the road, but you can visit the kiln ruins and the very good displays--that are very worthwhile and make your side trip here invaluable. The DISPLAYS explain the history of the town, the importance and process of making charcoal--with wood provided by the tie hackers, the relationship with the transcontinental railroad and eventual demise of the community. Likewise a walk across the creek over to the cemetery, accessible to the public, at least for me, became rewarding. At the cemetery take note how many of the children died in their infancy showing how difficult pioneer living was. You'll also notice that there have been a few burials recently, and flowers are placed on some of the graves….which gave me the idea that on Memorial Day, a visit to the cemetery might just make possible meeting people connected to Piedmont--living or dead!

So on Memorial Day in 2013 I was at Piedmont waiting at the cemetery when a real live Kelly Crompton Bussio, and her husband J.D., drove up to the cemetery and a very rewarding visit ensued. Kelly's first husband, Brent Crompton, was buried in the cemetery in 1996. Kelly's mother-in-law, Faye Byrne Crompton, is a direct descendant of Moses Byrne, one of the pioneer founders of Piedmont.

Faye was still alive in 2013, 87 years old living in Orem, Utah and I went to visit her and husband. She was raised in Piedmont until she graduated from high school and had some interesting stories to tell, and showed me some original paintings/drawings of Piedmont, one seen above, and permitted me to photograph them and newspaper articles about Piedmont, reporting it once had a population of 11,000. Once a year the Byrne Family has a reunion in Robertson, Wyoming, and they make the trip to Piedmont to decorate the graves. Kelly gave me permission to go on to the private property and take close-up photographs of what remains, all part of the Piedmont photo/essay on my website:

https://cordellmandersen.com/2013/05/ The property now belongs to the Guild family, the other pioneer founders of the community, with a very large cattle ranch covering the entire area. Now back to the LOOP TOUR:

p. 50

FOR THE "NORTH SLOPE TOUR"—if not interested in Ft. Bridger, you can follow part of the Old Mormon Trail west on CR-173 back to Highway 15o near Sulfur Reservoir & Bear Town, or from Piedmont west on CR-171 that goes by Piedmont, Guild and Byrne Reservoirs which road then joins CR-173, either way about 16 miles returning to WY150, and from there 18 miles back to the North Slope Road, where your total will be 142 miles.

ODOMETER: Evanston (80), to Exit #24 (20), Piedmont (8), then following the Piedmont Scenic Backway on CR-173 back to SR-150 (16), to North Slope Road (18), TOTAL = 142 miles If you're interested in Ft. Bridger, you can hold off on going to Piedmont until doing Ft. Bridger and from there continue to Mt. View, then go south & west through Robertson on SR-410, then CR-204 to Piedmont for a total of about 21 miles then return 16 miles to WY150 on CR-173 as mentioned, and 18 more to North Slope Road, for total of 55 miles. FOR THE PAVEMENT TOUR, from Piedmont, you can return to I-80 and continue the tour, having witnessed some wonderful western history with a side trip of around 15 miles.

FORT BRIDGER Back to the tour: From Exit 24 on I-80, we will continue 13 miles to the east, leaving the freeway at the Fort Bridger exit, with 2 miles more in to town. Here is another extremely worthwhile WYOMING STATE HISTORICAL SITE & MUSEUM focusing on famous mountain man and explorer Jim Bridger--connected to the Uinta Mountains. Here one can spend a handful of enjoyable hours learning more of our great Western History.

We can add that between the freeway and the town we cross the Blacks Fork River--born in the Uintas, where in 1847 Wilford Woodruff, with the first company of Mormon pioneers immigrating to Utah, introduced fly fishing to the West with equipment acquired on a mission to England.

p. 51

If you need to stay for the night, Ft. Bridger has the place that has been my place of refuge more than once when coming out of the Uintas dead tired, once after having survived quite miraculously a heart attack and making it out the final 8 miles on my own--by the grace of the Lord, and then on to the Wagon Wheel Motel.

Just don't count on the Motel on the Labor Day weekend, as Fort Bridger fills up with 50,000 visitors for a few days making the town one of the largest in Wyoming with the

MOUNTAIN MAN RENDEZVOUS.

ON TO ANOTHER "GATEWAY TO THE UINTAS" From Ft. Bridger we drive 6 miles, to the east to Urie, then south a couple of miles to MT. VIEW and find this impressive GATEWAY to get back to the Uintas.

p. 52

But, before getting back to the Uintas, best make a stop at the FOREST SERVICE RANGER STATION, just past the Gateway to the east on Lone Tree Road Highway 414, where there is another tie hacker cabin, that was also transplanted from the Steele Creek Commissary ghost town on the North Slope of the Uintas. The displays are very good, with artifacts from the tie hackers, like a broad ax, and other tools they used and you'll notice a wood stove that indicates that this cabin is from the 19121936 period.

ODOMETER: KAMAS to MT. VIEW including PIEDMONT TOUR: 80 miles to EVANSTON to Exit #24 (20), Piedmont & back to I-80 (15), then to FT. BRIDGER (15), to Mt. View (8), TOTAL=138 miles.

FOR THOSE TAKING THE ADVENTUROUS NORTH SLOPE ROAD SCENIC BACKWAY & THE ENTIRE PIEDMONT SCENIC BACKWAY Follow the instructions given in the preceding pages from Evanston to Fort Bridger. From Ft. Bridger continue on to Mt. View--where you should fill your gas tank, and from there follow what we can call the Piedmont Scenic Backway on WY-410 through Robertson and continue west eventually on dirt/gravel County Road (CR)-204 to the Piedmont ghost town, and it's kilns.

From Piedmont you can follow instructions on page 50 to return to WY-150 near Sulfur Reservoir & Bear Town. and from there 18 miles back to the North Slope Road.

p. 53

ODOMETER: THE complete PIEDMONT SCENIC BACKWAY LOOP TOUR from Kamas to Evanston (80), Ft. Bridger (35), Mt. View(8), then through Robertson to Piedmont (21), back to SR-150 (16), and return to North Slope Road (18), TOTAL= 177 miles. Doing this Backway from the North Slope Road, and back is a total of 127 miles bringing the total to 177 miles from Kamas. IMPORTANT NOTE-- SO, FILL UP WITH FUEL AT MT. VIEW IF DOING THIS TOUR, as on the North Slope Road it will be 148 miles more before you get to the UT-44 after the Geologic Loop Backway--and then 6 miles backtracking to Manila for gas. But. if you fill up at Mt. View, you'll make it fine--unless your vehicle is a real gas guzzler. We'll now continue with the PAVEMENT LOOP TOUR until it hooks up with the Adventurous North Slope Scenic Backway Loop, at which point we'll focus on the North Slope that gets you into close contact with the Uintas, a half dozen lakes and reservoirs, and a dozen or so Trailheads that point you south into the high country.

THE PAVEMENT LOOP TOUR FROM MT. VIEW NOTE: We will continue with the Pavement Tour until getting to Nila's Store & the Spirit Lake Scenic Backway where we will be confronted with a choice of how to continue. ODOMETER: 138 miles, MT. VIEW, WYOMING to LONETREE=22 miles , TOTAL=160 mi.

Soon we are through the badlands and begin seeing ranchland, and cattle grazing. Just before Lonetree we cross the Henry's Fork River that comes out of the Uintas and flows east finally emptying into Flaming Gorge Reservoir near Manila, where it is called Henrys Fork Creek, as 95% of its water is used to irrigate the farms and ranches along its course. In LONETREE there isn't much to see except a home attached to an old store, closed since 1986, complete with its parking meter out front….but with a few cobwebs—so, might be a good idea to insert a nickle or a dime.

p. 54

continue east soon passing by a turnoff that connects to the North Slope Scenic Backway, and the Beaver Creek Drainage, Hole in the Rock, Hoop Lake and more-but ignore it and continue on WY-414. From there we

Along the Henrys Fork River, if you keep a sharp eye out, you can see—in addition to healthy cattle, lots of wildlife, like geese, antelope and sand hill cranes29

In the 50 miles to Manila, Utah we will be paralleling the course of the Henrys Fork River that is born in the Uintas. This river and its now lush green ranch country, is of great importance in the history of the West as explained in a "must see display" on the right side of the highway between Burnt Fork and McKinnon, describing the first MOUNTAIN MAN RENDEZVOUS in 1825.

At that historic event--the first-- explorers, trappers, and Native Americans gathered to sell and trade their furs and replenish their supplies for the upcoming season. You'll want to stop and read every word about the great mountain men and explorers involved in "winning the West." I'll insert a few lines to whet your appetite so you will stop and read about this great event where most of THE GREATS gathered:

29

See, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandhill_crane

p. 55

The actual site where the rendezvous took place is not marked but seen above--down the valley a ways from the display and off to the north across the Henrys Fork River following CR-01 which road takes one to Green River. At the junction of WY-414 and CR-1, seen below, we find the sign directing us to the SPIRIT LAKE (SCENIC BACKWAY )--towards the south up into the High Uintas, and it is at this junction that we find NILA WILD'S STORE .

ODOMETER: To Junction with CR-1 & WY-414 and NILA'S STORE, TOTAL = 172 miles Here we are confronted with the decision whether we leave the pavement and follow a well cared for dirt/gravel road or continue on the pavement to Manila, but first let's meet Nila in her store in 2013 on the left--when undergoing chemotherapy for cancer. After picking out a few snacks, we attempt to fill up out front at the .28.9 cents/gallon price, that had her laughing a bit--in fact, a lot. Then, meet Nila in 2017 on the far right. This is the only store between Mt. View and Manila. Nila has been here for half a century.

I SUGGEST YOU LEAVE THE PAVEMENT--- FOR 40 MILES TAKING THE SPIRIT LAKE SCENIC BACKWAY, where 8 miles up into the Uintas we meet up with the route of those adventurous souls who chose to do the NORTH SLOPE SCENIC BACKWAY.

p. 56

THE PAVEMENT TOUR THROUGH MANILA & ON TO THE MAGNIFCENT SHEEP CREEK CANYON GEOLOGICAL BACKWAY If the weather is real bad, those of you on the "PAVEMENT TOUR" can continue on the pavement following WY-414 8 miles to the Utah border, and then on UT-43 another 8 miles to Manila. At Manila I suggest you fill up with gas, then drive about 15 miles south on UT-44 going past the lower entrance to the Geological Backway and on to the higher entrance that leads you to the junction with the North Slope Scenic Backway. At that Point we'll put on hold those of you on the "Pavement Tour" and go back and bring also to this point those of the Adventurous North Slope Scenic Backway tour.

ODOMETER: Nila's Store to Manila and on WY-414 & UT-43 (172+16)--Then on UT-44 to Dowd's Hole Displays just off of UT-44 on FR-218 (15), then 4 miles on FR-218 to junction with FR-221--North Slope Road, & beginning of the Sheep Creek Geologic Scenic Backway for a TOTAL =207 miles.

NOW--for those of the Pavement Tour wanting to do the

THE SPIRIT LAKE SCENIC BACKWAY (which I highly recommend) WE'LL BACKUP TO NILA'S STORE & HEAD UP WY- CR-01 that turns into FR-221 & HOOKUP WITH THE ADVENTURERS DOING THE NORTH SLOPE BACKWAY

Up this Backway, we begin on dirt, then at the Utah State line it turns into pavement for a few miles until we get up the canyon, then on dirt/gravel again, now back in Utah on FR-221. Eight miles from Nila's Store we meet up with the route of our "adventurous" friends—seen way up ahead in the third picture--who took the North Slope Scenic Backway--96 miles to that point from the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway, and from here follow the same route to finish out the North Slope Road where it meets the pavement and the Geological Backway loop.

p. 57

THE NORTH SLOPE ROAD

Google

©2018 Google LLC, used with permission. Google and the Google logo are registered trademarks of Google LLC

We'll back up to the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway, near the Bear River Lodge where you find the sign inserted above, and follow the North Slope Road Scenic Backway (my labeling it), for 138 miles along the very edge of the High Uintas Wilderness Area, pinpointing the many important Trailheads, lakes, ruins, and ghost towns of what I have coined, The Tie Hacker Culture, crucial to the Transcontinental Railroad that in 1867 was being constructed to the north crossing Wyoming, and then into Utah. A basic understanding of this crucial history will help make all of your experience on the Uinta's North Slope much more exciting and meaningful--you might even make some original discoveries as I have done. Some historical information has been shared already in the INTRODUCTION, and more information will precede some of the upcoming sections of the book describing the North Slope Scenic Backway. So before we continue east I’ll insert one more important item about the tie hackers, specifically about the Hilliard Flume. It originated on the west side of the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway, a few miles south up the Byway, and to the west. The view on the next page will be a GOOGLE EARTH view of the Gold Hill area west of UT-150, accessed via the Whitney Road, showing what I have discovered concerning the path of the tie hacker culture, namely the Hilliard Flume.

As far as I know I'm the only one to do such an exploration and map the findings—which included discovery of cuts for the flume to keep it at a constant 15% downgrade, diversion dams to move water into the flume, remnants of loading platforms, the pathway itself, and on up the canyon to the site of the Mill City ghost town where the tie hackers lived. I have pinpointed them on the following GOOGLE EARTH view. In Chapter 3, The WESTERN UINTAS, I will show pictures of the discoveries. One mystery is that the creek just doesn't presently have enough water to actually operate the flume—except perhaps for a month or so at run-off. After the GOOGLE EARTH view below I’ll insert a picture of the creek.

p. 58

Above we are seeing Mill City Creek, which I have never seen with enough water to make the Hilliard Flume effective. There must have been more water back then, but they also had to construct the Howe Feeder Flume on Main Fork of the Bear River to add more water to the flume and get their wood products the 30 miles to Hilliard, Wyoming & the kilns. p. 61

The NORTH SLOPE SCENIC BACKWAY TOUR

This is the sign you will see first on the North Slope Road going east, the North Slope Road [Forest Road] FR-058, indicating the 16 mile segment shown on the map--to the Blacks Fork area. After leaving the pavement it is 1.7 miles to the turn-off--FR-059, to the Scout Camp and the East Fork of Bear River Trailhead, where there are some very worthwhile Forest Service displays. About the Trailhead & trail: The first 3 miles of the trail along this major tributary of our famous Bear River that leads into the high country, is dotted with many ruins of the tie hackers.

For the lovers of the high country there are wonderful options with details in Chapter 2 to guide your hikes and backpacks to: Lake Lorena, Norice, Priord and Allsop Lakes, with majestic peaks such as Mount Beulah, the Cathedral and Yard Peak…..with feisty Native cutthroat trout awaiting you.

At mile 7 you come to Mill Creek where from the road are visible the ruins of a tie hacker splash dam as seen in the picture below on the left. In the middle an old picture of the ties behind a splash dam at the time of the thaw. Later I'll tell you what happened next. This was the site of the Mill Creek Commissary that supplied the tie hackers.

p. 62

A couple of miles ahead on a straight-away we come to McKenzie Creek where a slight distance from the road to the south is found a quite large number of tie hacker ruins, called the McKenzie Compound. Below is the GOOGLE EARTH view, with my labels.

A little further along on a big swing in the road uphill to the north there is a road taking off to the southeast—seen below. You could take a short hike up this road along which you can see the remains of one of the tie hackers sleds, ruins of a cabin and loading platforms.

Following the old tie hack road we eventually found piles of slabs cut off from the logs at a time after the process was mechanized with the first tractors with a power take-offs, all of this evidence of portable saw mills and mechanization which eventually made the tie hackers obsolete.

p. 63

From that point the road begins a steep climb up to ELIZABETH RIDGE or DIVIDE, 12 miles from the pavement where you'll find the above sign. This is Utah's version of the Continental Divide, the North Slope rivers to the east joining to help create the Green River that swings southeast forming Flaming Gorge Reservoir, and eventually south to join the Colorado River that flows southwest and on to the Gulf of California and the Pacific Ocean. The Bear River and its tributaries are west from the divide flowing north, as mentioned, into Wyoming, then swings west into Idaho and circles the northern tip of the Wasatch Mountains, then south back into Utah and empties into the Great Salt Lake making the 500 mile long river the largest in the Northern Hemisphere that doesn't empty into an ocean.

NOTE: The Preface for the Bear River Drainage in Chapter 2 will have a special article on the Bear River. From Elizabeth Ridge you begin to drop into the Black Fork drainage, seeing to the south our first 13,000+ mountain, 13,165 ft. high Tokewanna Peak. The western flank drops into the West Fork of Blacks Fork with many tie hack ruins from the 1867-80 period--which are mostly rotted away, others destroyed in a forest fire.

As you go down from the Ridge, if you look carefully through the pines to the south, you will notice a quite large lake that few ever see. As the road takes a sharp turn to the right, you will see a road taking off to the west that is gated. A short walk in will reveal first a sign indicating it is private property, then some cabins, and FISH LAKE you see below. A surprisingly large, beautiful lake--this eastern end on private property.

I just talked to Bernard Asay, Trail Supervisor for the Forest Service on the North Slope and learned about the lake: From the gated road, approximately 3/4 mile down FR-058 there is a

p. 64

pullout and bulletin board, and from there a two-track trail leads 1/2 mile to the dam--built to enlarge the original lake, part of which is on Forest Service land, and open to fishing for brook trout--be respectful of Private Property signs. Few if any even know about this lake. At 18 miles from the pavement we come to a junction with a sign we see below that gives us two options:

ODOMETER: At the sign--NORTH SLOPE SCENIC BACKWAY = 18 miles from from UT-150, plus the complete Piedmont Tour = 195 miles. First option: A sharp turn to the right is the West Fork of Blacks Fork road. This would be a detour from our tour, but if interested the road is fine for about 5 miles, with many places you can camp and fish the stream, then it gets a bit rougher, fording the river and taking you to the Trailhead which is little used.

A SUGGESTION: On my exploratory trips, after fording the river I had to contend with a ruined tire. On a previous trip in the Hoop Lake area, had one too. For my 3rd exploration, I had tougher tires, and two spares--enough insurance to not have any more trouble, even in the Dry Gulch Drainage! BE WARNED! HAVE GOOD TIRES.

The West Fork of Blacks Fork trail takes backpackers 10 miles up to Dead Horse Lake and Pass, and the Highline Trail that heads east climbing Red Knob Pass--from where the photo below was taken looking towards the Deadhorse area. From Red Knob Pass the trail drops into the South Slope Lake Fork Drainage.

p. 65

Second option: Is to the left taking you north, where the ATV's are heading, 1/2 mile to Little Lyman Lake--then 1/2 mile more to Lyman Lake. There you can camp and do a little fishing. I'll insert below pictures of the Campground, and each of the Lyman lakes.

Continuing on the "Adventure Tour" on the main North Slope Road, FR-058 takes us 2 miles to the east and a junction where we see the sign inserted below, FR-058, continuing to the left swinging north 8 miles to the Meeks Cabin Reservoir, historical site and campground mostly in Wyoming, and then continues on to Robertson and Mountain View, Wyoming.

WEST FORK JOINS EAST FORK OF BLACKS FORK With MIDDLE FORK JOINING ALSO ODOMETER: At the junction of FR-058 and FR-065, NORTH SLOPE = 20 miles, plus the Piedmont Tour = 197 miles.

p. 66

EAST FORK OF BLACKS FORK To the south on FR-065 we can go 6 miles to the East Fork of Blacks Fork Trailhead from which the pickup and travel trailer are coming in the previous photo panel. A mile before arriving at the Trailhead, we see a sign on the right designated as the CACHE TRAILHEAD, basically just a point along the North Slope Highline Trail which started at the East Fork of Bear River, and continues east. From the East Fork of Blacks Fork Trailhead, the trail leads south 1-1/2 miles then divides, the left hand fork taking you up Little East Fork of Blacks Fork where in the Preface to Chapter 2, Section 8, I will tell the sort of mystical story of my encounter with Big Foot-even with a picture. The trail continues on to Squaw Pass then down to the Oweep Drainage and Porcupine Lake, and the Highline Trail. The right hand fork takes you past two tie hacker sites then up to what I call East Fork Pass, 12,150 ft. high, where you see me below in the midst of one of my survival experiences--with 13,219 ft. Mt. Lovenia in the background.

A mile further along the spine of the High Uintas the trail drops down to Red Knob Pass and the Highline trail. From the attention I'm giving this area, you can rightfully imagine it is a special area for me, which I'll explain in Chapter 2, Section 7--where in the Preface, I'll

describe the above mentioned SURVIVAL experience, what saved me, and what we all can learn from it-- to avoid becoming a sad story on the 10 o'clock News. From the East Fork of Blacks Fork Trailhead, you can also access the Bald Mountain Trail that continues on to the Red Castle Lakes area.

MIDDLE FORK OF BLACKS FORK Back to the North Slope Road junction, just over the bridge south on the west side of the road is a hardly noticeable crude gate in the fence from which a road takes one 2 miles to the unofficial Middle Fork of Blacks Fork trailhead--which only I call a "trailhead." The last mile of the road is impossible. The road ends with a barrier, then the trail and the majestic beauty of the Middle Fork--rarely visited by anyone.

p. 67

The little used trail takes you up to the slopes of Tokewanna Peak and Bob's Lake, but along the way are scattered more ruins of the tie hackers than anywhere, which on my first two backpacks I didn't know what they represented--until meeting Teresa and Bob Fascineli, described further along at the Hewinta Guard Station--when I asked them, "Do you know

what the heck was going on up Middle Fork of Blacks Fork with more ruins than anywhere?" Their reply and introduction to the tie hackers, prompted my 3rd trip up Middle Fork, resulting in me being the first to map, measure, photograph and report on all the ruins. I only found one lone site from the early 1867-1880 period--mostly rotted away, with evidence of a fireplace inside and use of square nails. It was the first found going up the drainage.

Counting that one, I documented 14 tie hacker sites, the upper one with one very large ruin-in the middle above, with signs of having had a rustic floor--the conclusion being that it was likely the kitchen and dining room, also used by the tie hackers for social gatherings-since tie hackers from the 1912-1936 period were more sociable--mostly being of Scandinavian origins where communities were established. Nearby there were two ruins of sweat houses, common among Scandinavians. My conclusion was that it had probably been a Swedish community of tie hackers from the 1912-1936 period. From the early period, 1867-1880, most of the tie hackers were Irish immigrants. The MIDDLE FORK OF BLACKS FORK is not frequented by backpackers. Actually on my first two trips up there I saw signs of only one other person having been in the area. What I did find was a profusion of wild flowers like nowhere else in the Uintas, and the ruins of cabins, some quite large as mentioned in the previous paragraphs. On two of my backpacks I continued up to the slopes of Tokewanna Peak where is found one named lake, Bob's Lake, with feisty Tiger trout.

p. 68

THE OLD BLACK'S FORK COMMISSARY GHOST TOWN We'll now continue our tour following FR-058 to the north 1/2 mile and come to road FR073 that heads due east crossing the Blacks Fork River, but first we'll continue north for another mile to view a very important tie hacker historical site on the west side of the road: The Old Blacks Fork Commissary ruins. This was a fairly complete community that serviced the tie hackers, with general store, livery stable, a school. saloons and even--some say, a brothel.

We'll now return a mile to FR-073 and head east.

ODOMETER: At the junction of FR-073 after visiting the Black Fork Commisary ruins-NORTH SLOPE = 23 miles, plus the Piedmont Tour = 200 miles. We're heading for the Hewinta Guard Station area on what has mostly been a logging road, still in use, so we have to proceed with caution. This is also a section of the Forest Service Road that has at times been a little tough making having a 4-WD vehicle a bit safer. Along this 6 mile stretch several tie hacker ruins are seen right along the road. You will also observe the Forest Service supervised effort to thin out the Lodge pole pines that often are "thicker than weeds" reducing the harvest of productive trees. After removing the commercially useful logs, the debris is piled up, and in the winter--with no wildfire danger, Forest Service employees go in on snowmobiles and burn the debris.

p. 70

SUICIDE PARK Six miles later we come to a junction where we take another side-trip, taking FR-074 north for 2-1/2 miles to visit the tie hacker's SUICIDE PARK right on the Utah side of the border with Wyoming.

Back at the time of the tie hackers there didn't exist Social Security retirement nor any Welfare Programs. Some tie hackers as they grew old and unable to continue working with their broad axes to support themselves, and later when mechanization made many of them obsolete, some who didn't have family to fall back on, gave up and took their own lives. Three of them are buried at this simple memorial site, with nice plaques--one of which I'll insert to help us gratefully remember these "unsung heroes without whom the West might not have been won!" Now, back at the junction:

ODOMETER: At the junction-- NORTH SLOPE = 34 miles, PLUS the Piedmont Tour = TOTAL 211 miles.

the complete

We continue on FR-073 passing over Steele Creek and within 1/4th mile turn off to the right on FR-209 to drive a quarter mile where a very often muddy road takes off to the right that leads shortly to the Steele Creek Commissary ghost town site. It's more than worth it to walk around this important site of the tie hackers period 1912-1936.

THE STEEL CREEK COMMISARY GHOST TOWN Below we notice that after the mud, where many of us have got stuck, the Forest Service has a warning post I have inserted a picture of--warning us to: USE ONLY WHEN DRY. I actually tried to pull it up and move it back where the quagmire began--to be an effective warning, but it was firmly anchored--besides, who am I to deprive others of the opportunity of getting stuck and having a great story to tell on returning to civilization? The walk in is just 1/4th mile or less.

p. 71

You should recall that the tie hacker cabins at the Bear River and Mt. View Ranger Stations came from this site which is from the 1912 to 1936 tie hacker period when they were getting really civilized, even with an outhouse--tipped over in the 3rd picture above. The cover is the 4th picture.

HEWINTA GUARD STATION & WEST FORK OF SMITHS FORK TRAILHEAD Then back on FR-209 we continue about a quarter mile and come to the Hewinta Guard Station. You'll notice it is a log cabin…..and, yes, it was made by the tie hackers in 1928, and with a few modern updates has served the Forest Service for many years. NOTE: In 2018 I

found the Hewinta sign gone, replaced by a small Historical Display relating the history of the cabin. The cabin was not being used at that time.

But, it was here in 2007, where I met Teresa and Bob Fascineli you see above inside the cabin, followed by a picture of the West Fork of Smith's Fork Trailhead--1/2 mile past Hewinta, and me--with a tie hack ruin behind me, I was ready to go up the trail to the North Slope Highline Trail, and from there bushwhack up to Bald Lake nestled under Bald Mountain (11,776 ft.), obviously not the same as the one near Mirror Lake. But, I first talked to Bob and Teresa, who worked as a Wilderness Ranger in the summers. They were the ones who opened up a whole new world to me--the World of the Tie Hackers, which journey since has made my backpacks into the High Uintas so much more meaningful and enjoyable. That same day, at the Trailhead--which you see has a sign and register, even though NGS and Forest Service maps don't list a trailhead being here-- you see behind me the ruins of a tie hack cabin, then within the next mile I was to find more ruins along the trail, including a Model T Ford truck the tie hackers wore out. Then once past the Wilderness Area boundary, we find the best preserved tie hacker splash dam. Note: Behind it they would

accumulate ties during the winter, and then with the run-off in the Spring filling their temporary dam, they'd blow it with dynamite and with a "SPLASH" the ties would be washed downstream into Wyoming where they'd be picked up by workers from the Transcontinental Railroad. I'll insert a few photos of all of that.

p. 72

This chance visit led to intensive research, explorations and discoveries, and even evolved into me giving speeches on the subject to Historical Societies in Evanston, Wyoming and Coalville, Utah. THANKS TERESA AND BOB!

In relation to Teresa--since 2007 when we met, years have come and gone with a lot of water gushing by under the bridge of life…..that brought me to 2015 and a failed effort to get to my lake--Little Andy Lake, Utah's highest lake at 12,302 ft. in the eastern shadow of South Kings Peak. High Altitude Sickness had me backing off and coming back down the trail--that had me stumble into one of those coincidental experiences for which I'm most grateful. Some Forest Service personnel were coming up the trail--one, a lady on horseback. I stopped to say hello when she screamed at me! It was Teresa, still a Wilderness Ranger, who recognized me and explained she had Googled my name a while ago and found an obituary for a "Cordell M. Andersen" who had died in Council Bluffs, Iowa in 2010--causing her to scream at the ghost--me, what's in her picture.

Now back to the LOOP TOUR. From the Hewinta Guard Station, return to FR-073:

ODOMETER: At the junction--Hewinta/FR-073, NORTH SLOPE = 36 miles, PLUS the Piedmont Tour = 213 miles. As we head south on FR-073, before coming to China Meadows, there is a fairly rough road that heads north east that takes you to CHINA LAKE, which in addition to trout, has arctic grayling. I somehow missed this lake and didn't drive in to check it out, but will insert here at least a map showing the Lake and its location along with a picture of an Arctic Grayling.

Map courtesy of
