p. 73

THE JUMP-OFF POINT TO UTAH'S GREATEST MOUNTAIN SCENE We continue on FR-073 southeast 6-1/2 miles and come to the CHINA MEADOWS TRAILHEAD that is a fairly busy one as it is the GATEWAY to what many think is the most stunning mountain scene in Utah: RED CASTLE PEAK & LAKE. But first we see an early summer photo of beautiful China Meadows.

It was likely in this area where on weekends, the tie hackers would "tie one on" with some heavy drinking to break the monotony of their difficult life. Chinamen would come to the camps to do their laundry, and allegedly--with tie hack drinking out of control--would once in a while kill a Chinaman that made necessary a clandestine cemetery for the poor victims. I've searched, but not found anything….yet.

SMITH'S FORK - RED CASTLE The trail up into the high country follows the East Fork of Smith's Fork--we see below, named after famous mountain man and explorer, Jedediah Smith. He and his team of trappers were the first to trap beaver in this area during 1824-25.

p. 74

You've already seen in the INTRODUCTION a mountain--Utah's 5th highest 13,387 ft., I named MT. JEDEDIAH for this greatest of the explorers and mountain men--whose adventurous life accomplished more than any other in such a short life of only 32 years. His

story will be summarized in the Preface to Section 10 of Chapter 2.

"THE SCENE" LIKE YOU'VE NEVER SEEN IT BEFORE What some call "The Greatest Mountain Scene in Utah" famous for its frontal view, as seen below--which picture was published in the January 2010 issue of BACKPACKER MAGAZINE. See APPENDIX 1.

But my favorite, seen below, includes Red Castle Lake, the 2nd largest in the Uintas, located at 11,295 ft., well above timberline in the Uintas. This view shows us the western flank of the Peak. The eastern flank, guarding East Red Castle Lake is similarly magnificent-I'll include it in Chapter 2, Section 10, along with pictures of the two largest native cutthroat trout I've ever caught--both from the Red Castle area.

NOTE: You won't see these scenes from the Road, but only after a 14+ mile hike.

p. 75

ODOMETER: At the China Meadows Trailhead-- NORTH SLOPE = 43 miles, plus the Piedmont Tour = TOTAL 220 miles. Our "North Slope Road" now becomes FR-072 and we drive north 1.3 miles and come to Marsh Lake on our left with campgrounds in a number of areas. In the panel of photos below, Marsh Lake comes first, then a fisherman. Next, Bridger Lake--2.7 miles to the turnoff road on the right--with a 1 mile drive in to the lake and campgrounds. Then, back to FR072, another option for camping, and/or fishing is the large Stateline Reservoir on the west side of the road.

North 1/2 mile there is strangely a short piece of pavement and a "Dump station," important for those with RV's. Another mile north our road takes us a couple of miles into Wyoming where we come to a junction and turn right on FR-017--Henry's Fork 8, and proceed 5.7 miles south back into Utah and a junction with FR-077 (middle picture) which we follow south towards the Henrys Fork CG (3 miles), and the junction of FR-082 and FR-077.

Below we are viewing what we will be enjoying as we travel back from Wyoming towards the Henrys Fork Trailhead--viewing on the left Gilbert Peak, Utah's 3rd highest peak at 13,442 ft.

To continue east we will take FR-082 to Hole in Rock, but a swing past the Campground and to the Henrys Fork Trailhead is a good idea--it being the launching area most use to climb King's Peak, Utah's highest at 13,528 ft. seen on the next page on the left.

p. 76

I’m with Grace and Isaac (Hirschi), my TRAIL BUDDIES. When we met in 2016. I was coming from my first successful exploration of my lake--Little Andy Lake,30 Utah's highest seen on the right. My trail buddies were on their way to climbing Kings Peak the first time with their father, Jake. They began calling me their "trail buddy," and we have kept in touch. During the 2018 season in 3 separate climbs they climbed the peak including with a new little sister, Nora--just turned 7, but for right now I was just advised of a climb--an incredible feat by Grace and her father, which story I tell with some great photographs in Chapter 2, Section 11 on the Henry's Fork, page 256. Thereafter the new stories of Isaac and Nora are told in the Preface to Chapter 2, Section 22 on the Grandview Trailhead page 386. HENRYS FORK TRAILHEAD, I'll have much more to say about this beautiful area, and especially a couple of INSPIRING SURVIVAL STORIES that I'm told have already saved lives…..and can save many more.

ODOMETER: At the Henrys Fork Trailhead -- NORTH SLOPE = 60.5 miles, plus the Piedmont Tour = 238 miles. We now continue northeast towards the Beaver Creek Drainage, and Hole in the Rock, following FR-082, and travel 4 miles--passing through Bullocks Park-- to a junction with the sign we see below on the left

The Henrys Fork Rd refers to the road from Henry's Fork toward Mt. Home, so don't worry about it. I did drive up it just a mile or so to get the view seen below.

We make a right hand turn towards West Beaver Creek, and in one mile pass by the West Beaver Creek Trailhead, I've inserted on the previous page, along with a photo of the main area the trail takes you too-- Gilbert Lake and Gilbert Peak. We continue on towards Hole in the Rock, passing by many beaver dams. We are now in a vast northeast area of the Uintas geologists call "hogbacks" one of which we get a shadowy glimpse of to the left in the previous photo. I'll insert a better shot of one below.

Below is a good view of a hogback, looking back to the west from the junction of the Middle Beaver Creek Trailhead road. The mileage included next will include the 4 mile roundtrip to the Trailhead, the sign indicating some of the areas the trail will take you to.

From the sign coming out of the Middle Fork road, to the junction of the road coming from Lonetree, and continuing to Hoops Lake, it is 1 mile. This is a good point to insert our mileages:

ODOMETER: At the junction where FR-082 meets FR-078 coming from Lonetree and continuing to Hoop Lake -- NORTH SLOPE = 80 miles, plus the complete Piedmont Tour = 257 miles. From the junction where FR-078 comes from Lonetree and the highway on the north, our North Slope Scenic Backway Tour now continues following FR-078. This is the spot where we can see HOLE IN THE ROCK, with a zoomed-in photo of it shown on the next page.

p. 78

We continue through a rough, but beautiful rock portal in a hogback that welcomes us back towards the snow dotted crests of the Uintas.

p. 79

All throughout the Uintas, from the foothills up to Kings Peak, there is a profusion of wildflowers, and on my last exploratory trip in mid-June I found a few new ones that boosts my total to over 320. So this is a good place to insert a few of the new ones, along with old standbys, to stimulate your curiosity to keep a sharp eye out for these divine VISIONS OF NATURE.

We'd best get moving on to Hoop Lake where there are two Trailheads, plus great camping areas and fishing, even for arctic grayling…..but as we move along under one of the hog backs we have to stop to see a display on the Rocky Mountain Bighorn sheep that, due to the efforts of the Division of Wildlife Resources, are multiplying in the area, and I'll include a shot of a good one on the right.

Four miles from the junction on FR-078 we arrive at Hoop Lake, that--as many bodies of water in the Uintas, dams have been built to increase the size and storage capacity, and with outflow controls, can be released downstream for the farms and ranches. Such is the case with Hoop, and, as happens almost everywhere, the level drops towards the end of the summer as you can see in the Lake with the picture below taken in the Fall.

There are nice campgrounds, and on the western end one of the two Trailheads with trails that head up into the Wilderness Area as listed in the signs below.

From there we drive back across the dam and head up FR-86 and soon get a good view of the lake from the east. Then we come to the access road to other camping areas, and the 2nd Trailhead on the eastern edge of the lake.

p. 82

We continue east on FR-86 3 miles and come to a Trailhead sign, we see below--which is the BURNT FORK TRAILHEAD, with a trail that takes one up to the North Slope Highline Trail, accessing Fish Lake and others in the Wilderness Area. NOTE: Seems like in

some areas they call it "The North Side Highline Trail," but since we are on the North Slope-thus the excuse for my slip of the tongue.

A short distance east we cross Burnt Fork, which would be a great stream to wet a line in and you could camp out most anywhere. From the Trailhead we drive 2.2 miles and come to BEAVER MEADOWS RESERVOIR where the road crosses the long dam. There is a Trailhead you find by taking a quite rough road just before crossing the dam.

p. 83

With the dam behind us, seen to the right in this fisheye view of the reservoir we, continue.

From Beaver Meadows Reservoir the road is wider and smoother and at some point becomes FR-058, which was the designation of the North Slope Road from the beginning for about 20 miles. In 5 miles we arrive at the junction with the Spirit Lake Scenic Backway, FR-221, that begins at Nila's Store, 8 miles down to the north in Wyoming along WY-414. Here we join up with those of the Pavement Tour who have opted to drive with us on dirt for 40 miles. FR-058 is the one the pickup is turning onto seen below.

ODOMETER: At the junction where FR-058 meets FR-221 coming from Nila's Store & our North Slope Scenic Backway joins the Spirit Lake Scenic Backway -- NORTH SLOPE RD. = 96 miles, PLUS the Piedmont Tour = 273 miles

ON TO SPIRIT LAKE Now on Forest Road 221, we drive 2.7 miles further east and come to the Spirit Lake road junction, and turn right to drive on FR-01 the 7 miles to the most remote resort area in the Uintas--with Lodge, restaurant, cabin and boat rental, plus full-service Forest Service campgrounds around Spirit Lake, and 3 Trailheads along the road, with several more at Spirit Lake, including the last really important one giving access to the Wilderness Area.

p. 84

We are now in the Sheep Creek drainage where work is being done by the DWR--Division of Wildlife Resources (Fish & Game) working to restore and preserve the Colorado River Cutthroat trout, native of the area. You'll also notice cattle grazing as this is a Multiple-Use Forest with grazing, and logging activities closely supervised by the Forest Service.

Soon we come to a double Trailhead, one on each side of the road--not the elaborate trailheads with register and such to guide the hikers as is usually the case for the Wilderness Area.

Only one of the destinations listed, Fish Lake, is in the Wilderness Area, so for sure we are now in the Eastern Uintas, a guide to which will be Chapter 4. A couple more miles and we see another Trailhead—seen below.

We have driven 7 miles from the junction and arrive at beautiful Spirit Lake, and drive around the eastern shoreline, and soon see another Trailhead sign.

p. 85

This trail takes the hiker east to lakes out of the Wilderness Area, one of which--Browne Lake we will get to on the road in just a little while. In another mile or so we come to a very nice Forest Service Campground with good rest rooms, and a little further to the Spirit Lake Resort. If you were hoping for a bit of civilization you will be disappointed as the gate has been locked for several years--of course you could remedy that by responding to the FOR SALE sign, and becoming the owner of the most remote resort in the Uintas.

Below you can see the way it was back in 2005. The year before I had met Clay Zimmerman on the Lake Fork River near Crater Lake and he invited me to go with him on his annual 100 mile goat pack trip from the Hayden Pass Highline Trailhead to Spirit Lake. My daughter, Mahana, went with--and WE MADE IT! Here she is happy to be rewarded with a MAMA MOOSEBURGER, and me with my PAPA MOOSEBURGER.

Clay is still in business, so if interested here is his contact information: CLAY ZIMMERMAN, "The Goat Whisperer," HIGH UINTA PACK GOATS, 614 Spring Creek Rd., Evanston, WYOMING 82930-4628; Tel. 1-877-722-5462; 307-701-4628 EMAIL: clay@highuintapackgoats.com

p. 86

Near the closed gate to the Lodge, is a most important Trailhead you see below, which is where we came out of the mountains after our 100 mile hike from the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway, most of it on the Highline Trail.

We have now done the 18 mile round-trip to Spirit Lake and are back at the junction ready to move east.

We soon see up ahead Long Park Reservoir and anticipate the turn-off road.

p. 87

At 2.4 miles from the Spirit Lake junction, we come to the turn-off to Long Park Reservoir and take the short drive.

Soon we pass the stream feeding the reservoir, and also see a very important notice about the cooperative effort to restore the Colorado River Cutthroat trout. In 1.7 miles we come to the reservoir and observe campers and fishermen.

We have now returned to the main road, FR-221, after a 3.3 mile round-trip, and in about another 3 miles turn-off to visit Sheep Creek Lake, where the DWR has a trap to catch spawning Cutthroats and get their eggs to take to the hatchery for efficient raising of trout that will be planted all over.

Here you can read about the restrictions, as part of the restoration program, which include use of only artificial lures and flies. I'll insert the sign so you can see how your fishing is to be controlled.

p. 89

In another mile we come to another junction, seeing a pickup pulling a travel trailer, followed by others, which for several reasons I feel is important, as I will explain.

Browne Lake is a popular destination for campers, glampers, fishermen and hikers.

Just after we turn onto this road, we see in the long meadow to our right another Trailhead, but very importantly see a historical marker--as coming down this meadow we have been paralleling the route of the CARTER MILITARY ROAD, constructed in 1881 and used until 1924 that had the purpose of traveling between Fort Bridger and the railroad on the north to supply military outposts in the Uintah Basin. It followed one of the two routes used by the Native Americans to cross the Uinta Mountains--the other one being up the Henrys Fork, over Gun Sight Pass to the Uinta River Drainage and down to the basin. But, the Carter route made possible supply wagons--even though the distance of 60 miles still was a long torturous trip with a wagon. The story of the Carter Military Road is told on page 474.

It also was the route used by the Vernal sheriff in 1896 to clandestinely--in the dark of night, take a prisoner, Matt Warner, to avoid him being lynched, to the railroad in Wyoming and then to Ogden. He was followed by Butch Cassidy and his Wild Bunch, who had the intention of freeing their buddy, Warner, on which ride they stayed at Piedmont, then went on to rob the bank at Montpelier, Idaho to get the money they needed to spring Warner from jail. We will follow the route of the Carter Road down to Browne Lake where we will see a historical display.

p. 90

This is a great spot for spending a night, admiring the wildlife, doing a little fishing, taking in the history--like of the CARTER MILITARY ROAD--the display's print too small to read here--so you've got to do the tour. Here you can see your hiking options from several Trailheads, and admire the view to the south of Leidy Peak and others.

We have now returned to FR-221, having made the 5.5 mile round-trip, and proceed another 4.8 miles and come to the pavement, turning left to take the SHEEP CREEK GEOLOGICAL SCENIC BACKWAY--10 miles of breathtaking views of millions of years of history recorded in the stunningly colorful geologic earth layer recordings of history.

p. 91

ODOMETER: At the junction where FR-221 and our North Slope & Spirit Lake Scenic Backways meet the pavement and the Sheep Creek Geological Loop Backway--FR-218-NORTH SLOPE RD = 138 miles, PLUS the Piedmont Tour = 315 miles. At this point in our Tour, we are where those who remained on the paved highway (SR414) from NILA'S STORE continued to Manila, and from there on Utah State Highway 44, headed south for 14.5 miles, having passed the lower entrance to the Sheep Creek Geologic Loop and climbed to the higher starting point that we see below.

They will have the advantage of a little better understanding of the "Making" of the Uintas, but those of us "adventurers" will be able to see that later after the Geologic Loop, and possibly a short detour to Manila to fill up with gas.

THE SHEEP CREEK GEOLOGICAL SCENIC BACKWAY Let me introduce the upcoming most spectacular 10 mile drive of your life, by quoting from official sources: "This route winds through the dramatic geologic formations of the Sheep Creek National Geologic Area. The Uinta Fault, which runs for more than 100 miles along the north slope of the Uinta Mountains, is clearly visible in the extremely twisted rock layers along the upper part of the loop. But stunning scenery isn't the only reason to keep your camera ready on this Backway. Expect to catch a glimpse or two of Rocky Mountain bighorn sheep as you wind through Sheep Creek's awe-inspiring rock spires. This relatively small area is home to an impressive diversity of birds and other wildlife. Sharp eyes will spot the gravesite of the mysterious Cleophus Dowd along the western end of the loop. 31

31 www.flaminggorgecountry.com/Sheep-Creek-Geological-Loop

p. 92

Much more information is available on the internet, such as from the Forest Service, their leading paragraph being: The U.S. Forest Service designated nearly 3,600 acres of land as the Sheep Creek Canyon Geological Area on May 13, 1962, to preserve the spectacular geology of the canyon for future generations. This remarkable area is located along part of the Sheep Creek drainage west of Flaming Gorge National Recreation Area (figure 1). Sheep Creek Canyon is an excellent place to learn about the Earth's geologic history. 32

At the point above we were fortunate to see two young Rocky Mountain sheep, the youngest with an ear tag, and a collar with transmitter--part of a Division of Wildlife Resources effort to restore to the area a species once native.

32

https://www.utahgeology.org/road_logs/uga-29_first_edition/OP_guide/sheepcrk.pdf

p. 93

Down in the bottom of the canyon, you could stop for a picnic lunch at Palisades Memorial Park, where there are restrooms, picnic tables and shade. The park is dedicated to 7 victims of a flash flood in 1965, from the Woodruff and Swenson families.

A short hike can be taken along the way to see the source of a spring that gushes out of the base of the cliff and adds considerably to the size of Sheep Creek.

No camping is allowed in the canyon, but further down, out of the area, is this Forest Service Campground we see below. For those low on gasoline, a 6 mile drive can be made to Manila, so I'll give you a little tour of that loop drive, next.

p. 94

ODOMETER: After the Geological Loop, we are at the junction of FR-218 and UT-44 For the "Adventure Tour," -- 148 miles from SR-150, plus the Piedmont Tour = 325 miles. I will just keep track from here on for said, "Adventure Tour" people. The rest of you can keep track, but it will be somewhat less.

A QUICK LOOP THROUGH MANILA FOR GAS….or WHATEVER From the junction of FR-218 and UT-44, it is 6 miles north to Manila we are approaching in the picture below.

You can gas up, and cross the street to check on whatever at the friendly FOREST SERVICE office, where this smiling face not only was refreshing, but Maddy (Woodward, p.227) gave me a picture she took of foot prints she swore were from Sasquatch or Big Foot--I'll share that with you in the Preface to Chapter 2, Section 8, on Little East Fork of Blacks Fork . Down the main drag to the east there is an ATM from Zion's Bank, and if you need a change from camping, there is a good Motel, seen below.

p. 95

We'll now head back to our tour driving the 6 miles to where we left Sheep Creek, but just past that junction also notice there is another opportunity for learning.

It is very worthwhile to take the Nature Trail, only a mile or so, and learn about "nature" such as the annual spawn up Sheep Creek of the Kokanee salmon from Flaming Gorge. We continue on our tour, switch-backing up the mountain, and look back on the Sheep Creek portion of this huge reservoir.

Fourteen miles from Manila we come to the higher entrance to the Geologic Loop at Dowd's Hole Overlook with the displays shown a few pages ago that should have been seen already by those on the Pavement Tour. The rest of you should drive the 100 yards or so off UT-44 to see them and learn how the Uintas were made in 3 displays, like the one I'll insert again below:

p. 96

ODOMETER: After the Dowd's Hole Displays we are at the upper junction of FR-218 and UT-44 For the "Adventure Tour," -- 168 miles from UT-150, plus the Piedmont Tour (127) = 345 miles. We now proceed south on UT-44 and note that the forests in the eastern Uintas are very healthy, with rarely any sign at all of dead trees from the Pine borer beetle--so frequent in other areas of the mountains.

In a few miles we see the following sign with a nice pull-out with restrooms, a Nature Trail, and a pond where the children can fish.

Soon we come to a primary junction where UT-44 ends, our highway becoming U.S. 191 that comes from Vernal and at this junction turns east towards Flaming Gorge Dam and Recreation Area….as I recall 6 miles to the dam, which entire area is another destination you've got to see-- but for now let's stick to the Uinta Mountains to the west of U.S. 191.

p. 97

ODOMETER: At the junction of UT-44 and U.S.191, from Kamas, including the Piedmont tour plus the North Slope & Sheep Creek Geological Scenic Backways, plus a loop through Manila and back to here, TOTAL OF = 363 miles. We continue on U.S. 191 and in 6 miles or so we see an almost unnoticeable trailhead sign pointing to the west-- ironically for THE MOST FAMOUS TRAILHEAD IN UTAH.

We drive in about 1/2 mile and find the real beginning--or end, of the HIGHLINE TRAIL that we saw 106 trail miles to the west on the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway. A couple of years ago the Trailhead here had one of the worst trailhead signs in all of the Uintas--but after a bit of lobbying with the Forest Service, some improvement was realized, as you can see below, the 1st photo from the left being the 2016 version, the 2nd as it is presently in 2018, and the 3rd, an enlargement of an addition seen below of the great organization that has taken charge of maintaining the trail, and with some improvement in the sign--even though I'd like this great trail to be dignified a little more, even with a register. Maybe I'll mysteriously do the favor.

It is important to note that most people mistakenly think the Highline Trail ends at the Leidy Peak Trailhead, about 76 miles from the UT-150 trailhead. Rather it continues another 26 miles to this ending of the Trail. We'll shortly visit Leidy Peak and mention more about this. We'll now continue our tour towards the south stopping just a short way up the highway to see more Forest Service displays--called the CART CREEK MEADOW INTERPRETIVE SITE, then continue climbing up to the Pass, on Highway 191 we see below.

p. 98

This pass at 8,428 ft., compared to the Bald Mountain Pass at 10,759 ft. on the other highway that crosses the Uintas, shows graphically the difference between Eastern, and Western Uintas, basically a 2,331 foot elevation differential--U.S. 191 maintained open during the winter, while UT-150 is closed for at least 6 months a year buried in snow.

The elevation here is basically in what is called the "Lodgepole pine belt" all around the Uintas where lodgepole pines through natural seeding become too thick for good productivity and need to be thinned, and then replanted with other conifers more commercially important such as we see in the above photo. As we descend towards the south, 9 miles from the Highline Trail, we come to our next detour, the RED CLOUD LOOP SCENIC BACKWAY, first stopping to see more Forest Service displays, use the restroom, etc. The next 66 miles will be on good dirt/gravel roads that are well graded, so this should be an exception for those of you on the "Pavement Tour," but well worth it.

p. 99

I'll insert below the southern half of the Uinta Loop Map we used for the north. Below is a simple map--much more accurate than the previous one that shows the entire Red Cloud Loop Scenic Backway and at the apex of the brown colored route is where we add a blue route which is a very important side-trip right into the heart of the eastern high country, traveling to the Leidy Peak Highline Trailhead, and Hacking Lake.

Google EARTH MAPS Additional road by author

Google We are traveling first through beautiful Quaking Aspen forests, which I emphasize as it is the Queen of Utah's trees--the STATE TREE, which we'll see further along is the primary vegetation that saves first areas devastated by forest fires.

According to an article by Erin Alberty in the Salt Lake Tribune, and reported by Adam Eakle on KSL (TV) OUTDOORS, March 2, 2019 from Fish Lake in Central Utah, they describe the single organism that is “the largest, most dense ever found on earth” located on the Southwest bank of Fish Lake and calculated to weigh 13 million pounds. It is a stand of QUAKING ASPEN TREES spreading over 106 acres all from a single male quaking aspen, now composed of over 40,000 trees, some over 130 years old, all connected through the root system. It was discovered by researchers in the 1970’s and recently confirmed by geneticists, and given the name, PANDO, which is Latin for “I SPREAD” and variously described as “the heaviest,” 34 “the most dense,” and “the most massive” organism on earth. 34

https://www.sltrib.com/author/ealberty/

p. 101

As we climb higher the forests begin to be dominated by beautiful conifers, that are all very healthy.

We pass by very nice Forest Service Campgrounds, and then at 13.4 miles come to a junction with these signs that will guide us. We will continue to Oaks Park.

The road behind us comes from Vernal as indicated by the sign below, called The Taylor Mtn. Rd.-- which is another access road for the Red Cloud Loop coming from Vernal on 2500 West and traveling due north 21 miles to this point from U.S. Highway 40.

Four miles further along we come to the turn-off road to Oaks Park and drive 1.2 miles to the Reservoir, which I'll have to admit was a bit disappointing….as the water level was very low….even early in the season. I won’t bother showing a photo of the reservoir.

p. 102

We're back to the main road, FR-018 and continue through vast meadow areas 3.3 miles and come to the junction with FR-043, the road to Leidy Peak and Hacking Lake.

We drive the 8 miles up to the junction where a very rough road goes in a short distance to Hacking Lake, but we continue up another mile to the Leidy Peak Highline Trailhead.

Along the way we see where the HIGHLINE TRAIL leaves the road and heads down from above timberline east through 26 miles of forest to reach the end of the trail we have seen near U.S. 191 close to Flaming Gorge. And there's another Trailhead that goes down to Browne Lake--do you recall? -- Where we saw the trail marked going to Leidy Peak, with the Peak in the distance. So we are getting around.

Below we are looking at the trail coming 76 miles from the Highline Trailhead on the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway.

p. 103

And, here is Leidy Peak, 12,028 ft. high, taken from timberline, the confers gradually thinning out, at 11,000 ft. with the Highline Trail heading west.

A short hike up the trail towards Leidy Peak, revealed that Fall the following fascinating mushrooms. At other times of the season it would be incredible wildflowers, or other kinds of mushrooms.

Some of them reminded me of marshmallows toasted in our campfire--but be careful as about 25% of mushrooms are deadly poisonous. Best not risk it, unless you are an expert and are sure what you're doing. See pages 396-402 for an article on Mushrooms. At the parking lot we take a short walk 50 yards south through the trees and look east at the 26 miles of forest to the eastern end of the Highline trail.

p. 104

From the same spot we swing a just a little to the south and get a heavenly view of Hacking Lake, and feel more than grateful for having made an 18 mile round trip to be inspired by these--and many other VISIONS OF NATURE! If you want to fish, you can catch cutthroat, rainbow and/or tiger trout.

We are now backtracking to the RED CLOUD LOOP and pass a sign indicating a trail back down to Browne Lake, in relation to the Carter Military Road we learned about there.

We are traveling along the North Fork of Ashley Creek, and now find ourselves officially on the High Uinta's SOUTH SLOPE, as Ashley Creek flows down through the Uintah Basin and into the Green River.

Here again we are grateful to find our Division of Wildlife Resources (DWR) working for us, and from a display seen below, we learn about the wonderful native cutthroat trout that we can catch in the stream that is being enhanced to help the trout.

p. 105

Sorry I can't enlarge the display more so you can read it--you'll just HAVE TO TAKE THE TOUR and ENHANCE YOUR LIFE!

What the heck, here at least is a somewhat enlarged shot at least showing the headlines.

We are now back to the RED CLOUD LOOP SCENIC BACKWAY, and turn south as does the North Fork of Ashley Creek, and soon we will be on another fork of Ashley Creek

p. 106

Keep your eyes open as you proceed, as on my last exploratory trip here I came around a turn to see dashing across the road ahead of me a bobcat. Of course he was gone by the time I could screech to a halt and grab my camera. But for those who might not be familiar with this beautiful animal, here's a picture…… 35 and next a bit of interesting history.

It reminded me of my youth when I worked as a hunter and trapper on a wildlife research project for the University of Utah at Dugway Proving Grounds in 1954-55. On one of my field trips I got a bobcat and as I was skinning him the hind quarters looked pretty good. I recalled reading in one of our reference books--from which we had to learn the scientific names of the 40 mammals we were dealing with, that the mountain men and Indians considered bobcat meat a delicacy. So I carefully prepared it with spices and cooked it in an autoclave we had in our laboratory, then passed out slices on paper plates for my companions, including some G.I's from Brooklyn. Everyone raved over the meat and thanked me, until one of the G.I's asked me what kind of animal it was. I was pretty dumb back then, and so didn't hesitate to tell the Jewish G.I's that it was bobcat--which had them going berserk and wanting to execute me on the spot as they had eaten a prohibited, unclean animal and were doomed forever! We soon come to the South Fork of Ashley Creek, and pull off at a display area with a restroom, and learn more about the efforts of the DWR.

35

Image of bobcat: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobcat

p. 107

Wow! What a beautiful spot to do a little fishing and stay the night. I'll insert the display large enough to arouse your curiosity--and hope you'll TAKE THE TOUR to actually be able to read all about the area and what is being done with our tax dollars.

We continue to drive through dense forests, now in the Lodge pole belt with them growing as thick as weeds, and see efforts to thin them out, get something of commercial value, and eventually have a more productive forest. Soon we begin a steep descent down into Dry Fork Canyon............and all of a sudden are in a different, quite hot, world……..

……… seeing more Forest Service displays--interestingly one about another FLUME--but this one designed with the hope of it bringing more effectively water to the farms and ranches below.

p. 108

You can learn all about these pioneering efforts, and even take a hike to view up close some of the history. You'll also notice a great change in the temperature--now down into a more desert-like environment, with corresponding scenery.

Eventually we get down out of the steep canyon where it widens into ranching country from where we look back up from where we had come.

There's one more display you can pull out and see, reading about a flag we see way up above the ranching country -- that makes a pretty picture to end our RED CLOUD LOOP SCENIC BACKWAY.

p. 109

Shortly we are in Vernal passing 2500 West which is the Taylor Mountain access road taking one up to where we have been for the last 66 miles.

ODOMETER: At end of the Red Cloud Loop in west Vernal, distance including round trip to Leidy Peak = 66 miles, our TOTAL = 448 miles. I now suggest, before continuing back up into the Uintas, driving to downtown Vernal and, at a very special MUSEUM, meet some of the magnificent creatures that roamed the Uinta Mountains over its millions of years of history--address: 496 E. Main St., Vernal

NOTE: There is also the very worthwhile, UINTA COUNTY HERITAGE MUSEUM, 300 E. 200 So., Vernal, Tel. 435-789-7399.36

CONTINUING THE SOUTH SLOPE SCENIC BACKWAY BEGINNING WITH THE ELKHORN LOOP & WHITEROCKS DRAINAGE ODOMETER: After running around Vernal, we continue with the SOUTH SLOPE SCENIC BACKWAY=66 miles, and a TOTAL of 454.

FOR THOSE WHO DON'T WANT TO LEAVE THE PAVEMENT NOTE: You'll have to follow U.S. 40 to Roosevelt, then up UT-121 to Neola, then CR-17 to see the Uinta Canyon. 36

https://www.tripadvisor.com/Attraction_Review-g57155-d536172-Reviews-Western_Heritage_MuseumVernal_Utah.html

p. 110

NOTE: For each area mentioned check out its description, with pictures, in the "Adventurous" South Slope Scenic Backway tour……. taking note of what I suggest for each area. Then from the Uinta River Canyon back down to U.S. 40 and to Duchesne, then up UT-87 and continue to Mountain Home, and from there on to the Moon Lake area where you'll see a resort with store, cabins and boats for rent, and of course Forest Service Campgrounds, plus the Lake Fork Trailhead giving access to many alpine areas. From there return to Mountain Home--with store, gas station and Bed & Breakfast, and take the road that goes west and northwest to the Rock Creek Area and the Stillwater Reservoir where there is also a resort with store, cabins for rent, and Campgrounds. Then return to Mt. Home, and on CR-87 back towards Duchesne--stopping for sure at PINN WILLIES--store & museum, but then further down the road turn off on UT-35 to visit Tabiona, Hanna, the North Fork of the Duchesne River to Defa's Dude Ranch. Then return to UT-35 and drive up over Wolf Creek Pass, Woodland, Francis and back to the starting point at Kamas. Make sure and read all the historical descriptions of the Adventure Tour. From there you can follow the instructions that will be given to all to drive north to Oakley and up the Weber Canyon, visiting the areas that will be suggested, then back to Oakley, and on to Coalville, where I suggest the tour end by visiting the Court House, meeting NaVee and the unique Museum in the basement she put together, which will end the Auto Loop Tour of the Uinta Mountains.

FOR THE REST OF US on what I'm calling unofficially

"THE SOUTH SLOPE SCENIC BACKWAY" We've done the RED CLOUD LOOP and now our destination is the WHITEROCKS RIVER DRAINAGE going first west to the town of Whiterocks. From downtown Vernal we get on 500 North and go west, it soon becomes State Road UT-121. It will continue west until the turn-off to Whiterocks--on the "Whiterocks Highway" taking you through the community (25.5 miles)--on the Ute Reservation, and continue north on the Whiterocks Hwy……….as you see on the map.

Map from

UTAH ROAD & RECREATION ATLAS, Benchmark Maps 2012

p. 111

It becomes the Farm Creek Road that turns north, then back to the east, then north to the Elkhorn Guard Station, where you will see a sign turning left onto a well graded dirt/gravel road, which is the ELKHORN LOOP RD. as you see on the map.

This road is Forest Road FR-117 that takes you up into the Whiterocks River Drainage of the Uinta Mountains. Let's insert here a simple map of where we are going from Whiterocks to the Uinta River. Map by GOOGLE EARTH MAP with labels by author

©2018 Google LLC, used with permission. Google and the Google logo are registered trademarks of Google LLC. Highlights, new routes and labels by author

p. 112

As you climb up out of the Uintah Basin, you will see a nice display well worth your time, concerning the ever present danger of forest fires and its effect on the environment. You will later see in person areas devastated by fires and how they are recovering.

As you see on the map, we will at one point leave the Elkhorn Loop Road, and continue up to Chepeta Lake, but then return to continue on the Loop until getting to the Uinta River Canyon. We soon get up into the forest and are warned about the TIMBER OPERATIONS….so be careful always.

We again are on a wonderful road that will take us right up to near timberline at Chepeta Lake, where once again we cross the Highline Trail. At 14.2 miles after leaving the pavement, we come to a junction where the ELKHORN LOOP ROAD turns west to Pole Creek. Here we will take the important side-trip up into the high country at Chepeta Lake. After our side-trip we will return to the Elkhorn Loop Road, but we've got to see the high country in this wonderful drainage which is east of the Wilderness Area but with important Wilderness trails.

Five miles further we come to the sign to the West Fork Trailhead, the picture below actually taken when I was coming down.

p. 113

We drive .6 of a mile in to the Trailhead, which is a very nice one—the nicest in the Whiterocks Drainage, with extensive corrals for horses used a lot in this area.

In Chapter 4 on the Eastern Uintas I'll tell in the Preface my "John Wayne look-alike" experience in climbing from here Queant Fox Pass that is right on the eastern edge of the Wilderness Area and the Uinta River Drainage.

Over the next 6.8 miles we pass several trail markers I'll insert below, including where the Highline Trail continues to the east after leaving the trailhead that is up the road on the west side and called the CHEPETA TRAILHEAD, .3 of a mile down from the lake--I'll insert a picture of the Trailhead before showing the lake.

p. 114

In Chapter 4 on the Eastern Uintas, I will give details of all the lakes that can be accessed from the Trailheads, and trail signs we have seen, but for now it's getting dark and I wanted to get to CHEPETA LAKE for a photo or two and camp out, so we'll move .3 miles up to the parking lot at Chepeta Lake. I was too late for a picture of the lake, but as the next day dawns I got a beautiful shot of the sunrise.

As you can see, Chepeta Lake was also enlarged with a dike raising the level and making it more useful for the Uintah Basin below. To the left of the mountain in the middle of the picture is 11,360 ft. Fox Queant Pass, and to the right 12,226 ft. North Pole Pass.

p. 115

ODOMETER: When ready to leave Vernal for the 2nd segment of the SOUTH SLOPE SCENIC BACKWAY we were at a TOTAL of 454 miles. From Vernal through Whiterocks and to the Elkhorn Loop turn-off, we traveled another 36.2 miles, and up to Chepeta Lake, 26.2 miles, for a TOTAL of 516 miles. The SOUTH SLOPE SCENIC BACKWAY total beginning at the RED CLOUD LOOP--to Vernal & to here, is 128 miles Early, a mule deer doe is cleaning up one of the camps near the lake, while the campers snooze.

From Chepeta Lake there are a number of good alpine lakes that will only require short hikes, as we see below:

p. 116

We head down the canyon and cross the headwaters of the Whiterocks River, and wave to an early rising fly fisherman getting ready to give it a try. It's pleasing to see at every access point to meadows in this high country, signs that prohibit ATV's.

I screech to a halt for a brief photo-shoot with a colony of yellow bellied marmots.

And take one more admiring scan of the high country to the north.

Then head slowly down FR-110, impressed often by the healthy forests, recalling that yesterday, as the shadows were long and deep approaching Chepeta Lake, I was lucky to see

p. 117

elk on the road ahead of me, but wasn’t able to get any photos. But this morning I once in a while eased to a stop to photograph a deer, and then find another new wildflower.

We've soon passed the West Fork of Whiterocks River, noting that we should be going slow enough to even stop and fish--which few do, making such streams almost virgin. Then we pass by the entrance to the West Fork Trailhead, and continue to the junction with FR-177 and the ELKHORN LOOP, and turn west soon driving past the very nice Poll Creek Campground with the lake down through the forest to the south. We have now come about 12 miles from Chepeta Lake, and are on a narrow Forest Service road, so take extra caution-even though I saw no other vehicle, as we very soon begin dropping down to the west through a vast forest fire area.

It's not visible in the above photo, but tiny pine trees have already been planted in this area. As we proceed we get into deep canyons where such reforestation is not so easy, but much of the area of the fire was in areas of Quaking Aspen as seen on the right on the next page in a small section untouched, but in the middle and on the left a lot of forest was burned, but look what is happening--all that green vegetation in the middle photo is the QUEEN OF UTAH'S TREES--THE QUAKING ASPEN that is propagated by the root system that usually survives forest fires and is the first living thing to take over and protect the area from erosion, and gives life to flowers and wildlife.

p. 118

We soon begin our descent into the Uinta Canyon, and come to the junction with the pavement. From that point we'll drive up the canyon 3.5 miles (part of it gravel) to see the Uinta Canyon Trailhead, and then take a walk to view what was once for me the greatest resort--THE U-BAR WILDERNESS RANCH, which has been closed for many years since a flash flood roared down the mountain and cut it off from road travel and the Forest Service determined it dangerous to continue. I'll tell you a little of my history with it on page 119, and in Chapter 2, Section 16, page 285, as one of my very real PLACES OF REST & REFUGE.

This is one of the truly GREAT TRAILHEADS with trails leading you through great areas in the very large Uinta River Drainage, and then to the east on the Highline Trail over North

p. 119

Pole Pass to the Whiterocks Drainage, on to Leidy Peak and to the end of the Highline Trail near Flaming Gorge; to the northeast over Divide Pass and on to the Spirit Lake area; to the northwest over Gunsight Pass to the Henrys Fork and the North Slope; and to the west on the Highline Trail to Anderson Pass and King's Peak then following the spine of the Uintas all the way to the Trailhead at Hayden's Pass and the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway.

I think of it as a FINISH LINE of what for me were gigantic adventurous efforts. First, in 1954 when my original and still--Uinta buddies, Ted Packard, and Charlie Peterson, and me took two weeks to backpack the entire HIGH UINTAS PRIMITIVE AREA, a picture of us below at the Uinta Canyon Trailhead.

Second, in 2003 on my 206 mile no-resupply "expedition," that started my High Uintas Wilderness Project, the U-Bar Wilderness Ranch became an incredible "finish line," with Jan preparing me a "lunch for a King," of tuna fish sandwiches, green Jello and soda pop. Then a warm shower, and rest in the Rainbow Cabin! Wow, how wonderful it was!

How I've missed it since. Maybe one of you can talk the Forest Service into letting you take over, reconditioning the lodge, cabins, laundry/shower cabin, and horse facilities for taking people on pack trips up in the high country! I promise you I'll be a grateful customer. Read on pages 285-287 my article, with photos, of The Ghost of the U-Bar Wilderness Ranch.

THE "DRY GULCH" segment of the SOUTH SLOPE SCENIC BACKWAY We are now down the canyon 3.5 miles past where the Elkhorn Loop comes from the east, and driven 4 miles more to where the pavement turns left, but we make a sharp turn to the

p. 120

right and begin switch backing our way out of the canyon on the DRY GULCH ROAD. Let's do the mileage thing here before proceeding.

ODOMETER: From Chepeta Lake we have driven 25 miles to the pavement in the Uinta River Canyon, a TOTAL of 51 miles for the Whiterocks Drainage. Then to the Uinta River Trailhead and back, plus 4 more miles down the canyon to begin our 3rd segment for a TOTAL of 553 miles. The SOUTH SLOPE SCENIC BACKWAY total is 165 miles

A FRANK WORD OF CAUTION I'm determined to actually create the SOUTH SLOPE SCENIC BACKWAY, keeping us as close to the Uintas as is possible, such as was done on the North Slope. So I had to connect the Uinta River Canyon to the next drainage which is the DRY GULCH DRAINAGE-the smallest in the Uintas, and then YELLOWSTONE CANYON. To do so we have to traverse Ute Indian Reservation lands--that we are permitted to do, but warned to not leave the road, and not park or run the risk of having your vehicle towed--although I don't know by whom as in several trips over this road I've never seen another human being! It is a hot dry area more like a desert than anything else--which area provides little reason for good maintenance. So, we have ahead of us 10 miles or so of quite rough roads, with some stretches that would be tough during heavy rains. So, don't tell me one day I didn't warn you. At 10.1 miles we come again to Forest Service lands and FR-119 for 8 miles before coming to a much better road in Yellowstone Canyon. THE OTHER OPTION, would be to drive down to Roosevelt, then on U.S. 40 to Duchesne, then back up to Moon Lake, then Rock Creek, as I suggest for those who didn't want to leave the pavement. Here goes and it doesn't seem so bad, but it gets worse!

This is Route 10-BIA (Bureau of Indian Affairs) that switch backs up out of the Uinta Canyon, then heads west through quite barren country. 10 MPH is about as good as you can do for the 10 mile stretch. You won't likely see another human being. At 10.1 miles we gratefully come to a cattle guard leaving the reservation and are on FR-119, right at the point where FR-122 heads north up Dry Gulch Creek where there is--at road's end, according to one map a TRAILHEAD with trails to the Wilderness Area.

p. 121

As we drive the 7 miles back to a better road I will mention especially my cherished experiences in the drainage at CROW BASIN, but along with those experiences I've always wanted to check out this canyon, but I won't recommend it to anyone. Follows a few photos of my experience.

The first stretch on the left below is where I got stopped a few years ago as it was raining a lot and then a quagmire, but dry this time. A couple of miles up there was a continual chain of beaver dams in the creek. I had to go slow to avoid the large boulders, and it got worse as I continued, then I came to a Forest Service sign--which seemed to be a warning of some kind, but so weathered and rotted away it was hard to decipher.

At a bit over 4 miles I came to a gate that was locked, at which point there was a pickup and a camp, but no one around. No designation as a trailhead, even though the Forest Service Wilderness Map does indicate "TH." There were no signs saying where the trail led, but I knew it was the Lowline Trail beginning in the Uinta Canyon, swinging by this point and continuing to Heller Lake. Another to the Lily Pad Lakes, and then descending into Crow Basin--but very little used. The National Geographic High Uintas Wilderness Map doesn't designate this as a Trailhead, showing only a single trail ending at Heller Lake.

p. 122

We're now back on the main Dry Gulch Road, FR-119. NOTE: I won't include in our mileage totals the 8+ miles of that little side trip. We continue west about 3 miles and come to FR120--that becomes an extremely rough jeep road leading 4 miles north way up the mountain to barriers from which the trail goes to Jackson Park, and on to the Timothy Lakes area in the Swift Creek Drainage. Jackson Park is a vast green meadow and the jump off place to literally descend into Crow Basin. This is another of those areas never to be forgotten with high adventures and the most amazing outdoor experience of my life--which I'll share with photographs in Chapter 2, Section 17 on the Crow Basin, pages 308-318.

I was aided on my 3rd (successful) try by a High Uinta Friend, Jonathan Jausi, who took aerial photographs and gave me a set, that helped me finally get down into Crow Basin--like a box canyon, from beautiful Jackson park you barely see on the left in the aerial photo above. I'll use these spectacular photographs further along in the book but insert one of Jackson Park below.

p. 123

We continue another 3 miles and descend into Yellowstone Canyon, and at the sign you see below, turn right to drive 4 miles up to the Swift Creek Trailhead where there are some invaluable historical Displays we shouldn't miss. As we begin to descend into Yellowstone Canyon, we see this wonderful Uinta scene.

After switch backing down, we come to a well graded gravel road and turn north to drive around 4 miles to the Swift Creek Trailhead in Yellowstone Canyon.

Here we find ourselves in another of the pristine and remote areas of the Uintas, with the convergence of two important streams, Yellowstone and Swift Creeks, with major trails going up each into alpine areas second to none, with several dozen alpine lakes to explore and fish. Much more will be said in Chapter 2, Section 18.

p. 124

As is the case from almost all the trailheads, beautiful, unforgettable destinations await you like my wonderful time at Milk Lake--the day ending with the following breathtaking sunset.

Followed that night at my stealth camp by literally being surrounded by a herd of elk. Of great importance the Forest Service has some crucial displays, a taste of which you can see below--each of them important to be able to understand the past and the present of the Uintas. Don't miss them, and help your children understand.

We now turn back and head down Yellowstone Canyon, and soon cross a bridge over what was a creek, but now called the Yellowstone River, and from there climb up out of the canyon. We get a nice view down below of a ranch or two and cabins--which spot years ago attracted me to hope one day to have there the "cabin" I dreamed about as a child reading books about the mountain men and explorers of the west..

p. 125

HELLS CANYON & THE CENTER PARK TRAILHEAD We then come to a sign--the view below taken from the west side, of our next suggested side-trip--10 miles up Hells Canyon to the Center Park Trailhead--one of the highest in the Uintas at 10,400 ft. on one of the ridges coming off the spine of the Uintas.

As we approach the Trailhead we see beautiful meadows where healthy cattle are grazing, and see fences made years ago with the abundance of the forest--and gaze way down below through the trees of similar fences made in pioneer times, now deteriorating.

Soon we come to the high country Trailhead that is on the ridge that leads up to Swasey Hole Basin, and then higher to the above timberline Garfield Basin where I had a couple of revealing survival experiences I'll tell in Chapter 2, Section 19, p. 332 & Section 20, p. 343. Up the trail on a saddle, that should be named a 11,000+ ft. pass, you see me doing my darndest--during said Survival at Swasey Hole experience --to build up my resolve to save myself reading about "Cortez Collects Fresh Strength" from Bernal Diaz' book about the CONQUEST OF MEXICO,37 with a magnificent view of the spine of the Uintas taking in 180 degrees of my view, enlarged below.

37

CONQUEST OF MEXICO, by Bernal Diaz

p. 126

We are now back down on the Yellowstone Canyon road, working our way towards the pavement we meet after crossing the Lake Fork River. To the South, Mt. Home, to the north Moon Lake which will be our next destination.

ODOMETER: From Uinta Canyon, through Dry Gulch (18), Yellowstone Canyon to Trailhead (4), then to Hells Canyon junction (7), to Center Park Trailhead & back (20), then to the pavement turning towards Moon Lake (7), a TOTAL of 56 miles Uinta Canyon to here. TOTAL of 619 miles. The SOUTH SLOPE SCENIC BACKWAY total is 221 miles We turn right and head north towards Moon Lake, the Resort, and the Lake Fork Trailhead. Seen below.

Trails from here lead way up the Lake Fork to the Highline Trail, and another up to the Brown Duck Basin and beyond, all of which will be described with important details in

Chapter 2, Section 20. There are great Campgrounds here, and also:

"OUT OF THIS WORLD Moon Lake Resort BUT STILL IN UTAH" With everything you might want or need--shown below, owned by Bill & Julie Reardon

www.moonlakeresort.com

p. 127

The cabins are luxurious compared to what we usually think about as a "cabin" -- they have gas heaters, refrigerators, hot and cold water, etc. but you do have to provide your bedding.38 We'll now head back down the canyon, pass the turn-off road to Yellowstone Canyon, and continue on to a junction at Mountain Home, where we are welcomed by the following:

THE MOUNTAIN HOME INN & STORE: FUEL -- STORE -- BED & BREAKFAST

39

We note that this place is up for sale, right in the middle of the Uintah Basin, and one of the Gateways to the Uintas. Tel. 801-706-9941

Go to the website for up-to-date information and prices. There are comfortable beds, TV and anything you might need in the store.

PINN WILLIES Before proceeding to the Rock Creek Area, there is an interesting place to see down the road towards Duchesne 6.6 miles, which is a small restaurant, store & museum, owned by Larry Peck since the beginning 30 years ago.

38

www.moonlakeresort.com ; Facebook: Moon Lake Resort; Tel. 435-454-3142

39

See: www.mountainhomeinnutah.com

p. 128

Inside and outside he has accumulated a lifetime of artifacts that are interesting to see. So, once again another real MUSEUM, including a wooden artificial leg his daughter once found in a tree! As we drive back to the junction at the Mountain Home Inn & Store, we are welcomed by another Gateway sign to the High Uintas.

At the junction we turn left--west and head for the ROCK CREEK AREA.

Once again we are passing through lands of the Uintah and Ouray Indian Reservation so make sure and obey the signs. Eventually we leave Indian lands and enter the Forest again, paralleling Rock Creek as we continue northwest up into the Uintas with plenty of spots to picnic, fish the stream and camp.

Twenty-two miles from Mt. Home we pull into the ROCK CREEK RANCH, meeting at the Lodge Brenda Karren, the owner, and get information on cabin rental and other services available and get a cold Mountain Dew.

p. 129

In addition to cabins, there are available modern units that include Satellite TV, microwave, fridge with bedding/linen provided.40. Right in front of the entrance to the Rock Creek Ranch resort, there is a Forest Service building with a visitors Center, but it was closed on my last trip so I don't know what to expect, but you should check it out.

Up the road a mile we come to the dam, multiple displays that explain how water is taken out of this dam, going underground to the Current Creek Reservoir, and from there to Strawberry Reservoir, all part of the Central Utah Project. See Appendix 11.

40

For information call: 435-3332

p. 130

I'll insert below a map of the area, and multiple faceted outdoor opportunities available.

A little further west we come to the Rock Creek Trailhead in a beautiful mountain setting. We are now in the area that was one of the jump off places for those searching for the Lost Rhoades, and Spanish gold mines, as well as Aztec treasure caves. I'll tell some of those stories later in Chapters 2 & 3, including quoting the directions of how to find them with the hope of becoming the richest man, or woman in the world.

THE SOUTH FORK OF ROCK CREEK & THE BLIND STREAM CORKSCREW ROAD This is the mountain we have to now climb.

p. 131

WARNING: If the weather is REAL bad with a lot of rain, and you don't have a 4WD vehicle, best not proceed as the road in spots gets a little muddy, rather go 25 miles back down to Mt. Home, then get on UT-87 to Duchesne, turning off on UT-35 to Tabiona and Hanna--a drive of about 63 miles, rather than the 17 on the Blind Stream Road. If the weather is not too bad, any car with a good driver can do it fine. A little rain won't be a problem. It is a spectacular drive, 3 miles up what I'm calling a "corkscrew road," of switchback after switchback after switchback. I've driven down it 4 times and it is breathtaking. Driving up it might be a different experience--just be careful. I'll insert below a GOOGLE EARTH view of it. I recall counting 17 switchbacks.

©2018 Google LLC, used with permission. Google and the Google logo are registered trademarks of Google LLC. Highlights, new routes and labels by author

Where the Google Earth view ends, above, is the 10,300 ft. Blind Stream Pass. Then downhill to Hanna. To get there from Rock Creek we drive for a couple of miles along the South Fork of Rock Creek, and then come to a junction where the fun begins.

p. 132

NOTE: The road going straight away is to Arta Lake, 3-4 miles up the canyon, and from the end of the road a short hike to Arta Lake, and a bit more to Survey Lake, but the importance is that from there you bushwhack up to the East Grandaddy Saddle--and, as you're coming to it a scene opens up that boggles the mind it is so overwhelmingly stunning--of Grandaddy Lake and Basin, with Mt. Agassiz and Hayden Peak in the distance. WOW! The first backpack after 35 years in Guatemala--then beginning my HIGH UINTAS WILDERNESS PROJECT, was to that spot, the first picture in my PREFACE taken on that trip, and then one with my buddy, Ted Packard, inserted is used again on page 13 of the INTRODUCTION, and page 142, and elsewhere. This is a take-off spot worth remembering when you're ready to go backpacking. Back to the task at hand. Up we go, and up, and up. I'll insert a panel of a couple of three views during the corkscrew climb--although the pictures are all going down.

We now approach Blind Stream Pass, 10,300 ft.

From the pass we drop down quickly but should be careful on the narrow road, as those in the know use this shortcut to Rock Creek--so others could be on the road. We should also keep a sharp eye out for elk herds which I have jumped on this road--motivating me to go elk hunting here once--so maybe time for a………

I was unsuccessful for elk, but it is the only place in the wilds where I have actually seen a cougar, and I came close to shooting an ATV! -- Maybe I'd best explain: It was after struggling for two days backpacking way up on the mountain only to find--as I sneaked carefully up to the top of a ridge to get a shot at a giant elk--rather found

p. 133

an ATV parked there--like laughing at me, saying, "No problem getting to the top of the mountain!" For an instant I was so angry that I thought……jokingly about shooting it! But, then I thought, "You know, I bet that ATV hunter, never saw a cougar, and never heard during a moonlit night under the stars the howling of a pack of coyotes, nor a whole bunch of other things my closeness to nature experienced,"--so I made a big effort to conger up a feeling of pity and I forgave him and didn't pull the trigger!

Soon we are down to the pavement seeing the sign pointing up from where we had come, and then head east for a couple of miles enjoying the agriculture of Hanna

Most who come into this area have on their minds, "GOING TO THE GRANDADDIES" -- an alpine basin in the High Uintas accessed from here, and don't know we are now in the area known 100 years ago as:

"LITTLE ITALY" We'll soon help you appreciate what it once was--as it makes going through this area much more interesting, but let's first move 5 miles further east from where we planned on getting some refreshment at Hanna's Country Store, and come into the area properly at its gateway:

p. 134

THE GATEWAY TO THE GRANDADDY LAKES

It is the community of Tabiona, 5 miles down UT-35 from the Hanna COUNTRY STORE which was really what was on our mind--to get some refreshment. Tabiona is a quite complete community--the 2010 census saying the population was only 171, but surrounded by ranches, with a school that has all the grades--kindergarten thru 12th grade, an LDS Chapel, and more, including out on the highway a café and minimart, called the SAGEBRUSH INN, with rooms to rent, where we can eat a nice meal, and say hi to owner, Charlie Strebel--and shoot the breeze about the interesting history of the area. For information you can call Charlie at 435-848-5637.

Tabby Mountain is guarding the community to the southwest seen in the middle picture, it and the community bearing the name of a famous Uintah White River Ute chief, Tabby--we'll

p. 135

see his picture when we backtrack to Hanna, and among other things, visit a unique museum. Now we're back to Hanna and the COUNTRY STORE where we traditionally go for refreshment after coming out of the GRANDADDIES--and if you need gasoline, they’ve got it too

Across the street is the Café with rooms for rent, and the Lounge. Looks like a popular place for the bikers too. NOTE: But, please be careful guys and gals as just yesterday, July

19, 2018, 3 bikers lost their lives near here in an accident

As was the case with the COUNTRY STORE, the Café & Lounge originally was created by legendary folk hero, Frank Defa--we will meet in just a moment. The Country Store is still owned by the Defa family, but the Café & Lounge is now under new ownership since June 2018, and a new name, THE HANNA HILTON CAFÉ & BAR. I just met the new owners, Timmy & Brandy Giles, we see below, who served us delicious lunches, very much appreciated after a three day backpack into the Grandaddies.

p. 136

You see my two buddies above, Ted Packard on the right checking out his son, Mike, getting kicked out of the Hanna Hilton Bar, for being under age! Hey, I’m joking!

NOW TO FRANK DEFA & LITTLE ITALY We pronounce DEFA -- "Dee-fay" and I will now fill you in on Frank Defa, whose original name was, Francisco Di Fabrizio. Sounds Italian, right? Here's the fascinating story.

When starting my HIGH UINTAS WILDERNESS PROJECT in 2003, I had known about the Defa's Dude Ranch since 1952, but decided I had to begin learning details, so in 2003 me and my boys, Jesse and Nephi, decided we'd rent one of their cabins for a night and the next morning go on a day hike from the Grandview Trailhead to Grandaddy Lake, fish a little and then make it back to the car doing like 8 miles. So, at the Saloon we signed up for a night and, noticing some historical items framed on the walls about Frank Defa, I got talking to the bartender asking questions. His response, "Oh, so you want to know about the history? -- Here's a personal handwritten journal by Charley D. Fabrizio." I thumbed through the pages, fascinated by some of what I was seeing and asked if I could borrow it over night. We headed for our cabin with that journal, and since we were ambushed by learning no bedding was provided and we didn't have sleeping bags, we had a problem. Soon the coolness of the night had us frantically putting on whatever extra clothes we could find in the car, and wrapping ourselves in our ponchos. It didn't work well for me, so I stayed up all night reading the journal and taking notes. Years afterwards I tried to find it again but failed. But, another few years sped by and in 2015 I learned on another investigatory trip that the journal had been added to and published and I spent an entire morning at the saloon photographing every page, along with newspaper articles about "folk hero" Frank Defa, the legendary "King" of the clan. Here's a brief summary of what I learned.41 41

CHARLIE: The Legacy o Charlie D & Rosie Defa Fabrizio, by Tom Fabrizio Odgen, Agreka Books, 800-360-5284, www.historypreserved.com

p. 137

Charlie was Pasquale Pasqualetti, an orphaned child in Italy taken in by Angela Di Fabrizio, but he was eventually abandoned, and at 16 somehow made his way to the U.S., struggled to survive, finally making it to Magna, Utah. Over the years he survived from there to Sunny Side's coal mines, to mines in Colorado, then back to Magna and due to hard work bought a house, and eventually married Rosie Di Fabrizio from Hanna, and with her influence they soon moved to Hanna. Rosie was the daughter of Francisco Di Fabrizio born in Italy in 1880 who had migrated to the U.S. at 12, struggled to survive polishing shoes, and selling the Salt Lake Tribune in Salt Lake, and much more, and along with others from Italy attracted to Hanna when in 1903 Reservation lands were opened to Homesteading (that, by the way is explained at the Forest Service displays at the Swift Creek Trailhead in Yellowstone Canyon.) In 2005, at the confluence of West and North Duchesne Rivers, he built a cabin and turned it into a saloon which soon evolved into a community prospecting for gold, which story I'll tell later, calling it, "A FAKE GOLD RUSH at STOCKMORE." Later, Frank returned to Italy and was drafted into the military and was an interpreter, earning tips and accumulated enough to after the war tour Europe and the Middle East, eventually returning to the U.S. penniless, but with a wife, Maria, and knowing 4 languages, and went to work. The Italians modified their names in the U.S. Pasquale Pasqualetti became Charlie D. Frabrizio; Francisco Di Fabrizio became Frank Defa whose wife, Maria of course became Mary. They had children, Joe, Rosa (Rosie), Leo, Alfonso and Tracy--who we will meet born December 6, 1919. Charlie married Rosie--the book about their legacy. There were other Italian families, some relatives of the above two men, and others unrelated who migrated to the area, all leading to it at one time being called "LITTLE ITALY." About legendary folk hero, Frank Defa, the Salt Lake Tribune on December 12, 1948 said:

p. 138

"Did you ever hear of Frank Defa? He makes the sweetest mountain dew in 17 counties. He homesteaded some of Utah's wildest country. He piled up a fortune in what still is considered a wilderness. He's Utah's shrewdest backwoods 42 businessman."

After homesteading he went into business buying wild horses from the Indians for $5 each, and sold them for $10, accumulating $8,000 which he invested in stores, lumber mills, etc. and his dance hall during prohibition was known as the "rip-roaringest dance hall west of Denver." He distilled his own "white lightning" whiskey and many credited him for saving their lives with it during the Spanish Flu epidemic of 1918-19. He was eventually caught and put out of business as a bootlegger, his sentence being exile from Duchesne County for 18 months, afterwards returning to his businesses that have survived until today:43 Frank passed on in 1952. The Country Store, and Defa's Dude Ranch, thereafter was run by Frank's son Alfonso, and then a grandson, Geno, who passed on in 2010, now run by Geno's children.44 NOTE: At the Country Store I was once approached by a woman telling me in a hushed voice, glancing around nervously to make sure someone wasn't listening, that on her ranch she had some secret evidence about Frank's life as a bootlegger, which information scared the heck out of me--so much that I can't reveal it…..yet.

RIGHT NEXT TO THE COUNTRY STORE….

……..A MUST SEE MUSEUM -- if it is still available to the public

A few years ago, in 2013, I went to see if a tour was available, and knocked on the door. Tracy Roberts answered, then 93 years old and using a walker, and agreed to open up the museum for me. Tracy Defa Roberts, is the last daughter of Frank Defa. Her husband, Lloyd "Snooks" Roberts, passed on in 2012. His autobiography is one of the books, listed in the Reference Section, and will be quoted here and there.

Back to 2013, I was amazed going through this museum, and took many photographs I'll put into a YouTube video of the LOOP AUTO TOUR, connected to my book--which video I hope will be available soon after the publication of the book. My reaction….WOW! I'll add a few pictures below to arouse your interest--in hopes that this unique museum will be still be available to the public. In the entrance was a framed photograph of Chief Tabby, seen below with the enlarged explanation, indicating he died at 117. I have seen elsewhere that he lived to 104.

The museum is made up of many items donated by many people who cooperated with Snooks and Tracy, showing things like: The evolution of washing machines, cream separators, and churners to

p. 140

make butter, and ice cream; Radios, including the first car radios & phonographs from back when there was a horn on top, etc.; Then typewriters, saws, cameras, etc., etc. All taking us on a journey into the past, including the last item seen below on the right Can you imagine what they were? Snooks was a Mormon, but Tracy a devote Catholic. Did she use the "hobbles" to keep Snooks under her control? Come to the museum to learn….a lot.

We now continue our tour, traveling west on UT-35, and 5 miles from the Hanna Country Store and Snooks Antique Museum, come to a junction where County Road CR-144 takes us 5 miles north to Defa's Dude Ranch. Soon after turning onto it and following the North Fork of the Duchesne River, we pass a sign we see below:

Don't forget STOCKMORE -- we will get back to it and a fascinating part of history of the area in just a moment. On the National Forest we see campgrounds, and also many homes on private property, like we see below:

DEFA'S DUDE RANCH - COWBOY CAFÉ & SALOON

The weekends are busy, and evenings, "LIVELY!" closed during the winter.

You can get information at:45

It is

Frank Defa began the development of the "ranch" in 1938 and gradually turned it into what it is today, he himself building the cabins adding another every year. About that beginning, a few years ago I visited the saloon and got talking to some customers about the history. One of them told me that back in those early days "high stakes poker games" in the area were common. He went on, "not in the hundreds, but thousands." He then told me, "the property had been won in a poker game." 46 Other customers agreed. I haven't read that anywhere, but such was in harmony with the colorful history of Frank Defa.

It was on that visit that Mickey, the bartender, provided me with the published family history, CHARLIE….. that had evolved from the hand written journal I had read in 2003, and I spent the entire morning photographing every page of it for my records. 45

p. 142

THE GRANDVIEW TRAILHEAD: The REAL GATEWAY TO THE GRANDADDIES Fifty yards or so past Defa's you come to this sign, from which it is a 6 mile drive up Hades Canyon to the Trailhead.

Back in 1952, when I was introduced to the Uintas, described in the PREFACE, the Trailhead was down here and our hike to the Grandaddies a 10 mile struggle up to Hades Pass, from where you drop into the Grandaddy Basin. Today a 4 mile hike from the Trailhead. I've already told you how the area got its name back around 1906 when famous pioneer artist/photographer, George Beard, coined the name "the grandaddy of them all!" Resulting in the largest lake in the Uintas being named GRANDADDY LAKE, and the area THE GRANDADDY BASIN. See page 26.

Above we see it from the East Grandaddy Mountain saddle, the spot previously mentioned, accessed from the South Fork of Rock Creek.

p. 143

To make the loop tour complete, it might be best to actually drive the 6 miles up impressive Hades Canyon to the Trailhead. It can be done in any car--if you're careful. At about the halfway point we come to what is called THE SPLASH DAM, which until a few years ago had behind the old logs and deteriorating dam structure, a nice lake. But it was washed out in 2011 when there was a very heavy run-off.

The terminology, "splash dam" on the North Slope refers to the temporary dams built by the tie hackers, behind which they would accumulate thousands of ties created during the winter, then with the run-off they would blow the dams with dynamite creating a resultant "SPLASH" washing the ties downriver to be picked up by the railroad in Wyoming. But it didn't make sense for such to have worked in this extremely steep, rough Hades Canyon with at every turn logs jammed across the stream, etc. In email communications with the Forest Service in 2015,47 I was given the history which follows: In 1915 such a plan was devised for Hades Canyon, but the effort was a failure, as none of the logs made it to the bottom of the canyon. -- In 1979 there was a plan to build there a rock fill dam, but never realized, then in 2011 a high run-off moved the last remains of the log crib dam that had created the lake and the lake disappeared. Logs from the original effort can still be seen there, but the lake is mostly gone. Below we see a photo of the lake prior to 2011, and then what it is now, and in the 3rd picture we zoom in on some remains of the crib log dam.48

Seeing the vehicles at the Grandview Trailhead, makes it clear that any vehicle can make it up Hades Canyon--one of the more worthwhile side trips on our tour.

In Chapter 2, Section 22 we will get into all the possibilities in the GRANDADDIES, but you can also watch one of the more important YouTube videos49 I did on this area, showing all 26 lakes in the Basin. We now move back down the canyon, and come to the STOCKMORE JUNCTION

The Junction is in the middle-left, the Stockmore Ranger Station up to the right of the crossroad. At this point the West Fork of the Duchesne River comes in from the left, and joins the North Fork, creating the Duchesne River. That's the setting for our story:

Now THE FAKE GOLD RUSH (HOAX) ON THE DUCHESNE In reviewing the story of Frank Defa, do you recall that in 1905 he built a log cabin in this area and turned it into a saloon? This was when he began making bootleg whiskey. At that time two men came into the area and began buying up land all along the Duchesne River. They were Stockmore and his partner, Moore--both smooth talking con artists. When they were ready they sent a fellow--a prospector who had returned from the Klondike gold rush with a poke full of nuggets, to Park City, Salt Lake City, Provo and Heber and in saloons would make it seem like an accident for some of the nuggets to be seen--that immediately attracted attention. All wanted to know where he had found them. He acted cautious and tight lipped, but after he was bought a couple of drinks he finally blurted out,

"It was near the junction of the North Fork, and West Fork of the Duchesne River!" A rush ensued on the Duchesne, Stockman and More selling land hand over fist, and a tent city sprouted, along with quickly built wood structures: A general store, two hotels, livery stable, blacksmith shops, assay office and 3 more saloons, all around Frank's saloon--the new town was called STOCKMORE. When they were on the verge of electing a mayor, town council and sheriff, the scam became clear as no gold had been found, all discovered by a U.S. Marshall, but by then Stockmore and Moore had escaped with all the money. Reportedly one of them eventually was captured in Montana but escaped federal prison by pretending to be insane. The source of this information is in a book by Eldon Wilcken, who ends the description saying, "So far as my father knew the other man was never found." 50

"The town was torn down by the people who had built it. Many of the buildings were just abandoned and other settlers salvaged what they could for their own use."51

MY EFFORTS TO FIND THE STOCKMORE GHOST TOWN I went to the Stockmore Guard Station, seen above on the Google Earth view, knocked on the door, and then and later never found anyone to answer my questions. I walked all over that area, back and forth, up and down and found no remnants of old log cabins, etc. Then I did more research in Duchesne and learned that the original Forest Service Ranger Station had been built in 1914 on the other side of the highway by the river, and went

50

p. 146

exploring assuming it was close to where the town of Stockmore had been. 52 I found a whole series of old Forest Service buildings we see a few of below.

I learned that in 1999 the site was accepted into the National Registry of Historic Sites, and some efforts were made by the Daughters of the Utah Pioneers to restore and have one of the buildings as a Visitors Center, but nothing has come from any of that. Back at that time of discovery, I searched the entire area, walking back and forth, and fought my way though a tangle of willows and vegetation, and did find a few old remnants that might or might not have been from the Stockmore ghost town. I'll insert a few pictures of them below before we move on.

In the first picture down under the grass there is a log structure, like part of a foundation, but who knows. One day I'll do a bit more exploring in the area, but it is all a fascinating bit of history. Now, let's head up UT-35, but we'd best first catch up on the mileage.

WOLF CREEK PASS We have just returned to UT-35 from our swing up the North Fork of the Duchesne to Defa's and the Grandview Trailhead, and will now head west on the Wolf Creek Scenic Byway--up the last leg of the SOUTH SLOPE SCENIC BACKWAY.

This picture above is a drab introduction--taken in late Fall, of a beautiful drive over the Pass. Below we see it in its true character in the Springtime and early summer.

The bikers and the cyclists all love this gently winding road up to the pass and down.

p. 148

At the pass we leave behind us the South Slope, and bring an end to our SOUTH SLOPE SCENIC BACKWAY, so we'll bring up-to-date our mileage.

ODOMETER: From the junction with UT-35 & Stockmore we have driven 10 miles to here so The SOUTH SLOPE SCENIC BACKWAY total comes to 363 miles. The ENTIRE LOOP TOTAL to this point = 761 miles. We now descend quickly to the northwest. Along the highway there are frequently spots to pull over and stop to admire better the beauty of this area, and down the road a couple of miles you'll see a sign pointing to a short paved road on the left with a point of historic interest memorializing a Japanese aviator who in 1929 was attempting to fly over America, Europe and Asia, but crashed 3000 feet south east of here.

It's best to take advantage of the pullouts, to not miss what's important, not the least of which are the wildflowers. Often just a few steps off the road will reveal an astounding number of truly exotic ones. I should have said this in the beginning, but it would be fun for a family making the tour to see how many varieties of flowers they could see….and maybe photograph. I've showed you a few from the north slope, and here are a few from the South, all from the Wolf Creek Pass area.

p. 149

Best at this point take a glance at a map to see how our route takes us very close to the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway and then to Kamas.

From the pass we drop down 3,000 ft. and soon are traveling along the South Fork of the Provo River, through Woodland, and on to Francis, a rural community with around 1,347 residents. I'll insert below the welcoming sign seen as you come from the west.
