miles

For some this will seem like a great place to end our Loop Tour, but others of you might want to accompany me for two more segments to make it a complete experience.

p. 150

The first, and a major portion of the Western High Uinta Mountains, is the WEBER RIVER DRAINAGE, which includes several Trailheads from which you can hike up into the high country towards the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway. Last of all we have to give its due to SUMMIT COUNTY, which includes almost the entire North Slope of the Uintas, and the county seat, COALVILLE, where in the Courthouse you will find a large framed photograph of "Utah's Greatest Mountain Scene--RED CASTLE." A few years ago I donated it to the County to add to "The Greatest Little Museum in Utah," created by my friend, NaVee Vernon, who we see on the right in the photograph.

NaVee is the Summit County Historian. 53

THE WEBER RIVER DRAINAGE From Kamas we drive north 6 miles on UT-32 to Oakley, and at the junction we see below, turn right to Smith & Morehouse -- Weber Canyon.

As we drive up the canyon, we note that on both sides of the road it is private property with ranches and home construction going on here and there. 53

NaVee Vernon, Summit County Historian, nvernon@summitcounty.org , Tel.(435) 336-3015

p. 151

From Oakley we drive 11.7 miles to the sign we see below, and there turn right. We'll be back to this junction in a bit.

We drive 2.1 miles along a very nice stream, and then come to Smith & Morehouse Reservoir

We drive along Smith & Morehouse Reservoir and note shore fishermen, and others from boats, and recall this is one of the many places where you can now catch arctic grayling. From the dam we drive 2.2 miles and come to the Campground and then the Trailhead, noting that this trail leads up into the high country to places along the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway, like the Crystal Lake Trailhead, etc. In Chapter 3, Sections 7 and 8, I will give more details and include some Historical Notes about gold in the Uintas in this area.

From Oakley we've driven 22 miles to here. We'll now go back down to the Junction, and drive 8.7 miles up to the Gardner Trailhead. There are other minor trailheads, I'll describe in Chapter 3.

p. 152

We have now backtracked 20 miles to Oakley, and will begin our last segment.

COALVILLE & "THE BEST LITTLE MUSEUM IN UTAH" We get back on UT-32, and parallel the course of the Weber River to Rockport Reservoir, with its State Park, and all kinds of camping and recreation facilities. After Rockport we can get on I-80, or continue on UT-32 going through Hoytsville and on to Coalville, 18.4 miles from Oakley, and drive down the main street until coming to the Courthouse--and have finished our driving of the Auto Loop Tour of the Uintas. You will notice in the vicinity of the Courthouse, many displays of historical significance that are all worthwhile, like……this beautiful mural:

But our main interest is to meet NaVee, and see the unique museum she has created. Her MUSEUM can quite easily be missed, so best go in the Courthouse up a couple of floors and find the Historical Director, and she will be more than happy to take you back

p. 153

down a floor to a wide hallway, and on the right you'll see one of the old fashioned drinking fountains next to a door that could be the broom closet under the stairway…….

……. but NO, IT'S THE MUSEUM--down a narrow flight of stairs where you will find the whole basement COMES ALIVE WITH THE PAST. I'll just include a couple of panels of photos giving you a taste--which you'll want to see in real life to be able to appreciate what has been created. I'm sorry that some of the best were out of focus, as that day I only had a tiny point and shoot camera -- so ALONG WITH ALL OF YOU, I'VE GOT TO GO BACK AND SPEND HALF A DAY OR MORE and get good photos for the YouTube video.

You'll notice she has very good typed out historical explanations of everything, so the experience will be enlightening to say the least. After displays that review the Native American past, she goes on to the mountain men and the tie hackers in the Weber River

p. 154

Drainage, and on to logging with intricate models of the sawmills used. Then the pioneer history of the Mormons--showing impeccable rooms just like they were, and the mining industry--from which Coalville got its name. Then real life replicas of scenes from the past, like the soda fountain era, with price list that brings back fond memories for some of us.

And she reviews the two world wars, and honors veterans from the county who gave their lives for freedom.

There's much, much more to see, so don't miss it. Meeting NaVee in 2013, opened up the opportunity of speaking to the Historical Society from Coalville in 2014, which I did without visuals, but I videoed the speech and discussion afterwards that went on for another hour, and then carefully inserted pictures and visuals to show what I was speaking about. So there is a series of YouTube videos54 from that experience you see me in the middle of below which might be a good time to end this Auto

Tour of the High Uinta Mountains. ITS BEEN ONE INCREDIBLE TOUR.

We're now familiarized with the wonderful High Uinta Mountains--as good as, or better than some National Parks. Now it's urgent I focus on getting finished the GUIDE CHAPTERS on hiking, backpacking, horse & goat packing, including the SURVIVAL stories of those who didn't make it, and why, plus my 8 survival experiences and WHY I'm still alive & backpacking in my 84th year. I've been told that some of my internet reporting has already saved lives, and I'm convinced through this sharing many more lives can be saved, and everyone's enjoyment hugely enhanced of our Creators magnificent swath of color and wonderment we call the HIGH UINTA MOUNTAINS! Your TRAIL BUDDY, Cordell M. Andersen

Chapter 2: THE HIGH UINTAS WILDERNESS AREA Section 1: THE HIGHLINE TRAIL--following the spine of the Uintas *****************************

PREFACE ERIC ROBINSON EXPERIENCED MOUNTAIN BACKPACKER: LOST ON HIGHLINE TRAIL --FOR 5 YEARS August 7, 2011 A massive search, led by the Sheriff from Duchesne County, was triggered when Australian backpacker, Eric Robinson, was reported lost in the Uintas.

He had prepared meticulously his 60 mile backpack, even talking to those who had done the hike from Chepeta Lake on the Highline Trail west to the Trailhead at Hayden Pass on the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway. He was an experienced backpacker, and went prepared having posted carefully the route he would follow, had a GPS device, pepper spray for bears, and had his PLB--Personal Locator Beacon in case of emergencies. Sounds great….almost--right? He started on July 28th and was last seen on August 2nd by a group of Boy Scouts in the Yellowstone Creek Drainage, but seemed to be disoriented and had got off course as he was 2 miles south of the Highline Trail when seen. When he didn't arrive at the Trailhead on August 7th, he was reported missing. A massive search centered on the Yellowstone Creek Drainage area, but was eventually abandoned. 55 Jumping ahead 5 years on August 18, 2016, Kelvin Judd and his brother, Kimball, were trying to find a way to climb from Allsop Lake up to the Allsop saddle--at the headwaters of the East Fork of Bear River on the North Slope, when among boulders below perpendicular cliffs, they found scattered pieces of clothing, trekking poles, a red backpack, and a hiking boot with bone fragments inside. Of great importance they found an I.D. for Eric Robinson. 55

http://archive.sltrib.com/story.php?ref=/sltrib/news/52396506-78/robinson-hiker-trail-aug.html.csp

p. 157

Strangely they didn't know about Eric having been lost 5 years before, but they knew they had to report their find--but had no way to do so. The next morning they found in the area the camp of Dan Ransom and told him about their find. Dan was very familiar with the case of Robinson, and with his PLB device advised authorities, and soon Search & Rescue were sent via helicopter by the Sheriff of Summit County, and a thorough search ensued. The speculation since assumes that Robinson corrected his navigational mistake on the Yellowstone, got back up to the Highline Trail and continued west over Tungsten, Porcupine, and Red Knob Passes, taking him to the Deadhorse area at the headwaters of the West Fork of Blacks Fork. From there the Highline Trail climbs difficult north facing Deadhorse Pass, that often in early August still has some snow--and especially in 2011 as it was the heaviest winter in many years. That perhaps had forced Robinson to take the generally unknown (not on any maps), almost invisible mountaineer trail over the mountain to Allsop Lake, 56 and it is assumed that in his descent he slipped above the 40-70 foot high cliffs--upper left in the 2nd photo, to his death below where his remains were found.57

On the left, Allsop Lake seen from the saddle above Reconnaissance Lake. On the right viewing the saddle from Allsop Lake.

I speculate that he perhaps made it to Allsop Lake--but then wanted to return to the Highline Trail--the only way being to climb up to the Allsop saddle, from where the left picture was taken, and from there drop down past Reconnaissance Lake to the Highline Trail to continue his hike, but in so doing, he slipped and fell to his death. Whatever the details the case was closed. 56

Photo courtesy of Doug Perry

57

https://www.deseretnews.com/article/865661209/5-years-later-recovery-of-hikers-remains-provides-peacefor-Australian-family.html https://www.nationalgeographic.com/adventure/destinations/united-states/utah/missing-hiker-remains-foundutah/

p. 158

WHAT WAS THE MISTAKE….OR THE MISTAKES? I have said repeatedly that no one should go alone, unless they take all the precautions I take, which are:

1.) Leave a detailed itinerary where you're going to be each day, A duplicate set of maps showing itinerary left with family or friend, and/or on the internet.

2.) Have a satellite phone to give notice of changes, or emergency needs,,

3.) Have a (PLB) Personal satellite locator device--mine a SPOT TRACKER, and,

4. USE IT DAILY, which sends a reassuring email to 10 friends each time you hit the OK button, with a link that shows exactly where you are each time with Google Earth as seen above. Or, in case of an emergency need, hit the 911 button which shows exactly where you are and immediately triggers Search & Rescue to come for you. One first has to take the responsibility of being in optimum physical shape, and focus carefully on every step--each of which has to be taken with perfection--especially when alone. Robison had a PLB but didn't use it. He had no satellite phone--if he had of, a change in plans would have been known--where he was yesterday to narrow the search today. It might not have saved him, but sure avoided a massive search and 5 years before being found.

p. 159

One shouldn't take excessive risks such as choosing an extremely dangerous alternative route as was done. Several options could have been: 1.) I would have taken the time to carefully get around the snow and persist with the safer route--which I have done a few times on Deadhorse Pass. 2.) The mountaineering route to Allsop Lake was dangerous and never should have been attempted. Any of the following options should have been chosen. 3.) If he got safely to Allsop Lake, the very dangerous climb up to the Allsop Saddle to get down past Reconnaissance Lake and the Highline Trail, SHOULD NEVER HAVE BEEN ATTEMPTED--rather from Allsop Lake just go down the 10 miles to the East Fork of Bear River Trailhead, and hitch a ride to civilization. 4.) Or better still, backing up to Deadhorse Lake, just go the 15 miles down the West Fork of Blacks Fork Trail to the North Slope Road where he could stop frequent vehicles for a ride to civilization. Chapter 2: THE HIGH UINTAS WILDERNESS AREA59 The creation of the Wilderness Area in 1984 was reviewed in the INTRODUCTION, page 16.

Section 1 THE HIGHLINE TRAIL This trail, using terminology we have been introduced to already, is—

THE GRANDADDY OF THEM ALL! HOW TO GET HERE: It begins on the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway at Hayden Pass, 34 miles from Kamas, Utah, at an elevation of 10,382 ft. It follows the spine of the Uintas east going over 6 passes in the Wilderness Area: Rocky Sea (11,200 ft.), Deadhorse (11,600 ft.), Red Knob (11,700 ft.), Porcupine (12,256 ft.), Tungsten (11,400 ft.), Anderson (12,600); and three more a bit to the east: North Pole (12,226 ft.), Deadman (11,428 ft.), and Gabbro (11,740). Except briefly, from Deadhorse to Red Knob Passes, we are on the South Slope technically but we'll begin our GUIDE categorizing it as 59

©2018 Google LLC, used with permission. Google and the Google logo are registered trademarks of Google LLC. Highlights, new routes and labels by author

.

p. 161

sort of neutral all the way to the east. Thereafter we'll focus on the NORTH SLOPE, and then the SOUTH SLOPE. At 60 miles it crosses the first road at the Chepeta Lake Trailhead--where Robinson began his backpack. Then at 76 miles it crosses another road at the Leidy Peak/Hacking Lake Trailhead. It doesn't end there as many have erroneously written, rather descends below timberline into the forest and continues for 26 more miles to the easternmost Trailhead, elevation 8,200 ft., near U.S. Highway 191 close to Flaming Gorge--as I have already reported, a TOTAL distance of 102 miles.60

I will now outline the main options we can choose from to dive into the WILDERNESS from the HIGHLINE TRAILHEAD:

THE LAKES OF THE UINTAS OUR MAIN FOCUS All the information in the GUIDE CHAPTERS came originally from the Division of Wildlife Resources Pamphlets—LAKES OF THE UINTAS61 published from 1985 to 1999, and quite outdated, as is the case with all present Uinta guide books. I wanted to update, and have current and accurate information in this book. I therefore approached friend, Roger Wilson, who worked for many years with the DWR, and now Chairman of the Utah Anglers Coalition, as well as personnel from the DWR, to get updated information.

2018-2019 REVISIONS/UPDATING: A meeting was set for November 2018 of the UAC— Utah Anglers Coalition and the DWR with the only agenda item “dedicated to [updating] the Uinta Mountain Lakes.” But in the end for whatever reasons it never happened. Consequently a meeting was arranged between me and knowledgeable DWR personnel on February 4, 2019. Two met with me at the DWR offices in Salt Lake City: Randy Oplinger, Sportfish Coordinator, and Matt McKell, Regional Biologist of the North Slope lakes working out of the Ogden office, plus via phone hookup, Garn Birchell, Regional Biologist of the South Slope lakes, from the Vernal DWR office. We had a 3 hour session reviewing all of the “experimental “ and other changes with lakes of the Uintas over the past 34 years. In addition the DWR provided me with a link to all of their Stockings62 of lakes and streams from 2002 to 2018, plus those ongoing in 2019. All of that information was used over a week of intensive effort to update the more than 630 lakes of the Uintas described in this book, making it the only publication to date with updated information—for 2018, and at least one important one scheduled for 2019 at Crater Lake, plus planned for restoration projects for the Oweep, Ottoson, Garfield Basins and Fall Creek drainage of Rock Ck. Since, I have been advised by Roger Wilson, that beginning the summer of 2019 the Utah Anglers Coalition will be working with the DWR to put together an updated management plan for the High Uintas. He feels that this will help the DWR manage better many of these remote lakes in the future.

NOTE: The DWR pamphlets LAKES OF THE UINTAS, mention for most lakes whether there are campsites or not, spring water or not, but for most of us backpackers, we have ways of camping/bivouacking anywhere, and with our filter systems can get our water from the lakes, so I will not be including those commentaries. I will try and include when an area is impossible to access with horses.

DISTANCES are noted on the topographical maps at the end of each section.

OPTION 1: WILDER, WYMAN & PACKARD LAKES. Trailhead to Packard Lake cut-off trail, 2-1/2 miles, then on to Wilder, Wyman, and to Packard Lakes.

Note: Before coming to the Packard Lake Trail, you pass Scudder Lake, perhaps a nice spot to camp out, but the DWR pamphlet says: "subject to winterkill and does not sustain fish life." The following lakes have been planted in recent years.

OPTION 2: THE NATURALIST BASIN. From the Trailhead it is 4 miles to the Naturalist Basin Trail that heads north up into the basin nestled on the southeastern slopes of Mt. Agassiz. My suggestion is to swing to the west past a waterfall coming out of the Morat Lakes. From there climb up along the waterfall coming out of Blue Lake then swing around the upper lakes, then down to loop back to the junction with the Highline Trail, and return to the Trailhead. I'll list the lakes in order doing that loop, then back to the Trailhead for a total of 16 miles. A topographical map will be inserted showing the options west of Rocky Sea Pass. Below we see: On the left Lake Morat 1, and then up above, Blue Lake

BLUE (Z-32): 10,940 ft. elevation, 5-3/4 miles from TH, 19 acres., 36' deep, Brook & Tiger trout LECONTE (Z-33): 10,920 ft. elevation, 6-1/2 miles from TH, 9.5 acres, 15' deep, Cutthroat & Tiger trout SHALER (Z-34): 10,920 ft. elevation, 7-1/4 miles from TH, 13 acres, 7' deep, Cutthroat trout JORDAN (Z-35): 10,660 ft. elevation, 8 mile loop, 23.2 acres, 30' deep, Brook trout EVERMAN (Z-36): 10,520 ft. elevation 8-1/2 mile loop, 7.8 acres, 7', Brook trout, subject to winterkill. From Everman back to junction with 12 mile running total--including extras plus back to TH = 16 miles.

OPTION 3: THE EAST FORK PINTO LAKE TRAIL: 1.5 miles east from the junction with the Naturalist Basin Trail, or 5.5 miles from the TH, we come to another junction, this trail takes off to the south dipping down through the headwaters of the Duchesne River, then up the other side of the canyon to Pinto Lake--which has us in the Rock Creek Drainage and on the northern end of the Grandaddy Basin, which will be described as part of the SOUTH SLOPE. OPTION 4: CAROLYN LAKE & OUR FIRST CHANCE TO CATCH ARCTIC GRAYLING. Access is about 6 miles from the Trailhead and 1/2 mile short of the junction with the Four Lakes Basin Trail. Look for a trail taking off through a meadow to the south 200 yards to the lake. CAROLYN (Z-42): 10,430 ft. elevation, 6.1 miles, 5 acres, 17' deep, some B & C trout, plus grayling

OPTION 5: TWO OUTLIER LAKES & CYCLONE PASS' REMOTE LAKES-- THEN THE FOUR LAKES BASIN --all part of the Rock Creek Drainage. One half mile past the trail to Carolyn Lake, we come to a major junction: The Highline Trail veers to the northeast, but we'll put that on hold, and head south for 1/2 mile where there is another junction--a little used trail to the right heading south takes one a little over a mile to Bedground Lake--a small lake, but known for at times producing large brook trout. 8.1 miles from the TH. From there one can go off-trail 3/4 mile due east to famous Allen Lake where it has been said for years “the record arctic grayling” would be caught.

NOTE: On page 7 we have already seen the unofficial State record grayling caught by Ted Packard in 1962 from Lake Atwood in the Uinta River Drainage. BEDGROUND (Z-46): 10,500 ft. elevation, 2 acres, 15' deep, 8-1/2 miles from TH, Brook trout & Grayling ALLEN (Z-44): 10,390 ft. elevation, 15.2 acres, 16' deep, Brook trout & Grayling (AG).

I have twice fixed up the Forest Service sign seen below: The first time I scraped it to make it legible; The 2nd time picking it up off the ground.

p. 165

Afterwards some friends went in there with tools to fix it up right-- honoring Ranger Floyd Allen who lost his life here in 1938. Hope it's still there--standing! If not, let me know and I'll do what I can to keep honoring Floyd Allen. From Allen Lake you can bushwhack 1/2 mile due north to Daynes Lake and the Four Lakes Basin but you're in thick forest, so might be best to veer northwest 3/4 mile to hit the trail up to Daynes. Northeast of Daynes Lake you will intersect the trail that climbs 11,150 ft. Cyclone Pass. If you are ready for more adventuring, climb the pass--one mile from Daynes Lake, that isn't that hard, then drop down to the east with two options: One mile of boulder hopping to remote Thompson Lake--observing along the way what seems like more spiders than elsewhere. From the bottom of the pass you can also boulder hop 1.3 miles to even more remote Sea Lion Lake. On horseback you can't do either, so tie up your horse and boulder hop--carefully! THOMPSON (RC-8): 10,690 ft. elevation, about 11 miles direct from TH, 21 acres, 26' deep, Brook trout SEA LION (RC-11): 10,385 ft. elevation, 13 miles if doing Thompson too, 7.9 acres, 11' deep, C trout.

NOTE: My friend Jeffrey Probst, said in his original book…….. We don't recommend this hike. One word can describe it - inaccessible…..might be the most inaccessible lake in the High Uintas. Crazy fishermen might try to reach Thompson Lake. Big brook trout roam these waters, and will savagely attack……who knows how big some of the old monarchs are. This is a true wilderness experience that should only be attempted by the hardy, or the fool-hardy.64

Of course, this old "fool-hardy" guy, as part of his "expedition" in 2003, couldn't resist, so I got there, but failed to find any of the "monarch" brook trout--only normal feisty ones, and have learned that there are some even more inaccessible lakes in the Uintas, but it was a great adventure -- thanks, Jeff, for teasing this old "crazy," and " fool-hardy," guy into making it. I'll insert a photo of Thompson Lake below.

This is one of the few places I don't worry about filtering my water. From here, about 7 miles from the Trailhead, we begin the 1 mile climb to 11,200 65

OPTION 6: HIGHLINE TRAILHEAD TO ROCKY SEA PASS & THE UPPER ROCK CREEK DRAINAGE to DEADHORSE PASS & LOOP BACK TO HIGHLINE TH. From Rocky Sea Pass we drop down quickly and in 1.7 miles come to a junction. What is the actual Highline Trail (025), and the direct route, drops down east and in 1 mile crosses Rock Creek. At that point there is a junction with the main trail #069 coming 12 miles up from the Rock Creek TH.

--FORDING STREAMS: Let me confess a personal experience at this point early in my project--when I wasn't proficient yet fording a stream-especially at the time of early season high run-off, I arrived here coming from the east to find a raging torrent and no bridge. It was late in the day with deep shadows and poor visibility, and about half way across I made a misstep sliding into deep water and I went under and learned what it was like to try and swim with a backpack, and my camera waist pack. I finally struggled out of a dangerous situation to the bank. I was determined to get to civilization as fast as possible and maybe save my Nikon camera, so did a forced hike up over Rocky Sea Pass and down to Pigeon Milk Springs, when it was dark. I somehow got a fire going and began drying what I could and critically warmed myself to ward off hypothermia. My sleeping bag was alright as it was very compressed in a stuff sack and so didn't absorb water. I made it out the next day, saving the film, but not the camera--learning to not try and dry the camera, rather put it in a plastic bag and let the professionals save it. I learned to cross streams, first putting camera and such in a Ziploc bag, and in a really dangerous crossing loosening my pack's waist belt to be able to free myself from it. Then always use a stout pole to steady yourself with every step, facing upstream into the current, and making sure the pole is in a secure spot before taking another step.67 That trail takes one east 2.2+ miles up to the trail that swings around the upper basin (#122) which we are mainly interested in. So back to the junction, then 1/4 mile north to Brinkley Lake.

67

https://www.whiteblaze.net/forum/archive/index.php/t-105049.html

BRINKLEY LAKE, seen on the previous page, is one of my favorite photographs taken zooming in on Ostler Peak, clear over on the North Slope. At Rosalie Lake on my Expedition, at sundown I all of a sudden heard a pack of coyotes howling on the hunt up above some cliffs to the west, then the desperate bleating of what sounded like a young sheep--although none in the area, so it must have been a young Rocky Mountain goat I had seen some of. Then the bleating stopped followed by the triumphant howling of the pack of coyotes having a delicious supper. From Rosalie Lake we leave the trail to visit two off-trail lakes, easily found as we are now above timberline. UINTAH (X-131): 10,840 ft., 0.8 mile from Rosalie, 8.4 acres, 14' deep, Brook trout MARGIE (X-129): 10,980 ft., 0.8 mile from Uintah Lake, 7.5 acres, 11' deep, Brook trout From Margie just a short 1/4 mile back to camp at Rosalie Lake. From there the trail takes you north up above timberline to circle around the upper basin: GLADYS (X-128): 10,900 ft., about 12.6 miles from TH, 7.5 acres, 6' deep, Brook trout At 13 miles from the Trailhead, the trail begins to drop to the east with Lightning and Helen Lakes in view. That is the point from which you can take an off-trail climb up to the Ostler Saddle, and view on the North Slope beautiful Amethyst Lake seen below.

From Hellen Lake we have dropped down some and now with the point of the mountain to the north where the trail crosses a small stream -- we leave the trail and head northeast passing by several small lakes, and at about 1 mile from the trail come to a mountain scene that some feel rivals Red Castle as the most beautiful Mountain Scene

in Utah—TRIANGLE MOUNTAIN & RECONNAISSANCE LAKE. RECONNAISSANCE LAKE & TRIANGLE PEAK

RECONNAISSANCE (X-125): 11,145 ft., 16.6 miles from TH, 8.8 acres, 30' deep, Brook & C trout Small lakes and ponds in the area, like Bench and Triangle Lakes below Reconnaissance, and Doug and Jodie, are not even mentioned by the DWR, but they, along with connecting streams usually have pan-sized brook and cutthroat trout. From Reconnaissance Lake you can also climb the saddle to view below Allsop Lake to the north, near where Eric Robison was found. See page 157 for the view from said saddle. We continue past the trail coming up from Rock Creek, and on to Ledge Lake. SPECIAL NOTICE: The DWR is proposing poisoning with rotenone the lakes and streams of the Fall Creek Drainage, and then restoring the Native Cutthroat trout in the area. If approved it will be done, along with the other 3 areas (Ottoson, Oweep & Garfield) between 2022-2034. Including below: Ledge X-113, Continent X-121 See page 378 for others.

LEDGE ( X-113): 10,845 ft., 21 miles from the TH, 3 acres, 13" deep, Brook trout prone to winterkill. At this point there is a junction with one of the trails coming up 16 miles from the Rock Creek TH. We follow our trail for another mile and then leave the trail crossing arctic tundra to the west to visit our next important lake: CONTINENT (X-121): 11,285 ft., 22 miles from the TH, 27 acres, 23' deep, Brook & Cutthroat trout. Just for the view, it's worth doing a 1/2 mile hike to 11,600 ft. DEADHORSE PASS and look down on Deadhorse Lake we see below. The turquoise color is caused by glacial milk.68

We now do an about face to begin our loop back, but do so following another trail to visit another few lakes, before heading for Rocky Sea Pass. We backtrack about 3 miles to where we came out of the Reconnaissance Lake basin, and take the trail that goes to Jack and Jill Lakes, and two others: JACK (X-133): 10,460 ft., now at 27 miles of our Loop, 2.7 acres, 14' deep, Cutthroat trout JILL (X-111): 100 yards west of Jack, 3.6 acres, 25' deep, Brook trout OURAY (X-112): 10,380 ft., 27.5 miles in Loop, 4 acres, 6' deep, Brook & Cutthroat trout BLACK (X-132): 10,403 ft., 12 acres, 14' deep, 28.5 miles in Loop, used by Boy Scouts, Brook & Cutthroat We have now joined the trail we came in on between Brinkley and Rosalie Lakes, and begin our return climbing Rocky Sea Pass, where we have hiked 31.5 miles. From there to the Highline Trailhead it is another 8 miles, for a TOTAL OF 40 MILES-- having visited and fished in 15 lakes, plus a number of small lakes and ponds, in addition to seeing some spectacular mountain scenes, second to none! All of that plus the other options in the area to Wilder, Wyman, and Packard Lakes, Naturalist Basin--with 6 lakes, Carolyn, Bedground, Allen, Thompson and Sea Lion Lakes, and the Four Lakes Basin. Fifteen more lakes for a total of 30. Wow! 68

Chapter 2: THE WILDERNESS AREA—North Slope

Section 2: The HELL'S HOLE BASIN ********************

PREFACE "THE BIGGEST GRIZ!" The small Hell's Hole Basin produces a nice stream, Main Fork, which is one of several tributaries of what we should now recognize as a unique river in the Hemisphere--the Bear River. Its history will be told in the Preface to Chapter 2, Section 3. You might guess that the Bear River got its name in pioneer times because of bears, and the Main Fork--(of the Bear River), and where it is born--HELL'S HOLE BASIN, has the distinction of being mentioned by famous pioneer artist and photographer, George Beard.69 I'll insert his picture below, along with his wife, Lovenia--whose name George gave to Mt. Lovenia--one of the Uinta's named 13,000+ foot mountains.70 George was born in 1855 and died in Coalville in 1944.

About Hell's Hole Basin and Canyon, he once said:

"I here saw the largest grizzly I have ever seen!" I'm not sure when he made that comment, but I have it jotted down by him on a copy of one of his photographs, a set of which were given to me by a friend and a relative of George from Evanston, Shawn Moore. Apparently there was a time when bears were more prevalent in Utah, as evidenced by the bear trap I photographed in the Snooks Roberts Museum in Hanna, that had trapped 100 bears in the Blacks Fork area

of the Uintas North Slope. The last grizzly bear in Utah was known as "Old Ephraim," said to be "the curse of local sheepherders." He was tracked for 10 years by Frank Clark, a sheepherder, who finally got him in a trap chained to an 8" thick tree. Old Ephraim clawed down the tree and ran uphill with the trap on his foot--when Clark fired all his bullets into the bear before he dropped. That was on August 22, 1923, in Logan Canyon. On his death he stood 9 feet 11 inches tall and weighed 1,100 lbs. He was the last grizzly bear in Utah. A monument was erected where he is buried in 1966 by Logan Boy Scouts with a poem, by Nephi J. Bott, that is: "Old Ephraim, Old Ephraim, your deeds were so wrong yet we build you this marker and sing you

this song. To the king of the forest so mighty and tall, we salute you, Old Ephraim the king of them all." 71 69

Section 2:

The HELL'S HOLE BASIN TRAILHEAD--unofficial HOW TO GET HERE: The take-off point to hike to Hell's Hole Basin, is 9 miles down UT150 from the Highline Trailhead, or 43.5 miles from Kamas. When you are heading north and see the sign seen below pointing west to GOLD HILL & FR-081—a little further on the right, an unmarked road takes off…….

………. as seen below in the middle Google Earth view--turn down it carefully at the end of which a trail heads east crossing Hayden Fork, continuing east until you come to a road which you follow south to a sharp turn when it ends in a gravel pit. The Trail takes off on that turn climbing south up into the Hell's Hole Basin.

For me the importance of this area on the Main Fork, relates to its abundant water that was used by the Tie Hacker Culture and the Howe Feeder Flume that took water down-stream along the western bank of Main Fork, then at the point where the trail coming from the trailhead hits the road, the Flume veered west following that trail west and then north to join the Hilliard Flume, and give it enough water to carry its wood products 30 miles north to Hilliard, Wyoming and the charcoal kilns. The pathway of the Hilliard Flume is seen in the 3rd picture above. The Howe Feeder flume was first reported on by Forest Service archaeologist, James E. Ayres' Summary Report of Historic Sites--1978 & 1979,72 but no photographs are available. http://www.standard.net/Ogden-Area-History-Bin/2015/07/16/July-17-history-bin 72

SUMMARY EPORT OF 1978 & 1979 HISTORIC SITES SURVEY in the Evanston Ranger District, Wasatch National Forest, Utah, by James E. Ayres

p. 176

As far as we know, I was the first to re-discover the sites and report on this with photographs of the remnants of the 1870 flume. After crossing Hayden Fork, and hiking east you should notice off the trail to your left a log structure, which was one of the supports of the flume. Further along if you look carefully you'll notice some cuts in the hill on your left-the pathway of the flume. After coming to the road, you should notice on the left a level above the creek where I began discovering the last rotting remains of cabins--small, with rocks in one corner as they used fireplaces…….

……..and I began noticing square nails--all signs these sites were from the 1867 to 1880 period. I'll insert below a panel of 3 photographs. You can also see two YouTube Videos of my discoveries, never published before, of artifacts which are quickly rotting away.73 As I followed the clues upstream I began finding remnants of the flume, with braces, planks, and support structures, and always square nails. Now, 8 years later, maybe all gone.

NOW UP THE TRAIL FOR SOME FISHING HELL'S HOLE (BR-29): 10,340 ft., 5 miles from unofficial trailhead, 8.5 acres, 9' deep, Cutthroat trout.

p. 177

The DWR recommends bringing plenty of mosquito repellant, which I will emphasize with a few photographs on this subject crucial to enjoying a backpack into Hell's Hole where there are many marshy meadow areas, but of course important for any other area of the Uintas during the summer season, until into August in the high country where the life cycle of the mosquitoes is complete, and frosts finish off the stragglers.

Always use repellant with 98-100% Deet. The 30% version just doesn't get the job done. Some would say to put such a strong toxic substance on your skin is dangerous, but, as I have said: "I would prefer to run the risk of a little poison in my system for a short period, rather than be: First, driven insane, then dying--eaten alive by mosquitoes!"

I personally like the brand shown above as it is visible how much you have left and can resupply. A WORD OF ADVISE: It, as well as others, have a spray device, but it's a big waste to spray directly on your skin. Just squirt 2 or 3 times in the palm of your hand, then rub your palms together and lightly distribute over your legs, arms, and face. Then, at least early as I'm getting ready for the day, take your T-shirt off and treat the shirt, front and back--as the mosquitoes will penetrate your shirt, You might have to repeat several times the treatment during the day. ***************************************

Station on UT-150 to a well marked turnoff and then 2 miles southeast on the unimproved Lily Lake--Boundary Creek Road to the Lake.74 LILY (BR-11): It is a large beaver dam pond, 12.6 acres, 20' deep, 8,890 ft. elev., Rainbow trout

Section 3: CHRISTMAS MEADOWS/STILLWATER TRAILHEAD ************************** PREFACE So far, coming down the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway, we have been paralleling Hayden Fork, and reviewed Main Fork born in the Hell's Hole Basin. Downstream it joins the Stillwater Fork that is born in Middle Basin, and added to by a creek from West Basin, and from the east by Ostler Fork born in the Amethyst Basin--all together making Stillwater Fork a larger stream flowing through Christmas Meadows with majestic Ostler Peak, and Spread Eagle Mountain, forming the backdrop, as seen below in this beautiful scene.

A couple of miles downstream Main Fork joins Stillwater Fork, and in another mile is joined by Hayden Fork at which point all the Forks and creeks become the BEAR RIVER. In another 4 miles or so the East Fork of Bear River joins from further east and eventually the much smaller West Fork of Bear River joins the River. So, since coming north from Hayden Pass, WE HAVE BEEN IN THE BEAR RIVER DRAINAGE…..so let’s learn about this unique river.

THE BEAR RIVER THE BEAR RIVER became the first drainage from the Uinta’s North Slope to be worked by fur trappers as early as 1818, but visited as early as 1812 In Canada there had been a murderous trade war between the English Hudson Bay Co. and the Canadian North West Co, called “Nor”Westrs,” but it finally ended in a merger in 1821. But, as early as 1807 explorers were sent south from Canada to the Columbia River. In 1812 Robert Stuart was seemingly the first to visit our river, calling it “Miller’s River,” after his guide, Joseph Miller. But the name didn’t stick. By 1816 Donald Mackenzie was sent with brigades of trappers to the Columbia and by 1818-19 he had sent 3 expeditions east to the Snake River. One of them was the first to go through the Bear River drainage, and then cross what was later called the “Bear River Divide,” getting as far as the Green River Valley. Said “Divide” must be close to where today we find the sign we see below along the High Uinta’s North Slope Road.

p. 180

On the first expedition in 1818 French-Canadian, Michel Bourdon, a “young…..conductor of Trappers” for the Hudson Bay Co., made the “British discovery” of a river first thought by him to be the “Spanish River, the Colorado,” and later “a fork of the same,” and “named it the Bear from the great numbers of those animals on its borders,” both black and grizzly bears. The next year Michel Bourdon was killed by Indians along the river he named. By 1824 Jedediah Smith, one of the first members of The Missouri Fur Co., organized and owned by General William H. Ashley, and Major Andrew Henry, had crossed South Pass in Wyoming, then traveled southwest over the Bear River Divide and followed the Bear River trapping as he and his team traveled north for 100 miles, making two caches of 900 beaver pelts each—considered excellent for his brigade of 7 trappers in just 3 months. Others, like Jim Bridger, had followed the long course of the Bear River and learned where its long course led—making him the discoverer of the Great Salt Lake that was first thought to be an arm of the Pacific Ocean. Jedediah Smith wintered at the mouth of the Bear River in 1824-25 and it was at that spot in the summer of 1827 where the 3rd Mountain Man Rendezvous was held.75

This long and important river, born in the Uintas, as seen on the map above, flows north into Wyoming, then makes a big bend through Idaho to the northwest around the northern tip of the Wasatch Mountains, thereafter swinging south back into Utah emptying into the Great Salt Lake. All in all as it flows from the High Uintas, and drains a vast area of 4.8 million acres—with 150 lakes, reservoirs and streams making it the main tributary of the Great Salt Lake, and “the largest river in the hemisphere that doesn’t drain into an ocean.” All along it’s long 75

The brief history of the Bear River was summarized from, Dale L. Morgan's book, JEDEDIAH SMITH & THE OPENING OF THE WEST, Univ. of Nebraska Press, Lincoln, Nebraska, 1964, pages 124-128

p. 181

course it gives life to the agriculture and communities of an area larger than the sum total of Utah, Salt Lake, Wasatch, Summit & Morgan Counties. 76 In the INTRODUCTION, key references have already been made to the “Tie Hacker Culture” of the High Uintas North Slope, with much of it connected to the important Bear River, and the construction of the Transcontinental Railroad, crucial to the development and “winning of the West.” A greater understanding of this important history will enhance immensely and have come alive your enjoyment and appreciation of the High Uintas as you see firsthand the remnants of the past on which our present was built. IMPORTANT REFERRENCES TO THE BEAR RIVER:

Section 3:

The CHRISTMAS MEADOWS/STILLWATER TRAILHEAD HOW TO GET HERE: From Kamas to Christmas Meadows = 47 miles, then 4 miles to Trailhead TOTAL= 51 miles from Kamas, 91 from SLC. From Evanston, Wyoming, 30 miles to No. Slope Rd, plus 3 to turn-off and 4 to Trailhead, Total of 37 miles.

Forty-seven miles from Kamas, or 12.5 miles from the Highline Trailhead at Hayden Pass we come to a junction where we turn to the southeast on the road that takes us 4 miles to what we have always called the Christmas Meadows Trailhead, as do all my maps, but the sign calling it the Stillwater Trailhead.

Two miles from this junction is the beginning of the Bear River-Smiths Fork Trail, that many call The North Slope Highline Trail, or The North Side Highline Trail. Rather than following the spine of the Uintas, like the Highline Trail does, this trail is what maybe we could call a middle elevation trail, sort of mid-way between the Trailheads, and the high country, which in some cases can be used to make loop backpacks. Our focus will rather be on all the wonderful, even spectacular options from the “Stillwater” or “Christmas Meadows” Trailhead. I will outline 4 OPTIONS for good backpacks in the area. FROM THE TRAILHEAD, we hike 2.4 miles to a junction where the options begin: OPTION 1: To remote Seidner Lake with no trail in a side canyon to the west crossing the stream 1/4 mile before the trail junction, then follow the drainage 2 steep miles to the lake (not recommended for horses). This kind of lake get's my exploration juices flowing! SEIDNER (BR-31): 10,460 ft. elevation, 8.5 miles roundtrip, 3 acres, 8' deep, Brook trout by natural reproduction.

OPTION 2: Will be to KERMSUH LAKE in West Basin. From the key junction we continue straight up the canyon 2.1 miles and come to a sign pointing to the west, and soon come to a crossing of the fairly large stream--crossed by a single thin log quite high above the water-that scared the heck out of me, but I made it--today, 13 years later with balance not what it used to be would have me finding a safer crossing . You then switchback up into the solitude of West Basin, guarded by the east side of Hayden Peak as seen on the following page.

p. 183

KERMSUH (BR-20): 10,300 ft. elevation, 7 miles from Trailhead, 12 acres, 14' deep, Cutthroat trout, sustained by natural reproduction. OPTION 3: MIDDLE BASIN with Ryder and McPheeters Lakes, plus 3 small lakes which all could be combined with Kermsuh as one option or trip, which I did when exploring the area. To get there we are now back down on the main trail. From that junction it is 3.6 miles up to Middle Basin and Ryder Lake, a beautiful picture of which is seen on page 18 of the INTRODUCTION. From Ryder Lake a climb up to McPheeters Lake is a must--just head up the mountain to the northwest 1/2 mile. Along the way we look back at Ryder Lake with Mt. Agassiz in the background.

Below, McPheeters Lake, at timberline, makes an interesting picture--along with the whole basin, with Mt. Agassiz on the left, and Hayden Peak on the right.

p. 184

LAKE BR-17: 2.8 acre lake, 7' deep, south of Ryder Lake, Brook trout sustained by natural reproduction. Section 4: The EAST FORK OF THE BEAR RIVER **************************

PREFACE

LIVING & SURVIVING WITH WILD ANIMALS With the mention of bears in the Bear River Drainage, best talk a little about the precautions we should take in the Wilderness. We certainly don't have to worry as much as was the case in the days of George Beard when there were even grizzly bears, in addition to lots of black bears. Grizzlies were eradicated from Utah, and black bears greatly reduced in numbers. Let me just tell you of my experience. In 2006 I was on my way back from Reconnaissance Lake and met two backpackers and we got talking. They were backpacking for the first time, and wanted to know about wild animals. I started with deer, moose, and…..then they interrupted, saying, "What about bears?" I told them in all of my years hiking the Uintas I'd never seen one, and mentioned that earlier that summer I had met Dave and Alicia Evans in the Swift Creek Drainage where he was working for the Forest Service searching for wolverines. He had bait stations, with movement activated cameras and above 10,500 ft. had never photographed a bear, but had down along the rivers between 8,500 and 9,500. See page 323. So I told the backpackers that up in the high country where we were at that moment, no

problem, but to exercise caution coming up to the high country along the streams.

Two hours later I met a party of horse packers from the Uintah Basin, and I mentioned my intention of writing a book, so asked….do you have any exciting stories to tell me about? Immediately Steve, yelled, "Hey, Josh, come over here and tell Cordell your story." Josh, explained that in 2001 he was working for the Forest Service supplying, with pack horses, teams of Forest Service employees and volunteers from the east working on trails, bridges, etc. up Lake Fork above Moon Lake.. He would take letters out to mail, and bring

p. 189

them mail and packages. One kid from the east apparently was writing letters complaining

"the food is terrible, it rains every day, and the mosquitoes are eating us alive!" On one trip Josh brought a package for this kid, and when getting close to their camp at about 9,500 ft. he saw fresh bear tracks. So at camp he told everyone they had to have a clean camp as a bear was in the area. Apparently the contents of the package for the complainer was kept a secret--Oreo Cookies he didn't want to share, so hid them in the bottom of his sleeping bag. They got a good fire going, and put logs on to keep it going all night. At about 1:00 AM Josh heard the kid screaming and sat up to see the bear pulling the sleeping bag, with kid inside, out of the tent. He grabbed his 30-30 lever action rifle and fired a warning shot, and instantly the bear dropped the kid and bag, and charged Josh. He was chambering another round when the bear hit him, and literally had him in a bear hug. "I'M A GONER," he thought, then in a flash he remembered something he'd seen on the Discovery Channel--a guy in the jaws of a shark and he hit the shark in the snout as hard as

he could, and the shark dropped him. Josh went on, "I gave the bear my best Rocky Balboa punch, and he let me go. I quickly grabbed the rifle and killed the bear, and after some quick first aid, got on my horse and headed to civilization for help." "It's no joke," he said, "look at the evidence" ……as he pulled up his shirt showing me the scars on both sides.

So, I all of a sudden began exercising more caution, following the advice of keeping a clean camp, hanging my food in a tree at least 12-15' off the ground and 6 feet from the trunk as you see me doing below--and……..no Oreos in my sleeping bag!

p. 190

I even got some pepper spray and carried it on the trail a few times, but then thought--but

if a bear attacks in the night while I'm in my tent, the pepper spray would probably hurt me and not affect the bear. So, I went back to my Colt .45 Defender, with Corbon +P 230 grain bullets. But, as I've got older with the need of reducing my load, I've gone to my usual carry weapon, a Glock 43, 9 mm. and after extensive testing have it loaded in the mountains with +P Grizzly ammo. NOTE: I don't recommend everyone carrying a weapon, unless you have

training, a Concealed Carry Permit, and are level headed, but with a word of caution: If you carry, don't make the mistake of ignoring all the precautions recommended by the Forest Service and the DWR--DO ALL OF THAT FIRST & ALWAYS! WHAT HAS BEEN MY EXPERIENCE? HAVE I EVER HAD TO USE MY WEAPON? Four times, twice on clear moonlit nights, with my tent open--except for the mosquito netting, saw a coyote fooling with empty containers left outside. They are no danger to a humans and they were gone quickly with a "GET OUT OF HERE!" Another time at Deadhorse Lake on my expedition, I had left a pot outside soaking to make cleaning easy the next morning and I heard the lid knocked off and a "lap, lap, lap," some animal getting a taste of my high country cooking--and I had my Colt .45 ready to fire a warning shot, but hated the thought of making a hole in my tent, so with a shout….it was gone. The 4th time was at remote Margo Lake in the Grandaddies, something fooling with an empty water bottle about 25 feet away--and I was actually able to get a telephoto flash picture of a snow shoe rabbit for the first time. WARNING SHOTS? --Then, on the East Fork of the Bear River trail, I had passed a herd of cattle at a narrow point in the lower canyon, and then I stopped for a rest (frequent for this old guy), laying flat out using my camera waist pack as a pillow. With eyes closed still I all of a sudden was awakened hearing heavy breathing. I opened my eyes to see very close a Charolais bull who was trying to move his harem up the canyon, and I was in his way. I carefully reached for my camera in one hand for a picture, and my Colt .45 in the other. With a bit of exaggeration--snot was dripping from his nostrils, fire from his eyes, smoke from his ears, and he was pawing the ground ready to charge. My 35 years as a cattleman in Guatemala had taught me bulls were extremely dangerous. Just in time I fired a warning shot, and clicked the shutter as he wheeled out of there, seen below:

One other time on the trail to the Red Castle area, I found myself between a cow moose and her calf, and she was ready to charge when another warning shot ended that episode.

p. 191

Section 4: The EAST FORK OF THE BEAR RIVER HOW TO GET HERE: From Kamas on UT-150 to No. Slope Rd. = 50 miles, then 2 miles to junction with E. Fk. of the Bear River Rd., and 5 miles to Trailhead = 57 miles from Kamas, 97 from SLC. From Evanston, Wyoming, 30 miles to No. Slope Rd, plus 7 to Trailhead, Total of 37.

NOTE: No Trailhead is actually inside the Wilderness Area, but we are focusing on trails to lakes that are inside the Wilderness, with a few exceptions, beginning with Lily Lake on page 178, and here in this Drainage of the Wilderness. Two of them, Baker and Scow, are not accessed from the Trailhead, rather from a road at the Boy Scout Camp. The third will be the 1st described from the Trailhead--Lake Lorena. Baker and Scow Lakes, are accessed via the unmarked Boundary Creek Trail from the Boy Scout Camp, trail that is marked on the Topo map 4.5 miles to Baker Lake. Along that same trail, at 2.9 miles you will notice to the west a side canyon and as far as I can tell you have to bushwhack your way 0.9 miles to Scow Lake. SCOW (BR-12): 10,100 ft. elevation, 22.9 acres, 6' deep, B trout unpredictable due to possible winter kill. BAKER (BR-45): 10,420 ft. elevation, 3.6 acres, 8' deep, wary Brook & Tiger trout.

FOLLOWING IS THE TOPO MAP FOR BAKER & SCOW LAKES

p. 192

The EAST FORK OF BEAR RIVER TRAILHEAD Four lakes are accessed from this trailhead: Off trail Lake Lorena just outside of the Wilderness Area, then a little further along the stream divides: The Right Hand Fork leading to Norice and Priord Lakes; The Left Hand Fork leading to Allsop Lake. Now the details: LAKE LORENA (BR-46): 10,580 ft. elevation, 12 acres, 20' deep, stocked Brook trout. From TH hike 2.3 miles to where there are many tie hacker ruins, cross the stream, and make a very steep hike 1.8 miles up the steep mountain to the lake. It is not recommended for horses. Solitude is the name of the game.

NOTE: There is a YouTube video of my attempt in 2013 to get to Lake Lorena. 78 I was very interested in getting to the lake in part because of its remoteness, but also because I had heard from a Division of Wildlife Resources employee that they had gill netted a brook trout there that was very large and twice as old as the average brook trout for an alpine lake. At 3.8 miles from the TH you come to a sign pointing straight ahead to Allsop Lake, and to the right, crossing the stream, to Priord Lake which we'll study first. Following the Left Hand Fork, the trail climbs sharply along the river that cascades down the canyon, with scenes like seen below. At 5 miles from the junction, or about 9 miles from the Trailhead we come to Allsop Lake, which area we have seen in the case of Eric Robison.

ALLSOP (BR-42): 10,580 ft. elevation, 12.3 acres, 22' deep, Cutthroat trout by natural reproduction.

Access is 4 miles south of the Mill Creek Guard Station--at mile 7 of the North Slope Road--and then 2 miles northeast on the rough Lym Lake jeep trail to

the Lake. Be sure to take the left hand turn at the old tie-hack cabin sites in the large meadow.79 LYM (BR-7): 10,115 ft. elevation, 6.4 acres, 20' deep, Brook trout by natural reproduction. Next is Mt. Elizabeth Lake, in the Bear River Drainage. accessed 11.5 miles east from UT-150 at Elizabeth Ridge [or Pass] following the Elizabeth Mountain Road 4.5 miles to a point overlooking the lake, then on secondary logging roads using 4WD vehicles make your way to the lake. MT. ELIZABETH LAKE (BR-8): Follow instructions in preceding paragraph. 9,984 ft. elevation, 3.1 acres, 15' deep, stocked with Cutthroat trout.

The following lake is actually in the Blacks Fork Drainage, but described here as access is from Elizabeth Pass. Drainage of Blacks Fork 9,691 ft., 11.4 acres, 29' deep--with possible drawdown of 12'. Brook trout. 79

Section 5: The WEST FORK OF BLACKS FORK ***********************

PREFACE

THE STALKER! On thinking back on my experience in the West Fork Drainage--to tell here a story or two of benefit to my outdoor friends, a couple of things come to mind. First of all, where this trail

leads: Deadhorse Lake, and to the west, Deadhorse Pass, and to the east Red Knob Pass with the Highline Trail connecting them. I've mentioned one experience--while on my "expedition," and camped at Deadhorse Lake, related to wild animals: The "lap, lap, lap" heard during the night--some animal tasting from my soaking pot my high country cooking-- .45 ready to fire a warning shot, which worked out unnecessary. Also on that long backpack I had another unique experience with wildlife, seeing and photographing a beautiful mule deer buck near Deadhorse Lake. I'll insert the photo below, and then comment on why such an experience was possible--and review one of my techniques that might be useful to hikers really interested in the outdoors.

It was a telephoto shot in very low light with my Nikon film camera, a film of low ASA or ISO, making shots in very low light difficult, especially hand held with a telephoto lens while panning with the buck and clicking the shutter--totally blurring the background, but getting an interesting shot of the deer.

WHAT'S THE LESSON TO BE LEARNED? I have sometimes joked about my hiking speed as I've got into my 70's and 80's, calling it my "stalking speed." Yes, maybe I go that slow because I have no choice, but at least half of my motivation is so I won't miss any of the VISIONS OF NATURE that I've mentioned my "marathon backpacker" & ATV friends seldom if ever see. Here's another few examples:

LET'S TAKE IT SLOW & EASY and see the wonders of nature and not take a misstep!

p. 198

Chapter 2: THE WILDERNESS AREA--North Slope

Section 5: THE WEST FORK OF BLACKS FORK HOW TO GET HERE: From Kamas, on UT-150 to the North Fork Road (FR-058), then east 18 miles to the junction. TOTAL FROM Kamas = 68 miles, from SLC=108 miles. From Evanston, Wyo., east on I-80 to Ft. Bridger, east and south to Mt. View--total of 45 miles, then 9 miles on CR-410 to Robertson and end of pavement, turning south on CR-271 to Ut. border, then on FR058 to junction (24 miles from Robertson) with E. Fk. Blacks Fk. road, FR-065. Then 2 miles to the west. Total via Evanston=84 miles. From SLC 80 to Evanston + 80 miles to junction. TOTAL OF 160.

We'll begin this section with information about 4 lakes that are outside of the Wilderness Area, and accessible by road, the first ending with a jeep trail--needing 4WD. We back up to the Pass or Divide. Lym, Mt. Elizabeth & Moslander Lakes described on p. 194, map on 196. First, as we come from the west, the lakes accessed on a road that takes off to the north at the ELIZABETH RIDGE [PASS, DIVIDE] highpoint on the North Slope Road--12 miles from UT-150: The Mirror Lake Scenic Byway. FISH LAKE (mostly on Private Land) (GR-125): On coming down east from the Pass, after a hairpin turn in the road one comes to a gated road going into the lake where there are cabins from where we see the picture of the lake inserted below. Then, the following information in 2018 from Bernard Asay, Trail Supervisor for the Forest Service in the Evanston Office. From the gated road, approximately 3/4 mile down

FR-058 there is a two-track trail leading 1/2 mile to the dam--built to enlarge the original lake, part of which is on Forest Service land, and open to fishing for trout--but be respectful of Private Property signs. Few if any even know about this lake.81 See page 196 for a Google Earth view. In 2015 a survey was done finding the lake to contain a population of brook trout ranging approximately 7-11". It was later assigned the number GR-125. It was stocked in 2016 with 4,641 sterile brook trout.

Now we move further east to the junction of Lyman Lakes and West Fork of Blacks Fork. LITTLE LYMAN (G-25): At 18 miles from UT-150 at a 4 way junction, then 1/2 mile north to a full service Forest Service Campground, and the lake. 9,276 ft. elevation, 5 acres, 25' deep, stocked annually with Rainbow, Brook & Tiger trout. See photos on page 62.

81

Pages 62, 63 of this book.

p. 199

LYMAN (G-27): 1/2 mile northeast of Little Lyman Lake. 9,311 ft., 36.6 acres, 30' deep with small dam to enlarge original lake. Stocked with Rainbow, Brook & Tiger trout.

We now will deal with the lakes in this drainage that are in the Wilderness Area, beginning at the Trailhead and detailing small remote, off-trail lakes to the west as we go up the drainage, ending with Deadhorse Lake where the West Fork of Blacks Fork is born.

THE WEST FORK OF BLACKS FORK TRAILHEAD is found 5 miles up the canyon, then ford the stream and go about 1 mile further. LAKE G-82 : Access is 1/2 mile southwest of the Trailhead up a steep timbered ridge, 10,140 ft. elevation, 3.8 acres, 6' deep, difficult if not impossible for horses, Brook trout. LAKE G-81 : Access is 3/4 mile in steep terrain southwest of G-82 at the southern end of a cirque basin. 10,665 ft. elevation, 1.6 acres, 5' deep, stocked periodically with Cutthroat trout. LAKE G-78: Access is 1 mile south of the Trailhead on the 1st major stream from the west, then 1-1/4 miles to the lake. Difficult for horses. 10,660 ft., 3.2 acres, 9' deep. Stocked with Brook experimentally with brook trout in 1984 and 1990; follow up surveys done in 1986 and 1992 finding no fish--winterkill suspected; stocking was discontinued. LAKE G-79 : Access is 1/2 mile south of G-78 around the rocky ridge to the southwest. 10,820 ft., 2.5 acres, 5' deep. At the base of a SPECTACULAR rock face that rises 1,000 feet above the lake--IT'S ON MY BUCKET LIST! Don't try getting here on horseback. Stocked experimentally with brook trout in 1983 and 1990; follow up surveys done in 1986 and 1992 finding no fish--winterkill suspected; stocking discontinued. LAKE G-80: Accessed 2.5 miles south of the Trailhead to the upper end of Buck Pasture, then 3/4 mile west climbing the steep timbered slope to the basin. Difficult access should not be attempted on horseback. 10,580 ft. elevation, 1.8 acres, 8' deep. Stocked with Brook trout. LAKE G-81: It was stocked in the 1980s with cutthroat trout and continues to sustain a wild population of cutthroat. EJOD (G-76): Located 1/4 mile across alpine tundra northwest of Deadhorse Lake. 10,900 ft., 6.7 acres, 12'deep, contains Cutthroat trout by natural reproduction. DEADHORSE (G-77): 7.5 miles from the Trailhead, 10,878 ft., 16 acres, 41' deep, Cutthroat & Tiger trout. Emerald green due to glacial turbidity, seen on page 173 and below. Deadhorse Lake where the West Fork of Blacks Fork is born

Section 6: The MIDDLE FORK OF BLACKS FORK ************************

PREFACE SOLITUDE, TIE HACKS and SOLOMAN "SAM" GALLEGOS This has been for me one of the most fascinating drainages, even though it is literally unknown even for dyed in the wool backpackers. There are a number of reasons why it is special for me: It's solitude as in my first two backpacks up there I only saw footprints of one other person having been in the area. Then on my 3rd trip, as I was almost down the canyon, I ran into a couple. Nonetheless, still SOLITUDE, even though in the lower portion I have seen a few fishermen. Then there were the wildflowers, like I've never seen anywhere else. Of course if you've noticed, it was here I really started noticing lots of ruins, and eventually asked the right people--Teresa and Bob Fascineli, at the Hewinta Guard station--"What the

heck was going on up the Middle Fork--with more ruins than anywhere else?" So, I was introduced to the tie hackers, their culture on the North Slope , and so many fascinating stories about these "unsung heroes without whom the West might not have been won!" -- yet not even mentioned in the history books about the Transcontinental Railroad. All of these factors made the Uintas so much more interesting and even led to me making discoveries about the tie hackers with pictures published in this book for the first time--and this was so invigorating for me that it stimulated me to doing more research and other areas of fascination opened up to me, like: BIG FOOT or SASQUATCH, reportedly with quite a few sightings, and me making several backpacks up Little East Fork of Blacks Fork-purposely going off trail, with the lens cap off, and camera ready--just in case I would get to take a family portrait, and in Section 8 I'll relate my experience and insert a picture of those adventures and what I saw. My curiosity whetted, I did research into the first white men to view the Uintas--hoping my hero, Jedediah Smith, would be the first--and learned much more about him as one of the incredible heroes of the West, but then learned about Michael Bourdon, sent by the Hudson Bay Co., who in 1818 named the Bear River because of so many bears, but later killed by Indians on that stream--unique in all of North America as the biggest that doesn't

get to the ocean. So I had to conclude that the first white men were Spanish Priests, Escalante & Dominguez in 1776, and read about their exploits--but then STOPPED IN MY TRACKS, as they had come up "the old Spanish trail" from Santa Fe, New Mexico--so the trail was there before them…..so more research that got me into the Aztec Empire and their treasures allegedly brought to the Uintas in 1521 to hide them from the Spaniards--with the Utes as the "guardians" of vast riches, and the Spaniards creating the trail in 1540 searching for Montezuma's treasure…..and all the legends now of 7 Spanish mines, the secret cave with

p. 203

Montezuma's treasure, then the Lost Rhoades mine, and even the involvement of Butch Cassidy and his Wild Bunch as bodyguards for one of the factions--those stories still to be told in this book. WOW! Not only did I discover that the Middle Fork was most likely a community of Swedish tie hackers, complete with their sweat houses, but I also discovered that it was sort of the final resting place of a real lover of the Uintas when in my search off-trail for clues about the tie hackers, I all of a sudden found a cross-- complete with obituary, a few pictures of which I'll insert below. Maybe you can read at least portions of it. I should have done better with my photography.

p. 204

Chapter 2: THE WILDERNESS AREA--North Slope

Section 6: THE MIDDLE FORK OF BLACKS FORK HOW TO GET HERE: See Section 7 No official trailhead, nor even any kind of sign announcing one of the most incredible drainages in the Uintas. Let me tell you how to find it, showing a few pictures as a guide, and I'll relate one of the impossible to explain experiences--leading to the word…."MIRACLE!"

We are seeing above the bridge over the West Fork of Blacks Fork, with a yellow arrow pointing at a gate in the fence 150 yards from the bridge, which in the middle photo I'm about to go through. Doesn't say where it goes, but believe me it goes 2 miles to what I'm calling unofficially the MIDDLE FORK OF BLACKS FORK TRAILHEAD. With my vehicle, that is 4WD, I make it safely 1 mile then--especially if it has been raining, I park and shoulder my backpack. Less than 1 mile from the barrier--that we'll call THE TRAILHEAD, you come out of the Lodgepole pines and beautiful Middle Fork with its pioneer type fences and beaver dams--with 13,165 ft. Tokewanna Peak in the distances opens up before us.

I've mentioned that I have found more ruins here of the Tie Hack Culture than anywhere else, so I keep a sharp eye out for them, and try and determine whether they are from the early period--1867-1880, or the late period. Do you remember the characteristics? Early period: Small, no windows, rocks in one corner indicating a fireplace, square nails, rather than round, and mostly rotted away. Same for stumps…..from the early period, rotted a lot, almost disappearing. And keep a sharp eye out for beautiful wildflowers. Fishing the stream can be a lot of fun, but if high alpine lakes is what you want, keep moving up towards the slopes of Tokewanna Peak, and Bob's Lake, 11,150 ft. elevation and get ready for very strong, hard hitting Tiger trout. From Bob's you can check out the other two remote lakes that seldom see a fisherman. Now the information:

p. 205

BOB'S LAKE (G-73): As you hike up the drainage the trail becomes sometimes difficult to find, especially after the last tie hack ruins, but you can't miss by following the main stream, and when other streams come in from the southeast, keep to the right and follow it around west of the ridge that comes off of Tokewanna Peak, and you'll find the lake as you can see below--8 miles from the barrier, 9 if you had to park your vehicle a bit lower. 11,156 ft. elevation, 6.6 acres, 30' deep, The DWR pamphlet says it has Cutthroats, but the two times I have been there I've caught only Tiger trout.

Bob’s Lake under 13,165 ft. high Tokewanna Peak

Tiger trout

LAKE G-72 : The best way to get to this small alpine lake that is about 50' in elevation higher than Bobs, is to go due east over the ridge in the left of the picture, or just skirt around the end of the ridge and go a bit south into the glacial cirque where it is found. 11,198 ft. in elevation, 1.3 acres, 6' deep. It was stocked experimentally with brook trout in 1984; a follow up survey in 1986 found no fish--winterkill suspected; stocking discontinued. LAKE G-74 : Go 1/4 mile north down a grassy slope to the lake at 10,934 ft. elevation, only 3' deep so subject to winterkill, with wary Brook trout. Aerial stocked in 2018: Stocked on a 3 year cycle. To return to the main canyon just follow the drainage north and you will come to the Middle Fork and cross it to follow the trail down the canyon.

On my 3rd trip to Middle Fork, I went doing my best to be scientific in exploring, going back and forth as I worked up the drainage to find 14 sites of the tie hackers. With each I photographed from every angle, measured with my tape measure, and used my SPOT TRACKER to pinpoint the exact location of each. On my return to civilization I went to a rest area in Mt. View, Wyoming to clean up myself and all my equipment, but in the process couldn't find the memory card from my Nikon camera with its wealth of photographic documentation. I meticulously went through everything, including every nook and cranny in my car, and in my trailer, and NOTHING! I was literally sick, but determined to go back up there and do it all over again! -- No small thing for a then 77 year old, tired fellow. I went in the restroom to clean my pot to begin another backpack, and as I was doing so I heard something drop onto the pot cover--as though from heaven--and looked down to see…mysteriously…..miraculously, my memory card! Wow how grateful I felt, and celebrated at the Maverick Convenience Store with a big Mt. Dew and a donut!

p. 206
