Chapter 2: THE WILDERNESS AREA- North Slope

Section 7: The EAST FORK OF BLACKS FORK ********************

PREFACE

HIGH ALTITUDE -- THE SILENT KILLER

Late in the backpacking season for the Uintas, around the 10th of September, 2006, I left for the East Fork of Blacks Fork Trailhead on the North Slope--the intention being to hike the 16 miles to the base of Explorer Peak at Crater Lake--the Uinta's deepest at 147 ft. and get up on the ridge to the north for that one "perfect picture" of this spectacular scene. I had attempted it earlier in the season, but a snow drift had always blocked my climb to the saddle. I had actually tried to do the trip a few days before and was camped out about 4 miles up the trail when hit with bad weather that had me quickly setting up my tent and crawling inside a bit earlier than normal. Things were wet and there were drips here and there, but during the night the dripping stopped, and I discovered why--I was sort of in an igloo of frozen tent, and I couldn't get a drink as the tube to my water bladder had frozen. Then I discovered I had forgotten one of the two crucial medications I needed to take every day, and ended up going down the trail driving home for the medication. Then headed back for the North Slope. That seemingly gave the weather a chance to warm up some--and I hoped it would continue as I drove again to the Trailhead and headed for the high country. No tent this time, just my poncho used as a shelter. I made it 10 miles to my alpine camp north of 13,219 ft. Mt. Lovenia.

p. 209

The next day I switched-backed up to the saddle which I have called East Fork Pass. I used to say it was 12,300 ft., but since have recognized it is only 12,150 ft. From that vantage point I took a couple of the most stunning photographs showing what I have called "the spine of the Uintas," as seen below, first from the pass looking at Mt. Lovenia enshrouded in a menacing sky; then a panorama looking west--as you can see it was late in the season, winter approaching.

From East Fork Pass I went down to 11,700 ft. Red Knob Pass and there quickly put on my waterproof pants, and poncho, then continued down into the teeth of the storm crossing arctic tundra towards Crater Lake, pelted by rain and then snow, but made it to the base of the mountain. But soon found myself attacked by multiple problems: I was beginning for the first time in my life having problems with my teeth, with pain on one side making necessary chewing with the other--but all of a sudden a molar on my chewing side became infected and was so painful that I couldn't chew anything on either side. I began cutting up everything in little pieces and swallowing it whole--and soon upset my stomach with terrible gamboo! That coupled with feeling like I had the flu--fever, weakness, body aches, headache. I went to my Emergency bag: Started a 5 day crash treatment of antibiotic ( Azithromycin); then took gobbs of Redmond Clay paste (Bentonite Clay), with lots of water to settle the stomach/gamboo problem; Then soaked two big pieces of cotton with dental anesthesia & triple antibiotic, wrapping it around my infected molars. Then laid flat out under my poncho/shelter in a protected area of pines.

p. 210

As I rested I listened to the news and weather report on my tiny Grundig radio, hearing that snow was on its way in 2 or 3 days. I used my sat phone to call and let family know I would maybe need some help, but up against the mountain I couldn't get a signal and wore out one of my two batteries. After 24 hours my molar pain went away and my stomach settled down, and I could eat again. I had to give the antibiotic one more day to begin taking effect, so kept resting. Climbing up to Crater Lake now forgotten, as I focused on one thing--SURVIVAL and getting back up over the mountain and down to the Trailhead. I recognized that getting up over that mountain and down the other side was to be one of the great tests of my life, and I prepared myself with a lot of prayer, but something else: I was going to literally laugh myself up over that mountain, by recording on my tiny recorder all the jokes from a special Readers Digest I had brought with, featuring Reese Witherspoon, and more importantly a section entitled, LAUGH MORE--LIVE LONGER! When my need became acute I would pray and then listen to the jokes and laugh myself up the mountain!

On the 3rd day at the foot of Explorer Peak, I decided I had to get out of there and packed up. I started north--carefully enough so that the sickness wouldn't become aware it had a great chance to knock me down for the count. Two hours later I was at the last pines before the vast sea of arctic tundra between me and the 12,150 pass I had to go over. I got out the sat phone and got a signal and soon had on the line my good friend Ted Packard. He in turn called the Forest Service to get the weather report, then phoned me back with their message: "DON'T TRY AND CLIMB THAT

MOUNTAIN OR YOU WILL DIE! WAIT UNTIL TOMORROW WHEN THE WEATHER WILL

p. 211

CLEAR FOR THE MORNING." I was also advised that there were two female Wilderness Rangers in the area and I saw them way up ahead of me, then they disappeared. I set up my bivouac camp there and waited. The next morning the sun was out--and I saw the Rangers way up high across the arctic tundra, but moving in the opposite direction and didn't see them again. I packed up quickly and headed for Red Knob Pass, and as I was approaching it I began feeling sick-headache, weakness, shortness of breath with a feeling like something heavy weighed down on my chest, but I pushed myself carefully and soon was moving along the ridge up to East Fork Pass. When almost there the storm hit me with a vengeance--gale force winds, snow stinging my face, and then almost everything seemed to fall apart, including a throbbing pain in my heart/lung area, pain down my left arm. I quickly swallowed my blood pressure medication, a double dose of nitroglycerin, and a couple of Endurolytes and I'm not sure what else. Up on East Fork Pass I was too concerned with survival to think about taking pictures, so later, with Photoshop, I superimposed myself on the pass scene, but didn't know how to create the blizzard!

And, as I moved along and started down I got on the sat phone calling Russ Smith from Skycall Satellite. Soon it was a conference call between me and him, plus the Summit County Sherriff, and the University of Utah AirMed Helicopter Rescue team. Russ told me how to get my coordinates off the phone and….then I lost the signal. I had to get down where the helicopter could land, and, if needed where I could camp with some protection--so returned to my little clump of alpine firs and took my pack off. Still no signal, but I left the phone on and waited. Then it rang, the voice on the line saying, "The

helicopter is 4 minutes away. Put something bright on the ground so they can find you." I spread my red bivouac bag out--with rocks to keep it from blowing away, and all of a sudden here came the helicopter--of course, as you might imagine, me jumping and waving my arms like crazy, but smart enough to not yell as you see them do in the movies. He sailed overhead and disappeared over the next mountain. He didn't see me. But I was in constant phone contact with the dispatcher at the University of Utah Hospital, and he with the pilot, so we got him turned around and he came back over me, but still couldn't see me. I yelled into the phone, "Tell him to get lower!" Which he did on the 3rd pass, and was soon landing.

p. 212

By then I had come down 1,300 feet in elevation, and had rested for 30 minutes--and actually felt real good--relatively speaking. So I just thanked them for coming and said, "Just take me down to the Trailhead and I'll

drive home and on Monday see the doctor!" "No way," they replied.

Then I really got jovial and said, "At least take me to the Lavell Edwards Stadium--the game

starts in 30 minutes!" By then they had wrestled me to the ground, hooking their instruments up to me, and said,

"The oxygen in your blood is only 50….it should be in the 90's. Your pulse rate is 130, and your blood pressure sky high!" They shut me up with an oxygen mask on my face, lifted me onto a stretcher and loaded me and my pack in, and we were off to Salt Lake and the U of U Hospital where you see my mirror image in the ceiling thing.

They checked me out and released me the next morning--apparently dropping down 7,500 feet in elevation did the trick. My son Jesse picked me up and we drove clear out to the Trailhead and I drove my car home. I had multiple problems, but aggravating everything--I have concluded since, was one of

several forms of a failure, or slowness of the respiratory system, to adjust to higher altitudes--what we call High Altitude Sickness. If I had of understood that better on that backpack I could have saved a lot of money, and worry for others, by just not stubbornly insisting on going over that mountain to get to my

p. 213

car--rather just HIKE DOWN LAKE FORK TO MOON LAKE, and from there with my Sat phone, or at the Lodge with their phone, call my son to come and get me. But, due to ignorance, I had to be rescued--that, even with my insurance, cost me $1,000-the actual bill being $10,000! And, it's not just me. A case in point from 2017. HEALTHY, YOUTH WHO PLAYED SPORTS--DIED IN THE UINTAS DUCHESNE COUNTY, Utah -- A Boy Scout from Salem died during a hiking excursion in the High Uintas Saturday, one day before his 18th birthday. According to a press release from the Duchesne County Sheriff's Office, 17-year-old Douglas Jeffery Julian died as his Boy Scout troop began trying to hike out of the mountains to get him medical attention for an apparent illness Saturday morning. The release states Julian would have turned 18 Sunday. While a medical examiner will work to determine the cause of death, authorities say at this point they believe altitude sickness was a factor. “That’s the only possible reason we have,” stated Lt. Jeremy Curry of the Duchesne County Sheriff's Office. “Right now we have no reason to believe it was anything else.” The press release states the teen and his troop were camped in the Chain Lakes area in Krebs Basin Thursday when Julian began to complain of nausea and a headache. The teen was still sick Friday night, and the group decided they would pack up early Saturday to hike back to the trailhead and get him some help. Saturday morning a Scout leader set out earlier than the group and hiked for 8 to 10 miles until he was able to get cell phone service and call for help. Dispatchers sent a medical helicopter upon receiving that call, but the teen was deceased when the helicopter arrived. Deputies later learned the teen lost consciousness and collapsed about 50 yards from the troop's campsite once they began hiking out Saturday morning. Members of the troop began CPR but were unable to revive the teen. Julian was flown to Uintah Basin Medical Center in Roosevelt, and from there his body will be taken to a medical examiner for an autopsy. Curry said all indications are that Julian was a young and healthy teenager with no prior history of illness or medical problems. The press release notes the teen played high school sports. "Investigators suspect he may have succumbed to altitude sickness," the press release state s.

82

NOTE: If the group had a SATELLITE PHONE, as I have recommended for all groups and solo backpackers, or even a SPOT TRACKER, he could have possibly been saved!

LETS TRY AND UNDERSTAND HIGH ALTITUDE PROBLEMS--RIGHT NOW! In the simplest of terms, it is: "one of several forms of a failure, or slowness of the respiratory system to adjust to higher altitudes--that we call high altitude sickness."83 The mildest form called ACUTE MOUNTAIN SICKNESS (AMS)-- The symptoms: feeling dizziness, weakness, headache, muscle aches, nausea--some say like having a hangover, or the flu. 82

https://fox13now.com/2017/08/05/utah-boy-scout-dies-during-trip-in-high-uintas-authorities-suspect-altitudesickness/ 83

My words from this article.

p. 214

A more serious type is HIGH ALTITUDE SICKNESS (HAS)--or HIGH ALTITUDE PULMONARY EDEMA (HAPE)--a buildup of fluid in the lungs that can be dangerous and even life threatening. The most severe form of altitude sickness is HIGH ALTITUDE CEREBRAL EDEMA (HACE) when there's fluid in the brain, which is life threatening, with symptoms like:  Headache  Dizziness  Nausea  Vomiting  Fatigue and loss of energy  Shortness of breath  Problems with sleep  Loss of appetite Symptoms come on from 12 to 24 hours after reaching higher elevations, and then get better within a day or two as your body adjusts to the change in altitude. Other symptoms can be:  Loss of coordination and trouble walking  A severe headache that doesn't get better with medication  A tightening in your chest  Confusion  Shortness of breath, even at rest  A cough that produces a white or pink frothy substance  Coma The above information comes from WebMD84

NOTE: With several of the above symptoms, when going to higher and higher elevations, one should consider one of the forms of high altitude sickness. The prescription medication, DIAMOX, can help your body adjust quicker as you ascend higher into the mountains, but in 2006--not part of my Emergency Bag--it is now. I have mentioned in some of my reports how I actually had to turn around and abort the backpack, like when I ran into Teresa, she yelling at me, "NO, YOU'RE DEAD!" 85 Further on I will relate an even earlier survival experience in which high altitude had some responsibility, but I didn't know about it then. Said, other experiences, will be very helpful to all--so take note, in Prefaces to Section 11 for Henry's Fork and Bivouac on Kings Peak, and another at Survival at Swasey Hole, in Section 19 for the Center Park Trailhead, p. 332. I now take with me an OXIMETER--seen below, which on Amazon only costs around $25, and as I ascend into the mountains I check myself at rest stops.

At home (elevation 4,500 ft.) the oxygen count in my blood is 96. When in the mountains I climb slowly, and if the count drops below 90 I rest just a little longer and it usually normalizes at least to 90. At higher elevations, some people might need to rest longer, even for a day, to have your body normalize. But, in the end of it doesn't adjust and you get worse, the only solution is GO DOWN! 84

https://www.webmd.com/a-to-z-guides/altitude-sickness#2

85

Page 72 of this writing

p. 215

To conclude this long, but EXTREMELY LIFE & DEATH SURVIVAL SUBJECT, I will briefly relate the experience of probably the best backpacker I have ever known, who was so good he had no reason to ever think about high altitude problems--nor his brothers who were with him. They consequently didn’t go into the wilderness prepared for the emergency. NOW THE STORY OF THE BEST BACKPACKER I'VE EVER KNOWN I'll maintain his privacy and give him another name…let's say, BOB. His brothers we'll call Joe and Ken. Bob--at the time of this event, was probably 76. On the South Slope of the Uintas they backpacked up the Swift Creek Trail, swung by Farmers Lake and on to 11,663 ft. Bluebell Pass, and continued up Yellowstone Canyon to the Highline Trail, following it west over Tungsten Pass and from there were to drop down through the above timberline basin—all above 11,000 ft. elevation, fishing as they looped back down into the canyon to the Trailhead. At Tungsten Lake Ken first noticed in his big brother possible “muscle coordination problems” as he was casting into the lake, but didn’t really think about it until later. From there Ken and Joe were to head down the trail to Superior Lake while Bob remained behind filtering some water and would catch up. But when Bob stood up from his filtering chore he all of a sudden was light headed and almost passed out. His pulse was rapid, erratic, breathing labored and he had no strength. He slowly headed down the trail. In the meantime his brothers noticed Bob hadn’t showed up and so they headed back up the trail to look for “the old man,” and in a couple of hundred yards found him, according to Ken, “sitting on the high side of the trail, his pack off behind him…head on the back of his hands…leaning on his hiking pole. As Joe approached and said something, Bob looked up, his eyes rolled back and he passed out. He quickly came to, but all of a sudden our adventure had changed!” His face was “chalk-white” as were his fingertips, his nose started bleeding, but soon stopped. Color would come back into his face, then change to “as grey as his mustache.” His heartbeat was over 120 per minute, and of most concern was irregular, erratic. 3/8/19 Pulse just corrected at a shocking 200/minute! In a moment of Bob feeling better he shouldered his pack and slowly moved down the trail, but only made 50 yards and had to sit for fear of passing out. They laid him down for a while, but erratic heartbeat continued at 200+. Bob commented, “All three of us thought I could die right there!” They talked about the problem likely being High Altitude Sickness. Joe and Ken talked about evacuation by helicopter…..and thought, “Cordell, we need your SPOT Tracker, or your satellite phone.” They were 15 miles from the trailhead. The only solution was MOVE DOWN. Joe and Ken took all of Bob’s gear, including his pack, and they headed down, Bob struggling, and by nightfall they’d made 2 miles in 2 hours. They had dropped to 10,000 ft. elevation and camped for the night. Bob’s pulse didn’t slow, and continued irregular all night. Ken said, “Prayers were said (I think by all).” The next day, Joe and Ken still carrying all of Bob’s gear, they dropped to about 9,000 ft. and crossed Yellowstone Creek. Bob felt better, his pulse down to 80. In another 15 minutes his pulse was at 70 the arrhythmia gone, and Bob said, “BOYS, IT’S GONE!” He then shouldered his pack, and left his brothers in his dust in the 10 miles remaining, waiting for them in the parking lot, and as they arrived, smiling said to them, “WHAT TOOK YOU BOYS SO LONG?” On return to his home on the Pacific Coast, Bob had two visits with a cardiologist, they deciding his “problems were all related to high altitude sickness” with no apparent lasting effects from the frightening experience, but Bob commenting, “I do believe it was related to my sudden (2-3 days) ascent from sea level, followed by hard, uphill hiking. FROM NOW ON IT’S GOING TO BE SLOW ACCLIMATIZING AT ALTITUDE FOR ME.” NOTE: See Appendix 15, page 679 for new information& full disclosure.

In my case, and in Bob’s, plus that of the 18 year old youth and leaders, ignorance played an important part, but you'll notice I was READY FOR ALL THE EMERGENCIES (except for the OXIMETER), and in the end, it was the SATELLITE PHONE I had got from Russ Smith,86 and him getting me help that saved my day--my life. Thanks Russ! 86

The EAST FORK OF BLACKS FORK TRAILHEAD

The East Fork of Blacks Fork officially has no fishable lakes, except for a note recently received from friend, Roger Wilson, a now retired DWR employee, and current Chairman of the Utah Anglers Coalition. He said: “There is a single lake in the …East Fork of Blacks Fork Drainage with fish…. containing a natural population of cutthroat. In the 80’s I encountered an old sign at the lake calling it, WAGONWHEEL.”

WAGONWHEEL LAKE (G-105): With the help of Matt McKell from the DWR, the lake has been identified and shown on the topo map on page 219. 10,797 ft. elevation, at the northeast foot of 13,156 ft. Wasatch Peak. Matt sent me a picture of G-105 I’ll insert below. He said: Lake G-105 is very remote...I have no idea why or how anyone would pull a wagon to it...it's at the top of the drainage and a little southeast of Tokewanna Peak, ………..it has a population of genetically pure Colorado River Cutthroat Trout. The lake has never been stocked and the population is entirely natural and native. Here's a link to a [Google Earth] map of its location... https://goo.gl/maps/CmrsUHbRFG72.

THE LEGEND OF BIGFOOT--SASQUATCH Hey, you logically thinking guys--DON'T TURN ME OFF! Even the SURVIVORMAN, Les Shroud, decided he had to be scientific about it and do his best to check it out, resulting in a TV series, available on Amazon.87 If I recall his last episode was in Utah near the Uinta Mountains. A DWR employee, Lee Fielding, was camping in the Elizabeth Mountain area, we have mentioned in this book, and he reported that one night something stormed though his

camp and scared all the horses away. The next morning, his horse would not go in a particular direction, and then he met a group of hunters in another camp who told him they were spooked by seeing something they described as a Bigfoot!88 My interest was sparked in the beginning years of my HIGH UINTAS WILDERNESS PROJECT when once on Google Earth I was zooming in on the Uinta Mountains, and without requesting it alleged sightings of Big Foot were highlighted, and I recall vividly that most of them were from Little East Fork of Blacks Fork. So, you can imagine that soon I had a backpack up that mysterious drainage. I announced my exploration's purpose, GIVING BIG FOOT A CHANCE TO FIND ME TO TAKE A FAMILY PORTRAIT!

I went with an open mind, camera ready, lens cap off. I purposely went off-trail and had quite a time doing my best to quietly STALK through the forest. My camp was for sure a stealth camp, as you see below.

But, it was all just good exercise, and I was determined that I'd go again, exploring the whole canyon, climbing Squaw Pass and fishing in Porcupine Lake, and then stalk back 87

https://www.amazon.com/Survivorman-Season-6/dp/B00VK2UN6S

88

That incident and a list of alleged sightings: http://www.bfro.net/gdb/show_article.asp?id=184

p. 225

through--always with the camera ready. I actually announced my intention with a colorful opening page for the YouTube video I would make….as by then I had a digital Nikon capable also of taking good quality video.

Squaw Pass in the background

I'll add a link to the YouTube video. 89 I made it to the pass, and down to Porcupine Lake, and, as mentioned a few pages ago, caught some of the most colorful brook trout I've caught anywhere. On my way back going downhill it was easier to hike quietly, without the deep breathing, so I figured my chances of seeing Big Foot were increased--so I was ready.

Then as I was going down a ravine, I decided to stop in the shade and rest some, so took my pack off, setting my camera on a rock within easy reach, and got comfortable…… when

all of a sudden Big Foot appeared! Neither of us seemed surprised, nor scared and we attempted to communicate with sign language. I was asking him about his wife, and children, which he couldn't understand, but when I asked about what they ate--I used the sign language for eating used among the Indians in Guatemala, and he understood. He sort of got into a prancing position, like a deer running through the trees, he after him and jumped on his back and he made a sort of wrenching movement, like breaking its neck. Then, all of a sudden his son, Little Foot, appeared but riding a horse, and I recalled that a year or so ago a sheep herder had lost a horse up here. With this incredible scene I carefully--without frightening them, was attempting to manipulate my camera with just one hand and hope to be getting some pictures.

89

BIG FOOT in the Uintas Little East Fork of Blacks Fork: http://youtu.be/dyRAoXlkvCQ

p. 226

Then they communicated to each other--sort of laughing and pointing at me and my equipment--like saying, "These humans are so weak. They can't survive up here without their Osprey backpack, or their REI convertible pants, their Big Agnes tent, Golite sleeping quilt, and Salomon trail running shoes! We do just great without any of that--how pathetic are these humans!" With that they turned and without a goodbye headed towards the forest, and I lunged for my camera to at least get a shot of them before disappearing………do you see him…it?

Photoshop reconstruction of scene

……….. but, in lunging for the camera I knocked it off the rock, and it clattered down into the rocks…..and woke me up! But, it was so real, I thought, "Maybe I really did see all of that, and hopefully got some

pictures to prove it." I checked the camera and there was nothing--except I noticed that the fall had cracked the skylight filter--but saved my lens.

I sat there amazed and thought, "It was like the ancient prophets receiving visions in

dreams! Maybe the Lord was telling me there might just be something to the legends, so keep an open mind."

p. 227

But I then settled back to reality, which had "the giant" transformed into just a normal sized Rob Wilcox, mountain runner. We talked and I told him what had happened, and clicked off another shot of him as he was saying,

To get to this side canyon of East Fork of Blacks Fork, you leave the Trailhead crossing the bridge and then head south up the canyon, hiking for 1.3 miles where you cross the stream and then come to a fork in the trail, and take the left hand trail. If you keep your eyes open you'll start noticing many lodge pole pine stumps, at least 8" in diameter, Some are almost rotted away and you can be sure they are from the 1867-1880 period, and others still in fair shape from 1912-1936. There are no lakes along the trail that leads to Squaw Pass, rather they are all up on a high bench to the southwest of the stream, the first lake is in the pines……

…..to the right in the forested area in the above photo, the rest above timberline--or above the line of pines.

The third photo, below, is taken from the trail as it climbs the pass--the last two lakes are up high amidst the arctic tundra below the peaks.

The lowest, is accessed by an unmarked trail, after the 2nd ford of the stream. approximately 3.7 miles from the junction with the main trail, or 5 miles from the Trailhead. About 1-1/4 miles from the 2nd ford, there is a park with a small stream coming from the west and an unmarked, indistinct trail leading up SW 3/4 mile to the lake. LAKE G-69: 11,109 ft. elevation, 4.8 acres, 13' deep, accessible on horseback from main trail. Cutthroat trout sustain by natural reproduction.

View, Wyoming-- 6 miles on CR-410 towards Robertson, but go south on CR-283, for 7 miles then turn right on CR-285 for about 1-1/4 miles when the road enters Forest Service lands and becomes FR075 for 8 miles when you come to FR-073 and turn west for 2 miles to the Hewinta road--FR-209 you follow south for about a mile to Hewinta, and about 1/2 mile more to the Trailhead. From the West Smiths Fork Trailhead, you follow the trail 5 miles past the tie hacker camps, then cross the Wilderness Boundary, and continue south to the North Slope Highline Trail. From there you head southwest towards Bald Mountain for 1.5 miles to the lake. TOTAL 6.3 miles.

The first a steep climb, then dropping down, but hiking though beautiful alpine tundra--a wonderful hike. The West Fork, a gradual climb, and 1 mile less, while seeing lots of the Tie Hacker Culture. Section 10: EAST FORK OF SMITHS FORK *******************

PREFACE

The MOUNTAIN MAN of ALL MOUNTAIN MEN! In 2005 TNT presented a mini-series, that deeply impressed me--one of the first events in the movie depicted the famous experience of one of my youthful heroes, Jedediah Smith, being attacked by a huge grizzly bear--which I'll mention in a moment.

I was so impressed that I dedicated about a month of my life making VHS copies of that whole mini-series, and giving dozens of them to my family as their Christmas present. "DIAH" as he was often called by his friends, was born on January 6, 1799, in a family that were a breed of hard working, God-fearing, farmers and artisans that had just been part of the great 1776 Revolution, and infused with the desire for " greener pastures" in the movement towards the West, moving from New York, to Erie, Pennsylvania, and on to Ohio. Diah, the 4th of a group of 12 siblings, was given a second name, as often us parents do giving a special name to our kids in hopes they will follow in the footsteps of whoever, his second name being his mother's maiden name, STRONG, and with Jedediah--IT WORKED! The Smiths were tough frontiersmen, but Sallie Strong, was also from a breed apart, one of her relatives becoming the first to go over Niagara Falls, and live to tell about it! JEDEDIAH STRONG SMITH, even though living a short life of 32 years, would not disappoint. Most of the story I tell here comes from the first, well done biography of his life, I'll insert a picture of below.92

92

JEDEDIAH SMITH and the Opening of the West, by Dale L. Morgan, University of Nebraska Press, 1953.

p. 237

He grew up, working hard alongside his family, but helped the family also by hunting deer and squirrels, and while still in his teens was given a book that would inspire and guide him all of his life--an 1814 book about the famous 1804-06 first exploration all the way to the Pacific by Lewis & Clark. From then on Jedediah would carry this book with him always. His family had little money and so Diah followed his destiny west, and in 1922, at 23, found himself in St. Louis, Missouri. It was a booming frontier town because of the fur trade that was beginning far to the west in the Rocky Mountains. On February 13, 1822 the Missouri Gazette & Public Advertiser, had an advertisement that read: TO: Enterprising Young Men The subscriber wishes to engage ONE HUNDRED MEN, to ascend the river Missouri to its source, there to be employed for one, two or three years.--For particulars enquire of Major Andrew Henry, near the Lead Mines, in the County of Washington, (who will ascend with and command the party) or to the subscriber at St. Louis. Wm H. Ashley

Jedediah, contacted General William H Ashley and was accepted to go with him and Major Henry, as a "hunter." Ashley and Henry were adventurous men who believed they could become rich with the fur industry. Ashley had no experience in the West, but Henry had in 1808 as a partner in the Missouri Fur company, spent 3 years penetrating the headwaters of the Missouri, crossing the Continental Divide to the Snake and Lewis Rivers and established a post, but problems, not the least of which were with the Blackfeet and the war of 1812 with England, had driven them out of the mountains. Now they were organizing to return. Their names should be familiar to all who know the Uinta Mountains, as the South Slope is made up of the Ashley National Forest; The Henry Fork Drainage on the North Slope named after Major Henry, and the Uinta's Henry's Fork River, that later became the site of the First Mountain Man Rendezvous in 1825. The SMITHS FORK of the Green River, which we are dealing with in this section of the book, is named after Jedediah, as is the unofficial naming by me of Utah's 5th highest mountain, 13,387 ft. high MOUNT JEDEDIAH. I'll close this historical report with that mountain. Now, back to the history. Their first boat left St. Louis on April 3, 1822 led by Major Henry. Jedediah was on the 2nd boat, the Enterprize, that left on May 8, 1822. Their boats were "keelboats," propelled up the river by a square sail when the wind was right, then in deep water by twelve oars, six on each side. In shallow water the men would propel the boat forward with long poles, setting each pole and putting their shoulders into the task, each moving towards the stern, then move back for another set on each side. In certain situations they would resort to a cordelle, a thick rope on each bank pulled by the men moving them slowly up stream. The furry of Mother Nature was launched against them: Mosquitoes, wood ticks, nettles, climbing roses, buckthorn, etc. Jedediah, as a hunter was spared from some of the

p. 238

struggle, once in a while getting a deer, a turkey or a hog he would drag to the river's edge to be picked up; eventually his game would include bear, elk and bison. Another big chapter was their dealings with the Indians: The Mandans, the Rees, Kiowas, Sioux, Arikaras and more. Often the fatigue was so much that Diah couldn't sleep at night. It all sounds quite impossible. In fact they did meet with disaster and lost the Enterprize, salvaged what they could and set up a camp waiting for Ashley to send help. Eventually Jedediah was with a group that got horses from Indians and went overland, finally getting to the confluence of the Missouri and Yellowstone Rivers on October 1st, where Henry had built a fort--where by agreement began the Rocky Mountains. The replacement boat arrived two weeks later. Ashley then returned to organize the next year's trip, Henry remaining to get the men organized to begin trapping--as it was beaver pelts that would produce enough for expenses and the profit, which eventually would come. It can be said, this effort was the opposite of expeditions like Lewis & Clark--sent and financed by the government. All of Jedediah's amazing explorations and adventures over the next 9 years had to be paid for with beaver pelts--very similar to everything the Andersen Family Private Peace Corp accomplished over 50 years in Guatemala-- paid for by the sweat of our brows--producing and selling eggs, panela, broiler chickens, milk, butter, cheese, coffee beans and more.93 Even though Ashley & Henry's green recruits included many of the West's greatest, like Jim Bridger, yet in just one year--in 1823--Jedediah was head and shoulders above them all and named captain of one of two teams of 40 men. A year later he was Ashley's partner, and in another year--until he quit the Rockies, a senior partner--and, even though very young, was honored with the nickname "Old Jed!" Many were the accomplishments of Jedediah, but first perhaps was the re-discovery of South Pass, Wyoming. Described as: South Pass is the lowest point on the Continental Divide between the Central and Southern Rocky Mountains. The passes furnish a natural crossing point of the Rockies. The historic pass became the route for emigrants on the Oregon, California, and Mormon trails to the West.94

It had been overlooked by Lewis & Clark, their route taking them farther north, but South Pass had been discovered in 1812, then sort of forgotten, until the time of Jedediah Smith. Next, in moving south came the search for the Green River, they called Seeds-kee-dee, Siskadee, or Shetskedee, they not being the discoverers but, when they got to the Green River Valley on April 19, 1824 they concluded it was as fine a country for beaver as they

had found in the West.95 93

http://www.guatemalanfoundation.org/2018/05/the-final-report-twelve-strong-what_20.htm l

94

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Pass_(Wyoming)

95

JEDEDIAH SMITH and the Opening of the West, by Dale L. Morgan, p.93

p. 239

In exploring its tributaries in 1925 Ashley and his party moved southwest, and "Far to the

south, forty to fifty miles, the jagged crest of a mountain range lifted along the sky, the snowy heights glinting through the blue distances. Small wonder Jedediah Smith had ridden off in that direction the year before (1824)." Ashley was seeing the Uinta Mountains for the first time, where Jedediah and others had trapped beaver the year before, when with a party of eleven they had got to the Green River on April 19, 1824. They then divided into two groups to trap the head branches of the river "as far as Blacks Fork and made his hunt on that stream and its tributaries……it

is significant that one of the head branches of Blacks Fork has always been known as Smiths Fork." 96 So, our journey with Jedediah Smith, has now brought us back to where we started, on Smiths Fork of the Green River, and we'll bring it to a conclusion for this book--hoping that the tidbits I'm giving you will stimulate your interest to learn more, by telling the quite unbelievable story--vividly shown in INTO THE WEST, of the grizzly bear attack and its outcome. That amazing story will pretty well prepare us to believe the next point: A listing of the main accomplishments of this young mountain man, and a short paragraph about his character. I was going to quote the person who wrote a detailed description of the ordeal, Jim Clyman,97 but it is quite long, so we'll settle for a summarized version.98 On his second expedition, he was attacked by a grizzly bear. The bear…mauled Smith violently, throwing him to the ground, smashing his ribs, and literally ripping off his scalp. When the attack was over, the scalp was hanging on to his head by an ear. Smith instructed Jim Clyman to sew it back on. Clyman did the best he could, but thought nothing could be done for the severed ear. Smith insisted that he try. According to Clyman: "I put my needle sticking it through and through and over and over laying the lacerated parts together as nice as I could with my hands." After two weeks of rest, Smith resumed his duty as captain of the party.

Another version describes it this way: Smith and his party were the first Euro-Americans to explore the southern Black Hills, in present[30] day South Dakota and eastern Wyoming. While looking for the Crow tribe to obtain fresh horses and get westward directions, Smith was attacked by a large grizzly bear. Smith was tackled to the ground by the grizzly breaking his ribs. Members of his party witnessed him fight the bear, which ripped open his side with its claws and took his head in its mouth. When the bear retreated, Smith's men ran to help him. They found his scalp and ear ripped off, but he convinced a friend, Jim Clyman, to sew it loosely back on, giving him directions. The trappers fetched water, bound up his broken ribs, and cleaned his [31] wounds. After recuperating from his bloody wounds and broken ribs, Smith wore his hair long to [32] cover the large scar from his eyebrow to his ear. The only known portrait of Jedediah Smith, painted 99 after his death in 1831, showed the long hair he wore over the side of his head, to hide his scar. 96

Ibid. p. 94, 161,

97

Ibid. p.84

98

99

p. 240

JEDEDIAH SMITH'S MAJOR ACCOMPLISHMENTS 1. Re-discovery of SOUTH PASS 2. First man to reach California overland from the American frontier--in an amazing journey following basically Interstate 15, attacked by Indians, loosing almost all of his men, and all of their horses, crossing the Mohave Desert on foot. 3. The first to cross the Sierra Nevada following basically U.S. Highway 6 across Nevada to Utah. 4. The first to cross the length and width of the Great Basin. 5. The first to reach Oregon by a journey up the California coast. 6. Jedediah Smith, Sublette & Jackson were the first to take wagons to the Rocky Mountains.100 7. Survived the three worst disasters of the American fur trade: The Arikara defeat in 1823; the Mojave massacre of 1827; and, the Umpqua massacre of 1828, in which no less than forty men fell around him.

UNIQUE LIKE NO OTHER MOUNTAIN MAN In the INTRODUCTION I mentioned this great man and the mountain I have given his name in the Uintas, saying, He was unique among unbelievably tough mountain men and explorers, famous for carrying his Bible, “…didn’t use tobacco, liquor, never swore, and stayed away from loose women…” 101

Dale Morgan in his final chapter says: "Jedediah made the lone wilderness his place of meditation, the mountaintop his altar, and he made religion an active, practical principle, from the duties of which nothing could seduce him. His firm belief that faith must find expression in works emerges…." 102

In 1831 he returned to St. Louis having made a good profit--finally, from the sale of furs of around $17,000 (approximately $4 million in 2011), bought a house there, to be shared with his brothers, and, very aware of his family's needs, sent money to his family with which his brother Ralph was able to purchase a farm, and prepared a document which provided his father would receive an annuity of $200 the rest of his life. He then launched himself into one more project, accompanied by two brothers, Peter and Austin. It was a trading expedition to Santa Fe, in the Mexican Provinces. With Ashley helping him, the State Department issued him a passport, and a certificate of good character. 100

JEDEDIAH SMITH and the Opening of the West, by Dale L. Morgan, p.322

101

From, UTAH, 5 edition, p. 54 by Tom & Gayen Wharton

102

JEDEDIAH SMITH and the Opening of the West, by Dale L. Morgan, p.311

th

p. 241

They left St. Louis with a party of 74 men, twenty-two mule-drawn wagons, with others joining them later, leaving on April 10, 1831. They began having problems when several hundred mounted Comanche's made a charge on their wagons, scared off by firing a six-pound canon. Later in "the most dreaded stretch of the Santa Fe trail" which area was in the middle of a drought, they began having an impossible time finding water. Jedediah and another went searching, then divided, and Jedediah was never seen again. A fruitless search was made, then the company went on to Santa Fe. There, Mexicans, who traded with the Comanche's, on May 27, 1831 arrived at Santa Fe carrying his pistols and rifle, and recounted what they had been told. Jedediah was confronted by a hunting party of between 15-20 Comanche's. They paid no attention to his signs of peace and fired hitting him near his left shoulder. He leveled his rifle and killed the chief, and was then rushed by the Comanche's with their lances. Morgan ends his biography with:

"….yet was he modest, never obtrusive, charitable, 'without guile,' ……a man whom none could approach without respect, or know without esteem. And though he fell under the spears of the savages, and his body has glutted the prairie wolf, and none can tell where his bones are bleaching, he must not be forgotten."

LETS NOT FORGET HIM I have done my part in helping that this great mountain man and explorer of the West not be forgotten in Utah, by naming the previously no-name, 5th highest mountain in the Uintas (and Utah), 13,387 ft. high, MOUNT JEDEDIAH, we see on the next page, at the head of the Uinta River Drainage's Painter Basin, under Trail Rider Pass, and just down the ridge from Kings Peak, and at its foot no-name lake U-75. I hope and pray that the name will stick--it will with me. Up above 1,000 feet in elevation and 1 mile from lake U-75 is found Little Andy Lake. Also honoring this courageous young man: The Jedediah Smith Wilderness, the western slope of Wyoming's Teton Range; The Jedediah Smith Redwood State Park, in California; The Smith River National Recreation Area in Northern California; The Jedediah Smith Memorial Bicycle Trail in California; The Jedediah Smith Society, University of the Pacific; The Taming of the Wild West: The Legend of Jedediah Smith, documentary (2005), etc.103

CHAPTER 2: THE HIGH UINTAS WILDERNESS AREA--North Slope

Section 10: The EAST FORK OF SMITHS FORK

HOW TO GET HERE: From Kamas to North Slope Rd., 50 miles, then on FR-058 21 miles to FR-073 and continue 13.5 miles to China Meadows, TOTAL 81 miles from Kamas--121 from SLC. From Mt. View, Wyo. 6-7 miles on CR-410 towards Robertson, then go south on CR-283, for 7 miles to a fork and turn right on FR-072 and follow signs about 15 miles to China Meadows. Total= 29 miles from Mt. View--74 from Evanston, and 154 from SLC.

This area of the High Uintas has to be considered the most stunning area in the entire Uinta Range. We have already seen it in a BIG LOOP hike from the East Fork of Blacks Fork Trailhead in Section 7, returning to that Trailhead by way of the Bald Mountain Trail from the Red Castle Area. From this Trailhead, we will also introduce another LOOP by way of Kings Peak and the Henrys Fork Basin, and back to this Trailhead. But we'll begin with Option 1, a simple hike just in the Red Castle Area, seen below in a stunning view of Red Castle Peak with Lower Red Castle Lake in the foreground. Then details of the all the lakes.

OPTION #1: From TH to first bridge, 1.7 miles, then at 3.7 miles the No. Slope Highline Trail going east, with a possible side trip of 1.6 miles to the Hessie Lake area, but back to

p. 244

the main trail, at 7.6 miles the 2nd bridge. From there a steep climb up to above timberline and the junction with the Bald Mt. Trail at 8.8 miles. From there I suggest making the 10.2 mile Loop of all the Red Castle lakes, taking the left hand trail to Smiths Pass Lake, and there at 3 miles leaving the trail to go west to lake G-45, and then to East Red Castle Lake, which I'll insert a panel of pictures of below, including a magnificent Cutthroat trout I caught there--very heavy bodied and 19-1/2 inches long.

From East Red Castle, you continue off-trail, going down around the mountain--quite easily done if you're careful, and cross the stream above Lower Red Castle Lake and to the trail, continuing up to the jewel of them all--Red Castle Lake--a stunning panorama you see on page 74. On my last backpack there in 2004 on July 4th, I caught on successive casts three 16" native cutthroat trout, but then my hands were so cold I had to continue up to Upper Red Castle Lake--my main objective, a picture of you see below.

Why was this lake my main objective?

In 1962 Ted Packard and myself left the Center Park Trailhead on the South Slope, hiked up through the Garfield Basin to Porcupine Pass, and from there--somehow--skirted around the end of 13,095 ft. Mt. Wilson to dry ski down a chute, barely visible on the upper left of the above picture. As we were going down we noticed fish surface action in the lake and began catching very large cutthroat trout. Then we went down to the east side of Red Castle Lake where we camped on the cliffs high above the lake. The next day we hiked back up to the upper lake, and eventually I hooked the lunker of them all--for an alpine lake, seen below -- very heavy bodied, 21 inches long. (continued next page)

p. 245

We buried him in a snow bank, un-cleaned, to be able to take him out and get an accurate live weight. The next day we went to get him, and as we approached the snow bank, a marmot jumped down from the snow bank. I know marmots are not carnivorous, but something ate the heavier head half of my fish along with the guts. I lugged the lighter tail half to civilization by way of Smiths Fork Lake Pass. It weighed 3-1/2 lbs. Considering the head half would have been heavier, plus the guts, the weight had to exceed 8 lbs. So, I wanted to try it once more in 2004, but an iced in lake on July 4th stopped me. Now, back to our OPTION #1: From Upper Red Castle Lake, you backtrack down past Red Castle Lake, and continue down to the junction where the Loop began--a total of 10.1 miles, then back to the Trailhead for a total of around 28 miles--and a few miles more if you did the Hessie Lake loop. ONE OF THE MOST AMAZING BACKPACKS YOU WILL EVER EXPERIENCE. Now the details of all those lakes, plus a few others off-trail: HESSIE (G-18): Access 1.5 miles southeast on No. Slope Highline Trail, from the Red Castle Trail then 1/4 mile west to the lake. 10,620 ft. elevation, 13.2 acres, 18' deep, Cutthroat & Tiger trout via. LAKE G-58: Tiny 1.3 acre lake on Hessie outlet stream 5' deep, Cutthroat trout. LAKE G-59: 1/2 mile south of Hessie Lake, 10,740 ft. elevation, 3.2 acres, 24' deep, Brook trout. LAKE G-60: 250 yards south of stream crossing in Hessie Lk Basin, 10,500 ft. elevation, 2.5 acres, 9' deep, Brook & Tiger trout. LAKE G-61: 1/8th mile south of G-60 up steep timbered ridge following G-60's major inlet stream. 10,669 ft. elevation, 3.1 acres, 6' deep. With Brook trout recently stocked again. LAKE G-50: Situated 6.25 miles from Trailhead on the Red Castle Trail, to Broadbent Meadows then 1/2 mile west up the steep timbered ridge to the lake. 10,639 ft. elevation, 3.7 acres, 5' deep, Brook trout. LAKE G-51: Access is 7-1/4 miles from the Trailhead on the Red Castle Trail to the 2nd bridge. Without crossing the bridge follow an obscure trail southeast around a timbered ridge and across an open meadow for about 1 mile to the lake. 10,620 ft. elevation, 8.1 acres, 5' deep, with Brook trout.

NOW THE RED CASTLE LOOP -- Going east towards Smiths Fk Pass Lake LAKE G-13: Accessed 1 mile SE and visible from the Smiths Fk. Pass Trail. 10,860 ft. elevation, 7.9 acres, 17' deep, Fishing variable for Brook trout. SMITHS FK PASS (G-14): 2.5 miles from footbridge on Smiths Fk Pass Trail. 11,152 ft. elevation, 26.1 acres, 17' deep, Cutthroat & Tiger trout. LAKE G-45: Located 1/8th mile northwest of Smiths Fk Pass Lake, 11,220 ft. elevation, 3.1 acres, 12' deep, stocked with Brook trout. EAST RED CASTLE (G-17): Located 3/8th mile northwest of Smiths Fk Pass Lake, 11,190 ft. elevation, 21.1 acres, 58' deep, huge wary Cutthroat & Tiger trout. Lake G-49: Located on Lower Red Castle Lake inlet stream, 1/2 mile above lake, and 100 yards east of the trail's stream crossing. 10,830 ft. elevation, 3.9 acres but fluctuating, 11' maximum depth, varied population of brook, cutthroat and rainbow trout. Often overlooked by fishermen. RED CASTLE (G-15): Located 11 miles from TH. 2nd largest and deepest lake in the Uintas. Found at end of trail from Lower Red Castle Lake. 11,295 ft. elevation, 168 acres, 103' deep, Cutthroat & Tiger trout UPPER RED CASTLE (G-16): Located 1/8 mile above Red Castle Lake. 11,542 ft. elevation, 25 acres, 72' deep, Stocked with Cutthroat trout. Here is where I caught a heavy bodied 8 lb. Cutthroat trout.

p. 246

LOWER RED CASTLE (G-12): Located 9 miles from the TH at the foot of Red Castle Peak. 10,758 ft. elevation, 45 acres, 28' deep, Fishing pressure is heavy. Stocked with Rainbow trout, but Cutthroat and Brook trout also in lake.

OTHER OPTIONS: A BIG LOOP backpack has already been described in Section 7 from the East Fork of Blacks Fork Trailhead, to Crater Lake, then up the Oweep Drainage to Porcupine Pass, down through the upper reaches of the Garfield Basin, then over Smiths Fork Lake Pass, looping around the Red Castle Lakes, and then back to the East Fork of Blacks Fork Trailhead, via the Bald Mt. Trail. ANOTHER OPTION: BIG LOOP from the China Meadows Trailhead to the Red Castle Lakes Loop in reverse, coming out at the Smiths Fork Pass, then over to Anderson Pass and Kings Peak, then over Gunsight Pass to the Henrys Fork Basin, swinging around the upper lakes and down to the North Slope Highline Trail and back to the China Meadows Trailhead for a total of 42 miles. Section 11: THE HENRYS FORK & KINGS PEAK *************************

PREFACE

SURVIVAL

In 2004, during the 2nd season of my HIGH UINTAS WILDERNESS PROJECT, I made backpacks in July to the Red Castle and another to the Rock Creek areas, and mid-month, while walking across the kitchen in our Springville rental home, my "motorcyle knee" collapsed and I fell to the floor. A few days later surgery was performed to give me temporary relief, but I was told that eventually I would have to have complete knee replacement surgery.

By 6 weeks I was supposed to increase my therapy to begin carrying light loads on my back, but at that date, at the end of August, I was scheduled to be bivouacking on the slopes of Kings Peak to get unique photos with a sliver of a moon. So I rescheduled my therapy, speeding it up some, and by the end of August was in Henrys Fork limping towards Gunsight Pass, and then set up my bivouac camp on Kings Peak.

p. 252

It had taken me two days to get there--the first day doing about 8-9 miles and feeling as though I was getting sick, and unable to eat, but after taking my recovery supplements, felt alright and was able to eat, and the next day went on to Kings Peak where I again didn't feel too good, as it had been 6 weeks since getting any real significant exercise, but I took my recovery supplements I had learned on my long expedition really did the trick, and within two hours I felt like eating. Sleep was a bit difficult, and I once in a while was awakened with shortness of breath, but got through the night. The next day I wanted to go down to the little no-name lake (U-75) at the foot of the mountain I would eventually name Mount Jedediah, as on my expedition I had caught there a very large brook trout, and figured any survivors would really be big. So I did a 1.5 mile day hike, down 1,000 feet in elevation to the 11,400 ft. high lake, but as I was picking my way off-trail down through arctic tundra, I began feeling very sick. My digestive system was topsy-turvy, with gamboo, and I had a fever and a persistent headache, as well as continually getting weaker. But I was close to the lake and persisted and made it, and with one cast--in a flash, realized I couldn't have cared less about fishing. I had to concentrate on my SURVIVAL! I had an emergency antibiotic treatment--a Z-Pack of Azithromycin, and, even though I didn't really know much about high altitude sickness, did have in my Emergency kit, a bottle of Azetazolamide or Diamox, to help the respiratory system speed up acclimatization to higher altitudes. BUT THEY WERE IN MY TENT, 1.5 miles away and 1,000 feet higher, that--the way I felt, it seemed like a million miles away!

I looked up where I had to get to….and then raised my gaze to the heavens in very sincere prayer to the Creator, and instantly my mind was flooded with my motto: "NEVER, NEVER, NEVER GIVE IN!" I hadn't added yet at the end of that….EASILY! I knew that with the help of the Lord I had to make it! As I carefully started taking step, by step tackling that giant mountain, a prayer remained in my heart and I began going through what some at the seeming end of their lives go through: A life review. Mine entailed out loud talking to the Lord about crucial periods of my life, and at times my words were of confession, and remorse, asking for forgiveness, and at times of triumph and gratitude. It was getting steeper and harder, my strength on the verge of failing, and I had flash into my mind that unforgettable NBA Championship game between the Jazz and Michael Jordan in Salt Lake City when Jordan was visibly sick with the flu, but time after time made incredible moves and scored but with not even a hint of a smile on his face--he was obviously suffering, but determined and ending up beating the Jazz, him scoring 38 points! As I recalled that and was encouraged, I thought about the I.V.'s, and who knows what else was helping him get the job done--and I only had my

p. 253

determination, and my miraculous life-saving experiences--that convinced me of the helping hand of the Lord--who kept reminding me of events observed and experienced that filled me with determination. I gratefully made it just as a few snowflakes swirled around in the high, cold winds. Wow, what a heavenly refuge my tiny tent was, and soon with a few supplements and medications I began feeling awfully lucky. I got on my sat phone and called the family letting them know I was having serious problems but would probably be alright--and would rest there for a couple of days letting the antibiotic begin taking effect, and then carefully head for civilization.

Above is a conglomeration of some of the things I take, just in case, plus others I don't have pictures of at the moment--and especially back at that early time, I didn't have things like an Oximeter that I now don't go without, but you've got to go prepared. Back in 2004 I didn't have a SPOT Personal Satellite Tracker, you see above, but from the beginning of my project, I've always had the satellite phone--once afterwards actually using it for my own safety as related in the Preface to Section 7, but prior to that--on my expedition, it was useful in saving on two occasions Boy Scouts who had fallen and hurt themselves, and my Sat phone was used by the leaders in each case to call for help. Almost all of the lives lost

in recent years could have been saved if a satellite phone had of been part of their equipment. BACK TO KINGS PEAK: I rested for two complete days, but did have difficulty sleeping as once again I would often be awakened because of shortness of breath that awakened me feeling like I was suffocating. My heart beat stuttered at times, but I was used to it since about 1994. On the afternoon of the 2nd day of rest, or my 5th day of the backpack, I decided I would test my ability to hike out the next day by going up to Anderson Pass and down just a bit on the western side to get a picture at sunset of the peak--one of the mountains of gold I've mentioned, which you can see below.

p. 254

I wondered whether I'd be able to carry my backpack, but knew it had to go with me as in my condition there was no way I could do the whole 16 miles in one day. I started carefully--it being the first time I felt I had to be sneaky and take it so easy that

the sickness wouldn't become aware it had a great opportunity to take me down for the count. I rested often, but found I couldn't really rest much as each time I would doze off, I was then awakened with a suffocating feeling. I finally made it down to the meadows of Painter Basin and became a little lax and stumbled once, turning my left ankle. I was already limping with my right "football ankle," and operated on "motorcycle knee," but now had to continue LIMPING WITH BOTH LEGS! I kept moving up towards Gunsight Pass, trying to laugh myself along--remembering that in one of my last running's of the International Half Marathon in Coban, Guatemala, it was said that, "Andersen crossed the finish line running as fast as he could, limping with both

legs, and dragging one behind him!" I finally made the 8 miles to the Dollar Lake area and set up my tent, then called my daughter, Julie, to let the family know I was alright. I fixed my first cooked, hot meal in all those days, and prepared to hopefully relax that night.

As I laid there waiting for my fatigue to doze me off--I began calculating at what time the next day my slow, deliberate pace would get me to the Trailhead and my car…..when, all of

a sudden it felt like my heart was being jabbed repeatedly with a sharp butcher knife. I grabbed desperately my chest with all my strength feeling that if I didn't it would burst! And, I frantically shouted out an intense prayer,

"FATHER IN HEAVEN, MANY STILL DEPEND ON ME……HELP ME!" At that instant, my hands desperately clutching my chest, I literally felt my heart jumping around inside my chest….and then the pain stopped! I slowly released the chest pressure, finally removing my hands and just laying there staring up into the blackness of the night and offered once again a prayer of gratitude. I got through the night without further complications, and….even though very slow the next day I made the 8 miles to the Trailhead by 5:00 PM……….. ………….BUT I MADE IT AND WAS ALIVE.

p. 255

I drove to Fort Bridger and the welcome comfort and refuge of the: I noticed that night my irregular/stuttering heart beat was gone, and pulse very regular, and it has continued that way until today, March 23, 2019— the day I hope to have the book presented to the world—through my website. Back in Springville/Provo, Utah I was checked out thoroughly by a Cardiologist, and his Nurse Practitioner, and in the tests they ran finally concluded that I had experienced a cardiac event, but there didn't seem to be any permanent damage, in fact the irregular heart beat I had for years all of a sudden had disappeared. I started taking a very small dose of a blood pressure medication, and told I should always have with me some tiny little tablets of

nitroglycerin. CONCLUSIONS: At the time of the 2004 event described, I didn't have a good understanding of high altitude problems--described in the Preface to Section 7, which I had never experienced before. I conclude now, that most of what I experienced was precisely one form or another of High Altitude Sickness--likely brought on because of my weakened condition and poor physical conditioning, due to the surgery, and then going on a difficult backpack too soon for someone of my age--68 at that time. One has to go into the Wilderness prepared to save and preserve your life, with saving essentials, depending on what your condition of health is. You also have to let family and friends know specifically where you are going, and when you'll return, but you need to have communication devices, such as a satellite phone, to advise changes in plans, and of special needs; plus a personal satellite tracking device—acquiring myself, after this event a SPOT PERSONNAL SATELLITE TRACKER to advise family daily where you are, and be able to call or signal for help if needed. All of the above if you go alone, and if in a group, at least one satellite phone, one tracking device, one Oximeter, plus emergency medications.

"DEATH BE NOT BORING…… ...I'VE LIVED WELL, I'VE ADVENTURED WIDELY. I WILL NOT DIE POORLY." By Jonathan Dorn

……but,

"LET'S NOT DIE STUPIDLY!" 105

Chapter 2: THE WILDERNESS AREA--North Slope

Section 11: The HENRYS FORK TRAILHEAD I must add here, for those who perhaps are new to the Uintas, the HENRYS FORK TRAILHEAD is the main access point to climb Utah's highest mountain--KINGS PEAK, 13,528 ft. high. I must begin this section, with a picture of Kings Peak, and a wonderful historical note about a young 11 year old girl's climb of Kings Peak--actually her 3rd, but I think you'll agree it was AMAZING to say the least. I'll get to driving directions--next page.

:

One day in early July 2018, 11 year old Grace, and her father Jake Hirschi, decided to take advantage of the great weather and climb King's Peak, seen in the exact center of the picture. Grace zeroed in on it and then left her father in her trail dust!106

She climbed it the first time in 2016, when I met them on the trail, me returning from my successful climb to Little Andy Lake. That's when I was honored by her and her brother, Isaac, calling me their “trail buddy”….so all of us became TRAIL BUDDIES.107

I'm not sure at what time they made it to the peak, but after making it and taking a picture, they turned around and headed for the Trailhead, fueled by, I think it was 6 bags of special trail-mix, getting to their car by 8:00 PM that same day--28 miles. WOW! 106

Photos courtesy of Jake Hirschi

107

See page 75 and for Isaac's also incredible climb, as well as 7 year old Nora's, see Chapter 2, Section 22, Preface.

p. 257

HOW TO GET HERE: From Kamas to North Slope Rd., 50 miles, then on FR-058 21 miles to FR-073 and continue 13.5 miles to China Meadows, then 7 miles north on FR-072, then 8 miles south on FR-017, then at fork continue south 3 miles on FR-077 to Trailhead. TOTAL 103 miles from Kamas--141 from SLC. From Mt. View, Wyo. 6-7 miles on CR-410 towards Robertson, then go south on CR-283, for 7 miles to a fork and turn left on FR-072 for 4 miles and at another fork take left hand FR-017 for 6 miles, then on FR077 3 miles to Trailhead. Total= 27 miles from Mt. View--72 from Evanston, and 152 from SLC.

I will outline here two important options, even though there are others, such as the Loops to the Red Castle Area, and then back following the North Slope Highline Trail--already outlined from the China Meadows Trailhead. OPTION 1: To & from Kings Peak, which you'll see in the 1st topographical map. It is 5.3 miles to Elkhorn Crossing, from which you continue on the main trail south and up above timberline to Dollar Lake, for 7.2 miles.

Most who climb the peak, camp in this area, and then do a day hike--to and from the Peak and back to their camp: To Gunsight Pass, it is 10 miles from the TH, then down from the pass 1/3 mile it’s best to leave the trail and follow a short-cut directly south 0.8 of a mile to pick up the trail heading up and west to Anderson Pass. That short-cut will save you 1 mile. From the pass you boulder hop 0.8 mile up to the peak. Then return 7 miles to your Dollar Lake camp. OPTION 2: Henrys Fork Basin lakes LOOP. Seven miles to Dollar Lake, then 1 more to trail heading down-west to begin visiting all of the wonderful lakes in this drainage: Blanchard, G-4, G-43, Cliff Lake (from here you can continue off-trail to test G-98, but it is a questionable fishery), Castle, G-44, Henrys Fork, Island, Grass, G-39, G-10, G-40, Bear and Sawmill Lakes, which takes you back to Elkhorn Crossing, at which point you've come a bit more than 25 miles. A mile down the canyon, if you don't want to miss anything, you can bushwhack up to G-62, and 2.3 miles before getting to the TH, you can take a short hike to Alligator Lake. Total lakes -- 18 lakes, for a total distance of 34 miles. OPTION 3: To George Beard Basin (above Lake Atwood), and others along the way, like: From Trail Rider Pass we observe what I have named, GEORGE BEARD BASIN, above Lake Atwood we see on the left. It's 1st lake is George Beard Lake seen bottom left.

p. 258

U-76, U-75, Little Andy Lake, and Beard Lake (U-74). Proceed from TH to Elkhorn Crossing, then on to Gunsight Pass (10 miles) and follow main trail to a large rock cairn where the Highline Trail comes from Kings Peak and continues east. There, go south 1 mile to another junction and follow the right hand fork to climb Trail Rider Pass, 3.7 miles from the cairn, then down to the basin for a total of 16.1 miles from the TH. A swing past the 4 lakes in the basin begins with the only named lake, George Beard Lake where on my "expedition" I had the fastest fishing of my long backpack, catching on 20 casts, 15 feisty wild, self sustaining brook trout. All the lakes mentioned on this trip will be described in this section even though they are in the Uinta River Drainage. On returning to the Pass, just a little down to the west is Beard Lake (U-74) where on my expedition I hooked what would have been a Utah State record brook trout, heavy bodied, hook jawed, 28" long--1st in the panel below. Then at the north foot of Trail Rider Pass, you can make a loop 1st of no name U-75 where I caught a very large 17" long, very heavy bodied brook trout--2nd in the panel, then a year after my survival experience, went back and caught a 21" long brook trout--3rd in the panel, but emaciated and ready for the grave. The other no-name lake—U-76, is to the northwest about a mile where I took unsuccessful casts on my expedition, but could have fish—in fact recently stocked.

You could even do a 3 mile round trip to visit Little Andy Lake, then back to the trail--the loop being about 6-7 miles, then return to the main trail, and hike back over Gunsight Pass to the Trailhead. Total would be approximately 30 miles, seeing and fishing in 7 wild lakes, plus seeing Little Andy Lake (maybe by the time you get there I'll have convinced the DWR airplane to experiment by dropping a few Grayling into it). I'll insert next a panel of photos, first of a group of youth from Washington I met on Gunsight Pass, who went on to climb Kings Peak, then boulder hopping down the ridge to South Kings Peak--from which Elisabeth Johanson, on the left took for me the picture of Little Andy Lake.

p. 259

They then continued to Mt. Jedediah, and all the way down to Mt. Emmons, Utah's 4th highest peak--bagging Utah's highest, then the 2nd, 4th and 5th highest peaks. WOW! Now, let's look at the details of the lakes mentioned in this section, including those from the Uinta River Drainage. We will begin down close to the Trailhead and work our way south. ALLIGATOR (G-38): Access is 2.3 miles from the Trailhead, then west about 1/2 mile to the lake. It is 10,033 ft. in elevation, 14.5 acres, 26' deep, fished heavily for Cutthroat and Brook trout.

LAKE G-62: Access is 4.25 miles from the TH to a point where 2 small streams cross the trail in close proximity, then following the northern-most stream west for 3/4 mile to the lake. 10,630 ft. elevation, 2.2 acres, 7' deep, stocked experimentally with Brook trout in 1985. Stocked with brook trout in 1985, 1988, 1991, and 1994; a survey in 1987 found a single age-class of fish stocked 1985; due to potential negative effects to native cutthroat trout in the Henrys Fork drainage brook trout stocking was discontinued.

We will now follow the trail to Dollar Lake and then to the junction where the Basin Trail circles the drainage to the west. DOLLAR (G-2): Access is 7 miles on the Kings Peak Trail to the last patch of tall timber on the trail, then 250 yards to the east. 10,772 ft. elevation, 5.4 acres 12' deep, Brook, Cutthroat & Tiger trout.

LAKE G-42: Located in boggy meadow west of junction on the Basin Trail. 4.6 acres, only 2' deep, but has Brook and Cutthroat trout migrants from the streams.

BLANCHARD (G-3): Accessed by leaving the Basin Trail about 1 mile from the junction, and hiking cross-country southwest paralleling the lake's outlet stream .7 miles to the lake. 11,164 ft. elevation, 31.3 acres, 29' deep, Cutthroat trout.

LITTLE BLANCHARD (G-4): Right next to Blanchard Lake, Cutthroat trout. CLIFF (G-5): Located about 1 mile south of Blanchard Lake, in the large cirque basin. 11,443 ft. elevation, 33.1 acres, 69' deep, Stocked with Cutthroat trout that are very wary, with light fishing pressure, and the possibility of large fish. See next Note. Now added, Tiger trout.

BIG FISH NOTE: When I circled the entire basin once early in the season, the runoff had Cliff Lake's water a bit murky, and on my cast I was reeling in my Thomas Cyclone, but observing the scenery when all of a sudden a huge fish made an alligator like lunge for my lure, splashing water on me 20 feet away--that almost stopped my heart. He missed my lure, but it was the 2nd greatest attempt to grab my lure experienced in fresh water. Consequent casts produced nothing, but there was a big Cutthroat in that lake, seen below.

p. 260

ARCTIC PTARMIGAN, were seen frequently up in the area between Cliff and Blanchard Lakes, as well as on my hike above timberline to get to Little Andy Lake. On almost all of my backpacks in the Basin I've seen hunters with their shotguns.

Now back to the lakes. From Cliff Lake you can swing off-trail 2 miles across arctic tundra northwest to our next lake. CASTLE (G-11): It is located 3/4 mile northwest of Blanchard Lake. 11,363 ft. elevation, 11.5 acres, 11' deep, It has Brook & Tiger trout.

LAKE G-44: As you go down east from Castle Lake you can try this small glacial lake, 11,140 ft. elevation, 1.5 acres, 7' deep, that has experimentally been stocked with Cutthroat trout. Stocked experimentally with cutthroat trout in 1986; a follow up survey in 1988 found no fish--winterkill suspected; stocking discontinued.

HENRYS FORK (G-1): As you come down from Castle and G-11 lakes angling northeast, you come to the trail, and this picturesque alpine lake, at 10,830 ft. elevation, 19.7 acres, 19' deep, with an excellent population of Cutthroat trout. I'll insert a picture of it here.

ISLAND (G-9): Found 3/8th mile west of Henrys Lake, 10,830 ft. elevation, 10.4 acres, 5' deep, with a small island and shallow conditions with a wary population of Brook trout, some Cutthroat & Tiger trout

GRASS (G-8): Found 1/2 mile northeast of Henrys Fork Lake, or just follow the outlet stream from Island Lake. 10,740 ft. elevation, 5.5 acres, 4' deep, that in spite of not much depth, has a self-sustaining population of Brook and Cutthroat trout.

LAKE G-39: Just west of Grass Lake on the other side of the Basin Trail, 10,820 ft. elevation, 2.6 acres, 7' deep, Has received experimental stockings of Brook trout. A follow up in 1992 found no fish--winterkill suspected; stocking discontinued.

LAKE G-10: About 1 mile past G-39, the lake is visible from the trail 350 yards to the northeast. 10,772 ft. elevation, 5.4 acres, 12' deep, Brook trout.

p. 261

LAKE G-40: 1/8th mile downstream from G-10, 10,740 ft. elevation, 3.6 acres, 5' deep, experimental stocking has been done in the past. Managed for brook trout, stocked on a 5 year cycle.

BEAR (G-7): The lake is 1.5 miles from Elkhorn Crossing, where the Basin Trail joins the North Slope Highline Trail, and is also 8.25 miles from the China Meadows TH. deep, heavily used , stocked with Brook trout, with some Cutthroats.

10,767 ft. elevation, 16.9 acres, 37'

SAWMILL (G-6): Found a short distance downstream from Bear lake. 10,661 ft. elevation, 7.2 acres, 21' deep, Contains a large population of Brook and Cutthroat trout sustained by natural reproduction.

Castle Peak and Castle Lake, described in one Guide book as "mysterious," showing they haven't been there

LAKE U-75: Located at extreme western edge of Painter Basin, southeast of U-76. 11,390 ft. elevation, 6.9 acres, 18' deep. The DWR pamphlet says, "contains an abundant population of pan-sized brook and cutthroat trout." See the panel of 3 brook trout in this section, the middle one is from this lake--far from "pan sized." In 2014 Cutthroat trout were planted.

Last stocking was in 2017. See the 1st in the panel miles from Henrys Fork TH.

of brook trout, that could have qualified as a Utah State record and won the Field & Stream fishing contest that year, beating out usual winners from Canada.

GEORGE BEARD (U-21): Located 2 miles above Lake Atwood, at the northeast corner of the basin I have named THE GEORGE BEARD BASIN. 11,420 ft. elevation, 7.4 acres, 15' deep, Brook trout sustained naturally. My previous note indicated it was the fastest fishing on my 2003 expedition.

LAKE U-20: No information. LAKE U-19: Along with George Beard Lake, this is the only other of the 4 listed as being a fishery, although the others look good and are worth a try. 11,420 ft. elevation, 15 acres, 8' deep, good population of Brook trout and in 2012 GOLDEN TROUT were stocked. http://wildlife.utah.gov/blog/2014/theres-gold-inthe-uintas/
