Chapter 2: THE WILDERNESS AREA- North Slope

Section 12: THE BEAVER CREEK DRAINAGE PREFACE

INTRODUCTION TO THE BEAVER CREEK DRAINAGE For likely a vast majority, even those who know a lot about the High Uintas, we are getting far enough east on the North Slope to put this portion of the Uintas out of familiarity of most, so best introduce it by quoting from the UTAH NATURAL RESOURCES: Wildlife Resources publication No. 86-10 from 1986, Field Project Leader, Roger Wilson. The Beaver Creek Basin is a remote, medium sized drainage system located on the north slope of the Uinta Range some 10 miles south of Lonetree, Wyoming. This drainage is scenic and composed of steep walled alpine basins dotted with lakes near the crest of the range and broad timbered ridges to the north. There are three major drainage systems in this basin including the West Fork, Middle Fork and East Fork. The highest point of land is Gilbert Peak at the head of the West Fork Drainage which stands at 13,442 feet in elevation. Due to the isolated nature of this basin, fishing pressure is limited and most of the lakes are seldom visited by anglers. None of the backcountry lakes are subject to heavy fishing pressure, and this basin is a good choice for anglers and other recreational users seeking solitude. The Beaver Creek Basin contains some 40 natural lakes, one large reservoir and numerous small ponds and potholes. These waters are scattered and dissimilar and range in elevation from 9,230 feet at GR-160 to 11,295 feet at GR-152. Twelve of these waters currently contain fish populations, and nine more are scheduled for continued experimental fisheries evaluation. The more remote lakes commonly produce catches of brook and cutthroat trout, and rainbows are taken by anglers at the popular Hoop Lake in the East Fork Drainage. These populations are supplemented by occasional aerial socking of fingerling as needed. Major roads accessing the drainage are the Hole in the Rock Road from Lonetree and the North Slope Road from either the Henrys Fork Drainage to the west or the Burnt Fork Drainage to the east.. Trail access to the Wilderness Area is provided by the West Fork Beaver Trail from the West Fork Road, the Middle Fork Beaver Trail from the Georges Park Trailhead and the Burnt Ridge and Thompson Peak Trails from the Hoop Lake Trailhead. The Hoop Lake Trailhead also provides access to the Burnt Fork Drainage via the Kabell Meadow Trail. In general, trails are marked and in good condition with the exception of the Middle Fork Beaver Trail. This trail is poorly routed and is difficult for horses in areas. All trails are identified on the drainage map by Forest Service trail numbers. A full-service campground is available at Hoop Lake with tap water, restroom facilities and a boat ramp. Several picnic areas are provided in the Middle Fork Drainage below the Georges Park Trailhead. Road conditions are generally good with the exception of the North Slope Road in the vicinity of Fallon Creek and the West Fork Road which is extremely rough. U.S. Geological Survey topographic maps applicable to the Beaver Creek Drainage inclue the Kings Peak, Fox Lake, Hoop Lake, Hole in the Rock and Gilbert Peak NE quadrangles. These maps show topographic detail and are a useful supplement to the maps provided in this booklet.

p. 266

Chapter 2: THE WILDERNESS AREA--North Slope

Section 12: THE BEAVER CREEK DRAINAGE

Dominating the West Fork of Beaver Creek is Utah's 3rd highest, 13,442 ft. high GILBERT PEAK, with Gilbert Lake at its foot

THE WEST FORK of BEAVER CREEK TRAILHEAD HOW TO GET HERE: If you want to get here from the NORTH SLOPE ROAD coming from the west, go to the directions for Henrys Fork, page 257, then tack on 5 miles to the 103 from Kamas, for a TOTAL of 108 miles (148 from SLC)--58 miles on dirt/gravel VIA EVANSTON: Follow Henrys Fork directions, page 257, plus 5 more added to the 72, TOTAL of 77 miles (from SLC 157)--25 on dirt/gravel road. THE BEST OPTION with less on dirt/gravel roads: From Evanston 45 to Mt. View then on WY-414 -- 22 miles To Lonetree, then 1.7 more to the Hole in the Rock turnoff--now on dirt road--CR-295 and from border FR-078, total of about 7 miles to a fork, the left to Hoops Lake, the right for 4.4 miles to West Fork of Beaver Trailhead, TOTAL of 80.1 miles from Evanston (only 11.4 miles on dirt/gravel), and 160 from SLC. At 5.6 miles the gradually climbing West Fork Trail crosses the North Slope Highline Trail, which comes from Henry's Fork, and continues east to cross the Middle Fork of Beaver Creek Trail, and then continues on to Thompson Pass and Thompson, Kabell, and Burnt Fork Creeks and their drainages that end the North Slope drainages of the Wilderness Area.

LAKE G-154: It is a wedge shaped lake sitting at the foot of a talus ridge 2.5 miles east of Gilbert Lake in a small side drainage tributary to the West Fork Basin. 10,930 ft. elevation, 2.1 acres, 6' deep. No horse access. Scheduled for stocking of Brook trout in 1986. Stocked again in 2018.

GILBERT (G-160): Located at the end of the West Fork Trail, approximately 8 miles from the Trailhead. 10,905 ft. elevation, 15.2 acres, 2' deep. Often moose are seen feeding all over the lake. In spite of being very shallow, it has an excellent population of Brook and Cutthroat trout. Spin fishing with lures is frustrating due to being so shallow with water weeds. Fly fishing can be very fast.

LAKE G-151: Located 3/8th mile south of Gilbert Lake. 11,033 ft. elevation, 12.6 acres, 11' deep, Brook trout sustained by natural reproduction.

LAKE G-153: Located 150 yards west of G-151. It is a beaver pond, breeches of its dam at times reduces the size of this pond--as was the case when I visited there in 2010. 11,066 ft. elevation, normally it is 3.6 acres, 2' deep, with self sustaining populations of Brook and Cutthroat trout.

LAKE G-152: Located 3/8th mile south of G-151 following the stream to the top of the ridge. It is a small glacial lake high on the ridge, at 11,295 ft. elevation, 4.8 acres, 13' deep, often with ice until mid-July. 10 miles from the Trailhead. Stocked with Brook trout in 2012, and seldom visited by fishermen.

p. 267

THE MIDDLE FORK OF BEAVER CREEK TRAILHEAD -- older publications calling it the GEORGES PARK TRAILHEAD HOW TO GET HERE: From the West Fork of Beaver Creek Trailhead, you drive into the "hogback" area of the Uintas, past beaver dams, and on to a junction where you switch back down to a road going south with the following sign: At that point you have come a bit over 4 miles from the West Fork TH and will take a right hand turn and drive 2 miles to the Middle Fork of Beaver Fork Trailhead--or Georges Park TH. At that sign it is .8 of a mile north to a junction, and from there 8 miles to Lonetree, Wyoming. Directions for the West Fork TH will give you the details to civilization.

Below is seen the trail sign located at the Trailhead--here an example of what I call the North Slope Highline Trail being called the NORTH SIDE HIGHLINE TRAIL.

Many lakes are accessed from this Trailhead. There are a bunch to the west, which I will describe last, but first those that are up in the high country. At 5 miles the trail meets the North Side Highline Trail, and at that point we'll begin to learn the details of lakes in the drainage. HIDDEN (GR-149): Located on the northern side of the trail, 1/2 mile north of Long Meadow, easily found but not frequently visited. 10,148 ft. elevation, 6.5 acres, 18' deep, Brook trout and also Tiger trout.

DINE (GR-148): Located 1/2 mile west of Long Meadow up the steep timbered ridge, or 1 mile southwest of hidden Lake following the stream. 10,460 ft. elevation, 5.1 acres, 15' deep, with Brook trout.

BEAVER (GR-147): Located at the end of the Middle Fork Trail. 10,505 ft. elevation, 38.3 acres, 30' deep, Brook trout sustained by natural reproduction, plus a few Cutthroat trout.

COFFIN (GR-144): Located by following the stream southwest 3/4 mile to this scenic alpine lake, at 10,853 ft. elevation, 25.8 acres, 28' deep, with a shallow shelf that extends out into the lake on all sides. Cutthroat and Tiger trout.

LAKE GR-145: Located 1/8 mile south of Coffin Lake up the talus ridge. 11,020 ft. elevation, 5.6 acres, 11' deep, horse access is not recommended. Experimental stocking of Cutthroats trout in 1986 & Grayling in 2014.

LAKE GR-177: Access is 1.5 miles southeast of Beaver Lake over rough terrain. There is an obscure sheep trail into this basin, but the trail is difficult to locate and follow. 10,860 ft. elevation, 18.3 acres, 11' deep with glacial turbidity. Wary Cutthroat trout.

I will now describe the lakes to the west of the Trailhead, beginning at 2.1 miles from the Trailhead where a stream comes out of that area and will detail the lakes on the north and

p. 268

move east around the drainage ending with GR-164 near the trail. This area is described as "a steep walled glacial depression," characterized by pothole lakes, most of which have no inlet, and no outlet, that fluctuate according to precipitation patterns, and characterized by

an abundance of snags and deadfall. LAKE GR-173: It is a natural pothole lake, 9,490 ft. elevation, 3.9 acres, 7' deep, scheduled for experimental stocking of Brook trout in 1986 and in 2012. Stocked on a 2 year cycle.

LAKE GR-172: Located 100 yards northeast of GR-173, 9,490 ft. elevation, 3.6 acres, 15' deep, experimental stocking of Brook trout in 1986, and in 2012. Follow up surveys found no fish--winterkill suspected; stocking discontinued.

LAKE GR-163: Located in thick timber east of GR-172, 9,322 ft. elevation, 6.5 acres, 16' deep, but size varies in accordance with beaver activity across the outlet. A deep brown color due to an accumulation of suspended organic matter, received experimental stocking of Brook trout in 1985. Follow up surveys found no fish--winterkill suspected; stocking discontinued.

LAKE GR-164: No fish life. LAKE GR-162: Located northeast of GR-163. An oblong pothole in heavy timber at 9,344 ft. elevation, 6.5 acres, 18' deep. Wary Brook trout. Managed for brook trout, stocked on a 2 year cycle.

LAKE GR-161: Located 250 yards east of GR-162 in heavy timber, 9,250 ft. elevation, 4.3 acres, 41' deep. Received experimental stocking of Brook trout in 1985 and in 2005. Stocked experimentally with brook trout; follow up surveys found no fish--winterkill suspected; stocking discontinued.

LAKE GR-160: Located 1/4 mile north east of GR-162. 9,230 ft. elevation, 50' deep. Received in 1985 experimental stocking of Brook trout.

Section 13: EAST BEAVER CREEK DRAINAGE & HOOPS LAKE *******************

PREFACE MEETING A LIVE ENCYCLOPEDIA of MOUNTAIN HISTORY In 2013 I made a YouTube video entitled, #7-2013 500 MILE HIGH UINTA LOOP & 75 NEW FRIENDS.108 Part of it came from a trip I had made through Lonetree, Wyoming when I was parked by the closed store contemplating--with a smile--whether to park I had to put a nickel or dime in the parking meter?

Then I noticed I was being watched by a sort of big cowboy kind of guy in a pickup, who seeing I had noticed him, motioned me to come and talk.

With a great friendly smile he said "I'm Joe Hickey, and you?" I introduced myself and in a sentence or two explained my HIGH UINTAS WILDERNESS PROJECT, the eventual creating of a unique book, and told him,

"I'm making a swing around the Uinta Mountains looking for interesting information and stories about the whole area--and good photos." That's all he needed to open before me the book of his life, the Lonetree area, the Hickey Ranch--he pointed out to me to the north, and on and on.

108

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AcdVrMZuGKo&feature=youtu.be

p. 272

Once in a while he would grab a worn out old grubby paperback book--cover long gone, and quickly thumb through its pages to quote something about the history from Lonetree, all along the Uintas Henry Fork River, and down to Flaming Gorge. The book was what you see below, that I got later that day at the Forest Service office in Manila.

He was just getting warmed up when his cell phone rang. He had to go, but invited me to an outdoor lecture, he and his brother Mike would be giving the next day.

I drove down the Henrys Fork Valley towards Manila and marveled at the wonderful herds of healthy cattle and ranching country made green with our Uinta Mountain water. From Maddy I got the book, and she whispered to me about Big Foot's footprints and promised to email me photos. The next day I was back at Lonetree with the Hickey brothers, and a good sized group, mostly of elderly Mormon missionary couples that served at LDS historic sites around Wyoming.

We were held spellbound and fascinated by what Joe and Mike showed and explained to us about the history of the area, and the Native American Shoshoni's who had lived for

p. 273

centuries in this area. led by Chief Washakie. I took a lot of video and one day I'll find time to convert it into YouTube videos, but for now just insert a few pictures.

Joe, on the left, and Mike on the right, talked a lot about the Shoshoni's history in the area.

Mike talked about the history of Lonetree, pointing to the famous cottonwood tree for which the town was named, considered quite miraculous as it had survived a number of direct lightning strikes--that did stunt it, but it is still alive--as is Lonetree.

We also drove up into the badlands overlooking the Henrys Fork valley, and they showed us some sacred Indian ritual sites that are carefully preserved.

p. 274

Chapter 2: THE WILDERNESS AREA--North Slope

Section 13: EAST BEAVER CREEK, HOOP LAKE & TRAILHEADS HOW TO GET HERE: From here on we'll forget the long drive on dirt/gravel, and do most of it on the pavement, 80 miles from SLC to Evanston, Wyoming, then 45 to Mt. View, and on WY-414, 22 more to Lonetree, and here I'll show you with a few photos:

Note: The picture of the store was back a few years when there were still some gas pumps. Keep your eyes open, as on my last trip just over the bridge on the left in the middle picture, I all of a sudden saw just off the road a red fox with the tip of its tail strikingly pure white. From Lonetree, drive 1.7 miles to the Hole in the Rock/Hoop Lake turnoff--now on dirt road--CR-295 that changes at border to FR-078, total of about 7 miles to a fork, the left on FR-078--3.2 miles, past Hole in the Rock, and some magnificent portals (seen on page 78), to Hoop Lake, then right crossing the dam and come to the Trailhead.

Overflow from Hoop Lake goes into the East Fork of Beaver Creek, on which there are no lakes. There are excellent Forest Service Campgrounds, with restrooms, and water available.

The sign on the right deals with the East Fork of Beaver Creek, and you'll notice that said, BURNT RIDGE TRAIL is only called that until it goes along the western edge of Burnt Ridge, and then becomes--on the National Geographic Wilderness map, the THOMPSON PEAK TRAIL that goes around the northwestern flank of the peak, and then ends when meeting the North Slope--Side Highline Trail. The lakes it leads to are those in the Middle Fork of Beaver Creek area, that we have already covered. You'll see that on the NG map I'll insert for your interest, but continue to use mainly topographical maps for this section.

p. 275

There is also a Trailhead on the northeastern end of Hoop Lake, the trail from there connecting on to the Kabell Meadow Trail, on which you can backtrack to the western Trailhead from where you can follow the Burnt Ridge Trail leading to the Middle Fork. So that leaves only one lake to deal with in this area: HOOP LAKE (?): No. DWR info. It is a fairly large lake, about the size of Grandaddy Lake, but also is a reservoir with a dam made to increase its size and water storage capacity, but water level drops as the summer season progresses. It is found at 9,140 ft. elevation, with no major inlet stream--as it sits on sort of a divide, its outlet stream joins the East Fork of Beaver Creek. It is basically a lake with planted trout: Brook, cutthroat, rainbows, tiger, and now has arctic grayling too.

Now we'll deal with the other sign and the KABELL MEADOW TRAIL, and the lakes it can lead you to. KABELL (GR-139): Is at about 10,400 ft. elevation, 5 miles from the Trailhead. The NG Topographical Wilderness map states it "Kabell Lakes," because there is another lake nearby--GR-140. The map shows the trail ending at GR-140, but the directions to get to the lake lead to the other lake (GR-139), they are:

…..follow the trail from Hoop Lake to Kabell Meadows. At the upper portion of the meadows, the trail forks to the south and southwest. From here, take the trail south up Kabell Ridge a couple of hundred yards. A side trail then takes off to the southwest ending at Kabell Lake." 109 Dense timber surrounds the lake making fly casting impossible--Spin fishing is the solution. Now, info from the DWR pamphlet revised in 1996: 10,348 ft. elevation, 14.7 acres, 23' deep, C trout.

ISLAND (GR-132): This is a large lake with a dam, used for water storage, so level fluctuates a lot. 10,777 ft. elevation, 117 acres when full, 34' deep, self sustaining Brook and Cutthroat trout. 8.9 miles from Hoop Lk. TH, 9.6 miles from Spirit Lk. TH. It experiences fairly heavy usage fishing for Brook and Cutthroat trout. Better fishing can usually be experienced in other lakes in the area.

NOTE: From Island Lake, it is a 1.4 mile hike up to 11,240 ft. Divide Pass, and access to the Uinta River Drainage--shown in the panel of 2 photos below--my daughter Mahana--on our 2005 Goat pack trip with Clay Zimmerman, seen descending towards Island Lake, and then at the Pass seeing Divide Lake, one of the reputed best fishing lakes in the Uintas.

I was shocked in 2005 at Island Lake to see every vestige of dry, dead wood, branches on trees, etc. GONE as though purposely pruned up to the height 109

HIGH UINTAS BACKCOUNTRY of UTAH, by Jeffrey Probst & Brad Probst, Revised Edition in 2000, page 196. The revised version in 2016 by Brett Prettyman, on page 224 has a mistake in distance.

p. 276

of a man, and cleaned-up, which helped me understand the Wilderness Area's rules of no camping within 200 feet of water (streams and lakes), and no campfires within 1/4 mile of most lakes in the Area--in hopes that such areas will eventually (at least maybe in 50 years) recover to their natural state. So, take a small stove with you. To the east: ROUND (GR-131): Picturesque lakes located 0.4 miles southeast of Island Lake through heavy timber following the outlet stream. 10,662 ft. elevation, 24.3 acres, 38' deep, Cutthroat trout. SNOW (GR-130): In older publications called "Andrea Lake." Impossible for horse travel, surrounded on 3 sides by talus slides and ledges, located 0.3 miles east of Round Lake, 10,550 ft. elevation, 9.4 acres, 35' deep, planted Cutthroat trout. CRYSTAL (GR-128): Located off-trail, bushwhacking 2.8 difficult miles east of Island Lake, more easily accessed 6.7 miles from the Spirit Lake TH. 10,380 ft. elevation, 5.4 acres, 5' deep, self-sustaining population of Cutthroat and Brook trout. More will be said in the section on the Spirit Lake TH.

To the west: WHITEWALL (GR-133): Located in a large meadow 0.4 miles west of Island Lake. 10,900 ft. elevation, 14.5 acres, 3' deep. Not stocked but with Brook and Cutthroat trout that migrate from surrounding areas. LOWER BENNION (GR-134): An elongated lake at the base of North Burro Peak, located 0.7 miles west of Island Lake--across a large meadow and up a timbered slope. 10,950 ft. elevation, 7.7 acres, 13' deep, Brook and self-sustaining population of Cutthroat trout. UPPER BENNION (GR-135): Located a few hundred yards upstream from Lower Bennion. 10,970 ft. elevation, 2 acres, 3' deep, not stocked, but brook and cutthroat trout migrate up the short stream from Lower Bennion. HIGH NO-NAME LAKE: Located in a high glacial cirque 0.6 mile west of Upper Bennion, about 4 acres in size. Might be a hard climb, but lakes like this excite the exploring spirit in me. Try it and let me know what you find.

PREFACE

THE 1st MOUNTAIN MAN RENDEZOUS--1825 Northeast of the Burnt Fork Trailhead--10 miles as the crow flies, along WY-414, is found a very important display--I've already shown a small version of on page 54, but it is so important in the development of the West, that we've got to see it big enough now to read.

In case you're curious why so much effort and sacrifice only created $50,000 worth of furs, it's equivalent today would be more than $12 million--not bad for the new adventurers, like Jedediah Smith, whose incredible story is summarized beginning on page 236. On page 55 I've inserted a picture of the approximate location of the "Jubilee," chosen because of its abundant grass--which is still being produced with the help of the Uinta's Henry Fork River. A mural, actually from the Rendezvous later in the Grand Teton area, helps us visualize the great event, celebrated every year in Fort Bridger, mentioned on page 51.

p. 279

Chapter 2: THE WILDERNESS AREA--North Slope

Section 14:

The BURNT FORK & BEAVER MEADOWS TRAILHEADS HOW TO GET HERE:

80 miles from SLC to Evanston, Wyoming, then 45 to Mt. View, and on WY414, 22 more to Lonetree. From Lonetree, drive 1.7 miles to the Hole in the Rock/Hoop Lake turnoff--now on dirt road--CR-295 that changes at border to FR-078, total of about 7 miles to a fork, the left on FR078--3.2 miles, past Hole in the Rock, and some magnificent portals (seen on page 78), to Hoop Lake. From the eastern end of Hoop Lake, continue on 11 miles east where you find a sign TRAILHEAD, and drive 0.3 mile to the Trailhead. Continuing east you soon cross Burnt Fork--a very nice fishing stream, and at 2.7 miles you come to Beaver Meadows Reservoir. Just as you come to the Reservoir, before crossing the dam, the Trailhead is found to the right on a fairly rough road about 1/2 mile.

From the BURNT FORK TRAILHEAD--seen above, you hike about 4 miles to the North Slope Highline Trail. From there you can hike about 4 miles west to Island Lake, or 2 miles to Fish Lake, plus another mile to Burnt Fork Lake, but it's probably best to get to these lakes from the Spirit Lake Trailhead. These two lakes are the last in the Wilderness Area.

From the BEAVER MEADOWS TRAILHEAD, seen above, it is approximately 5 miles to the North Slope Highline Trail, and another mile to Fish Lake, and one more to Burnt Fork Lake. We'll deal with the lakes mentioned above in Section 15: THE SPIRIT LAKE TRAILHEAD. These Burnt Fork and Beaver Meadows trailheads can be seen on the NATIONAL GEOGRAPHIC WILDERNESS MAP I've inserted on page 276.

p. 280

Section 15: The SPIRIT LAKE TRAILHEAD *********************

PREFACE A GOAT PACK TRIP FROM MIRROR LAKE TO SPIRIT LAKE In the second year of my HIGH UINTAS WILDERNESS PROJECT I decided to tackle again Crater Lake, the Uinta's deepest at 147 feet, but the long way--to explore also new areas of the Uintas from the south. On that backpack, at the junction with the Highline Trail to Lambert Meadows, I met a herd of goats coaxed along by Clay Zimmerman, "The Goat Whisperer," and his daughter Crystal. They were on Clay's annual 100 mile pack trip. 110

By the time we got through talking, I was invited to go with him the following year. So in 2005, my adopted daughter Mahana, just having arrived from Guatemala, got introduced to the U.S.A. with Clay's help, and in the upper Rock Creek Drainage she experienced snow for the first time in her life.

At remote Reconnaissance Lake she caught her first fish, then further along, after a short rest she successfully climbed Dead Horse Pass.

Section 15:

The SPIRIT LAKE TRAILHEAD: Burnt Fork Drainage NOTE: Since our Chapter 2 deals only with the WILDERNESS AREA, this section will only cover the Burnt Fork Drainage, including the Island Lake area already explained, as it can be accessed from Spirit Lake. For the Sheep Creek Drainage we will revisit the Spirit Lake Trailheads in Chapter 4: THE EASTERN UINTAS. HOW TO GET HERE: You can get here following the instructions to get to the Beaver Meadows Reservoir, Total of 173 miles from SLC, then driving 5 miles on FR-058 to the junction with FR-221 you follow for 2.7 miles to the Spirit Lake Road--FR-01, then 9 miles to the Spirit Lake Area, for a TOTAL OF 190 miles from SLC. Let's see if we can't get there less painfully: From SLC 147 to Lonetree, than on WY-414, 12 miles to Nila's Store, then 11 miles up the Spirit Lake Byway to the Spirit Lake road, FR-01, and 9 more to Spirit Lake, for a TOTAL of 180 miles, 10 less overall, but 26 miles less on dirt/gravel.

For your convenience I’ll insert below information about the lakes accessed from here. FISH (GR-125): A large narrow lake with its entire southern shore a steep rock slide, sits atop a divide between the Burnt Fork and Sheep Creek Drainages. 10,685 ft. elevation, 38.3 acres, 23' deep, Brook and Cutthroat trout. BURNT FORK LAKES (GR-127): One mile from the western end of Fish Lake by a faint trail winding westerly along the base of a ridge and then cuts south over the ridge to the lakes. 10,630 ft. elevation, the main lake 9.8 acres, 25' deep, Cutthroat trout self sustaining naturally. CRYSTAL (GR-128): Accessed from Burnt Fork Lake 0.6 mile southwest down a steep, timber covered slope. Accessed also by following the outlet from Burnt Lake down to a wet grassy meadow. The outlet of Crystal Lake flows into the western side of the meadow. Follow the stream to the lake. 10,380 ft. elevation, 5.4 acres, 5' deep, self-sustaining population of Cutthroat and Brook trout. SNOW (GR-130): In older publications called "Andrea Lake." Impossible for horse travel. surrounded on 3 sides by talus slides and ledges, located 2 miles west of Crystal Lake, 10,550 ft. elevation, 9.4 acres, 35' deep, planted Cutthroat trout. ROUND (GR-131): ): Picturesque lake located 0.5 mile west of Snow Lake. 10,662 ft. elevation, 24.3 acres, 38' deep, Cutthroat trout. ISLAND (GR-132): This is a large lake with a dam, used for water storage, so level fluctuates. 10,777 ft. elevation, 117 acres when full, 34' deep, self sustaining Brook and Cutthroat trout. 8.9 miles from Hoop Lk. TH, 9.6 miles from Spirit Lk. TH. It experiences fairly heavy usage fishing for Brook and Cutthroat trout. Better fishing can usually be experienced in other lakes in the area. NOTE: From Island Lake, it is a 1.4 mile hike up to 11,240 ft. Divide Pass, and access to the SOUTH SLOPE'S Uinta River Drainage--shown

p. 283

in Section 14 a panel of 2 photos--of my daughter Mahana--on our 2005 Goat pack trip with Clay Zimmerman, seen descending towards Island Lake, and then at the Pass seeing Divide Lake, one of the reputed best fishing lakes in the Uintas.

Now, to the west of Island Lake WHITEWALL (GR-133): Located in a large meadow 0.4 miles west of Island Lake. 10,900 ft. elevation, 14.5 acres, 3' deep. Not stocked but with Brook and Cutthroat trout that migrate from surrounding areas.

LOWER BENNION (GR-134): An elongated lake at the base of North Burro Peak, located 0.7 miles west of Island Lake--across a large meadow and up a timbered slope. 10,950 ft. elevation, 7.7 acres, 13' deep, Brook and self-sustaining population of Cutthroat trout.

UPPER BENNION (GR-135): Located a few hundred yards upstream from Lower Bennion. 10,970 ft. elevation, 2 acres, 3' deep, not stocked, but brook and cutthroat trout migrate up the short stream from Lower Bennion.

HIGH NO-NAME LAKE: Located in a high glacial cirque 0.6 mile west of Upper Bennion, about 4 acres in size. Might be a hard climb, but lakes like this excite the exploring spirit in me. Try it and let me know what you find. On Google Earth it looks pretty shallow, so likely does not have fish.

Section 16: The UINTA RIVER TRAILHEAD *********************

PREFACE

THE GHOST of THE U-BAR WILDERNESS RANCH In 2003 I left the Highline Trailhead, near the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway, on what I called my "expedition," with a load of 83 lbs. on my back and around my waist, then in my 68th year. Shocked by 83 lbs.? There was to be no re-supply as is common among backpackers who do long hikes--they finding civilization every 3 or 4 days and getting a box of food, and clean clothes in the mail. I had prepared for my expedition for years, working on my farm in Guatemala alongside my Mayan employees, and a couple of times every week did 3-4 miles on the rolling hills with a 100 lb. bag of fertilizer on my back. NOTE: Since I've learned I could have reduced my load by 15-20 lbs. as explained at the end of Chapter 5. At this point I was a week or so into my expedition, pack weight down to 70 lbs. In the background is Explorer Peak, with Crater Lake in the glacial cirque at its foot

Nearly 4 weeks later, with 206 miles behind me following the spine of the High Uintas, with zigzags, north, and others south of the spine, I came down the Uinta River Trail to the end of my hike at the U-BAR WILDERNESS RANCH.

WOW! Pretty well sums up what this tiny bit of civilization meant to me--I'm admitting for the first time that I did feel a bit lonely at times. I met at the Lodge, Jan, and then the owner, Ed Baltz, and pulled out my Visa Card and signed up for a day of rest and food.

p. 286

My rest was to be in the Rainbow Cabin, including a hot shower in the shower/rest room-giving Jan time to fix me a "a Kingly lunch," -- I mistakenly said a few pages ago it was a tuna fish sandwich, but it was ham & cheese, plus a green Jello salad, Doritos, and soda pop.

As I was chowing down, I got out my satellite phone, and called my son Joe, asking him to come and get me the next day, and then headed for some welcome rest in the Rainbow Cabin.

Ed also needed a rest in one of the cabins after a hard day's work, seen next, helping his wrangler, Bill, prepare a load to be taken up into the high country for clients

The Ranch had been serving the public for many years, and I so appreciated it being there for me, but sadly in 2005 it all began coming to a screeching halt. In May 2005, a mudslide occurred on U.S. Forest Service land and entered the Ranch permit area, damaging one of the guest cabins. Although the Forest Service took responsibility for the incident and asserted that it would clean up the damaged area, it did not. In the spring of 2007, the Ranch complained to the Forest Service that it had failed to keep a drainage channel and culvert free of debris. In July 2007, after a minor debris flow, which resulted from accumulated debris in the neglected channel and culvert, the Forest Service issued a Special Closure Order against the Ranch and, in August 2007, suspended both the business and outfitter permits.111

111

https://www.mountainstateslegal.org/news-updates/news-releases/2013/02/07/utah-family-sues-forestservice-for-breach-of-contract#.W32_485KiUk

p. 287

You can read the whole legal story at the footnote reference, but it is sad that this great business, serving the public ended, and as indicated in the title of this Preface, has become a "GHOST Ranch," which I visited again in 2015, and took a few pictures I'll insert below.

The mud slide, or flash flood, came down from the east side of the canyon--the pathway seen above on the right, and, as what I quoted above said, damaging one of the cabins. For whatever reasons, the permit was cancelled and the U-Bar Wilderness Ranch ended, and, as we can see below, is rotting away.

What a great loss. I'll insert below another reference, 112 and then a link to an Ashley National Forest list of PERMITEES.113 112

http://www.loopnet.com/Listing/14150312/NEOLA-UTAH-NEOLA-UT/ and

https://www.fs.usda.gov/detail/ashley/specialplaces/?cid=stelprdb5270341

Chapter 2: THE WILDERNESS AREA—South Slope

Section 16:

The UINTA RIVER DRAINAGE & TRAILHEAD IMPORTANT NOTE: While the North Slope was magnificently scenic, historically fascinating and with captivating & humorous legends, plus compelling life saving survival stories, its hikes to the high country were usually only 10 miles or so. You will soon notice that on the SOUTH SLOPE, the hikes to the high country are 15-20 miles, and the number of alpine lakes are greatly increased--so WE'VE GOT A BIG & EXCITING TASK AHEAD OF US……and the history, legends, tall tales and survival stories will be equally informative, intriguing, and capable of saving lives. The South Slope will also reveal the most amazing outdoor experience of my life--which I obviously survived--and have a picture of! TO GET HERE: From Salt Lake City, Utah to Roosevelt in the Uinta Basin, go east on I-80, to Kimball Junction, then south on U.S. 189 to Heber, and U.S. 40 to Roosevelt for 143 miles, then 10 miles north on UT-121 to Neola, and continue on CR-17 for about 13 miles then on FR-118 for 3.5 miles to the Trailhead, for a TOTAL OF ABOUT 170 miles. You'll notice the main road is closed, so to get to the "GHOST of the UBAR WILDERNESS RANCH," you'll have to hike along with the rest of us for a mile or so. Kings Peak--in the direct center, Utah's highest peak at 13,528 feet, is found at the western edge of the Uinta River Drainage, and the Painter Basin. The lake seen is U-75. Picture taken from near Trail Rider Pass. The flower is, OLD MAN OF THE MOUNTAIN.

The UTAH WILDLIFE RESOURCES pamphlet, LAKES OF THE HIGH UINTAS--DRY GULCH & UINTA RIVER DRAINAGES, published in 1982, with a revised edition in 1997, says about the Uinta River Drainage, "There are 51 lakes in the drainage that contain trout populations,

or are under experimental fisheries management." 114 I know that there are some others that should also be on their list…..like, Little Andy Lake, so let's go to work and see how many we can list and give you information about, first following the trail right up the Uinta River Canyon to the Highline Trail, and begin on the east side of the drainage and swing around to the west all the way to Kings Peak. Then 114

Publication No. 97-6/First Printing 1982, Revised Edition, 1997 by Utah Division of Wildlife Resources

p. 289

we'll backtrack to the Sheep Bridge, 3.5 miles up the canyon from the trailhead, and do the Lake Atwood Trail and all of its lakes. WALL (U-99): Located up a side canyon to the east of the Rock Canyon Bridge 6 miles from the Trailhead. No trail, approximately 3 miles bushwhacking from Rock Canyon Bridge. Tiger trout & Grayling

LAKE U-100: Near Wall Lake. Stocked with Grayling.. MEADOW (U-66): Found up a Bluebell Creek side-canyon to the east of the trail, 7.2 miles from the trailhead. No trail, so off-trail in tough terrain, approximately 2.2 miles. No information.

WILD GOOSE (U-67): Near Meadow Lake. Approximately 1.8 miles. No information.

In this vicinity, in the early 60's, I climbed down to the Uinta River, near where Atwood Creek enters, and caught what for years I speculated as a possible cutthroat/golden trout hybrid, but experts from the DWR feel it more likely is just a very colorful native cutthroat trout

LAKE U-97:

Located up a side canyon to the east from the Shale Creek Bridge. No trail but approximately 1.9 miles. No info.

PENNY NICKELL (U-98): A pretty cirque lake south of U-97. Approximately 2.3 miles off-trail up the side canyon to the east of the Shale Creek Bridge, or 3.5 miles south of Fox Lake, 10,710 ft. elevation, 11.5 acres, 43' deep, stocked with Cutthroat trout, fishing pressure very light.

We have now hiked 11.2 miles up the canyon just past the Shale Creek Bridge and at a fork in the trail, take the right hand trail and hike 2.2 miles more and join the Highline Trail--at a point about 50 miles from the Hayden Fork western beginning of the trail. At this fork, to the northwest are two more lakes (U-57 and U-58) and another a short distance to the north and a little east (U-50). LAKE U-58 and U-57: Again with no information in the pamphlet. Not managed. LAKE U-50: We're finally hitting more pay-dirt. Accessed 1/4 mile northwest from G-49, U-50 is 10,882 ft. elevation, 18 acres, 8' deep, stocked with Brook trout.

DIME or DOLLAR LAKE (U-49): Located about 1/2 mile north of the trail where a small stream crosses the trail, as seen on the topo map, or 1 mile northwest of Fox Lake. We are now 15 miles from the trailhead. 10,704 ft. elevation, 11.5 acres, 6' deep, Has a natural population of Brook trout.

FOX (U-47): This is a lake/reservoir, a dike increasing its capacity for irrigation use downstream, so it fluctuates as the summer progresses. 10,790 ft. elevation, 102 acres at full pool, 47' deep, with Brook and Cutthroat trout. Heavily fished.

p. 290

CRESCENT (U-48): Near Fox Lake and easily found following Forest Service signs. It is 15.5 miles from the Uinta Trailhead, or 8 miles over Fox-Queant Pass from the West Fork Whiterocks Trailhead. It is another lake/reservoir with 4 feet of fluctuation. 10,830 ft. elevation, 31 acres, 23' deep, with mainly Cutthroat trout and some Brook. Use is moderate to heavy with Scout groups and others.

BROOK (U-53): Located about 1 mile east of the north shore of Fox Lake on the Highline Trail. 10,950 ft. elevation, 10 acres, 8' deep, stocked with Brook trout, with light fishing pressure.

DIVIDE (U-59): Located 1.6 miles north of Fox Lake on the trail leading to the North Slope and Island Lake. It is surrounded by arctic tundra at 11,217 feet elevation, 18.9 acres, 39' deep, has Cutthroat trout, with the reputation of being very good fishing for larger than normal fish. We went by it on our goat/pack trip, but I made the mistake of not testing the fishing. We will now backtrack to Fox Lake and the Highline Trail, and hike a couple of miles west where we can take Trail #104 that goes north near Samuels Lake, then swings up towards the Davis Lakes, then back down between the Kidney Lakes to the Highline Trail. My NG Topo CD/Rom map set doesn't have that trail, but I'll put the map back on my computer and rough it in. We'll call this basin….

THE KIDNEY LAKES -- RAINBOW LAKE BASIN SAMUELS (U-27): Accessed by taking Trail #104 for one mile, then where a small stream crosses the trail, we begin an off-trail loop of the basin, going north and slightly east 0.8 mile to the lake. 10,995 ft. elevation, 4.8 acres, 7' deep, horse friendly, abundant Brook trout.

DAVIS SOUTH (U-34): Go 1.7 miles west and then northwest following the edge of the mountain to the Lakes. U-34, 11,020 ft. elevation, 6.1 acres, 4' deep, horse friendly, Brook trout.

DAVIS NORTH (U-46): 250 yards north of U-34, 11,060 ft. elevation, 7.3 acres, 7' deep, Brook trout that move freely between the lakes.

WEEPING LEDGE (U-40): Located 1 mile west of U-3. Not managed. LAKE U-37: Located 1/2 mile south of U-40, 11,180 ft. elevation, 6.3 acres, 12' deep, stocked with Brook trout

LAKE U-38: Located 1/4 miles southwest of U-40, 11,218 ft. elevation, 15.7 acres, 13' deep, with Cutthroat trout.

LAKE U-42: Found 1/2 mile west of U-38, 11,350 ft. elevation, 7.6 acres, 7' deep, stocked with Cutthroat trout.

LAKE U-43: No information. LAKE U-44: No information. LAKE U-45: Located 1/2 mile north of U-43, 11,425 ft. elevation, 5 acres, 5' deep, Cutthroat trout. DIAMOND (U-39): Located 1.3 miles southeast of U-45, and 1/4 mile north of Rainbow Lake, 11,160 ft. elevation, 6.3 acres, 9' deep, stocked with Brook trout, and Grayling.

RAINBOW (U-33): Just south of U-39, 1.25 miles north of Kidney Lakes. 11,130 ft. elevation, 35.1 acres, 20' deep, Brook trout are self-sustaining, and maybe a few rainbows and cutthroats. At times heavy pressure.

LAKE U-35: Found 100 yards north of Rainbow Lake. 11,110 ft. elevation, 4.4 acres, 5' deep, Cutthroat and Brook trout.

p. 291

WILDERNESS (U-36): On outlet stream from U-35. Natural reproducing Brook trout. KIDNEY WEST (U-26): 100 yards west of Kidney East, 18 miles from Uinta Trailhead, 15 miles from West Fork Whiterocks Trailhead over Fox-Queant Pass. 10,850 ft. elevation, 20 acres, 4' deep, Brook trout heavily fished.

KIDNEY EAST (U-25): 10,850 ft. elevation, 13.7 acres, 12' deep, Brook trout with heavy usage. LILY U-23: Located 1/2 mile northeast of the Kidney Lakes. 10,919 ft. elevation, 5.3 acres, 15' deep, surrounded by yellow water lilies, horse friendly, Brook trout, fishing pressure is light.

BOWDEN (U-32): Located 1/2 mile southeast of Kidney Lakes, on south side of Highline Trail. 10,693 ft. elevation, 4.5 acres, 14' deep, Horse friendly, Brook trout.

VERLIE (U-41): West of Kidney Lakes 1 mile, "the last several hundred yards are inaccessible to horses," 10,906 ft. elevation, 10.6 acres, 12' deep, the lake has self-sustaining Brook trout, and some Cutthroats.

We'll now move a mile west on the Highline Trail to the junction with the trail that comes up from NORTH PARK, and go down this trail to the southeast 1.2 miles to NORTH PARK. Here we are 14 miles from the Uinta Trailhead. From here we can access our next area.

THE PAINTER LAKES BASIN This is not to be confused with the Painter Basin, which we'll get to in a moment. To get to this remote area, we have to ford the Uinta River--which I suggest you do late in the season when the river is not so high.

I know about this as early in my project I planned on getting to this area early in the season and found the river a raging torrent that I was not about to try and cross. So, we ford the river, then, quoting the DWR pamphlet, "Head due south for 2 very steep and rough miles up a vague trail (along a small creek) into the Painter Lakes Basin." 115 CRAIG (U-85): This is the first lake we come to after a 2 mile hike, 10,848 ft. elevation, 9.3 acres, 14' deep. Horse friendly. It has mostly Cutthroat trout.

LAKE U-88: This beautiful natural lake is the largest in the basin, 1 mile west of Craig Lake, 11,030 ft. elevation, 14 acres, 18' deep, with a self-sustaining population of Brook trout.

LAKE U-87: Is a small lake north of U-87 at the foot of the mountain, 11,667 ft. elevation. No information.

LAKE U-93: Is due west 0.7 mile from U-87, and is the farthest west and highest in the basin. 11,402 ft. elevation, 11.1 acres, 8' deep, stocked with Cutthroat trout.

LAKE U-90: We will now make the loop back, this lake 1/2 mile east of U-93. No information. LAKE U-89: Due west of U-90, and 100 yards southwest of U-88, 11,037 ft. elevation, 11.5 acres, 15' deep, Brook trout.

LAKE U-91: West of U-89. With Cutthroat trout. LAKE U-92: West of U-92. With Cutthroat trout. 115

LAKES OF THE HIGH UINTAS: Dry Gulch & Uinta River Drainages, Publication No. 97-6/Revised edition, 1997.

p. 292

We are back to NORTH PARK, and will go back up the trail 1.2 miles to the Highline Trail and then head west to the Gilbert Creek Basin. In two miles from where the Gilbert Creek crosses the trail we will continue another mile when we meet the creek again a bit upstream and from that point will make a 7.8 mile loop around the Gilbert Creek Basin.

THE GILBERT CREEK BASIN NOTE: As we will see only one of the lakes in this basin had fish at the time of the 1997 Revised edition of the pamphlet, but in hopes that since then there will now be fish in others--I'll leave them on the list awaiting new information I got for one of them. We begin the loop following the Center Fork of Gilbert Creek. LAKE U-79: From the Highline Trail you hike 1.7 miles to this lake that lies at the base of 12,718 ft. high Anna Peak. 11,239 ft. elevation. Has Cutthroat and Brook trout.

GILBERT U-82: Located 1.6 miles west of U-79, crossing to the other side of the drainage. 20.5 miles from the Trailhead, 11,459 ft. elevation, 14.6 acres, 20' deep, horse friendly, has Brook & Cutthroat trout.

LAKE U-81: From U-82 go southwest 1 mile. 12,010 ft. elevation. No information. LAKE U-80: This small lake is about 1 mile north of U-81 at 11,840 ft. elevation. No information. LAKE U-83: Located on Gilbert Creek about 1 mile below U-83. No information. Back at the 3.2 mile point from the previous junction on the Highline Trail, we proceed west and southwest crossing over the very rocky tip of the mountain, and as we begin to drop down, on a sharp turn in the trail--it is a good point to make a small loop hike to visit our next lake--and one that does have fish. MILK (G-73): It is located in a small cirque basin 0.6 mile from the above point on the trail going northwest--at this point we are 5 trail miles west of North Park, or 7 miles northeast of Trail Rider Pass. At 11,236 ft. elevation, 13.1 acres, 35' deep. Not horse friendly. Abundant Cutthroat trout, rarely fished.

LAKE G-72: Half-way between G-73 and Highline Trail, 11,153 ft. elevation. No information. We continue on the Highline Trail going southwest 2.1 miles to a major cross-trail. The Highline Trail coming from the northwest 3.3 miles from Anderson Pass--and Kings Peak, which trail is joined by the trail--coming 12.7 miles, from the Henrys Fork Basin TH crossing Gunsight Pass. From said cross-trail another trail goes east 7.3 miles to North Park. The other trail goes southwest 3.7 miles to Trail Rider Pass, then dropping down 0.8 of mile to the 2 mile long George Beard Basin Loop. Said trail from Trail Rider Pass, mainly is the Lake Atwood Trail, from the pass going 13.5 miles to the Sheep Bridge on the Uinta River, plus 3.6 miles more to the Trailhead, for a total from Trail Rider of about 17 miles. An additional option from this cross-trail, is to do a loop visiting U-76, U-75, Little Andy Lake, and Beard Lake (U-74) on Trail Rider Pass. This has been described already in Section 11, Option 3, pages 257, 258 and 263, 264. For your convenience I will insert here the details of the lakes involved that are part of the Uinta River Drainage's Painter, and George Beard Basins, with a few added notes.

p. 293

INFORMATION ON LAKES FROM UINTA RIVER DRAINAGE IN UPPER PAINTER & GEORGE BEARD BASINS LAKE U-76: Located on my "survival route" east of Kings Peak in upper Painter Basin. 11,475 ft. elevation, 6 acres, 15' deep, Brook and Cutthroat trout. Note: On my survival hike I took a half dozen casts

here with no results--but maybe airplane stocked trout hadn’t grown up enough yet.

LAKE U-75: Located at extreme western edge of Painter Basin, southeast of U-76. 11,390 ft. elevation, 6.9 acres, 18' deep. The DWR pamphlet says, "contains an abundant population of pan-sized brook and

cutthroat trout." Note: See the panel of 3 brook trout in Section 11, which I'll repeat below--the middle one--17" long & heavy bodied, is from this lake--far from "pan sized." The 3rd--21" long, is also from U-75, 2 years later when the few that were left were old, emaciated and ready for the grave.

LITTLE ANDY LAKE (U- 00):

Given my nick-name from my youth, on suggestion from the guys from KSL Radio Outdoors, that a lake be given my name. Located 1.3 miles from U-75, at 12,302 ft. elevation, making it the highest lake in Utah. Hopefully the DWR airplane will drop in a few Cutthroat trout or perhaps better arctic grayling, giving it an experimental try. BEARD (U-74): Located 400 yards northwest of Trail Rider Pass, 22 miles from Uinta River TH. 15.3 miles from Henrys Fork TH. . 11,740 ft. elevation, 9 acres, 15' deep, pamphlet says: "Stocked brook trout

grow well in Beard and fishing pressure is quite light." Note: See the 1st in the panel of brook trout, that could have qualified as a Utah State record and won the Field & Stream fishing contest that year, beating out usual winners from Canada. Heavy bodied, hook jawed, conservatively 28" long, likely 10 lbs. For Utah State Fish Records, see: https://wildlife.utah.gov/record-fish.html

GEORGE BEARD (U-21): Located 2 miles above Lake Atwood, at the northeast corner of the basin I have named THE GEORGE BEARD BASIN. 11,420 ft. elevation, 7.4 acres, 15' deep, Brook trout sustained naturally. My previous note indicated it was the fastest fishing on my 2003 expedition.

LAKE U-20: No information. LAKE U-19: Along with George Beard Lake, this is the only other of the 4 listed as being a fishery, although the others look good and are worth a try. 11,420 ft. elevation, 15 acres, 8' deep, good population of Brook trout and now stocked with GOLDEN TROUT.

Eastern brook trout from U-75 and Beard Lake - U-74, see above box for details

We will now take on last the Lake Atwood Trail lakes, beginning back down on the Sheep Bridge on the Uinta River, 3.6 miles from the Trailhead. At 2.5 miles up the Atwood Trail (or 6.1 miles from the TH), we come to the first possible side-hike, to the following lakes.

p. 294

ALBERT U-94: Located in a very steep and rocky basin, 4.5 miles south of the Atwood Trail, at 10,826 ft. elevation, 7 acre, 8' deep, the DWR says, "horses should not be taken into this basin," has Cutthroat trout sustained by natural reproduction. Rarely visited, and in the pamphlet it says, "a must for the rugged outdoorsman." The route recommended in the pamphlet, is "Access is to go northwest up a ridge 2 miles from Bollie Lake (U-96), then turn north and climb down a steep talus slope into the basin." Bollie Lake will be described as part of the Dry Gulch - Heller Basin. LAKE U-95: Smaller than U-94, but does have a number. No information.

We continue up the trail to the 4.2 mile marker where there are additional opportunities. LILY PAD (U-8): Located 1/4 mile to the east of the trail at marker 4.2, 8 miles from the Trailhead, 10,218 ft. elevation, 3.7 acres, 7' deep, contains abundant Brook and Rainbow trout sustained naturally.

At this point you can go off-trail to the west following the trail I have roughed in on the topo map to visit several lakes, which are: PIPPEN or on NG Wilderness Map, ISLAND (U-9):

Located 1 mile west of trail, at 10,450 ft. elevation, 3.2 acres, 3' deep, very horse friendly, with a natural producing population of Brook trout. LAKE U-?: Located 2.4 miles west of trail, at 10,900 ft. elevation. No information. KREBS U-10: Located 1.4 miles west and a little north of trail. No information. LOWER CHAIN 1 (U-3): The first of the Chain Lakes, at marker 5.1, 11.5 miles from Trailhead, at 10,580 ft. elevation. It is a lake/reservoir and so there is drawdown as the summer progresses. 62 acres at full pool, 38' deep, contains abundant Brook trout that reproduce naturally. Fishing pressure is heavy. MIDDLE CHAIN 2 (U-2): It used to be a storage reservoir but earth dam has washed out. 10,605 ft. elevation, 14.4 acres, 13' deep, abundant Brook trout that are self-sustaining. UPPER CHAIN 3 (U-1): Located 12.5 miles from the Trailhead. It is also a lake/reservoir, so experiences drawdown. 10,623 ft. elevation, 51 acres at full pool, 44' deep, with a self-sustaining population of Brook trout. CHAIN 4 (U-4): It is above Chain 3, at 10,870 ft. elevation, 13.5 acres, 31' deep, managed with Cutthroat trout. OKE-DOKE (U-5): This pretty cirque lake is found 1 mile west of the base of Roberts Pass, 15 miles from the Trailhead. 11,320 ft. elevation, 12.9 acres, 38' deep, has stocked Cutthroat trout. A great place to get off the beaten path for backpackers. LAKE U-6: Located along the off-trail hike to Oke-Doke Lake. No information. LAKE U-7: On the north side of the trail to Oke-Doke Lake. No information.

The CHAIN LAKES

p. 295

In 1954 I accompanied Charlie Peterson, and Ted Packard on what for us was an epic backpack crossing the High Uintas Primitive Area. The last leg of our trip was down the Lake Atwood Trail, and past the Chain Lakes. As we were walking across the end of I think the Middle Chain, the sand we were walking on seemed like walking on Jello making sort of waves as we moved across.116 Then all of a sudden Ted began sinking in and Charlie and me began carefully moving to form a chain with ourselves to save our buddy.

But, then we noticed he stopped sinking deeper, so rather than continue our daring rescue attempt, we got out our cameras and starting taking his picture, like the one above. For whatever reason, Ted got upset at us and in the movie Charlie was making you can see the mucky sand Ted was throwing at us….along with some choice words—he had apparently learned from his sheep herding uncles. He apparently didn't think it was funny, as we did…...so we just let him go horizontal in the muck and crawl his way to safety! Now, on to what always seemed like for me THE TOUGHEST PASS IN THE UINTAS-ROBERTS PASS, that takes you into the Lake Atwood area. Maybe it seemed tough as it was always done on our way out, after a tough backpack, when we were tired and hungry! Now for the last area in the Uinta River Drainage:

THE LAKE ATWOOD BASIN As soon as you get down from the rocky pass, and around the point of the mountain, you can begin a loop of all the amazing lakes in the basin. B-29 LAKE (U-18): You can see on the topo map that it is a short distance to the west of the trail. It is 17.5 miles from the Trailhead, at an elevation of 10,740 ft., 19 acres, 7' deep, horse friendly, with a large population of Brook trout. 116

Matt McKell & Roger Wilson, from the DWR, explain about “floating banks” in Uinta lakes: “On lake shores, masses, of Sphagnum moss of the genus Sphagnum (aka peat moss), form large, thick mats that grow out over the water, seen in the following: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DXZCLQqx8Ak” So, floating banks are composed of mostly mosses and vegetation and they are more like walking on sponges. In the case in question, alluvial deposition has washed over and covered the mats with fine sand, apparently with some soft areas, like Ted sank into, but likely stopped sinking on reaching the mat..

p. 296

CARROT (U-17): It is located west of B-29 Lake about 1/2 mile, 10,830 ft. elevation, 31 acres, 31' deep, horse friendly, good fishing for Brook trout.

ROBERTS (U-15): This deep natural lake is found high up in a cirque basin, 1.3 miles west of Carrot Lake, following a faint trail zigzagging up a steep ravine where you find yourself in windswept arctic tundra country at 11,550 ft. elevation, 23.3 acres, 38' deep, with a self-sustaining population of Cutthroat trout, with some Brook trout too. Light fishing pressure.

ALLEN or MT. EMMONS (U-13): Come down the ravine from Roberts Lake, and head east and a bit north 1/2 mile through timber to this pretty lake, 10,990 ft. elevation, 15.5 acres 21' deep, Brook trout, but many years ago it was planted with Golden trout, and recently the DWR has planted here Golden trout again.117

ALLRED (U-14): Located just north of Mt. Emmons Lake, and 225 yards south of the Lake Atwood dam, 10,995 ft. elevation, 34 acres, 30' deep, horse friendly, good sized Brook trout are found here, sustained by natural reproduction.

LAKE ATWOOD (U-16): Located 18 miles from the Trailhead, 11,030 ft. elevation, 200 acres makes it the largest lake in the Uinta River Drainage, 40' deep, but has a dam with its outflow controlled and used for irrigation in the Uintah Basin, so the depth and size fluctuates. It has a large Brook trout population, and years ago had Golden trout, and was stocked again in 2012 and 2014.

It's not mentioned in the DWR pamphlet, but it has had also huge arctic grayling.

HISTORICAL NOTE: In 1962, Ted Packard and myself led a group of 15 Explorer Scouts from the Center Park Trailhead, and up through the Garfield Basin, and on to Kings Peak, then down the Lake Atwood Trail. At Lake Atwood, we were doing our usual thing, spin fishing with red & white Daredevils, and began catching huge arctic grayling--that are usually caught on flies as they have small mouths, but these had HUGE MOUTHS, and were going for our lures. In a previous section I inserted a couple of pictures, and will repeat, but with a panel of pictures, as I, along with one of the boys, Steve Clark, also caught grayling 18" long, even though Ted got the largest, 19" long. The pictures are poor in quality as my camera was later dropped into one of the Chain Lakes, but we salvaged the following pictures:

117

http://wildlife.utah.gov/blog/2014/theres-gold-in-the-uintas/

p. 297

Sorry about repeating….again, Ted’s record arctic grayling, but it’s more than worth it as it is “history” in the making, and I got a nice 18” one too. For Utah State Records, see: https://wildlife.utah.gov/record-fish.html

In this section on the Uinta River Drainage, I have listed 74 lakes, 72 that have numbers, with 51 listed in the 1997 pamphlet as having fish, but some were experimental, and since then others, which I listed as "No information," might now in 2018 have fish. I will find out soon from the DWR the current situation.

Chapter 2: THE WILDERNESS AREA – South Slope

Section 17: The DRY GULCH DRAINAGE ******************

PREFACE My Struggle to get to Crow Canyon & SURVIVING A FALL & LIGHTNING AT JACKSON PARK Back in 2011, in my zeal to explore and photograph all of the Uintas, I discovered on my NG Wilderness Map what the DWR described as "the smallest drainage on the South Slope ……divided into two main basins: Heller and Crow." 118 The CROW BASIN, "long and narrow with steep side walls," like a box canyon, and basically without marked trails, attracted me most, and in that year I did my first explorations at a time when I was beginning to have a difficult time….actually becoming a cripple, that led in 2012 to my first back surgery fusing vertebras and trying to solve a pinched nerve problem. So 2012 became a year when I was not able to backpack. But my attempts in 2011 did result in one YouTube video about Crow Basin, entitled, "SAW IT, SURVIVED IT"119 but did not tell the whole story. What did come out of that effort was that one of my High Uinta Friends, Jonathan Jaussi, flew over the area and took aerial photographs and shared them with me. They ended up being a great help to me finally getting down into Crow Canyon in 2013, after sort of recovering from my back surgery. That resulted in my 2nd YouTube video, 120 done during Utah's PIONEER DAY CELEBRATION, my trip honoring my great grandmother, Alice Brooks, survivor of the Martin Handcart Company ordeal.

118

DWR publication No. 97-6, revised edition 1997, DRY GULCH & UINTA RIVER DRAINAGES.

119

Saw it, Survived It, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dUIQjy7WAjo&feature=youtu.be

120

2013 CROW BASIN--A PIONEER ADVENTURE, http://youtu.be/GVgBmNVTQ-o

p. 309

Let me first show you a collection of the best of the aerial photographs by Jonathan that he so kindly has given me permission to use. Then I will share with you the very important SURVIVAL experiences--that includes THE MOST AMAZING EXPERIENCE I'VE HAD IN THE OUTDOORS. NOTE: In all of what I describe I do so as though it was all part of one year's experience--but a combination of the two backpacks. An important part of it was getting some crucial help from Rocky Balboa's trainer, Mickie, to get down into the box canyon. I'll also include a panel of animal photos I experienced there, more than almost anywhere. And, last but not least introduce you to some HIGH UINTA FRIENDS, who had heard I was to make the attempt, and threw together a quick trip to meet me there. All of this, with many details in photographs you can see in the videos.

Looking north with 13,440 ft. high Mt. Emmons watching over Crow Canyon

Looking at Jackson Park from the south with the only water at its lower end coming from a spring in the little clump of conifers in the dead center, which is where I camped and where I found the only sign lying on the ground I'll insert on the next page.

p. 310

Of course. after the photo, I hung it on a nail as best I could

The 2nd line says, TIMOTHY LAKES - 13.5 miles. The trail to Jackson Park is actually an old jeep road, now with barriers, all the way to the Timothy Lakes, some of them with dikes and head gates--when machinery was used there as elsewhere in the Uintas before the Wilderness designation.

Looking south showing the escarpment crossing the picture that in my 78th year with balance and agility lacking a tad, I was hesitant to tackle as young people would do.

The southern or lower end of Jackson Park where I finally found a way down.

p. 311

Crow Canyon's 8-9 lakes that are managed fisheries of the DWR, Crow Lake in the upper dead center where we will be in a moment.

A WELL EARNED WORD OF APPRECIATION FROM ALL OF US: To: Jonathan Jaussi for what for me are the incredible photographs he got for me and for all of us, helping me to finally get into Crow Canyon, and helping all of us have a few moments of inspiration and awe of the HIGH UINTAS from these wonderful photographs. THANKS!

NOW, SURVIVING & GETTING DOWN INTO CROW CANYON I camped by the spring and early that morning hiked all the way up Jackson Park, got photographs of elk, saw bones of some critters that didn't make it, and got over along the escarpment going as high up as I could, but not finding a safe path. Then a drop or two of rain began falling and I hustled back to my pack and got under the protection of some pines, but the intensity of the storm increased and it quickly got quite cold with hail falling. I knew from previous experience that I had to avoid like the plague getting wet and cold that could bring on hypothermia--one of the three or four main killers in the Uintas. I stepped out of the protection and tried to quickly throw the poncho up over my head and pack, but hurried too much, and lost my balance, and stumbled backwards over a fallen tree and its entangled root. As I was going over it--my pack pulled me forcefully backwards. My left foot got caught in the root, firmly grabbing my toes and bending me backwards and down with tremendous force on my ankle ligaments, and I ended up hanging by my foot that was bending with such pressure that I was a sure it had to be broken, connective tissues, and ligaments torn--nothing could have withstood that much force!

p. 312

I struggled free of my pack, then lunged for a root and pulled myself up and got my foot out of the tangle--seen on the previous page on the left. My foot and ankle were sore, but not broken, nor ligaments torn—an extraordinary testament to the effectiveness of my supplements and continual exercise program! I got my pack and poncho on and moved up to the edge of the Park, and was careful to keep to the smaller trees that hopefully wouldn't attract lighting. Then the rain and lightning hit with a vengeance. THE LIGHTNING WAS RIGHT ON TOP OF ME--THE THUNDER & LIGHTNING HITTING AT THE SAME INSTANT……THE GROUND SHAKING! I STOOD THERE PARALYZED WITH AWE AS LITTLE WISPS OF ELECTRICITY DANCED IN FRONT OF ME.

The above reconstruction of the scene is quite accurate, and THE MOST AMAZING OUTDOOR EXPERIENCE OF MY LIFE--YOU HAD TO BE THERE TO APPRECIATE THE EVENT--ELECTICITY DANCING ALL AROUND ME.

Eventually--in the 2013 attempt, I moved on along the edge of the escarpment, and found a couple of places where a young person could likely get safely down into the canyon, but I continued down to the end of Jackson Park where there were boulder fields, and for the only time in my Crow Canyon experience found a Forest Service marker saying I was in the Wilderness Area--from the edge of Jackson Park down into the canyon. I was then faced with a decision: To the left it was very steep with dense timber and a lot of deadfall which I don't manage very well anymore; to the right was a boulder field. As I looked at my options I thought about Rocky coming back to his corner all beaten up, blood everywhere, eyes almost swollen shut, and Rocky said, "I see three of him!" Mickey yelled at him, "HIT THE ONE IN THE MIDDLE!" So, my decision was to GO TO THE MIDDLE, as you see below:

p. 313

It worked like a charm, as I found in the middle, between a tree and a rock, a faint trail and as I went for it diving--almost literally downward I yelled out, "YEE-HAW," it taking me down the mountain on what I called, "THE YEEHAW TRAIL!"

I had a wonderful time in Crow Canyon. On a trail past DG-1 lake I got the following great shot of two young elk, a female and her brother, his antlers just beginning to grow.

I then bushwhacked my way through a lot of deadfall up to Crow Lake where I set up my camp, and the next day had a great Sunday celebrating PIONEER DAY, thinking of my great-grandmother Alice Brooks, whose life had inspired me more than once during my project to "NEVER GIVE UP!" I had a great time also with the little critters, a panel of which I'll insert below, including the elk I'd seen up at Jackson Park--in fact, early that day I had heard the elk out in the park, and then a pack of coyotes howling happily on the chase--which I wish I could have seen, or at least got a recording of.

I even got a little religion in with my tiny Grundig radio, picking up the Mormon Tabernacle Choir. Their rendition of the pioneer hymn, Come, Come Ye Saints, had words that had special meaning for me as I was making tough journeys too. Then they really surprised me when they sang the one song of my infancy that I could still remember, Give said the little stream, give oh give, give oh give,121 which in a nature sense has great 121

Watch a wonderful rendition of this children's song at: https://www.thetabernaclechoir.org/videos/August-122018-4639-music-and-the-spoken-word.html

p. 314

meaning, but also it had me thinking how maybe those words--sang in my infancy, engraved on my mind and soul the idea of "giving," which I had been doing for more than 50 years among my needy Mayan brothers and sisters in Guatemala (www.guatemalanfoundation.org), and over all my years of the HIGH UINTAS WILDERNESS PROJECT, giving or sharing with all and helping all have safe, enjoyable and inspiring experiences in the Uintas—and TO

SAVE LIVES! Those thoughts were then interrupted when I heard voices--no, not heavenly, rather of four HIGH UINTA FRIENDS, who had noticed on my website that I was going to make another attempt to get to Crow Basin, so they quickly threw together their stuff and headed for Crow Basin to meet me. It was a great reunion. I'll insert their picture below:

Darren & Ryan McMichael, and Tyler and Tom Summerhays, & of course Little Foot

They had already tried all the upper lakes and just caught pan-sized trout, and since quite frankly I was pretty tired and sore from my hike in--still struggling some with my surgery recovery, I decided to just take their word about the other lakes. Besides I had somehow lost my poncho on the trail, and figured I'd better take advantage of the nice weather to get out of there. So, I'd fish a little in Crow Lake, and the next day head for home.

Fishing was good catching very nice Cutthroat trout, cooking this one in aluminum foil for my lunch. And, on my way out I found my poncho, so I was more than lucky and blessed on this backpack, and remember Crow Basin with great fondness.

p. 315

Chapter 2: THE WILDERNESS AREA—South Slope

Section 17: The DRY GULCH DRAINAGE & TRAILHEADS With this smallest drainage on the South Slope, we will first deal with CROW CANYON, and then with the HELLER BASIN. HOW TO GET HERE: From the Wasatch Front, 100 miles to Duchesne, (from Heber on U.S. 40) then north following the signs towards Yellowstone Canyon (29 miles) on the Road to Moon Lake, but turning east on the dirt-gravel road towards Yellowstone Canyon, then 4 miles before the campground and trailhead, turning east at the sign pointing to Dry Gulch, and then about 5 miles to FR-120. For 2 miles it's not bad, but then there's a stretch like the photo below, but if you can get by that, it will be another 2 miles up, and up and up, to the barriers, for a TOTAL OF ABOUT 134 miles. For the hike, consult the Topographical map for distances.

THE CROW CANYON DRAINAGE LAKE DG-1: This lake looks good to me, and sufficiently deep, but the DWR says no fish. CROW LAKE (DG-3): 10,350 ft. elevation, 18 acres, 26' deep, accessible to horses only from the Heller Basin Trail. Cutthroat trout. LAKE DG-4: No fish LAKE DG-6: 10,550 ft. elevation, 3 acres, 5' deep, Cutthroat trout. LAKE DG-7: 10,550 ft. elevation, 6 acres, 4' deep, Cutthroat trout that migrate from DG-6. LAKE DG-8: East of DG-7 70 yards, 10,550 ft. elevation, 7 acres, 8' deep, a few Cutthroat that migrate from DG-6. LAKE DG-9: Follow the inlet stream from DG-6 up to the rock escarpment above which lies this lake, 10,750 ft. elevation, 10 acres, 27' deep, Cutthroat trout. LAKE DG-10: Accessed by following the inlet stream north from DG-9 about 1 mile, 10,750 ft. elevation, 10 acres, 12' deep, Cutthroat trout. LAKE DG-14: Sits at the northeast head of the canyon 2 miles north of Crow Lake, 11,000 ft. elevation, 2 acres, 10' deep, Cuttroat trout. LAKE DG-15: Found at the northwest rim at the head of Crow Canyon, 10,950 ft. elevation, 3 acres, 9' deep, water level fluctuates, has a good population of fairy shrimp, Cuttroat trout at times subject to winterkill. LAKE DG-16: Located 100 feet south of DG-15, 10,950 ft. elevation, 3 acres, 8' deep, Cuttroat trout subject to winterkill. LAKE DG-17: Located 100 yards east of DG-16, 10,950 ft. elevation, 3 acres, 12' deep, has a large population of Cutthroat trout sustained by natural reproduction.

p. 316

THE HELLER BASIN HOW TO GET HERE: Follow instructions to Crow Canyon access road FR-120. From there, on FR-119, go east 3 miles to the Dry Gulch Road--FR-122, and drive 4 tough miles to gate, which some maps say is a Trailhead. See Chapter 1, pages 120, 121.

HELLER LAKE/RESERVOIR (DG-28): Accessed 2 miles following the jeep road from the gate, 10,108 ft. elevation, 12 acres, 37' deep, horse friendly but no feed available, pan-sized Brook trout, heavy usage. LAKE DG-30: No fish life LAKE DG-29: Is a small beaver pond accessed from Heller Lake, 1/4 mile northwest to a long park followed 1/2 mile then east 1/8th mile, horse friendly, not managed by DWR for fish. HIDDEN LAKE DG-27: At the head of the Heller Basin, accessed 2 miles north-northeast on a poorly marked trail from Heller Lake. 9,520 ft. elevation, 10 acres, 39' deep. Fair population of healthy Brook trout.

LILY PAD LAKES Upper DG-25: Beautiful meadow lake surrounded by conifers, accessed 2 miles cross country northwest of Heller Lake, or 7.5 miles via the Dry Gulch Rd. and pack trail over Flat Top Mountain. Horse friendly, 10,280 ft. elevation 12 acres, 37' deep, small population of healthy Brook and Cutthroat trout. Heavy pressure. Lower DG-26: Meadow lake covered with aquatic vegetation, access from Upper Lily Pad Lake, then 1/8th mile due east. 10,275 ft. elevation, 9 acres, 11 ' deep, Brook trout, light pressure.

BOLLIE (U-96): Natural lake surrounded by meadows accessed by trail from Lilly Pad Lakes, or via a primitive logging road 3 miles north past Jefferson Park to the canyon rim, then follow he trail2 miles along the rim until you reach the lake near the head of the basin. 10,660 ft. elevation, 10 acres, 15' deep, Cutthroat trout and I've been told it's the best fishing, pressure light.

In this section we have described 19 lakes.
