Section 18: YELLOWSTONE & SWIFT CREEK DRAINAGES *******************************

PREFACE

FROM AMAZING BACKPACKERS to WOLVERINES on the YELLOWSTONE CANYON/SWIFT CREEK TRAIL

Most of the river was inaccessible as you can see, but there were places where I could climb down and fish the stream and so my one night in the canyon was with a meal of a couple of nice brook trout that were tricked by a Mepps spinner.

In my 4th season of backpacking on my HIGH UINTAS WILDERNESS PROJECT, I achieved 1,000 miles of backpacking in the Uintas. One of those 2006 trips was in the amazing Yellowstone Canyon seen above, and then on to the Swift Creek drainage on the east side of that large basin, and as I reflect back on the adventure I am quite amazed at the 7 day experience--ending, sort of, with rare and tough WOLVERINES. First, because of the people I met on the trail. Then amazing indirect encounters with the critters, and what I learned about them My way of tackling the area was with a loop hike from the Swift Creek Trailhead, straight up Yellowstone Canyon for 10.8 miles, and then take off on a steep switch backing trail taking me east up into the high country. Within the first hour in the canyon I met Randy Thompson, one of those rare coincidences that in our conversation we somehow got into the intriguing subject of gold in the Uintas and the Lost Rhoades Mine. That chance encounter got me going on research that helped make the Uintas come alive for me--which I've mentioned some, and will more later on.

p. 320

Later that day I ran into the wonderful Arden Pope family from Springville, Utah--you see on the previous page, all with infectuous and well earned happy smiles--Arden and his wife, along with their five boys. They were on the last leg of an ambitious loop backpack, taking off at the sign you see below--going west up through the Garfield Basin, to the Highline Trail, then east over Tungsten Pass, across the headwaters of the Yellowstone past a major cross-trail and on to Anderson Pass, from where they climbed Kings Peak. From there they backtracked to the cross-trail--the Yellowstone-Smith's Fork Trail, bisecting the Highline Trail, and headed straight down the canyon 14.6 miles to the Trailhead, TOTAL, 50 miles.

You can see by the signs some of the great options from this junction located 8.5 miles up the canyon from the Trailhead. Did you catch the Forest Service error? From the next junction 2.3 miles past the above junction, there is a trail that climbs up to Milk Lake, and from there swings down, and then up to Bluebell Pass and into the Swift Creek Drainage. Up near Milk Lake, I met Joey Hoopes and his boy, Jesse. They were on their first backpacking trip heading for Kings Peak, but were doing it the hard way having come up the steep Swift Creek Trail, over 11,613 ft. Bluebell Pass, then up to Milk Lake, and down, way down to Yellowstone Canyon to then up to the Highline Trail and follow it to Anderson Pass, and from there climb Kings Peak.

NOTE: I hope my book will help a few--orienting them a little better. See the body of SECTION 18 for a comparative rundown of ways to climb KINGS PEAK--Utah's highest peak at 13,528 feet.

p. 321

Later I learned that they made it and got a picture of them on the highest point in Utah.

NOTE: Joey lives in Eagle Mountain, and is an expert mechanic, and in his spare time restores those old antique cars and pickups some of us fondly remember, and are amazed at when we see them in parades, and such. Keep up the good work Joey! I was soon at Milk Lake, another with a dike to increase its capacity and a head gate to control the outflow to help keep alive the Uintah Basin below us to the south.

NOTE: As mentioned in Chapter 1, the Swift Creek Trailhead has some wonderful displays that give the history of these water conservation efforts on the South Slope. DON'T MISS THEM. I soon had my camp set up on the north side of the lake, and went fishing, and ended the day recording on film (no digital yet, as I was being stupidly stubborn) some of the most wonderful photographs of my years in the High Uintas. I'd better insert a few of them starting with what for some reason I have called my "stealth camp," then the lake and fishing success, and one memorable sundown photo, with another to end this section, and then we'll get to the incredible WOLVERINES.

That night I heard several times a whole herd of whatever, all around my camp hearing their hoofs on the rocks, some coming very close to my tent. The next day I saw the hoof

p. 322

prints of elk. I think I mentioned this previously and maybe said I heard their musical sounds, but not true--that experience was later when camped out near Cleveland Pass. The next day: I couldn't say I'd explored the major features of the Uintas without, in addition to climbing Kings Peak, also visiting and photographing KINGS LAKE, so the next day I did a day hike going due north 2 miles, mostly crossing open, above timberline tundra, to visit and try fishing in KINGS LAKE. It is found on the southern flank of South Kings Peak, Utah's 2nd highest at 13,512 feet. I found a very old sign, but most of the name obliterated by the ravishes of time. I got out my small backpacking pocket knife and repaired it as you see below. The lake looked deep enough to have fish, and I tried working halfway around the lake, but had no strikes, and headed back to camp.

The next day I packed up and followed the trail towards Bluebell Pass. The trail first drops down some to the south, but then circles towards the east climbing the 11,613 ft. pass, of course photographing bluebell flowers, and others along the way. Then dropped down into the Swift Creek Drainage with its 18 lakes. Down from the pass I became entranced photographing some beautiful wildflowers, when surprised by two backpackers--two very young teenage girls. They were on their way to climb Kings Peak, not alone, but their father, Mike Ward and companion, Lynn Brown, had been left in the girl's dust! I eventually met the men, sorry for not having taken pictures of the girls. Eventually they did go on to successfully climb Kings Peak, and sent me a few pictures, I'll insert below….first in the panel, my picture of Mike, then their photos.

I went on to explore all the lakes in the drainage, and a couple of days later headed down the trail when all of a sudden surprised again, this time hearing hoofs on rocks, and ready with my camera to get a shot of a whole herd of elk, but it turned out to rather be Dave and Alicia Evans on horseback.

p. 323

It was again one of those coincidences you end up being grateful for.

We talked for the next hour. Dave was a Forest Service employee whose mission was to find and photograph wolverines in the Uintas. He had bait stations up around 10,500 ft. and higher where he would set up motion activated digital cameras, using road kill as bait. Once a week he would ride up to pick up memory cards, inserting new ones, along with new batteries, and then excitedly head for home and his computer to see what kind of luck he had. As close as he got was a blurred image looking to be the right size and color, but not clear. I asked about bears, and he said he had never got shots of a bear at his high country bait stations, but had down along the streams between 8,000 and 9,000 ft. Wolverines are rarely ever seen, and most people are only familiar with the Michigan or Utah Valley U. Wolverines, or maybe you have come to mind, what for me was a great movie about wolverines with Patrick Swayze--RED DAWN. "Great" as when a teenager in Provo, Utah--when we anticipated World War III with the Chinese and/or Russians invading our Pacific Coast and moving on to Utah…. me and my buddies had a plan to take off to the mountains with our deer hunting rifles and become guerrilla fighters, like the kids in the movie did--as ferocious fighters, calling themselves THE WOLVERINES, against the Russian and Nicaraguan communist invaders.

Wolverines in nature are bear like animals, but small about the size of a medium sized dog, around 50 lbs. with maximum around 70. They usually feed on small mammals, but are very strong and capable of killing animals several times their size, like a deer. 122 The picture below of a WOLVERINE is also from the Wikipedia site mentioned in the reference.

122

Wolverine: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolverine

p. 324

At the time of Dave Evans in 2006, the only previous proven case in Utah was in 1979 when one was killed on U.S. Highway 40 east of Vernal. Dave finally moved on to other tasks. Then in 2014 DWR motion activated night video digital cameras set up on the Uinta's North Slope in January, memory cards picked up in the Spring, and they had the first photographic evidence of a wolverine in the Uintas. In April of that year a trail camera also got pictures of a wolverine 20 miles south of Evanston, Wyoming, that would put it near the Uintas. Since wolverines are known to travel incredible distances and inhabit areas of around 350 square miles, there was speculation that the two cases might have been the same wolverine. 123 Let me insert one more incredible report about wolverines. This is fascinating, as you will see. The Wildlife Conservation Society reported in June 2009 that wolverine researchers had been tracking for almost three months one that had crossed into northern Colorado. Society officials had tagged the young male wolverine in Wyoming near Grand Teton National Park and it had traveled southward for about 500 miles. It was the first wolverine seen in Colorado since 1919, and its appearance was also confirmed by the Colorado Division of Wildlife.[54] In May 2016 the same wolverine was killed by a cattle ranch-hand in North Dakota, ending a >800 mile trip by this lone male wolverine, dubbed M-56. This was the first verified sighting of a Wolverine in North Dakota in 150 years.[55] In February 2014, a wolverine was seen in Utah, the first confirmed sighting in that state in 30 years.[56]124

More recently in 2016 a wolverine was killed on a highway one mile west of Laketown, near Bear Lake in Utah's northern Rich County. 125 With great satisfaction I headed down the trail after a very satisfying 7 days exploring the Swift Creek Drainage, and the eastern half of the Yellowstone Drainage--with the western half to be reported on in Section 19, from the Center Park Trailhead. Now on to the details of each lake. Below: THE SUN SETS OVER MILK LAKE

Section 18:

The YELLOWSTONE & SWIFT CREEK DRAINAGES and SWIFT CREEK TRAILHEAD HOW TO GET HERE: From the Wasatch Front, 100 miles to Duchesne, (from Heber on U.S. 40) then north following the signs towards Yellowstone Canyon (29 miles) on the Road to Moon Lake, but at the sign turning east on the dirt-gravel road and continue to Yellowstone Canyon, and the Swift Creek Trailhead. TOTAL of 129 miles.

OPTIONS FOR CLIMBING KINGS PEAK OPTION 1: Henrys Fork Trailhead on the North Slope……………………..……….…..…....15 miles (30) OPTION 2: Swift Creek Trailhead via Yellowstone Canyon…………………………..….. 18 miles (36) OPTION 3: Swift Ck. TH via Swift Ck., Bluebell Pass, Yellowstone Canyon…..22 miles.(44) OPTION 4: Uinta River TH via Atwood Trail, Trail Rider Pass…………………………..25 miles(50)

THE SWIFT CREEK DRAINAGE The first lake, actually in the Yellowstone Creek Drainage, as its outlet stream goes into the Yellowstone, will be accessed before the Trailhead about 1/2 mile at the well marked Grants Spring on the right side of the road. LILY (S-15) or on the NG Wilderness Map, WATER LILY LAKE: A very nice lake surrounded by pines and quaking aspen trees. Access is via a steep, well-defined trail that goes 1 mile to the lake with 1,250 feet of elevation gain. 9,346 ft. elevation, 20 acres, 39' deep. No horse feed at the lake. Stocked brook trout, heavily fished.

We will begin listing the rest of the lakes of the SWIFT CREEK DRAINAGE. After leaving the Trailhead, at about 0.1 of a mile you come to an iron bridge over Swift Creek, and shortly come to the sign pointing to the east up that drainage. Very shortly the trail turns north-north west and begins a sharp climb. LAKE S-2: No information. LAKE S-3: No information. GRAYLING (X-56): Access is 5 miles via the Swift Creek Trail to Swift Creek, then 1 more north along the creek to where the outlet from the lake converges, than follow the stream up to the lake. Not too horse friendly. 9,980 ft. elevation, 8.5 acres, 33' deep, Brook trout & recently stocked with Grayling, with heavy fishing pressure.

DEER (X-55): Located on the trail, 6 miles from the Trailhead, 10,240 ft. elevation, 12 acres, 47' deep, Brook and Cutthroat trout by natural reproduction. Heavy use . LAKE X-48: No information. LAKE X-47: No information.

p. 326

LAKE X-51: This is a very remote lake with no trail leading to it. It is located 1 mile west of the fork in the trail past Deer Lake. 11,000 ft. elevation, 5 acres, 8' deep, Cutthroat trout, very light use.

WHITE MILLER (X-54): Located about 1 mile north on the left hand fork, where the trail divides 5.8 miles from the trailhead, or a total of about 7 miles from the TH. 10,670 ft. elevation, 11 acres, 18' deep, surrounded by meadows and pine trees. Horse friendly, with stocked Brook trout, heavy pressure, abundant mosquitoes and horse flies during mid-summer.

FARMERS (X-23): Located on the trail, topographical map says 6.3 miles from TH, pamphlet says 8 miles. Is another lake/reservoir with a control system at the outlet. 10,990 ft. elevation, 63 acres, 24' deep, horse friendly, healthy population of stocked Brook trout. fishing pressure is moderate.

We are now up at the point where one trail goes towards Bluebell Pass, the other to the Timothy Lakes Basin--where we will go first going to East Timothy Lake and then to Center and up to West, then swing around the basin to the north and east. EAST TIMOTHY (X-16):

It is 9.5 miles from the trailhead, and is another lake/reservoir with drawdown as much as 30'. 11,000 ft. elevation, 40 acres, 35' deep, has a large population of Brook trout, and some Cutthroats. Good fishing in Swift Creek below the dam.

CENTER TIMOTHY (X-20): Located 250 yards west of East Timothy, 11,030 ft. elevation, 10 acres, 18' deep, with 3' dam, and 2' of fluctuation. horse friendly, Brook trout self sustaining.

WEST TIMOTHY (X-19): Accessed 1/2 mile northwest along the inlet stream to East Timothy, 11,100 ft. elevation, 45 acres, 45' deep, no fluctuation, horse feed sparse, Brook trout.

UPPER CARROL (X-18): Located at the head of the basin in rocky terrain, 3/4 mile north of East Timothy, 11,140 ft. elevation, 35 acres, 45' deep, good population of Brook trout that reproduce naturally.

LOWER CARROL (X-17): Located 1/2 mile north of East Timothy, 11,060 ft. elevation, 9 acres, 7' deep, horse friendly, has a large Brook trout population.

EAST CARROL (X-21): Located 1/2 mile northeast of East Timothy, 11,230 ft. elevation, 10 acres, 19' deep, may contain Cutthroat trout.

LAKE X-22: Located 3/4 mile east of East Timothy, 11,060 ft. elevation, 9 acres, 8' deep, horse friendly, Both Brook and Cutthroat trout.

We will now return to the junction of trails at Farmers Lake, and describe the lakes west of the trail and one to the east as the trail climbs Bluebell Pass. LAKE X-30: No information. TWIN (X-77): Access is 3/4 mile northwest of White Miller over a rocky, timbered ridge, 10,816 ft. elevation, 14 acres, 15' deep, horse friendly, a productive lake with Cutthroat trout.

LAKE X-50: No information LAKE X-24: Access is 3/4 mile west of Farmers Lake, 10,919 ft. elevation, 21.4 acres, 30' deep, horse friendly, Stocked with Cutthroat trout.

p. 327

LAKE X-25 Found 1 mile northwest of Farmers Lake at the head of the basin, 10,966 ft. elevation, 15.9 acres, 27' deep, horse friendly, has Cutthroat trout.

LAKE X-26 Is in open rocky terrain north of Farmers, and has no outlets, 11,008 ft. elevation, 7.7 acres, 23' deep, Brook trout.

The trail now takes you over Bluebell Pass, to the YELLOWSTONE DRAINAGE and then 2 miles to Milk Lake . MILK (Y-25): Located 14 miles from TH via Yellowstone Canyon Trail, or 11 miles using the Swift Creek Trail, 10,989 ft. elevation, 17.5 acres, 20' deep, fluctuates, horse friendly, Brook trout, light pressure.

KINGS (Y-22): Accessed 2 miles due north of Milk Lake, horse friendly, 11,416 ft. elevation, 10 acres, has Cutthroat trout, stocked in 2018. LAKE Y-23: No information. LAKE Y-24: No information.

In this Section we have listed 19 lakes that are active fisheries.

Section 19: The CENTER PARK TRAILHEAD— WEST YELLOWSTONE DRAINAGE-- THE GARFIELD & SWASEY HOLE BASINS

****************

PREFACE

SURVIVAL AT SWASEY HOLE126 The Center Park Trailhead--Swasey Hole/Garfield Basin Trail, brings back great memories as it is another of those inspiring areas of wonderful adventures in the High Uintas. The first one is from 1954 when I was with Ted Packard and Charlie Peterson on our two week backpack across the entire Primitive Area. As we came over Porcupine Pass and down into the upper Garfield Basin, the sky was dark and getting darker with a storm on about September 10th. We stopped to fish North Star Lake surrounded by arctic tundra. As the storm moved in on us with stiff, cold winds, then snow, all of a sudden the pan sized brook trout we were catching were pushed aside as giant brookies came up from depths and bullied the little fish aside to grab our lures. Before our hands were too cold to work our spinning reels, we all had experienced vicious strikes, and fish on, but Ted had actually caught two of them, then we decided to find a way to survive, and just headed down running hoping to find some trees and protection from the storm. We finally found a few trees and before it got dark set up our camp and took refuge in the one pup tent, me squeezing inside too, rather than use my poncho/leanto. The sun warmed us the next day, and Charlie clicked a shot of a tough looking Ted with his two brookies, and me cooking our breakfast--complete with my several pound, heavy leather jacket--not having yet learned much about light-weight backpacking.

126

For more info see Chapter 1, page 125

p. 333

A few years later, Ted and me took our group of 15 Explorer Scouts up from the Center Park Trailhead, through the Gilbert Basin, then east to climb Kings Peak, and then down the Attwood Trail to the Uinta Trailhead. Then in 1962 it was Ted and me alone hiking north from Center Park, up through the Garfield Basin to Porcupine Pass, and somehow skirted around the western end of 13,091 foot high Wilson Peak to dry ski down a chute to the Red Castle upper lakes, mentioned in Section 10, on page 244 with the huge 8+ lb. cutthroat, then with the 3.5 lb. tail half circled around over Smiths Fork Pass, and back through the Garield Basin to this Trailhead. As part of my HIGH UINTAS WILDERNESS PROJECT in 2003 I had again gone through the upper Garfield Basin on the Highline Trail as part of my expedition, and caught pansized brookies in North Star Lake--too early for a blizzard and the big ones, and camped there. Later I wanted to visit again the area in 2011, and so in late July found myself at the Center Park Trailhead, prepared to do an 8 day backpack to explore again the entire area and all of its many lakes.

To that point I had gone through--during my PROJECT, like 7 surgeries, 2 radiation treatments, mostly overcome my metatarsilitis (balls of my feet feeling like stepping on a rock), and survived a heart attack, plus hypothermia on the Red Castle Trail (I'll sneak that in as the Preface to Section 20), and a number of times, to one degree or another experienced High Altitude Sickness--but which I didn't really understand yet--as I was only 75 and admittedly a SLOW LEARNER! I did a YouTube video127 -- the title page above, of that experience, but will relate it very briefly here so we can finally—hopefully, learn our lesson.

127

SURVIVAL AT SWASEY HOLE: http://youtu.be/SG1i1EFxV3s

p. 334

I had got a late start the first day, but by the 2nd was going over an area that should be considered a pass at 11,100 ft. where the breathtaking panorama—on the previous page-of the spine of the Uintas opens up before you. We can see the trail in the lower right corner. From there you drop way down into Swasey Hole, before climbing up from there into the Garfield Basin. In Swasey Hole I made the mistake of trying make a loop of the lakes bushwhacking through a lot of downed timber and really wore myself out.

I finally camped, feeling fatigued, nauseous not able to eat, had a headache, and stomach upset with gamboo! – I’m using the Guatemalan/missionary definition which is intestinal! I mixed and swallowed the supplements that had worked for me many times--5 gms. of glutamine, calcium/magnesium--both known among marathoners to avoid getting sick, plus ENDUROX for recovery.128 Within 2 hours I was finally able to eat something. I had also learned about Diamox to help speed up acclimatization to higher altitudes, and took two tablets, knowing that it helped me sleep when experiencing such problems.

The next day I packed up and moved up the trail out of Swasey Hole towards the Garfield Basin, but as I approached again the 11,000 foot elevation began feeling real sick and shocked as all of a sudden there erupted from deep in my lungs an ugly, gurgling sounding cough like I had never experienced in my life. I stopped shocked, saying to myself, "Where did that come from?" 128

Supplements towards the end of the post GEARS/SUPPLEMENTS: https://cordellmandersen.com/2015gearsupplements/

p. 335

NOTE: I knew something was seriously wrong, but wasn't sure what--but suspected it had to do with my fatigue, and the altitude. What we learned in Section 7, pages 214, and 215, we should now remember. I quote: HIGH ALTITUDE PULMONARY EDEMA (HAPE)--a buildup of fluid in the lungs that can be dangerous and even life threatening. The most severe form of altitude sickness is HIGH ALTITUDE CEREBRAL EDEMA (HACE) when there's fluid in the brain, which is life threatening, with symptoms like:  Headache  Dizziness  Nausea  Vomiting  Fatigue and loss of energy  Shortness of breath  Problems with sleep  Loss of appetite129

I stopped, knowing something was seriously wrong, and decided quickly I had to go back down into Swasey Hole. I got out my SPOT Tracker, not to send a 911 or help signal, but rather an OK signal to show where I stopped to then go back down the trail into the Swasey Hole, where I hit the OK button again. My friend, Luke Hopkins back in Springville, who was tracking me, noticed and knew something was wrong, and almost jumped in his jeep to head for the Uintas to help.

He decided to wait a little because I was hitting the OK button. But he suspected there was trouble. If I had really thought I couldn't make it I would have hit the 911 button, and got on my satellite phone calling for help--but I still felt I could make it on my own-if I proceeded carefully. Back in the Hole at my previous camping spot, I set up my camp to rest, take my supplements to see if I could restore my appetite to get some strength. It finally worked, but only two foods appealed to me: Dee's Cereal, and my powdered eggnog drink laced with the supplements mentioned.

129

https://www.webmd.com/a-to-z-guides/altitude-sickness#2

p. 336

The next day I felt a bit better, and decided to head for the trailhead, with the big challenge climbing over the 11,100 foot pass. I felt confident I could make it, but had to move along carefully, and rest often--even if it took me a couple of days. As I was slowly working up the rocky trail I rested often, but prayed constantly, then at one rest stop noticed down off the trail a backpack. I checked it out and didn't find any identification but noticed it had been there a while. I finally assumed it belonged to someone like me, but who decided, "With my pack there's no way I can get up out of this suckin hole!" and jettisoned his pack!

A littler further along I saw down off the steep trail a bunch of bones and worked my way down close enough to see that they belonged to some critter who hadn't made it-but not from a human. It took me a while--but not as long as I had feared--to get up to the pass, and took my pack off to rest, say a prayer of gratitude, and while resting pulled out the book I was reading on this backpack: THE CONQUEST OF NEW SPAIN, by Bernal Diaz, and marveled at the tough times the Spaniards had endured in the conquest--and in perspective realized my ordeal was like child's play, even while realizing that it could have been deadly if I hadn't of gone at least somewhat prepared. The chapter I was reading was, "Cortez Collects Fresh Strength," which I had been blessed with too, actually having throughout a deeply spiritual experience.

I made it to the Trailhead and the car by 7:30 PM, feeling a lot of gratitude and relief. I drove down the steep road from this 10,400 foot high Trailhead, and found a spot down in the Uintah Basin to park and rest for the night. I was dead tired, but alive and better prepared for my next adventure. I stopped at the Forest Service Ranger Station in Duchesne and reported the abandoned pack so they could check it out.

p. 337

Chapter 2: THE WILDERNESS AREA—South slope

Section 19: The CENTER PARK TRAILHEAD: WEST YELLOWSTONE DRAINAGE--THE GARFIELD & SWASEY HOLE BASINS HOW TO GET HERE: From the Wasatch Front, 100 miles to Duchesne, (from Heber on U.S. 40) then north following the signs towards Yellowstone Canyon (29 miles) on the Road to Moon Lake, but at the sign turning east to Yellowstone Canyon on the dirt-gravel road and continue to the sign to Hells Canyon (about 122 miles to that junction), then drive 10 miles to the Trailhead. TOTAL = 132 miles.

For more details, see Chapter 1, page 125.130 First, we'll learn about one lake accessed best from this trailhead, but which is in the Lake Fork Drainage. TOQUER (LF-25): This lake is the headwaters of Fish Creek that flows into Moon Lake. It can be accessed 7 miles via the Fish Creek National Recreation Trail from Moon Lake, or 3 miles via the Hell's Canyon Trail from the west end of the Center Park. 10,470 ft. elevation, 11.1 acres, 32' deep, horse friendly, has both Brook and Cutthroat trout, with light fishing pressure.

Now we'll move up the Swasey Hole/Garfield Basin Trail.

SWASEY HOLE -SWASEY (X-58): It is 6 miles from the trailhead, accessed by following the main stream 1 mile northwest, horse friendly but sometimes trail not well-marked, and with deadfall. The other option is to continue up the main trail and then go cross country along the edge of the mountain to the lake, 10,715 ft. elevation, 36 acres, 30' deep, has Brook and Cutthroat trout sustained naturally. A popular lake with heavy use. LAKE X-59: Located 50 yards southeast of Swasey Lake, 10,706 ft. elevation, 4.5 acres, 13' deep, has Brook and Cutthroat trout. LAKE X-60: Located 1/3 mile northwest of Swasey Lake up a trail-less slope. 10,810 ft. elevation, 8 acres, 30' deep, stocked with Cutthroat trout, with light pressure. LAKE X-57: Found 1 mile--with no trail, west of Swasey Lake up a rocky, timbered slope, not horse friendly, 10,976 ft. elevation, 8.8 acres, 30'deep, has naturally sustaining Brook trout.

We now move up into the GARFIELD BASIN basically doing a loop following the main trail up to the Highline Trail, then exploring the lakes near Tungsten Pass, and up the trail northwest, then swing down around the basin crossing open tundra visiting all the lakes. SPECIAL NOTICE: The DWR is proposing poisoning with rotenone the lakes and streams of the Garfield Drainage, and then restoring the Native Cutthroat trout in the area. If approved it will be done, along with the other 3 areas (Ottoson, Oweep & Fall Creek) between 2022-2034. SPIDER (X-109): It is located 11 miles from the trailhead, along the main trail, horse friendly. It is a pretty lake with several finger-like bays, at 10,876 ft. elevation, 20 acres, 31' deep, has Brook and Cutthroat trout. with heavy use. LAKE Y-33: No fish life.

GEM (Y-34): Accessed by following the outlet stream 1/2 mile from Five-Point Lake. 10,830 ft. elevation, 11.1 acres, 15' deep, horse friendly, with Brook trout sustained naturally & Tiger trout

FIVE POINT (X-106): This is a large lake/reservoir with a fluctuation of 10 feet. It is found 12 miles from the trailhead, horse friendly trail, but feed sparse. 11,009 ft. elevation, 82 acres, 21' deep, pan-sized Brook trout are abundant. Heavy use. SUPERIOR (X-103): Also a lake/reservoir with fluctuation during the season. Found along the trail 13 miles from the trailhead, 11,163 ft. elevation, 36 acres, 26' deep, horse access easy, but feed is sparse, has Brook trout sustained naturally, with moderate fishing pressure. My topographical measurement has it at 13.7 miles (plus the 15% error I have mentioned=2 miles, putting it near the pamphlet mileage). 11,344 ft. elevation, 13 acres, 13' deep, with Brook and Cutthroat trout, and moderate use. LAKE Y-19: This natural lake is found 1/2 mile east of Tungsten Lake, just over Tungsten Pass, 16.5 miles from the trailhead. 11,268 ft. elevation, 6.2 acres, 15' deep, with Brook trout, with light pressure . LAKE Y-20: Located south of Y-19, and 1/4 mile southeast of Tungsten Pass, 11,176 ft. elevation, 5 acres, 20' deep, with Arctic grayling & Brook trout.

NORTH STAR (X-108): Located along the Highline Trail, 16.5 miles from the trailhead, 11,395 ft. elevation, 14 acres, 15' deep, horse friendly but sparse feed. The fish? Remember what happened during a blizzard in 1954 with Ted's two large brookies. The pamphlet says, it contains a few pan sized Brook trout sustained by natural reproduction. LAKE Y-2: Accessed by following North Star inlet stream 1 mile. 11,670 ft. elevation, 1.8 acres, 20' deep, natural population of Brook trout, with light pressure. LAKE Y-4: Located a short distance north of Y-2, 11,679 ft elevation, 5.8 acres, 12' deep, natural population of Brook trout. If I ever get another chance, I'll take a few cast in each. North Star Lake is on the right, with Tungsten Lake beyond it. Y-32 & 33: With Arctic Grayling. DRIFT (Y-41): A lake/reservoir with extreme fluctuation. Found 1.25 miles southwest of Five Point, or 1/2 mile west of Spider. 11,064 ft. elevation, 14.8 acres, Brook trout with light pressure.

BLUEBELL (X-110): Access is by following the east inlet stream from Spider 1/4 mile west through thick willows. 10,894 ft. elevation, 38.3 acres, 32' deep, Brook trout abundant with some Cutthroat maintained by natural reproduction, pressure moderate. Note: I had a friend from the Army Reserve,

back in the early 60's, who said he caught here a brook trout that weighed over 8 lbs.

LAKE Y-37: Sits 1/3 mile south of Bluebell. Horses not recommended. 10,823 ft. elevation, 13 acres, 12' deep, Brook trout with light pressure.

LAKE Y-36: Located a short distance east northeast of Y-37 or 1/4 mile from trail at marker 8.3 miles from trailhead surrounded by conifers. 10,820 ft. elevation, 14 acres, 15' deep, horse access easy, but no pasture. Has a few Brook trout, pressure light.

With that we have finished a 23.2 mile loop, and in this Section have described 28 lakes that are active fisheries.

Section 20: THE LAKE FORK DRAINAGE & TRAILHEAD *************

PREFACE

HYPOTHERMIA -- It is a killer! "…. bone fragments found in the Uinta Mountains are those of a mother and daughter who got lost and died of hypothermia on a hike last fall…….. They probably died by the first night…" 131

A HYPOTHERMIA SURVIVAL SUCCESS: I knew about that report by KSL.com in 2004--a mother and daughter just going on a DAY HIKE….. and with that knowledge, and my own experience in the Uintas foremost in my mind, I headed up the trail to the Red Castle area at the end of July, 2007. I was still working on recovery from the reconstruction of my "football ankle" that had caused me to slightly limp since I was 17 years old. It had entailed a tendon transplant, and 3 titanium screws to straighten it out and hold it together. The recovery had turned into a hellish and complicated ordeal that had lasted 3 months, and had weakened me a great deal. For that backpacking season, in my 72nd year, I had to wear a special high-top boot you see in the picture, and carefully increase the length of my hikes to regain my strength, and endurance. I had to rest often on the trail as otherwise I would begin feeling as though I was getting sick. I had to be careful and have whatever I might need for emergencies.

Towards the early afternoon I was doing my darndest and sweating quite profusely, when a storm quickly moved into the area, and a light rain began. I moved off the trail looking for trees I could get under for protection--as often quick rain storms move on soon and don't require putting on all the rain gear. 131

Missing Hikers Likely Died First Night, posted on KSL.com, July 9, 2004:

https://www.ksl.com/?sid=83779

p. 344

But then everything quickly changed drastically with a real deluge pouring down. I got my poncho on covering me and pack--me with a sweaty body and dampened clothes, and the small trees I was under didn't help much. I looked for better protection, but there was none nearby. Then, just as quickly the temperature took a nose dive, the problem being under my poncho I just had on a sweaty T-shirt. I waited too long to remedy that, and in the process exposed myself, my clothes, and the jacket I put on--all getting a little wet. The intensity of the storm increased like I'd never seen in the Uintas, and as I sat huddled underneath my poncho, it got worse with water running underneath me. NOTE: Later, I got

a report from friends who at the same time had been in the Wind Rivers up in Wyoming, and forced back to civilization by what they called “a monsoon!” It didn't let up, and I was beginning to feel the temperature plunge even more, and pretty soon I was shivering with cold. I knew some about HYPOTHERMIA--and that being wet could speed up the progression as much as 25 times, and feared that could happen to me, as had been the case with the mother and daughter who had died. I had to do something quick before my body completely lost the ability to warm itself that would then have my condition deteriorate to not being able to think clearly, nor have the physical ability to do anything about it. Even though to do what I had to do meant momentarily even exposing myself more, I had no choice. I stood up, moved quickly to find a spot with tree protection on one side, took my pack off and quickly used my poncho to set up a lean-to, then underneath laid down my bivy bag with air mattress and sleeping bag inside. Note: I wasn't using yet a sleeping quilt instead of the bag, and my poncho and bivy bag were being used instead of a tent. I always add grommets around the edges of my poncho to use it as a shelter. I placed my pack with water, energy snacks and supplements within reach under the semi-protection of the leanto. Critically--I took off all my wet clothes and slithered down inside my bag.

As I laid there shivering--which actually was a good sign--proof that my body was still capable of trying to warm me--I then moved to help it, by doing isometric exercises with my whole body, then my legs, next my arms, then repeat. It is basically exercise to speed up

circulation by stiffening, tightening, hardening, or flexing the body or a muscle group and holding it in a static position, then release, and repeat……time after time, after time. Apparently my body had not got to dangerous hypothermia, as it finally warmed up, and I stopped shivering. I was able to say a word of thanks, relax, eat and drink some energy food/supplements, especially items I have mentioned that would help me avoid getting sick after a physically demanding experience--when normally the immune system is weakened.

p. 345

If I had of degenerated into hypothermia, my body would not have been capable of warming itself, and to save me would have required some kind of exterior heat source, one of which we'll see next. Luckily the next day the sun came up and I was able to spread around all my wet stuff to dry. I needed to do a little cooking too, but the normal dry twigs, pine needles, etc. around the base of trees was all totally soaked, but my little Zip-lock bag labeled "Fire making," did the trick for me, as you can see in the panel of pictures below.

Fire of course is one of the things that can warm a hypothermic person, but you must have with you--even on a supposedly short day hike, a plastic bag in your pocket with what you need to make a FIRE. My little kit, I go nowhere without, is made up of pine pitch you can get off a tree--seen on the left, wherever you're at, but best have always a good chunk in your bag--as it will burn even when wet, burning hot and burning long to dry out wet twigs, and small branches. My kit now always has also STORMPROOF MATCHES you see above. They will burn long enough to get your fire going regardless of wind or weather.

NOTE: Prior to Stormproof Matches, I used strike anywhere matches and those Magic Birthday Candles, you can't extinguish, and a mixture of Fire Paste & kerosene or diesel fuel to liquefy it-- in a squirt bottle--which I still carry. An interesting note is that in the above experience I couldn't find a dry rock to strike my “strike anywhere matches” on, but used the file on my Leatherman tool. In my experience, related above, getting a fire going during a monsoon would have been impossible. So, in such a case when my body can't warm itself, I carry with me a little bag of those chemical warmers (1 lb. of them), you see below, and would distribute them inside my sleeping bag. But also a must are the items along the bottom edge of this picture.

Your Emergency Kit, even for a day hike should include a small compass, tool--with blade, pliers, file, and leather punch, and a headlamp with good batteries--used for signaling, and moving at night. There's a good reason to insert me too. I have learned better to live with storms which are frequent in the Uintas, and other alpine mountains. You'll need a water-proof: Hat, parka, and poncho. Also a warm lightweight jacket (mine weighs 12 oz.), plus other layers of clothing like long and short sleeved T-shirts that can be layered if the cold becomes extreme.

p. 346

They should not be cotton, rather synthetic materials. Cotton, when it gets wet loses its insulating qualities, and is slow to dry. The synthetics will last you forever, dry quickly, and retain some of their insulation capabilities even when damp. I also usually take with a lightweight pair of water-proof pants zippered on each side so I can put them on without taking off my shoes/boots. Let me just tell you about the above picture of me. It was towards the end of August, late in the backpacking season, of 2016 when I finally made it to Little Andy Lake, at 12,302 ft. high in the east shadow of South Kings Peak. I couldn't hang around long as snowflakes were in the wind, and I returned to my camp at Lake U-75. It snowed that night a few inches. The next day began sort of clear, but as I headed towards Gun Sight Pass, it quickly closed in on me. I was in open tundra and would need protection from high winds, driving rain, and maybe snow. I quickly stopped, put on my water-proof pants, my warm jacket with waterproof parka on top, put my camera in its waist pack inside my pack, and covered the pack with its water-proof cover you see. I was ready for Mother Nature to throw anything at me. I comfortably continued hiking in the rain all day, up over the Pass, and down the other side to where I had water, and set up my tent. It's always a bit bothersome to set a tent up in the rain, but I was dressed for it, my camera safe in my pack and covered, and I got the job done with no trouble--no getting wet, no feeling cold, much less feeling any danger of HYPOTHERMIA. I was up at 6:00 AM, to give my satellite phone report on KSL OUTDOORS RADIO. The tube to my water container was frozen, but I was dry, warm and cozy & happy to have finally learned to manage my High Altitude problem as well as the rain, snow & HYPOTHERMIA!

The sun came up the next morning and quickly melted off the thin layer of snow on Kings Peak and the Henrys Fork Basin, but was slow to warm my tent and me, as I had failed to set it up where the sun would hit it early. But I had awakened early anyway to use another of the essentials for one who goes alone backpacking, or is responsible for a group, like Explorers and Scouts--a SATELLITE PHONE.

I repeat: A satellite phone is an essential for one who goes alone, or is responsible for a

group, like Explorers and Scouts—I repeat… A SATELLITE PHONE.132

NOW LET'S READ ABOUT A TRAGIC CASE OF HYPOTHERMIA & see what was done wrong. 132

MOTHER & DAUGHTER MISSING IN THE UINTA MOUNTAINS On Saturday, September 13, 2003, 58 year old Carole Wetherton, and her daughter, 39 year old Kim, missed their scheduled flight back to Florida, prompting concern among the family and an investigation began. They had last been seen on Sunday the 7th at their hotel in Park City, Utah from where they intended to do some hiking. Their rental vehicle was found parked at the Crystal Lake Trailhead in the Uinta Mountains.133 One hundred search and rescue volunteers and specialists, using dogs, horses, and a helicopter intensively searched the area for two days without finding trace of the mother and daughter. Almost a week had gone by since their likely disappearance and at that time of year temperatures could drop into the teens. In fact the weather had suddenly turned quite extreme on the day they likely had gone missing, and the next day even worse, and hope of finding them alive dimmed. Over the next few months officials learned that a Forest Ranger saw the women near the trailhead on September 8th and told the women they would need heavier clothing in case the weather quickly changed as is frequent in the Uintas. 134 Apparently in the area that same afternoon rain fell and temperatures dropped below freezing, and the next night snow fell in the area. Later it was discovered they did not have rain gear, nor a compass--even though they did have a map, but left it in their vehicle. They had no [waterproof] matches, nor any emergency items like a headlamp, much less any kind of communication devices. They had not left any specific information with anyone of their planned for hike. NOTE: One report says matches were found with their remains, but didn't use them, likely they were the wrong kind, and wet! NINE MONTHS LATER - Reported on June 27th: On June 24th, 1 mile north west of where searchers scoured the area last September, and 1/2 mile from any trail in rocky timbered terrain, bone fragments were found in a crude shelter made of pine boughs in a natural formation of rocks, along with clothing, personal items, a set of car keys, 135 and a camera. "It appeared they were huddled in a small stone, kind of a shelter, and looked like they'd removed some of their clothing to dry," he said. "They probably died by the first night, and definitely by the second."136 "Hypothermia occurs when the body loses more heat than it generates, and the condition can be fatal. The pair could survive in the dropping temperatures if they could start a fire to stay warm and dry their clothing. But shivering and without means to make a fire, their core body temperatures began dropping, and eventually they sank into a hypothermic state and died."137 133

Mother, daughter still lost in Uintas, https://www.deseretnews.com/article/510054604/Mother-daughter-still-

lost-in Uintas.html 134

https://www.deseretnews.com/article/510054604/Mother-daughter-still-lost-in-Uintas.html

135 136

137

Remains found in Uintas, https://www.deseretnews.com/article/595073455/Remains-found-in-Uintas.html

Reported on KSL.com on June 27, 2004: https://www.ksl.com/?sid=83779 http://climb-utah.com/Uinta/losthiker.htm

ABOUT THE CAMERA: The photographs are water-stained. Some have horizontal lines running

through them. But Summit County investigators say the story they tell of a day hike that turned deadly is remarkable. The pictures document a trip a Florida woman and her daughter took into the High Uintas in September 2003. While there, they encountered a fierce storm, got lost and died of exposure. It took nine months for searchers to find the bodies of Carole Wetherton, 58, of Panacea, Fla., and her daughter, Kimberly Beverly, 39, of Tucker, Ga. A camera was among the belongings found with the bodies near the Crystal Lake trailhead. Summit County Sheriff's Capt. Alan Siddoway said a roll of film inside the camera was developed at a special lab in Montana. Many of the pictures are of scenery the mother and daughter saw during their hike. They also took pictures of each other. One of the earlier pictures on the roll shows a fuzzy image of a smiling Kim Beverly wearing a cap and sweatshirt. Jim Wetherton, Carole's husband and Kim's stepfather, told KSL News radio about that tragic day and what he saw in the pictures.

"They had maps and were prepared in that respect. I think there's a number of things in the area that they didn't know about that they probably were not prepared for," he said. "They had started out on a well-marked trail. They were somewhere in the neighborhood of 10,000 feet elevation, looking — actually the picture shows, behind them that they weren't paying that much attention to the weather." A later photo, shows Carole Wetherton sitting at the shore of a lake in a T-shirt. Later she's on a rocky ridge looking to the horizon, gray clouds still high in the sky. "Folks that are familiar with the weather patterns in the High Uintas could explain to me what exactly was going on with the weather," Jim Wetherton said, adding that he was told if locals had seen that weather developing, they would've "run for

home." Four photos later in the sequence, an image shows hazy fog topping the trees and heavy rain hitting a lake's surface. Investigators say the temperature dropped dramatically as the day progressed, as did the cloud cover. "As the pictures progress, you start to see the weather changing. You start to see some urgency on the faces of the individuals," said Summit County Sheriff Dave Edmunds. The second-to-last photo shows a still-smiling Carole Wetherton. But now her thin jacket is on, the hood pulled over her head. Siddoway, a trained forensics investigator, saw more. "Posturing and body language.

You see there that the (picture) by the side of the lake it's more relaxed, and then the last one there with the coat, you know, she's fairly rigid." Investigators theorize that in one of two passes, surrounded by similar-looking mountains, cold, wet and possibly disoriented by the storm, the pair turned left toward the Middle Fork of the Weber River rather than right, toward the trailhead. "They couldn't have been in a worse spot, really, to try to survive the temperatures and the moisture that they were forced to endure," Edmunds said. Siddoway said it's obvious by the evidence found with their bodies that the hikers tried to seek shelter and may have even tried to dry some clothes by laying them out on some rocks. He said they had a thermal blanket, a map, some coats, some water and some matches in their pack, but there was no evidence of a fire. Jim Wetherton believes one thing: Global positioning satellite equipment may have given the pair a chance to survive. "I know that without a GPS, I would have gotten lost while I was hiking up there." Wetherton said he hopes others get the message that "it's not a park up there " and that, “people need to be

prepared.”138

138

https://www.deseretnews.com/article/650194370/Photos-record-day-that-turned-deadly-in-Uintas.html

THIS IS SO CRUCIAL W'EVE GOT TO GIVE YOU INFORMATION from Web.MD What Is Hypothermia? Hypothermia is a potentially dangerous drop in body temperature, usually caused by prolonged exposure to cold temperatures. The risk of cold exposure increases as the winter months arrive. But if you're exposed to cold temperatures on a spring hike or capsized on a summer sail, you can also be at risk of hypothermia. Normal body temperature averages 98.6 degrees. With hypothermia, core temperature drops below 95 degrees. In severe hypothermia, core body temperature can drop to 82 degrees or lower. What Causes Hypothermia? Possible causes of hypothermia include: Cold exposure. When the balance between the body's heat production and heat loss tips toward heat loss for a prolonged period, hypothermia can occur. Accidental hypothermia usually happens after cold temperature exposure without enough warm, dry clothing for protection. Mountain climbers on Mount Everest avoid hypothermia by wearing specialized, high-tech gear designed for that windy, icy environment. However, much milder environments can also lead to hypothermia, depending on a person's age, body mass, body fat, overall health, and length of time exposed to cold temperatures. A frail, older adult in a 60-degree house after a power outage can develop mild hypothermia overnight. Infants and babies sleeping in cold bedrooms are also at risk. Other causes. Certain medical conditions such as diabetesand thyroid conditions, some medications, severe trauma, or using drugs or alcohol all increase the risk of hypothermia. How Does Cold Exposure Cause Hypothermia? During exposure to cold temperatures, most heat loss -- up to 90% -- escapes through your skin; the rest, you exhale from your lungs. Heat loss through the skin happens primarily through radiation and speeds up when skin is exposed to wind or moisture. If cold exposure is due to being immersed in cold water, heat loss can occur 25 times faster than it would if exposed to the same air temperature. The hypothalamus, the brain's temperature-control center, works to raise body temperature by triggering processes that heat and cool the body. During cold temperature exposure, shivering is a protective response to produce heat through muscle activity. In another heat-preserving response -- called vasoconstriction -blood vessels temporarily narrow. Normally, the activity of the heart and liver produce most of your body heat. But as core body temperature cools, these organs produce less heat, in essence causing a protective "shut down" to preserve heat and protect the brain. Low body temperature can slow brain activity, breathing, and heart rate. Confusion and fatigue can set in, hampering a person's ability to understand what's happening and make intelligent choices to get to safety. What Are the Risk Factors for Hypothermia? People at increased risk for hypothermia include:

   

The elderly, infants, and children without adequate heating, clothing, or food People with mental illness People who are outdoors for extended periods People in cold weather whose judgment is impaired by alcohol or drugs What Are the Symptoms of Hypothermia? Hypothermia symptoms for adults include:

    

Shivering, which may stop as hypothermia progresses (shivering is actually a good sign that a person's heat regulation systems are still active. ) Slow, shallow breathing Confusion and memory loss Drowsiness or exhaustion Slurred or mumbled speech

p. 350

  

Loss of coordination, fumbling hands, stumbling steps A slow, weak pulse In severe hypothermia, a person may be unconscious without obvious signs of breathing or a pulse Hypothermia symptoms for infants include: How Is Hypothermia Diagnosed? Recognizing the symptoms is the first step in diagnosing hypothermia. A specialized thermometer, available in most hospital emergency rooms, can detect very low core body temperatures and confirm a diagnosis. Temperatures for mild, moderate, and severe hypothermia generally range from: Mild hypothermia: 89-95 degrees Fahrenheit Moderate hypothermia: 82-89 degrees Fahrenheit Severe hypothermia: Lower than 82 degrees Fahrenheit Because response to hypothermia varies among individuals, temperatures may differ. What Is the Treatment for Hypothermia? Hypothermia is a potentially life-threatening condition that needs emergency medical attention. If medical care isn't immediately available:

     

Remove any wet clothes, hats, gloves, shoes, and socks. Protect the person against wind, drafts, and further heat loss with warm, dry clothes and blankets. Move gently to a warm, dry shelter as soon as possible. Begin re-warming the person with extra clothing. Use warm blankets. Other helpful items for warming are: an electric blanket to the torso area and hot packs and heating pad on the torso, armpits, neck, and groin; however, these can cause burns to the skin. Use your own body heat if nothing else is available. Take the person's temperature if a thermometer is available. Offer warm liquids, but avoid alcohol and caffeine, which speed up heat loss. Don't try to give fluids to an unconscious person. If the hypothermic person is unconscious, or has no pulse or signs of breathing, call for emergency help right away. CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) should be given immediately if a pulse can’t be felt and there is no sign of breathing. Feel for the pulse for up to a whole minute before starting CPR, because the heart rate may be extremely slow and you should not start CPR if there is any heart beat present.. CPR should be continued, in the absence of signs of breathing or a pulse, until paramedics arrive or the person is taken to a hospital. In cases of advanced hypothermia, hospital treatment is required to re-warm the core temperature. Hypothermia treatment may include warmed IV fluids, heated and humidified oxygen, peritoneal lavage (internal "washing" of the abdominal cavity), and other measures. Complications during recovery can include pneumonia, heart arrhythmias, ventricular fibrillation (a dangerous "fluttering" rhythm of the heart), cardiac arrest (a sudden stopping of the heartbeat), and death. Seek immediate medical help for anyone with hypothermia. Call 911 if you suspect severe hypothermia.139

139

https://www.webmd.com/a-to-z-guides/what-is-hypothermia#3

p. 351

Chapter 2: THE WILDERNESS AREA—South Slope

Section 20: The LAKE FORK TRAILHEAD & DRAINAGE140 HOW TO GET HERE: From the Provo, Utah 100 miles to Duchesne, (from Heber on U.S. 40), then north following the signs to Moon Lake--another 32 miles, for a TOTAL of 132 miles from Provo, 146.7 from Salt Lake City. The sign in Duchesne, Uintah Basin, 100 miles from the Wasatch Front.

NOTE: Remember in Duchesne there is a Forest Service Ranger Station, 85 West Main St, where you can get up-to-date information, maps, and other pamphlets and books dealing with the Ashley National Forest on the South Slope (telephone 435-738-2482). The LAKEFORK DRAINAGE, is another of the very large ones typical of the South Slope. It is divided into a number of creeks and their drainages, beginning on the east: Fish, Oweep, Lake Fork, Ottoson, East Basin, and the Brown Duck--drained also by Clements and Atwine Creeks that actually join directly the Lake Fork River that flows into Moon Lake/reservoir. MOON LAKE/Reservoir: Has Rainbow, Cutthroat, Brook, Tiger & Splake trout. I'll group them into a number of options for excellent backpacks.

OPTION 1: THE FISH CREEK NATIONAL RECREATION TRAIL141 to Toquer Lake. It begins at the Moon Lake Dam and ascends northeast up to Center Park, and on to Toquer Lake, climbing from 8,200' to 10,300', to near the Trailhead for 5 miles, and another 2 miles to Toquer Lake. It provides special views of Moon Lake and the Brown Duck Basin, and, I quote: The trail passes through a ponderosa pine, mountain mahogany and juniper zone; aspen zone; open parks; lodgepole pine zone; alpine fir and spruce zone; to a subalpine park. The proposed Arboretum Trail can highlight a number of tree and shrub species existing together in a natural amphitheater of high sandstone and conglomerate cliffs.

Information was given on page 337, in Section 19, since its access is closer from the Center Park Trailhead, but repeated here for your convenience. TOQUER (LF-25): This lake is the headwaters of Fish Creek that flows into Moon Lake. It can be accessed 7 miles via the Fish Creek National Recreation Trail from Moon Lake--see instructions above, or 3 miles via the Hell's Canyon Trail from the west end of the Center Park. 10,470 ft. elevation, 11.1 acres, 32' deep, horse friendly, has both Brook and Cutthroat trout, with light fishing pressure.

140

For information on Moon Lake/Lake Fork, go to page 126 of this book.

141

http://www.nrtdatabase.org/trailDetail.php?recordID=2359#three

p. 352

OPTION 2: "A TRUE WILDERNESS EXPERIENCE" -- It will be to another single lake I have called the most remote in the Uintas, but I'll show a short route requiring fording of the Lake Fork River, then up a no-trail tough canyon-side. It is described by the DWR pamphlet as "a true wilderness experience." EAST SLIDE (LF-44): It hopefully can be accessed 8 miles up Lake Fork from the trailhead at the confluence of Lake Fork and Oweep Creek. A ford will have to be found sufficiently downstream to avoid the gorge the Lake Fork comes out of. Then off-trail bushwhacking your way northeast switch backing up to the lake. 10,314 ft. elevation, 5 acres, not horse friendly, stocked periodically with Brook trout. Extremely rare fishing pressure. From East Basin Pass we get the following view of where East Slide Lake is.

On the left we are looking up the Oweep Creek Drainage, and on the right zoom in on the route to East Slide Lake

We will now describe Option 3 --taking us from the trailhead all the way up Lake Fork to its large area of arctic tundra, and include a must visit to Crater Lake, the Uinta's deepest at 147 ft., then move up Oweep Creek for the lakes in that remote drainage.

OPTION 3: CRATER LAKE & THE OWEEP BASIN -- From the trailhead, proceed 8 miles up Lake Fork to the confluence with Oweep Creek, and continue past the junction with the Ottoson Basin Trail at 9.1 miles, then at 9.5 miles cross gratefully a bridge, then keep moving up to the junction with the Highline Trail at 13.6 miles from the trailhead where it continues east towards Lambert Meadow and Oweep Creek. NOTE: It was near this junction where Josh had his encounter with a bear, described on pages 188-190. But, to do the Crater Lake Loop, stick to the left on the Highline Trail to where it crosses the stream.

p. 353

At that point leave the trail and go cross-country to the base of Explorer Peak where you can camp in the protection of conifers along the stream that comes out of Crater Lake.

You could also do as I did once, bivouac way up there near the lake in scrub alpine firs, for an early morning shot. If you camped down below, you then carefully work your way up to this gem of a lake nestled in a glacial cirque. CRATER (X-94): As described above Crater Lake is 17 miles from the Lake Fork Trailhead. We have already described the beautiful lake and getting here from the North Slope's East Fork of Blacks Fork Trailhead, 16 miles--just one mile less than from Moon lake, but you see THE SPINE OF THE UINTAS LIKE NOWHERE ELSE which makes it worth every bit of the greater elevation gain. Lies at 11,268 ft. elevation, 28 acres, 147' deep. Brook trout, that prolifically self-reproduce., plus Tiger trout and in summer 2019 SPLAKE trout will be stocked—a cross between Brook & Lake trout. Potentially a much larger fish.

Still with OPTION 3, we leave Crater Lake and return to the Highline Trail and go down 0.2 mile to the junction and turn left towards Lambert Meadows and on to Lambert Lake, 2 miles from the junction--out of sight down to the south of the trail. From Lambert we continue on the Highline Trail up above timberline about 4 miles where on a turn to the left, you can stop there to make an off-trail 2.4 mile round-trip hike to visit rarely visited Oweep Lake. Then, back on the trail we continue around that bend where we come to the trail to Squaw Pass and Little East Fork of Blacks Fork. Just a short distance up that trail you will see off to the east a short distance Porcupine Lake, which most hikers just cruise right on by, but it's worth wetting a line for the most colorful brook trout in the Uintas.

To this point we have hiked about 20.6 miles from the Trailhead, plus an 8 mile round trip to Crater, and 2.4 more to Oweep Lake, for a total of 31 miles. Then a return of 20.6 miles, give us a ROUND TRIP TOTAL OF 52 MILES, and one heck of a backpack!

p. 354

Now the details for the Oweep Creek lakes. SPECIAL NOTICE: The DWR is proposing poisoning with rotenone the lakes and streams of the Oweep Drainage, and then restoring the Native Cutthroat trout in the area. If approved it will be done, along with the other 3 areas (Ottoson, Garfield, Fall Creek) between 20222034. If done we’ll eventually have to look elsewhere for “the most colorful brook trout.” LAMBERT (LF-21): This lake is found 1 mile southeast of Lambert Meadows along the Highline Trail, 17 miles from the Lake Fork Trailhead. It is 10,990 ft. elevation, 6.6 acres, 15' deep, horse friendly, with stocked Brook trout. Moderate pressure. LAKE LF-35: Located just east of Lambert Lake. Possibly has Brook trout with natural reproduction. OWEEP (LF-30): It is located next to the southern talus ridge bordering Oweep Basin in Upper Lake Fork. About 4 miles from Lambert Meadows on a big turn in the trail, head 1.2 miles southwest crosscountry to the lake. Horse friendly. At 10,865 ft. elevation, 6.4 acres 16' deep, has a population of Brook trout. PORCUPINE (LF-22): Located about 20 miles from the Lake Fork Trailhead, or 6 miles from Lambert Meadows, and found at the southern base of Squaw Pass--easily accessed by horses, but feed scarce, 11,301 ft. elevation, 12.8 acres, 14' deep, has a natural population of Brook trout.

We have now returned to the trailhead, and will review another option from the Lake Fork Trailhead.

OPTION 4: The BROWN DUCK BASIN, hiking 7 miles to Brown Duck Lake, then continue on the trail past Island Lake and then Kidney and up to Tworoose Lake and Pass. From there you can backtrack to the outlet of Brown Duck Lake and from there explore off-trail other lakes in the area, like to the south. Little Dog, and Big Dog Lakes. Then head north on the East Fork Pass Trail exploring off-trail lakes to the west of the trail: X-45, 61, 62, and Aspen, and X-67 to the east. Then to Atwine Lake, and north to Clements where a camp could be set up to extend out for exploring Stewart, X-78, X-75 and even farther west to Twin Lake, and LF-8 on the inlet stream to Clements. There are lots of exploring possibilities in the basin. Next I'll describe the details of each of the lakes in the Basin. BROWN DUCK (X-31): Located 7 miles from the trailhead at 10,117 ft. elevation, 30.7 acres, 38' deep-fluctuating, both natural and stocked Cutthroat trout inhabit the lake, heavily used, horse access easy but sparse feed. ISLAND (X-34): Located west of Brown Duck Lake, 8 miles from the trailhead, horse accessible as all these lakes, but sparse feed, 10,250 ft. elevation, 66 acres, 48' deep-- fluctuating, mainly Cutthroat trout. KIDNEY (X-35): Found 9 miles from trailhead, horse accessible but heavily used, 190 acres maximum but as lake/reservoir, like the other two, has a fluctuation of as much as 20 feet, but 112' maximum. Cutthroat and Brook trout, moderately fished. TWOROOSE (X-36): Located 11 miles from the trailhead, 10,310 ft. elevation, 21.9 acres, 37' deep, horse friendly, but sparse feed, has a natural Cutthroat population moderately fished. LILY PAD (X-37): Found on the main stream connecting Tworoose to Kidney Lakes, horse access possible, 10,275 ft. elevation, 1.4 acres, 8' deep, with a natural population of Cutthroat and Brook trout. LITTLE DOG (X-33): 1/2 mile southwest of Brown Duck, 10,230 ft. elevation, 4.5 acres, 17' deep, horse friendly, with stocked Brook trout, pressure light.

p. 355

BIG DOG (X-32): Sits at a talus ridge in the far south end of Duck Basin, accessed 1 mile south of Brown Duck, horse friendly but sparse feed, experimentally stocked with Arctic grayling under light pressure. LAKE X-45: Too shallow for fishery. LAKE X-61: It is the 2nd in a series of 3 meadow ponds 1/4 mile northeast of Island Reservoir dam in the Brown Duck Basin. From the trail junction at Brown Duck follow the East Basin Pass trail 1/2 mile north to pond X-45, then the stream to X-61. 10,265 ft. elevation, 5.2 acres, 10' deep, horse friendly, population of Cutthroat may still exist—stocked in 2018.

LAKE X-62: This is the 3rd in the series of 3 ponds. 10-,300 ft. elevation, 6 acres, 10' deep, horse friendly, may still have Cutthroat trout. Lake X-67: No fish life. ASPEN (X-63): Has no surface inlet or outlet, but fed underground and has extremely clear water. Sits 1/2 mile northeast of X-62, or 1/2 mile southeast from Atwine Lake, with no trail. 8 acres, 26' deep, no horse feed, stocked with Brook trout, fishing pressure moderate. ATWINE (X-64): A large natural lake surrounded by timber next to trail, 10,150 ft. elevation, 32 acres, 35' deep, horse feel limited, has abundant population of Brook trout. MUD (X-66); Found by following the inlet stream from Atwine west past the trail--is the first lake on the stream, horse friendly, 10,340 ft. elevation, 2.5 acres, 5' deep, stocked with Brook trout and Grayling CLEMENTS (X-74): is a lake/reservoir surrounded by timber, trail crosses dam 11 miles from the trailhead, 10,444 ft. elevation, 79.2 fluctuating acres, 50' deep, horse friendly, natural Cutthroat trout population with moderate fishing pressure. LAKE X-75: Located 25o yards west of Clements, horse friendly, 10,450 ft. elevation, 4.4 acres, 10' deep, has Cutthroat trout with light pressure. TWIN (X-77): To locate follow the inlet stream from Clements 1 mile west, horse accessible but sparse feed, 10,594 ft. elevation, 12.9 acres, 15' deep, stocked with Brook trout, & Grayling, with light pressure. STEWART (X-79): Access is trail less through timber northwest of Clements dam for 1/2 mile, not horse friendly, 10,530 ft. elevation, 9.2 acres, 22' deep, Brook trout stocked with light pressure. LAKE X-78: Located 1 mile north of Clements through timber past Stewarts Lake, 10,636 ft. elevation, 17 acres, 18' deep, not horse friendly, Cutthroat trout, light pressure. LAKE LF-8: This lake has a little island and is by rocky, timbered terrain. Access is cross-country 1.5 miles southwest of Clement's dam, horse access difficult, 10,498 ft. elevation, 7 acres, 17' deep, may have winterkilled, fishing pressure light for Brook trout.

I will insert here a photograph of Clements lake/reservoir. Clements Lake/reservoir in the Brown Duck Basin of Lake Fork

p. 356

OPTION 5: EAST BASIN -- We hike 7 miles from the Trailhead to Brown Duck Lake, then take the trail north 2.1 miles to Atwine Lake, and continue another mile to Clements Lake/reservoir, and on to East Basin Pass--a low pass in the pines at 10,650 feet--the lowest in the Uintas, where we have hiked 11.3 miles. From there we get a view to the north towards 13,219 foot high Mount Lovenia.

From there we drop down into East Basin. At the 13.5 point we can go off-trail hiking southwest swinging by Hook Lake and from there hike northeast and around the point of the mountain west to beautiful Picture Lake, then north to Lake X-83 and east to the main trail for a 3.3 loop hike. To take advantage of being in East Basin, we can go up the trail northwest 1/4 mile and then leave the trail to head northeast to make a nearly 2 mile loop around the Three Lakes (X-86, 84 & 85), then back to the center of the basin from which it is a 14,5 mile hike back to the Trailhead, a Grand TOTAL of about 35 miles. The lakes in East Basin are: HOOK -- on some maps called HORSESHOE (X-81): Located in East Basin, 17 miles from the Lake Fork Trailhead, the last mile is somewhat difficult bushwhacking southwest following the outlet stream from where it is the first to cross the trail, not horse friendly, 10,722 ft. elevation, 21 acres, 19' deep, has Brook trout, fishing pressure light. PICTURE (X-82): To access continue from Hook northeast bushwhacking around the end of the mountain 1.2 miles to the lake, 10,731 ft. elevation, 20 acres, 13' deep, Rainbow trout were experimentally stocked, pressure light. It can also be accessed from the main trail 14.5 miles from the trailhead, going southwest following the outlet stream. In 2014 Arctic Grayling were stocked. LAKE X-83: Found north of Picture 3/4 mile, is 7.9 acres, 9' deep, and in 1996 didn't have fish and not stocked between 2012-2018.

THREE LAKES: A 1.9 mile loop. LAKE X-86: After climbing the trail towards Cleveland Pass about 1/2 mile leave the trail and take a course northeast first to the lower and largest lake, horse access somewhat difficult, 10,819 ft. elevation, 6.9 acres, 12' deep, with stocked Brook trout, with light pressure. LAKE X-84: Located next to the talus slope, horse pasture sparse, 10,815 ft. elevation, 4.6 acres, 18' deep, stocked Brook trout with light pressure. LAKE X-85: The highest and most northerly of the three, 10,860 ft. elevation, 4.7 acres, and 14' deep, has Brook trout with light fishing pressure.

TOTAL MILES for the EAST BASIN OPTION round trip would be about 35 miles.

p. 357

OPTION 6: EAST BASIN -- OTTOSON BASIN BACKPACK -- Lake Fork Trailhead to East Basin Pass (11.3 miles), on to Cleveland Pass (+5.1 miles), then to Ottoson Basin (+2 miles) and the Ottoson Basin loop (+4 miles), and from there down to the Lake Fork Trail (+2.5 miles), and return to the trailhead (+9.1 miles) for a Grand TOTAL of 34 miles. SPECIAL NOTICE: The DWR is proposing poisoning with rotenone the lakes and streams of the Ottoson Basin, and then restoring the Native Cutthroat trout in the area. If approved it will be done, along with the other 3 areas (Oweep, Garfield, & Fall Creek) between 20222034. In my experience I only caught cutthroat trout there anyway. DETAILS OF THE OTTOSON BASIN LAKES: AMEBA (X-90): Located in the Ottoson Basin on Ottoson Creek, about 1 mile north of the base of Cleveland Pass, horse friendly, 10,850 ft. elevation, 4.6 acres, 4' deep, has stocked Cutthroat trout, fishing pressure light. LAKE X-89: This small tundra lake at 11,110 ft. elevation, 3.4 acres, is about 1/2 mile southeast of Upper Ottoson Lake. Has Cutthroat trout. UPPER OTTOSON (X-87): Located in open tundra at the head of the basin, at 11,099 ft. elevation, 12.4 acres, 30' deep, horse friendly, has Cutthroat trout, pressure is light. LOWER OTTOSON (X-88): Lies 1/4 mile south of Upper Ottoson, 11.075 ft. elevation, 9.1 acres, 8' deep, has a natural Cutthroat population, fishing pressure light . Upper Ottoson Lake native cutthroat

Above we see the inlet to Upper Ottoson Lake, and my dinner & breakfast from Ameba Lake.

OPTION 7: EAST BASIN - CLEVELAND PASS - SQUAW BASIN -TWOROOSE PASS LOOP -- From Lake Fork Trailhead through Brown Duck Basin to East Basin Pass (11.3 miles), then through East Basin and on to Cleveland Pass (+5.1), then make a loop exploring southwest

the lakes of Squaw Basin (+13.4), then over Tworoose Pass and back to the Lake Fork Trailhead (+10.5), TOTAL OF 40.3 miles plus extras in Brown Duck Basin and East Basin & you could even drop down and make a swing through the Ottoson Basin, that would be a WOW TRIP! Squaw Basin is part of the Rock Creek Drainage, but from the Lake Fork Trailhead, this makes a great loop backpack, encompassing three important basins in one trip--be it backpack, horse pack, or goat pack.
