Chapter 2: THE WILDERNESS AREA – South Slope

Section 21: THE ROCK CREEK DRAINAGE & TRAILHEAD ************************

PREFACE

THE LEGENDS OF GOLD IN THE UINTAS On July 13, 2013 I was parked in my tiny travel trailer on 400 East in Springville, Utah, working away doing research for my High Uintas Wilderness Project, when someone spoke to me, "Hey, Cordell. What are you doing?" It was Bishop Beach. I explained to him I was researching some of the legends of gold in the Uintas for my book. He didn't know about the book, so I explained that it would be a unique guide book for the Uintas that would have intertwined the history, the survival stories, and even the legends of Big Foot, gold, and mentioned I was just learning that possibly as early as 1540 Spaniards had come into the Uintah Basin looking for what was called "Montezuma's treasure," hidden in the Uintas with the Utes left as guardians of the treasure. He perked up having something to say, so I shut up to listen.

"Once we were on a little vacation driving along Rock Creek. We stopped for a break and were looking around along the stream, when all of a sudden two Utes appeared and asked, 'What are you doing here?' They were real serious and suspicious, so we moved on." That reminded me about the summer before when I was stopped at the Mountain Man Rendezvous display on the North Slope, and a car pulled in. The fellow had been drinking a little and wanted to talk, and on hearing about my work to write a book about the history and legends of the Uintas, told me of an experience also near Rock Creek when something similar to the Bishop’s experienced happened, and they knew enough to get out of there quick! I hadn't gone looking for these kind of stories, but they reminded me of a 3rd related experience with a High Uinta Friend who had come to buy from me a CD of my "Thousand Mile Backpack" slide show. He told me of an experience when he and a friend were hiking in the upper Rock Creek drainage when, "All of a sudden we saw a beautiful Indian woman

sitting on a paint horse. We were surprised and wondering, 'What?' when all of a sudden a shot rang out with a bullet whistling close by. Someone was shooting at us, and we got out of there fast." Now that we are dealing with Rock Creek in this book, where the three stories I heard all happened, best say a little more about the way the story goes, that does mention specifically this area, as well as others.

p. 368

In the INTRODUCTION, on page 24 and 25, I introduced the way some of such legends began with Montezuma's treasure in a Sacred Cave, brought from Central Mexico in 1521 that eventually had the Utes as guardians of the treasure--part of it also a series of rich mines. As the story evolved, it became more alluring with Butch Cassidy and some of his Wild Bunch as bodyguards of one of the groups looking for the mines/caves. Books have been written about many such legends in Utah, so we can all smile a bit and enjoy ourselves while--I promise I'll condense as much as I can what seems to be a pretty fascinating story taken from the book by Kerry Ross Boren and Lisa Lee Boren. 142 Ute legends tell about the "Old ones" who had been in their area and had mines, but then in 1169 they left leaving the Utes as guardians of the mines. Reputedly they were Aztecs, who centuries later in 1521 sent from Central Mexico 1,500 royal porters north carrying Montezuma's treasure to hide it from the Spaniards, following "the trail of the old ones," which treasure was stored in a large cave that came to be called "Carre-Shinob" meaning

"where the Great Spirit Dwells." As explained in the INTRODUCTION, Cortez then in 1540 sent an expedition north in search of the treasure creating what for hundreds of years was known as "The Old Spanish Trail" from Santa Fe, New Mexico to the Uintah Basin. From those expeditions were born the legends of Spanish mines along the South Slope of the Uintas, and even over into the Weber River Drainage. Then in 1847 the guardianship of mines and the Sacred Cave was given by the medicine men to Chief Walker, who in 1843 had a visionary experience of a man to whom would be given the secret location of the treasure. After the Mormon pioneers came into Utah, Chief Walker went to visit and among the Mormon leaders saw one he recognized, and remarked, "I have seen you. You will come and

live among my people. We will be brothers." A few months later said man, Isaac Morley, led a group of 244 pioneers to colonize what today is Sanpete County, and Manti, there living in the midst of the Utes. On March 13, 1850 Morley baptized Chief Walker and his brother Aropene. Morley was soon told by Chief Walker that he was the man seen in his vision, and would learn about the treasure, and eventually was taken to the location in the Uintas, and returned with 58 lbs. of gold. Morley convinced Chief Walker that Brigham Young and the LDS Church should be benefactors of the riches. 142

THE UTAH GOLD RUSH: The Lost Rhoades Mine and the Hathenbruck Legacy, published in 2002 by Council Press of Springville, Utah. DISCLAIMER NOTE: Author, Kerry Ross Boren, is today (2018) in the Utah State Prison, and some question some of his writings, yet he is a celebrated historical author in Europe and elsewhere, whose books were published by a close and trusted friend.

p. 369

An oath was taken, under penalty of death, that only one person would know the whereabouts of the Sacred Mine and be permitted to go there. By 1852 Thomas Rhoades was appointed Church Treasurer, and had been selected as the one person who would know of the whereabouts of the Sacred Mine, and be permitted to go and remove gold. Thomas Rhoades made his first trip to the Sacred Mine, taking 14 days, and brought back 62 lbs. of gold, and apparently made many more trips alone to the mine(s). It's even rumored that the gold used to cover the Angel Moroni on the Salt Lake Temple, was from the Sacred Mine, which over the years became known as The Lost Rhoades Mine. On January 29, 1855 Chief Walker died, his body packed in snow and maintained frozen in a cave waiting for springtime to be taken to the Uintas. He had wanted Isaac Morley to be present for his burial in the Sacred Cave--Carre Shinob. He was to make the trip along with Thomas Rhoades, but Thomas was ill and couldn't make any more trips to the mountains. His 19 year old son, Caleb was chosen to accompany Morley, along with the Indian burial party, in late April 1855. Note: That would seem to indicate the mine was not in the higher

elevations of the Uintas, that wouldn't be accessible until at least June. At the burial, Chief Aropene, told Morley, "You no come here anymore." Morley replied, "Don't worry. I'm too old." He was then 69 and passed on in 1865. Caleb, from then on became the designated person who could visit the Sacred Mine, and bring gold for Brigham Young and the Church--and apparently for 50 years did so for his own use too. There was a distinction between the "Sacred Mine," and "Carre-Shinob," with the following paragraph: A distinction must here be made between Carre-Shinob and the Sacred Mine. CarreShinob is a series of nine great caverns in which reposes the treasure of the Aztecs, as well as other ancient artifacts, and the remains of numerous "Old Ones," former leaders of the Uto-Aztean nation. The Sacred Mine is one of seven ancient caves from which the sacred gold was mined, and from which, according to Indian belief, their ancient race emerged from the underworld.143

Caleb's younger brother, Enock was engaged to be married and begged Caleb tell him where the Sacred Mines were so he could get enough money to start his new married life. Caleb told him he had sworn an oath to not tell, but he knew where there were Spanish mines not covered by the oath, and gave him a map and instructions where to find one "somewhere in the Upper Rock Creek area of the Uintahs." Enock found the mine and filled his bags with as much rich ore as he could, and headed down the canyon, but was ambushed by Indians and had to abandon his pack animals and fled with an arrow in his back making it as far as the Strawberry Valley where the Indians caught up with him and killed him. 143

Ibid. page 17

p. 370

This made Caleb more resolved to not tell anyone about any of the mines, without having permission from the Utes, but as he once wrote, "as long as President Young was alive the

Indians proved friendly enough, but since, they have shown a very ugly disposition. Going back to the Uintahs has become very dangerous." 144 In 1861 the Uintah and Ouray Reservation was established by the U.S. government in the Uintah Basin, bringing together three bands of those known as Utes: From the Sanpete, Utah and Heber Valleys, as well as from the Moab area. For the rest of the 19th century this limited access to the areas where the Sacred Mines and Caves were located eventually created a power struggle between two groups of white people trying to gain access to the area, find and exploit the hoped for riches. It was during those years of struggle when Caleb Rhoades began employing Butch Cassidy, and a number of individuals from his Wild Bunch, as bodyguards--the Sundance Kid also mentioned. One such event in Dry Fork Canyon, north of Vernal, has already been mentioned involving Matt Warner, one of the Wild Bunch, in a shootout landing him in jail, and then to avoid lynching was secretly taken up the Carter Military Road over the Uintas to the railroad to be transferred to jail in Ogden. Then followed by Butch and his gang, story told on page 89. Warner also prominently part of the SHOOTOUT AT SCOUT LAKE, page 447. But, what Caleb needed was a partner who was both a politician--capable of influencing the political power brokers in Washington, D.C., and also someone who was trusted by the Indians and capable of recruiting their cooperation. One such unique individual was a European immigrant, F.M.C. Hathenbruck, who in 1894 became Caleb's partner. He was a bigger than life kind of individual of illegitimate royal lineage who at one point in his life almost became the Kaiser of Germany, but rather won degrees as a medical doctor and mineralogist who migrated to the U.S. moving from being a physician for the Army, to Telluride, Colorado with a Medical Clinic & Assay Office. Then he, along with many, flocked to Park City where a major mineral discovery had been made, establishing again his clinic and assay office. Then in an emergency he was called on to fix a large auger clogged with ore and got his right arm caught up to the elbow--mangling the arm and trapping him in the machine. He sent a runner for his medical bag and proceeding to save himself by amputating his own arm! He ended up in Provo, Utah with a store, and his medical practice. He was already very knowledgeable of Indian cultures and soon came to know well the Utes gaining their trust. Many would make the difficult 100 mile trip from the Uintah Basin to Provo to be treated by this Dr. who they trusted. 144

Ibid. page 18

p. 371

He was always a mineral seeker, and soon partnered up with Caleb in efforts to gain access to and through Reservation lands so they could exploit the mines. Caleb died in 1906, and Hathenbruck continued until at least 1920 making efforts to find and exploit the mines, with several assassination attempts, with one of the last events told in the Preface to Chapter 3, THE WESTERN UINTAS, in the Section describing the Pass Lake Trailhead and hike to Scout

Lake. See page 447. Let me just conclude this brief summary of the subject by quoting some of the mentions of areas where some of the mines might have been--areas near and dear to many of us, adding interest and enticement to our trips in said areas.

"The mine is definitely located in the upper Rock Creek-Grandaddy Lakes Basin area." p. x145 "Matt Warner worked alternately with Hathenbruck and Rhoades….as bodyguard, guide, camp-tender, interpreter…..helped in the construction of a cabin for [them] in the Grandaddy Lakes Basin in the vicinity of their mine…." p. 45 "……there was only talk over the fabulous Mines….termed the Rhoades Mine…..in the second left hand fork--going upstream from the narrows of Rock Creek-- about 4 miles above the confluence of this fork with the main stream--" "Hathenbruck's directions are somewhat vague but he seems to be inferring that the….claims are on the second left hand fork of the West Fork of Rock Creek…..about 4 miles above the confluence of this fork with the main stream. This places it in the Lodgepole Lake area where Rhoades and Hathenbruck had a cabin." p. 49 "……Hathenbruck had been working the upper Rock Creek-Grandaddy Lakes Basin even prior to the opening of the reservation, in spite of the restraining order and threats against his life. But he dare not venture into the reservation alone, and surrounded himself with a bevy of gunfighters as bodyguards, as many as ten or more at times. Among them are the names of men who were, only a few years earlier, associated with Butch Cassidy and the Wild Bunch: Matt Warner, Elza Lay, Henry 'Hen' Lee--and, a little later, even the notorious Sundance Kid [Harry A. Longabaugh]." p. 51 "Their two Klondike claims were described as being '2 miles up the West Fork of Rock Creek, 4 miles from the big lake [Grandaddy Lake] in Rock Creek Basin, 8 miles above the [Upper] Stillwaters and 1 mile above the ranger or government cabin [located near the mouth of Cabin creek], on the left Hand Fork.'" p. 54 "Near sunset they arrived in the vicinity of Mirror Lake and found the cabin, just as Landreth had predicted. It was a dilapidated old structure situated on the edge of present-day Scout Lake (near the Boy Scout summer camp called Camp Steiner). A well defined trail led from the cabin up the mountainside….." p. 60 Note: This refers to the event described in the 145

Ibid, p. x, p. 45, 49, 51, 54, 60.

p. 372

Preface to the Pass Lake Trailhead, in Chapter 3, that resulted in a shootout with at least 5 dead.

FINAL COMMENTS In 2016 I made a backpack into the Grandaddy Basin, with the objective of getting to Fern Lake. I went around the south end of Grandaddy Lake, and camped the first night in a meadow above Grandaddy Lake to the southeast. From there I bushwhacked my way down along the edge of East Grandaddy Mountain, and when past the escarpment between Grandaddy Lake and Lodgepole Lake, I veered a bit to the north to go over a hill to navigate east towards Fern Lake. When, all of a sudden I found some artifacts--a rusty old shovel and its handle.

On the left you see my camp at the base of East Grandaddy Mt. In the middle, if you look carefully you can see the escarpment above which is Grandaddy Lake, here on the level of Lodgepole Lake--and you can see the rusty shovel and its handle

I started looking around and nearby found scattered all over the remains of an abandoned camp, that from the deterioration I deduced that it had been several years. Papers and documents were totally faded and weather worn and illegible, except for one empty plastic napkin bag from the RAINBOW HOTEL & CASINO, in Wendover, Nevada.

I looked for bones, outside, and then inside the collapsed tents, but found nothing. I widened my search but found nothing. IT ALL SEEMED VERY MYSTERIOUS! Except that on returning from Fern Lake, I did find and photograph the ruins of two cabins in the vicinity of Lodgepole Lake, as mentioned in several of the quotes.

p. 373

To conclude this segment, let me say, F.M.C. Hathenbruck was introduced saying he could have--almost, become Kaiser of Germany, but not mentioned was that about him it was also said "he could have become the richest man in the world," but--for those of us excited about GOLD IN THE UINTAS, let's also remind ourselves that quite a few lives have been lost in the search, and about Hathenbruck who lived for years under death threats, it was also said, He was always a mineral seeker, had a store in Provo--he neglected by seeking for mineral riches, and in 1920 organized a serious, last ditch effort to find the Lost Rhoades mine resulting in a deadly shootout, but by 1928 was selling sewing machines and life insurance door to door in Provo to survive.

Even the author of the book the UTAH GOLD RUSH said in his Forward: I am neither a treasure hunter nor a prospector. I have a peculiar over view. My interests are primarily concerned with history. It might surprise the reader to hear that I would prefer the mines remain forever hidden and undiscovered. To my mind, THE GREATEST TREASURE THAT CAN BE FOUND IN THE UINTAH MOUNTAINS ARE THE MOUNTAINS THEMSELVES. (my emphasis, Cordell)

With that said, I remind the reader that in the INTRODUCTION I mentioned I had even found and photographed whole mountains of gold in the Uintas--which you'll notice is a bit of a tongue-in-cheek stretch, nonetheless I'll conclude by showing a couple of three of them:

p. 374

"the greatest treasure…..the mountains themselves."

Chapter 2: THE WILDERNESS AREA—South Slope

Section 21: The ROCK CREEK DRAINAGE & TRAILHEAD HOW TO GET HERE:

From the Provo, Utah 100 miles to Duchesne, (from Heber on U.S. 40), then follow the signs to Mt. Home--18.6 miles, then another 23 miles to the Trailhead, for a TOTAL of 142 miles from Provo, 156 miles from Salt Lake City.

From the Division of Wildlife Resources pamphlet, ROCK CREEK DRAINAGE, Revised Edition, 1997, Publication No. 97-7, we find the following: ROCK CREEK IS THE LAEGEST DRAINAGE ON THE SOUTH SLOPE OF THE UINTA MOUNTAINS. It can be subdivided into four drainage systems. 1. The eastern-most, Squaw Basin, is drained by Squaw Basin Creek and the East Fork of Rock Creek. 2. Mainstream Rock Creek and Fall Creek drain the northernmost central basin. 3. The Grandaddy Basin is drained by Fish Creek and the West fork of Rock Creek. 4. The smallest basin is located south of East Grandaddy Mountain drained by the South Fork of Rock Creek. A majority of the 120+ lakes and ponds are between 9,000 and 11,000 feet in elevation and located at the heads of the individual basins. The lakes in the Grandaddy and Squaw basins are generally surrounded by heavy timber. Lakes in the higher central basins are located in heavy timber or on the gently rolling tundra of upper elevations. The Rock Creek drainage is noted for its scenic beauty and vast panoramas, especially at the head of the central basin. The major point of access is located at the trailhead of Upper Stillwater--ROCK CREEK TRAILHEAD. A well-maintained Forest Service trail follows the mainstream of Rock Creek up the central drainage basin, Spur trails split from the main trail and follow (1) the West Fork of Rock Creek and Fish Creek to points in Grandaddy Basin, (2) the East Fork of Rock Creek and Squaw Basin Creek to Squaw Basin and the Rudolph lakes area, abd (3) Fall Creek to areas in the eastern section of the central basin.

Access to the Squaw Basin and Rudolph lakes area has already been mentioned from the Lake Fork Trailhead on page 357, but details of those lakes will be included in this section. Access to the upper central drainage of Rock Creek has also been described via the Highline Trail over Rocky Sea Pass in Section 1 of Chapter 2, on pages 170-173, and descriptions of those lakes can be found on those pages. Access to the Grandaddy Basin will be described in this section, but the details of those lakes will be described in Section 22, The Grandview Trailhead, which is generally the point of access to the basin.

p. 376

At the trailhead we find the sign on the right. The Rock Creek Trail 069 is the one that goes right up the middle of the drainage--to where I learned my lesson about Fording Streams (page 170), and at which point it crosses the Highline Trail (025), then continues all the way up past Lightning Lake and to Helen Lake (and trail 122) at the very head of the drainage. The Squaw Basin Trail (o63) leads to Squaw Basin and continues on to Cleveland Pass and to the Ottoson Basin then down to the main Lake Fork Trail (061), the Fall Creek Trail (071) divides from Trail 069 nine miles up the canyon and continues to join trail 121 coming from Squaw Basin, and shortly joins the Highline Trail before it climbs Dead Horse Pass. The old sign in the middle is what was once found up the trail about 2.5 miles just past the end of the Upper Stillwater Reservoir, called LaMarla Lake Trail (073) to the Grandaddies, probably a total of about 8 miles to Grandaddy Lake from the Rock Creek trailhead. We'll see about distances when we create the topographical maps, where you'll see distances from the Trailhead to all the destinations. Maybe it's worth mentioning that in 2003 to begin my Project, one of my warm-up backpacks was up the La Marla Lake Trail which appeared to be very little used and not maintained and was a very tiring jumble of downed timber. As mentioned in the Preface, about GOLD IN THE UINTAS, the trails up Rock Creek, and up to the Grandaddies are featured in some of the legends. Rock Creek fills the Upper Stillwater Reservoir we see here. The trail follows the western shore of the reservoir for about 2.5 miles and soon forks, the western fork leading to the Grandaddies, and a little further again forks to the Squaw Basin, the main trail leading to the headwaters of Rock Creek

Now let's look at the details of the lakes in the Squaw Basin, and mention others along the trails leading up to the Upper Basin we have described already--that we'll just list here.

p. 377

First two lakes above Rock Creek before getting to the Reservoir, and the trailhead. AUDRY (RC-45): "Access is difficult by foot and likely impossible on horseback. The Miners Gulch jeep trail leads from the main road along Rock Creek to Bear Lake. Audry Lake is located 2.5 miles northwest along the timbered rocky mountainside." At 10,021 ft. elevation, 13.2 acres, 25' deep, with Brook trout by aerial stocking. Pressure very light.

BEAR LAKE (RC-43): No fish life in 1997.

THE SQUAW BASIN -- southeast basin -- East Fork of Rock Creek DIAMOND (X-43): It is located 9 miles from the Rock Creek trailhead, 1/2 mile southwest of the trail in rocky timbered terrain, but difficult to find. It can be found by following the outlet northwest of Mid Lake 1/2 mile. At 10,230 ft. elevation, 13 acres, 45' deep, with Brook trout maintained by aerial stocking. HORSESHOE (RC-38): Located at the base of a talus slope 3/4 mile west of Diamond Lake, difficult to find without a topographic map, surrounded by a boulder field and inaccessible on horseback, 10,118 ft. elevation, 2.9 acres, 20' deep, has stocked Brook trout, rarely visited. MID (X-42): Located in heavy timber due north of Rudolph Lakes, 10.2 miles from trailhead. 10,380 ft. elevation, 5.1 acres, 3' deep, with stocked Brook trout, moderate pressure. RUDOLPH (X-39): Located 10.3 miles from the Rock Creek trailhead, or 9.8 miles over Tworoose Pass from Lake Fork. The largest of 3 Rudolph lakes, at 10,420 ft. elevation, 25.6 acres, 46' deep, stocked with Brook trout, moderate pressure. RUDOLPH (X-40): The middle lake, 2.9 acres, 9' deep, stocked Brook trout, moderate pressure. RUDOLPH (X-41): Smallest of the three, 2.4 acres, 14.5' deep, winterkill with some migrating Brook t.

CABIN (RC-42): Located 1.2 miles southwest of Rudolph Lake over a rough, rocky saddle following an old sheep trail. Not horse friendly. 10,450 ft. elevation, 4.3 acres, 16' deep, good growth of stocked Brook trout, light pressure. LAKE X-71: No information LAKE X-37: With Arctic Grayling.

LAKE X-36: With Brook trout.

SQUAW BASIN -- northwest upper basin -ROCK 2 (X-97): Located 10.8 miles from trailhead, follow the East Fork of Rock Creek upstream 1/2 mile to the lake. 10,550 ft. elevation, 7.7 acres, 17' deep, horse friendly, has stocked Brook trout, fishing pressure light.

ROCK 1 (X-96): Lies 150 yards northwest of Rock 2, at 10,559 ft. elevation, 4.8 acres, 19' deep, horse friendly, abundant Brook trout, pressure light. SQUAW (X-95): Located 9.8 miles from the Rock Creek trailhead, surrounded by open meadows, horse friendly, 10,483 ft. elevation, 10,4 acres, 9' deep, stocked Brook trout, pressure heavy. SHAMROCK (X-98): Located 1/2 mile southwest of Squaw Lake and 300 yards east of Amlen Lake, 9 miles from the trailhead, 10,365 ft. elevation, 18.2 acres, 33' deep, stocked Brook trout, moderate pressure. AMLEN (X-99): Located 9 miles from the trailhead, access for last 1/4 mile is cross country, easiest approached from the southwest, 10,340 ft. elevation, 7.3 acres, 9' deep, horse friendly, a productive lake with stocked Brook trout, moderate pressure.

p. 378

From Squaw Basin we will now move up the Ledge Trail #121 and describe the lakes before it reaches Ledge Lake and the Highline Trail. SPECIAL NOTICE: The DWR is proposing poisoning with rotenone the lakes and streams of the Fall Creek drainage, along with the other 3 areas (Ottoson, Oweep & Garfield) between 2022-2034. Including lakes X-100, 116, 118, 117, 119, 120 and Ledge X-113, & Continent X-121. YOUNG (X-100): The lake is 10.5 miles from the trailhead, 1/4 mile west of the Ledge Trail through rocky timber, impossible for horses, 10,310 ft. elevation, 4 acres, 19' deep, has stocked Cutthroat trout, with light fishing pressure. LAKE X-116: No information. LAKE X-118: No information. ANDERSON (X-117): Located 13.8 miles from the trailhead, 100 yards east of the trail, and 300 yards south of Phinney Lake, 10,590 ft. elevation, 5.8 acres, 12' deep, horse friendly, natural Brook trout population, and possibly some Cutthroat trout, moderate to heavy fishing pressure. 2.3 miles from Dead Horse Pass, and 15.6 miles from Hayden Pass Highline Trailhead over Rocky Sea Pass. PHINNEY (X-119): Located 13.6 miles from Rock Creek Trailhead, 15.4 miles over Rocky Sea Pass, 1/4 mile north of Anderson Lake. 10,625 ft. elevation, 13.6 acres, 30' deep, horse friendly, has stocked Brook trout and some Cutthroats, pressure moderate. LAKE X-120: No information.

We'll now move to the main Rock Creek Trail #069, as some you will notice a couple of lakes way up to the west of the trail, before you come to Sea Lion and Thompson Lakes which are part of the Rock Creek Drainage--but already described in Section 1 of Chapter 2, pages 165, 166, as an option from the Highline Trail. The two are: FRANCIS (RC-15): described as "does not sustain fish life." SLIDE (RC-14): Also described as "does not sustain fish life." That takes us to the UPPER ROCK CREEK AREA, already described in Chapter 2, Section 1, on pages 171-173, and are: HUNTLEY PONDS (RC-3): just before Brinkley Lake, with Brook trout. BRINKLEY (RC-4): 10,460 ft., 10 miles from TH, 4.2 acres, 18' deep, Brook trout ROSALIE (X-130): 10,910 ft., 11.6 miles from TH, 8 acres, 8' deep, Brook trout UINTAH (X-131): 10,840 ft., 0.8 mile from Rosalie, 8.4 acres, 14' deep, Brook trout MARGIE (X-129): 10,980 ft., 0.8 mile from Uintah Lake, 7.5 acres, 11' deep, Brook trout GLADYS (X-128): 10,900 ft., about 12.6 miles from TH, 7.5 acres, 6' deep, Brook trout LIGHTNING (X-127): 10,819 ft., 13.5 miles from the TH, 14 acres, 23' deep, Brook & Cutthroat trout. HELEN (X-126): 10,869 ft., 13.7 miles from TH, 8.4 acres, 14' deep, Brook trout RECONNAISSANCE (X-125): 11,145 ft., 16.6 miles from TH, 8.8 acres, 30' deep, Brook & C trout BOOT (X-124): 11,096 ft., 1/2 mile southeast from Reconnaissance lake, 9 acres, 17' deep, Cutthroat trout LEDGE ( X-113): 10,845 ft., 21 miles from the TH, 3 acres, 13" deep, Brook trout prone to winterkill. CONTINENT (X-121): 11,285 ft., 22 miles from the TH, 27 acres, 23' deep, Brook & Cutthroat trout. JACK (X-133): 10,460 ft., now at 27 miles of our Loop, 2.7 acres, 14' deep, Cutthroat trout JILL (X-111): 100 yards west of Jack, 3.6 acres, 25' deep, Brook trout

p. 379

OURAY (X-112): 10,380 ft., 27.5 miles in Loop, 4 acres, 6' deep, Brook & Cutthroat trout BLACK (X-132): 10,403 ft., 12 acres, 14' deep, 28.5 miles in Loop, used by Boy Scouts, B & C Remaining in the Rock Creek Drainage, is the South Fork of Rock Creek, the road to which is mentioned on page 131, 132. The two lakes, not in the Wilderness Area, are: ARTA (RC-23): This lake is located 1/2 mile west from the end of a logging road along the South Fork of Rock Creek, at 10,450 ft. elevation, 5.4 acres, 6' deep--but fluctuates 2-3 feet each summer. Stocked Cutthroat trout, pressure light.

SURVEY (RC-20): Located 200 yards northwest of Arta, atop a high bench, 10,700 ft. elevation, 6 acres, 12' deep, horse friendly, has stocked Brook trout, pressure light.

NOTE: It is from Survey Lake that you can bushwhack your way up to the saddle of East Grandaddy Mountain, and be overwhelmed with the view of the High Uinta's largest lake, GRANDADDY, and its Basin. After being absent from Utah and the Uintas for quite a few years, this was my first backpack trip to begin THE HIGH UINTAS WILDERNESS PROJECT.

Section 22: THE GRANDVIEW TRAILHEAD

GATEWAY TO THE GRANDADDIES ******************

PREFACE THE GATEWAY…..yes--for the Grandaddies, but ALSO FOR ME and I'll tell here the

GATEWAY STORY for THREE MAGNIFICENT CHILDREN In the PREFACE I tell my story of this area being a sort of GATEWAY for me--opening up a lifetime of interest--BACKPACKER MAGAZINE called it "a love story" --with the Uinta Mountains and its towering, never ending VISIONS OF NATURE that for me are divine witnesses of our Creators interest in, and love for all of us.

Us original TRAIL BUDDIES--Little Andy, Ted Packard and Charlie Peterson, are still trail buddies--66 years later for which I'm most grateful, and it was the GATEWAY TO THE GRANDADDIES where it had its beginning, and reserves a special place in my heart and soul. Thanks, Ted and Charlie!

NEW TRAIL BUDDIES & A GATEWAY FOR THEIR LIVES On page 75 I told the 2016 story of being lucky to meet on the King's Peak Trail, two children on their way, with their father, Jake Hirschi, to climb Utah's highest peak the first time. They were, Grace, 9, and Isaac 10. They honored me by calling me their trail buddy.

p. 387

Later Jake sent me a note about what for me was an amazing accomplishment--not just for the kids, but for their awesome father. Cordell, Nice to meet you on the trial last weekend. We spent one night at Dollar Lake and headed for Kings early the next morning. my 9 and 10 year olds made it to the top of Kings Peak by 11:30am. We then stomped all the way out to the car that day by 8:30 PM just as darkness closed in. We easily made it home that night in time for school on Monday morning. Mom was impressed. First mountain peak for my 9 year old. She did great on this long trek. My 10 year old had done Mt Ogden 2 times and Ben Lomond 1 time before. They both helped motivate each other. I took the tent, one sleeping bag and one pad and our stove to the peak for safety. We were set for self containment in case of accident or need to help others along the trail. We had good weather and no accidents. Not one trip or fall. Kids did great. Some sore feet but they didn’t seem to mind after a little doctoring Your TRAIL BUDDIES, Jake & kids

For 2017 I was pleased we continued as trail buddies, and learned they did it again, but a little different as you can see in the panel of photos below, showing they had camped right up on the side of Kings Peak, similar to what I did in 2004-- my camp shown below in about the same spot. NOTE: That was when I had one of my greatest survival experiences re-told in Chapter 2, Section 11, on pages 251-255.

Isaac is the one posing as the "highest man in Utah" at that moment.

With the above photos, their message in 2017 was: We enjoy the newsletter. Thanks for keeping us updated and motivated trying to keep up with you. Hirschi family here, met you on Henry Fork Trail last year. Wanted to update you with some photos taken from this season. This is Isaac on his second ascent of Kings. On the hike in, he remembered exactly where we met you on the trail. He said as we hiked by, “hey, isn’t this where we met our trail buddy”? Dollar Lake was so crowded we ended up camping high in the basin. We were happy to see a forest ranger at the trailhead teaching Leave No Trace to everyone hiking in for the busy weekend. Way to go Rangers! Thanks for educating and reminding all backcountry users! Beautiful and empty below Kings Peak. Looking forward to your book. Regards Hirschi Family

p. 388

The 2018 backpacking season was an even more wonderful one for my trail buddies. On page 256 I have already introduced Grace's feat with her stunning picture and description of her doing the peak, car to car--28 miles, all in the same day. Isaac wasn't able to make that trip with his sister, but did his darndest to keep up with his little sister, so Jake wrote:

Isaac, 12, reached the top of Utah July 7, 2018 in a single day, car to car, push. He was excited about the whole hike. This has been an incredible summer seeing these guys push themselves in the outdoors.

He added: My third, Nora, cried when she couldn’t come with Grace. Nora also has good conditioning from being in formal gymnastics classes. She just turned 7 and we need to plan a couple of nights in the basin to get her up Kings. She is motivated but we take these things in steps and stages so we are prepared and reasonably safe. I'll have my wife or my brother join when we take Nora to the top of Utah. JAKE

With all of that as an introduction, I'll present the latest chapter with a picture, similar to the one of Grace, but this time of 7 year old NORA, heading for Kings Peak enshrouded by a storm, with winter coming on--all the green and colorful flowers gone.

p. 389

Jake wrote: Nora, 7, reached the top of Kings over Labor Day weekend. With a light snow falling with intermittent rain we hiked past dollar lake and into the high meadows. We made it with one ultralight bivi near to Gunsight Pass on Saturday Night.

Reached the peak by 12:00 on Sunday then beat the trail out that evening before dark. She is an excellent hiker and has a fast pace for such a young kid. Feel free to use the photos to help encourage others to love the mountains. All the best to you and your amazing goals. Your trail buddies Isaac, Grace, Nora and Jake

Hey, all you Hirschi trail buddies,

Have you noticed the serious problem you are causing by so many of you going to Kings Peak? The peak used to be 13,528 feet high, but your sign now says it is 13,527 feet high. ONE FOOT LOWER THAN IT USED TO BE! Must be that with so many of you on the peak IT HAS SUNK ONE FOOT BELOW NORMAL! ***************** HEY YOU HIRSCHI KIDS, the truth is that all of these impressive accomplishments are GATEWAY experiences for all of you, opening up the way for many future successes of all kinds throughout your lives--and additionally be a blessing in the lives of many--old and young--inspired in all the good ways by your example. You kids have got to be humbly grateful for your father and mother helping you lay the groundwork for amazing things you will each achieve during your lives! Hope to see you all on the trail in 2019!

Chapter 2: THE WILDERNESS AREA—South Slope

Section 22: THE GRANDVIEW TRAILHEAD--GATEWAY to the GRANDADDY PORTION OF THE ROCK CREEK DRAINAGE HOW TO GET HERE: From the American Fork Utah 31 miles to Heber, then to Francis (46.3), and on Ut-35 over Wolf Creek Pass and down to the North Fork of the Duchesne River (78.3), then 6 miles past Defas Dude Ranch (84.3), and 6 miles up Hades Canyon to the Grandview Trailhead a TOTAL of 90 miles from American Fork, Utah, about 105 miles from Salt Lake City.

The GRANDVIEW TRAILHEAD, located at around 9,000 ft. elevation--is one of the more picturesque.

As shown on the last two topographical maps, what a few years ago was called the LaMarla Lake Trail up the West Fork of Rock Creek, leads to the Grandaddy Basin, but I found it a difficult option, as being little used, it also was poorly maintained. So, most of us lovers of the Grandaddies, get to them from Hades Canyon on the North Fork of the Duchesne River, as described in the PREFACE on pages 1-4, of my first High Uinta experience in 1952 when I was 16 years old. That was a real GATEWAY for me. We visited Hades Canyon again on the Auto-Loop Tour, pages 140-144, seeing that the Grandview Trailhead--we see above, is now 6 miles up the canyon, making the hike to Grandaddy Lake only 4 miles. As you will see, from there are many trail options--and a few off-trail options, taking the adventurous explorer to the 26 named lakes in this great basin-all in the forest with no arctic tundra as is the case in other basins along the spine of the Uintas. A few of its lakes are part of the Duchesne River drainage, but almost all are described in the Rock Creek DWR pamphlet--1997 Revision that we will use again to give the details of our many options. I could add that you can get a good introduction to the Basin through my YouTube video entitled THE GRANDADDIES.146 A couple of named lakes are missing, Range and Jeff, which I visited and photographed in 2017, and added to the photo/essay. 146

YouTube "The Grandaddies," https://youtu.be/vIDv9oyIkIg

p. 391

Now let's review our many options not alphabetically, rather as I did in the video and as you might do if attempting visiting all of them in one backpack: HADES (D-11): This one is just 3/4 mile northwest of the trailhead, with no trail accessibility, so is not visited often. It is also part of the Duchesne River drainage--via Hades Creek, located at the foot of the steep talus ridge. Accessibility would be to go up the trail past the 7 switch-backs, and then using your map navigate your way to this lake, not horse friendly, 9,980 ft. elevation, 6.3 acres, 32' deep, stocked with Rainbow trout, possibly with Brook t. NOTE: I believe I failed to include this lake in my YouTube video.

HEART (X-13): Located just east of Hades Pass--the first lake you will see descending into the basin, 2.6 miles from the trailhead, and 1/2 mile southwest of Grandaddy Lake. 10,500 ft. elevation, 5.7 acres, 19' deep, horse friendly, stocked with Cutthroat trout, heavy pressure.

GRANDADDY (X-9): Located 4 miles from the Grandview Trailhead, and 13.4 miles from the Mirror Lake Trailhead, 10,310 ft. elevation, 173 acres--THE LARGEST LAKE IN THE UINTAS, 40' deep, horse friendly, has Cutthroat and Brook trout sustained by natural reproduction. The amazing Cutthroat spawn can be observed in the 3 small streams on its western shore during the first few weeks of the season. Said creeks are closed to fishing until mid-July, after the spawn has concluded.

Proceeding east from Grandaddy: LODGEPOLE (X-3): Located on the trail that follows the Grandaddy outlet stream that cascades down the escarpment to the level below. 4.1+ miles from the Grandview Trailhead, 8.6 miles from the Rock Creek Trailhead, and about 13 miles from Mirror Lake, horse friendly, 10,140 ft. elevation, 20.4 acres, 29' deep, has Brook and Cutthroat trout, moderate pressure.

LA MARLA (00): Not listed in pamphlet. Apparently does not have fish. FERN (X-5): Located northeast of East Grandaddy Mt., 5.3+ miles from the Grandview Trailhead, 8.1 miles from the Rock Creek Trailhead, accessed via a faint trail that cuts off the main trail just south of La Marla Lake. 9,890 ft. elevation, 19.3 acres, 19' deep, sort of horse friendly, stocked with Brook trout, with moderate fishing pressure.

On the left we see Fern Lake, with me and Ted & then me on top of East Grandaddy Mt. with Fern Lake seen directly over my head, and Doc's Lake at the far tip of the mountain showing the heavy forest you have to bushwhack through to get from Fern to Doc's. Then, on the right, Ted casting at Doc's Lake you can see is at the tip of the main ridge of East Grandaddy Mt.

DOC'S (X-15): This isolated lake is found at the northeast tip of East Grandaddy Mt. Off-trail several miles of bushwhacking southeast of Fern Lake, or 3 miles of hard climbing west of the Rock Creek Bridge, not possible for horses, 9,882 ft. elevation, 14.5 acres, 45' deep, pressure light for stocked Brook trout.

We will now return to Grandaddy Lake and go to the junction at its northern end where in 2003--when I started my Project, I found the sign--seen on the next page--in several pieces on the ground and stood it up for a picture. It shows we will next visit Betsy Lake, and from there the trail we will take goes down across the basin to Rainbow Lake, with 4 lakes along the way, with one trail continuing on to the Four Lakes Basin we have already visited when dealing with the Highline Trail. Then after 3 more lakes in that area, we will loop back

p. 392

by climbing off-trail to Margo Lake & pass, then down to Pine Island Lake and others returning to this same junction, having completed a loop of the basin lakes.

BETSY (X-7): Located a few hundred yards north of Grandaddy Lake. 10,350 ft. elevation, 33.8 acres, 44' deep, horse friendly, with Brook and Cutthroat trout, heavy pressure. NOTE: In the pamphlet the spelling

used is both "Betsey," and "Betsy," but the NG & Forest Service Wilderness maps spell it "Betsy," as does the sign above. So we'll go with "BETSY."

At the midway-point of Betsy we take the trail heading east, that soon drops down below the escarpment I'll show a picture of below, with Ted Packard and his son Mike.

Once you switch-back down you come to Brinton Meadows and a trail junction with a sign pointing north about 1/2 mile to our next Lake.

PALISADE (Z-28): Located 5.3 miles from the Grandview Trailhead, 11 miles from Mirror Lake. 10,140 ft. elevation, 22.7 acres, 44' deep, horse friendly, with Brook and Cutthroat trout. SHADOW (X-1): Approximately 1/2 mile east on the main trail from the trail to Palisade, the trail takes a turn northeast, and at that point there is a trail leading 1/4 mile south to the lake, 9,940 ft. elevation, 18.2 acres, 33' deep, horse friendly, large population of Brook trout, and some Cutthroats both sustained by natural reproduction. Pressure is moderate.

Snooks Roberts, in his autobiography, mentions Shadow Lake as one they would visit on horseback in 1927, and using rafts caught and took back to civilization as many as 300 brook trout.147 LOST (Z-29): This lake is found along the trail 3/4 mile northeast of Brinton Meadows, 5.8 miles from the Grandview Trailhead, 11 miles from Mirror Lake. 10,030 ft. elevation, 14 acres, 15' deep, horse friendly, tends to sometimes winterkill, but stocked with Brook trout, pressure is moderate. POWELL (Z-30): Located 1/4 mile east of Lost Lake, 6.3 miles from the Grandview Trailhead, 11.1 miles from Mirror Lake, horse friendly, 9,980 ft. elevation, 22.4 acres, 15' deep, stocked with Cutthroat trout, moderate pressure. RAINBOW (Z-25): Trails converge here and is a popular lake, the Fish Creek trail is one--9.8 miles from the Rock Creek Trailhead, 8 miles from the Grandview Trailhead, 8.7 miles from Mirror Lake, horse friendly, 9,930 ft. elevation, 17.9 acres, 15' deep, stocked with Brook trout, pressure heavy. RANGE (00): Located 1/4 mile east of Rainbow Lake, not listed in pamphlet but does have a name. JEFF (00): Located 1.4 mile east of Range lake. Not listed, but I swear I saw fishing rising. GOVERNOR DERN (Z-24): Located .7 mile northwest from Rainbow Lake, 8.7 miles from Grandview, 9.1 from Mirror Lake, 9.5 from Rock Creek, 9.,990 ft. elevation, 32 acres, 9' deep, horse friendly, stocked with Brook trout, but Cutthroats caught too, heavy pressure. PINTO (X-22): Located 200 yards northwest of Governor Dern, 8.8 miles from Grandview & Mirror Lake, 10 miles from Rock Creek, horse friendly, 10,020 ft. elevation, 46.6 acres, 36' deep, stocked with Brook trout, heavy pressure. MARGO (Z-23): Located 1/2+ mile west and above the west inlet of Pinto Lake, but from my recent experience the trail soon disappears and you just have to bushwhack your way to the lake. 10,420 ft. elevation, 11.1 acres, 29' deep, has Cutthroat trout that seem to be different than others, with light fishing pressure. On the right- the pass between Margo & Pine Island Lakes looking to the north-10,700 ft. 147

PINE ISLAND (X-8): This large picturesque lake is located 6 miles from the Grandview Trailhead, but on the loop I'm taking you on, I continued off-trail to a pass between Margo and Pine Island, and then bushwhacked down to the lake and the trail. 10,300 ft. elevation, 79.6 acres, 44' deep, horse friendly (not my bushwhacking route), has Brook trout, fished heavily, but has a large rocky shore with many areas untouched.

LILY PAD (X-2): 200 yards southeast of Pine Island, 10,270 ft. elevation, 9.5 acres, 14' deep, horse friendly, with Brook trout, moderate pressure.

FISH HATCHERY (X-6): Located 5.3 miles from the Grandview Trailhead, 11.8 miles from Mirror Lake, horse friendly, 10,230 ft. elevation, 37.2 acres, 28' deep, stocked with Cutthroat trout, but I've noticed them spawning too, also Brook trout, fishing pressure heavy.

FARNEY (X-14): Accessed bushwhacking 1/2 mile up the ridge west of Fish Hatchery, located on saddle, not horse friendly, 10,320 ft. elevation, 12.6 acres, 14' deep, stocked with Arctic Grayling. Duchesne drainage.

From Farney it might be best to return to trail near Fish Hatchery and continue up the trail to a junction north of Betsy lake, and proceed west up to Mohawk Lake. MOHAWK (X-10): Located 1+ mile from Grandaddy Lake, and 1/2 mile west of Betsey Lake, 10,380 ft. elevation, 50.8 acres, 23' deep, horse friendly, has a large population of self-sustaining Brook trout, plus Cutthroat trout, heavy pressure as it is popular with Scout groups.

MARSELL (X-11): For access the pamphlet says, "Leave the trail 1/2 mile north of Betsey Lake and go west [up a draw] along the edge of a talus ridge to the Lake." My way is at a point halfway between Betsey and Mohawk Lakes, leave the trail and go north until dropping down into a draw and go up it to the lake. Horse friendly, 10,470 ft. elevation, 16.4 acres, 50' deep, stocked with cutthroat trout, pressure moderate to light. Duchesne Drainage.

The sign was on the ground. With my tiny pocket tool, drilled a hole and hung it.

SONNY (X-12): Located about 1 mile southwest of Farney Lake, and 150 yards northwest of Marsell Lake. Best to access Sonny by going to Marsell. Horse friendly, 10,460 ft. elevation, 5 acres, 13' deep, has stocked Brook trout, with light pressure. Has a tendency to winterkill . Part of the Duchesne River Drainage.

I'll insert a picture of a Sonny Lake brook trout. Fishing here was also always good for me catching very healthy, and nice sized brookies.

One last lake listed in the pamphlet which I have overlooked in my reports and videos. GIBBY (RC-30): This pothole lake is located 75 yards north of Grandaddy Lake's northeastern arm, 10,320 ft. elevation, 1.9 acres, 25' deep, stocked with Brook trout.

Section 23:

THE MIRROR LAKE TRAILHEAD **************************

PREFACE

MUSHROOMS….Fascinating & Beautiful, but… EDIBLE? DEADLY POISONOUS? In the Fall of 2017 I was driving around the Uintas getting a few photos I would need for the book. Strangely I had never been to the Mirror Lake Trailhead, so I pulled into the parking lot, got a picture of the trail sign, with a woman and her daughter(s) coming up the trail with a basket full of mushrooms. I got their picture and asked how sure they were about the edibility and safeness of the mushrooms they had gathered. She agreed that for most eating wild mushrooms can be dangerous, but explained their family's history of doing this every year--and WE ARE STILL ALIVE!

Mushrooms are one of the most mysterious life forms, sometimes with new varieties seemingly coming from out of the blue. The Greeks believing they came from Zue's lightning because they appeared after rains and reproduced and grew inexplicably.149 Some in the new world and the Nords called them, the food of the Gods. Mushrooms have often been referred to as food of the Gods because of their various hallucinogenic properties and other affects. One must be extremely cautious when eating mushrooms and know exactly what kind they are eating. Some will cause hallucinations, some will have the death trance affect, and yet another will cause types of crazed behavior.150

149

NATIONAL AUDUBON SOCIETY FIELD GUIDE TO MUSHROOMS, A Borzoi Book, published by Alfred A. Knopf, 1981 150

Vikings Wanderer: Other Strangeness, https://timeslipsblog.wordpress.com/category/mushrooms-as-food-of-the-gods/

p. 397

Michael Kuo, author of 100 EDIBLE MUSHROOMS, says: "I love mushrooms….Most of the best meals I've eaten in my life included wild mushrooms……But the truth is…wild mushrooms scare me……Even when I am 100 percent sure of a mushrooms' identity and the species has been eaten safely by thousands of people, my intellect has trouble….The two times I have suffered from relatively minor mushroom poisoning, it was not pleasant. So my goal with this book is only partly to give you the means to collect and cook up edible wild mushrooms. The bigger goal is to get you interested in mushrooms--edible or not. They are so fascinating, and so little is known about them!.......The fungi are integral to life on earth, and mushrooms deserve our respect and admiration! ……If you want to eat the devil's urn (p.94) or pickled stinkhorn eggs (p. 197), have at it, by all means. But don't say I didn't warn you!"

In MUSHROOMING WITHOUT FEAR, the author says, If you're absolutely sure about the field mushroom, then pick it by all means. But unless you are 100 percent certain, HUNT FOR FIELD MUSHROOMS AND OTHER SPECIES WITH GILLS IN THE SUPERMARKET ONLY151. (my capitalization for emphasis)

More than 10,000 varieties have been identified in North America, but that's only 10-20% of the total, so it's a wide open field of study. They are famous for being poisonous, but only about 20% are, with around 1% being totally deadly. Some common names tell the tale with beautiful names, like: Fairy ring, Pretty, Prince, Honey, Sweetheart and Fried chicken. But then there are the sinister ones, such as: Poison pie, Hated amonita, Slimy cap, Deceptive milky, Corpse finder, Death cap, and Destroying angel, and the ones mentioned above, devils urn, and pickled stinkhorn eggs. Identification is the problem as it is sometimes difficult and frustrating even for the experts, a qualification among them is being humble and ready to admit error. 151

MUSHROOMING WITHOUT FEAR, by Alexander Schwab, published by Skyhorse Publishing in 2006.

p. 398

The unbendable rule--especially if we are deciding edibility is to never accept identification unless all evidence confirms. Many things have to be considered to make such an identification: Shapes or stature types, whether with gills or not, tubes, spines or ridges underneath rather than gills, rings, collar, skirt, around the stalk, or not, or volva around the base of the stalk, odor (watermelon, cucumber, rotten, etc.), texture (waxy, smooth, sticky, dry, wet, rough, scaly, etc.), and for sure identification only with microscopic spore print. So far I haven't said anything to make anyone confident about eating wild mushrooms, and I hope--if you really want to eat what you find in the Uintas, DO YOUR HOMEWORK, using some of the books I have quoted, and you see pictured below.

The experts suggest we first learn to recognize those that are deadly, and I'll insert below a few pictures of them.152

DESTROYING ANGEL, that is more deadly than cyanide. Symptoms of poisoning include: Vomiting, diarrhea, cramps, kidney/liver dysfunction, and without quick treatment results in death. 152

NATIONAL AUDUBON SOCIETY FIELD GUIDE TO MUSHROOMS, A Borzoi Book, published by Alfred A. Knopf, 1981

p. 399

About the same for Hated Amanita, and Death Cap,153 for which symptoms are often "delayed for 10-14 hours or more and begin with severe" symptoms similar to those outlined above. "A remission occurs after a day or so, and the victim believes he is better. By the 3rd or 4th day, signs of serious kidney and/or liver dysfunction appear and can, without adequate treatment, cause death in 5-10 days."154 In some cases of survival, organ transplants are necessary.

I'LL EMPHASIS THE DIFFICULTY and DANGER, with one of my pictures from the Uintas-in my notes I identify the mushroom below as, GRAY PANTHER, Amanita spissa, but didn't add a reference where I got that identification.

If that identification is correct, its toxins cause delirium, raving and a coma-like deep sleep. But in trying to confirm that identification, I came up with it possibly being rather FLY AGARIC, Amanita muscaria. For a decision, I would need more information, being able to see its underbelly--whether it had gills or not, and the stalk, whether it had rings, a skirt, or a collar, plus more information. It would still be poisonous but rather "cause delirium, raving, and profuse sweating," but "Unlike its Siberian relative, this induces no visions."155

153

Ibid. pages 113 and 114.

154

Ibid. pages 543-544.

155

Ibid. p. 539.

p. 400

Other symptoms caused by poisonous mushrooms are:

"blurred vision, dizziness, lack of coordination, delusions, staggering, delirium, lack of coordination, a fall in blood pressure, and slowing of the pulse, deep sleep."

Then others may cause "mood shifts, which can range from the pleasant to the apprehensive; symptoms may often include unmotivated laughter, hilarity, compulsive movements, muscular weakness, drowsiness, visions, then sleep." With some, recovery can occur in a few hours, or a few days,

and in others death will occur if diagnosis and treatment is not done quickly.156 To say the least it's a big subject you've got to learn about if you're going to entertain the idea of eating any of them. There are a lot of them in the Uintas, as you'll notice from the montage I'll insert below, with just a few of the thousands.

My purpose in this discussion is first, TO SAVE LIVES, making sure you don't attempt eating any without being 1000% sure of the identification. But, at the same time, your hikes into the Uintas will become much more fascinating knowing how interesting they are, how beautiful they are in their own way, and of great 156

Ibid. p. 872-874.

p. 401

importance, how important and crucial they are for the cycle of nature to function. Without them the decomposition of dead wood and other organic matter just wouldn't happen like it does. Fungi, which mushrooms are, along with related organisms, described as: Any of a diverse group of eukaryotic single-celled or multinucleate organisms that live by decomposing and absorbing the organic material in which they grow, comprising the mushrooms, molds, mildews, smuts, rusts, and yeast, and classified in the kingdom Fungi or Plantae.157

And, it's a lot more important and widespread than most could ever imagine, as an important part of this CYCLE OF NATURE has fungi forming a symbiotic, or partnership relationship, with algae to create another organism in nature we call LICHENS which we all notice live on rocks, and trees. The fungi and the algae each fill a role in the survival of the other, and together the resultant lichen fill a slow, but crucial role in the process of breaking down the rock or the tree they live on. We see below a few examples in the panel of photographs. s

Above on the left we see as the dominant lichen, one called PINCUSHION ORANGE - xanath oria polycarpa, but there are others there. On the right we see a multiple crustose lichen garden with at least a half a dozen varieties from among the 3,000 that have been identified in the Rocky Mountain area. This is another fascinating life-form that will enhance our hikes in the Uintas, as we will see lichens everywhere, and, by the way Rocky Mountain goats eat lichens as an important part of their diet. Let me just attach the first line and then a paragraph about them: "Lichens are fungi that have discovered agriculture" —Trevor Goward[39]

A lichen is a composite organism that emerges from algae or cyanobacteria living among the filaments (hyphae) of two fungi in a mutually beneficial symbiotic relationship. The fungi benefit from the carbohydrates produced by the algae or cyanobacteria via photosynthesis. The algae or cyanobacteria benefit by being protected from the environment by the filaments of the fungi, which also gather moisture and nutrients from the environment, and (usually) provide an anchor to it. Although some photosynthetic 157

https://www.dictionary.com/browse/fungi?s=t

p. 402

partners in a lichen can survive outside the lichen, the lichen symbiotic association extends the ecological range of both partners, whereby most descriptions of lichen associations describe them as symbiotic. However, while symbiotic, the relationship is probably not mutualistic, since the algae give up a disproportionate amount of their sugars (see below). Both partners gain water and mineral nutrients mainly from the atmosphere, through rain and dust. The fungal partner protects the alga by retaining water, serving as a larger capture area for mineral nutrients and, in some cases, provides minerals obtained from the substrate. If a cyanobacterium is present, as a primary partner or another symbiont in addition to a green alga as in certain tripartite lichens, they can fix atmospheric nitrogen, complementing the activities of the green alga. 158

Let's just finish our little discussion--which, as you can see--with 10,000+ varieties of MUSHROOMS identified, and then 3,000+ varieties of LICHENS, is no small matter, but hopefully our interest has been sparked to learn more, and take notice as we trek through the Uintas, just like we do with the wildflowers, the wildlife and the rocks. Let's just remember that mushrooms can be dangerous, just as also is the case with high altitude, cold climate changes, lightning, and wild animals, plus other dangers we have to understand and learn to live with. Lets just remember some of the rules of the game of MUSHROOMS: 1. Never consider eating any of them without being 100% sure of your identification--which should be based on true understanding. 2. If there is any shred of doubt about one, forget it. And a few rules given in the book, MUSHROOMING WITHOUT FEAR: 1. Read the entire book twice in order to understand the approach 2. Study the "Gills," "Tubes," "Spines" and "Ridges" sections until you're confident you can correctly distinguish these features: then you're ready for a foray. NOTE: If you don't know

what those things are, YOU AREN'T READY! 3. Double check at home by going through the full identification process step-by-step outlined in the book. Rules: 1. Never, never take a mushroom with gills!!! 2. Only take mushrooms with tubes, spines and ridges and the mavericks portrayed here. 3. Only eat mushrooms which you have clearly identified with ALL the positive ID marks. 4. If a mushroom smells rotten, it is rotten and if it feels soggy, it is soggy. 5. Never, never eat wild mushrooms raw. 6. If in doubt, LEAVE IT!159

Section 23:

THE MIRROR LAKE TRAILHEAD-- ANOTHER GATEWAY to the GRANDADDY BASIN HOW TO GET HERE: From the American Fork Utah 31 miles to Heber, then to Kamas (17), and on Ut-150-The Mirror Lake Scenic Byway, over Bald Mt. Pass and down to Mirror Lake (32), a TOTAL of 80 miles from American Fork, Utah, 72 miles from Salt Lake City.

Mirror Lake as seen from Scout Lake

With this segment we have come to the MIRROR LAKE TRAILHEAD, and full circle back to near where we started on page 160 at Hayden's Pass and the Highline Trail, that among other places leads the hiker to THE EAST FORK PINTO LAKE TRAIL, 5-1/2 miles from the TH, this trail taking off to the south dipping down through the headwaters of the Duchesne River, then up the other side of the canyon to Pinto Lake--which has us in the Rock Creek Drainage and on the northern end of the Grandaddy Basin, which is described as part of the SOUTH SLOPE. The MIRROR LAKE TRAILHEAD has two trails, one that in 2 miles connects to the Highline Trail 0.6 mile from the trailhead at Hayden pass. Following the Highline for 4.7 miles takes you to the junction with the East Fork Pinto Lake Trail that in 2.1 miles takes you to Pinto Lake where you are at the northern tip of the Grandaddy Basin. The other trail from the Mirror Lake Trailhead takes you down into the Duchesne River canyon and follows the river for 12.2 miles to the Mill Flat Trailhead. Over all of its course following the river it parallels the Wilderness Boundary on the east side of the river. This would be a great hike giving you 10 miles of access to the river and some great fishing, most of which sees few fishermen.

p. 404

There is no trail, but can easily be located. 9,000 ft. elevation, 5 acres, 14' deep, with regularly stocked Brook trout.

FERN (X-5): Located northeast of East Grandaddy Mt., 5.3 miles from the Grandview Trailhead, 8.1 miles from the Rock Creek Trailhead, accessed via a faint trail that cuts off the main trail just south of La Marla Lake. 9,890 ft. elevation, 19.3 acres, 19' deep, sort of horse friendly, stocked with Brook trout, with moderate fishing pressure. DOC'S (X-15): This isolated lake is found at the northeast tip of East Grandaddy Mt. Off-trail several miles of bushwhacking southeast of Fern Lake, or 3 miles of hard climbing west of the Rock Creek Bridge, not possible for horses, 9,882 ft. elevation, 14.5 acres, 45' deep, pressure light for stocked Brook trout. HEART (X-13): Located just east of Hades Pass--the first lake you will see descending into the basin, 2.6 miles from the trailhead, and 1/2 mile southwest of Grandaddy Lake. 10,500 ft. elevation, 5.7 acres, 19' deep, horse friendly, stocked with Cutthroat trout, heavy pressure.

PREFACE

The High Uintas Preservation Council and THE PROPOSED MT. WATSON WILDERNESS AREA We've been introduced to the Wilderness Area, including all the trails that lead into the roadless area of 456,705 acres (714 square miles), Utah's largest we see below. Basic map by GOOGLE EARTH MAPS, labels & color lines by author

Now, we'll learn about the WESTERN UINTAS, basically from the Mirror Lake Highway west. This is where are born the Provo and the Weber Rivers. Much of it is also a road-less wilderness, where 100,000 acres were proposed a few years ago as another Wilderness Area, and it's good for many of us to know so we might possibly be of influence in reviving this effort that was put on hold in 2010, when the High Uintas Preservation Council was retired. However, their website is still very much alive, with hundreds of interesting reports in their Archives. Let's learn about their efforts and the fascinating Western Uintas, first seeing below a map of the proposal--that's sort of convoluted due to roads into the area.

p. 411

160

THE PROPOSED MT. WATSON WILDERNESS AREA

This is incised and convoluted country. It is the heart of the Kamas Ranger District of the Wasatch-Cache National Forest. It is still wild enough that it can’t be encircled by a car in a day. You can feel its size and diversity by a drive from Kamas up the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway and west over the dirt road at Whitney Reservoir. Or try driving from Oakley up the Weber River to Smith-Morehouse or Holiday Park. In between all of this is a roadless area of over 100,000 acres; outside of the roadless country adjacent to the High Uintas Wilderness, it comprises the largest chunk of roadless Forest Service land left in Utah! Stroll up or down any of the major drainages of what the Forest Service calls the Lakes Backcountry and your wonder will be awakened as to how wild the place is and why it was never included in the Utah Wilderness Act of 1984. The slickrock cascades of the Middle Fork of the Weber, one of the wildest spots in the Uintas, will reward you with utter silence except for coyote families, moose, black bear and pine marten. The upper benches of the Middle Fork are dotted with dozens of small lakes, wet meadows and beautiful ancient stands of spruce, creating a patchy landscape of open rock slopes, towering peaks and ridgelines. This is rugged, high elevation country. The main fork of the Weber River is a larger drainage typified by dense stands of spruce and lodge pole pine tapering down to pine and aspen. The forest and river’s edge become one. The high peaks and ridges of the Uintas simply disappear into a wild forest. 160

http://www.hupc.org/Archive/newsletters/Oct.,%201998/mt._watson_article.htm

p. 412

A walk up Smith-More-house Creek into Erickson Basin opens up dramatically. Long 10,000 foot ridges dominate the horizon; the forest is open with patchy stands of aspen. Here the sky reigns. But try a hike from the Smith-Morehouse into the Middle Fork of the Weber through the convoluted topography of Hell's Kitchen with its false summits, small isolated basins and steep lodgepole pine slopes, and it is possible to believe it is the first stroll in this country! From the barren pass between Smith-Morehouse and the Middle Fork stretches a vista unmatched-green forests, open parklands, alpine peaks and acre after acre of untouched wildness. A hike up the North Fork of the Provo River, Shingle Creek, Yellowpine or Boulder Creek offers another view of this landscape. Here aspen and douglas-fir forests, sagebrush flats, and parklands dominate an open landscape. High peaks are steady companions. The country imperceptibly changes from a measured landscape into steep, rugged and deep canyons typical of the higher elevation pine and spruce forests of the Uintas. The North Fork of the Provo now runs with force all year as the nearly dozen small impounded lakes (dammed in the 1920s) have been stabilized as natural inflow/outflow lakes at or slightly above natural lake level (all of the "dam-works" have been removed). With the one exception of Marjorie Lake, none of these lakes will again have to be maintained as reservoired lakes by way of motorized access. This has added to both the wildness of the region and high quality wilderness characteristics! The Lakes Backcountry (we think it should be the Mt. Watson Wilderness) is not of one place. It is a diverse region. Half a dozen peaks top 11,000 feet. Over 100 lakes and numerous rivers/streams slice through the area. Cougar grace the most rugged corners of the area. Black bear haunt the richer habitats. Pine marten and goshawk find the old crumpled forests essential. It is integral to protecting the entire High Uintas. Dick Carter

11,551 ft. high Mt. Watson and other peaks of the proposed Mt. Watson Wilderness

Chapter 3: THE WESTERN UINTAS We will once again leave Kamas, Utah and head east following the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway--UT-150, and stop at each Trailhead and learn about the possibilities for adventuring, lots of them in the area. We will visit the trailheads on the west side of the Scenic Byway--primarily looking at the areas at least mid-way to the far western lower Weber River Canyon Trailheads. Last we will go to those low-country trailheads up Weber Canyon and examine the possibilities more practical from those access points. We will also detail the possibilities to the east of the highway not in the Wilderness Area, like the Murdock Basin. HOW TO GET TO KAMAS: From the American Fork Utah 31 miles to Heber, then to Kamas (17) for a TOTAL of 48 miles from American Fork, Utah, 40 miles from Salt Lake City. Then proceed on Ut-150The Mirror Lake Scenic Byway.

Section 1

THE LOWER PROVO & WEBER RIVER DRAINAGES To familiarize you with the areas we will cover, let me quote some from the DWR pamphlet, Provo and Weber River Drainages, Revision 1999.162

161

©2018 Google LLC, used with permission. Google and the Google logo are registered trademarks of Google LLC. Highlights, extra routes and labels by author 162

Lakes of the High Uintas: Provo and Weber River Drainages, publication No. 99-22 (1983) Revised Edition, 1999.

p. 414

PROVO RIVER DRAINAGE The Provo River Basin is a diverse drainage system on the western flank of the Uinta Mountains. The terrain is composed of wide drainage basins with timbered ridges and scattered high dome-like mountains. The highest point in the drainage is Bald Mountain which stands at 11,943 feet in elevation This area is one of the major water producing zones in the Uinta Mountains. Most of the lakes…are situated north and west of the Mirror Lake Highway which begins at Kamas, Utah. There are 80 natural lakes (15 of which have been modified and enlarged by dams for water storage) and well over 150 ponds of less than 2 acres in size. Of these waters, 57 contain game fish or are under experimental fisheries management. Lakes vary in elevation from 9360 to nearly 10,500 feet. Access to the major portion of the drainage is excellent due to the Mirror Lake Highway and associated Forest Service roads including the Upper Setting Road, the Norway Flats Road, and the Spring Canyon Road. Of the managed fish producing lakes, 19 are directly accessible to vehicles and a number of other lakes lie within a short walking distance of the road. Access to most of the back country lakes is provided by the Crystal lake Trailhead in the vicinity of Trial Lake on the Lake Country Trail, the Watson-Clyde Trail, and the Notch Mountain Loop Trail. The first two are well marked. The Watson-Clyde Trail is unmarked, difficult to locate, and becomes indistinct at times. This trail begins at the northwestern end of Upper Lily Lake in the vicinity of the Crystal Lake Trailhead. Other established take-off points in the drainage include the Bald Mountain and Upper Setting trailheads which primarily provide access to Weber Basin lakes. Additional forest Service trails in the Provo Drainage include the Norway Flats, Shingle Creek, North Fork, Weir Lake and Upper Setting Trails. Each of these trail systems are identified on the map by Forest Service trail numbers. Most of the fishing and camping activity in the Provo Drainage is concentrated along the highway corridor and adjacent to Forest Service roads and major trails. Full-service campgrounds are available at Trial, Lost and Lilly lakes and fishing pressure at these waters is very heavy. Several lakes on the popular Lakes Country Trail receive high levels of angling pressure as well. However, the remote lake basins away from the major trails and road have much to offer for those seeking solitude. The most abundant fish species is the brook trout, with some cutthroat trout. Arctic grayling are present in Marjorie and Weir lakes. U.S. Geological Survey topographic maps applicable to the Provo River Drainage include the Mirror Lake, Erickson Basin, Iron Mine Mountain and Soapstone Basin quadrangles.

The sun sets over the once proposed Mt. Watson Wilderness Area

p. 415

NOW THE WEBER RIVER DRAINAGE The Weber River is a large drainage system on the western extremity of the Uinta Mountains. There are 59 natural lakes and 80+ ponds of less than 2 acres. Eleven of these lakes have been enlarged by dam construction for water storage purposes. Access is provided by Highway 213 east of Oakley and Highway U-150 east of Kamas, Utah. Starting points along Highway 213 include the Erickson Basin Trailhead in the vicinity of the Ledgefork Campground. Other trails originate from Holiday Park but it is on private property and the Forest Service right-of-way road has no trailhead development or parking. NOTE: We will deal with the Trailheads on the Weber River after we examine first those along the Mirror Lake Highway. The major access points to the Weber Drainage are scattered along UT-150 and include the Upper Setting Trailhead, the Crystal lake Trailhead, the Bald Mountain Trailhead, and the Weber River Trail near Pass Lake. Trails originating at these points drop over the top into the major headwater regions of the Weber Basin. Some of the more inaccessible lakes in the Uinta Mountains lie within this drainage. Forest Service trails are not well developed or maintained with the exception of the Notch Mountain Loop Trail, the Lofty Lake Loop Trail, the Smith-Morehouse Trail, and the Yellow Pine Trail. Several trail systems, particularly in the Middle fork are no longer in existence due to light foot and horse traffic. Self-sustaining populations of Arctic grayling are present in Sand, Round and Fish lakes in the Dry Fork Drainage. USGS topographic maps useful in the Weber River Drainage include Whitney Reservoir, Slader Basin, Hidden Lake, Mirror Lake, Erickson Basin, and the Hoyt Peak quadrangles.

Now for the details: About 6 miles from Kamas you come to the first trailhead on the north side of the highway, THE YELLOW PINE, at an elevation of 7,080 ft.

From this point follow the Castle lake

Chapter 3: THE WESTERN UINTAS

Section 2: THE SPRING CANYON/TRIAL LAKE ROAD *******************

PREFACE INTRODUCTION: In this section you will notice we deal exclusively with lakes that are part of the Provo River Drainage, and it should be of great interest to all to know some about where the name "Provo" came from, so follows is a great article that introduces us to the mountain man after whom the river, and the city of Provo was named. Later we will also do the same for the Weber River.

Etienne Provost "THE MAN OF THE MOUNTAINS"163 Although he does not have the wide recognition of Jim Bridger or John Colter, Etienne Provost was considered by his contemporaries as one of the most knowledgeable, skillful, and successful of the mountain men. Provost gave his name (phonetically) to the Provo River and the city of Provo. It seems likely that most of the early settlers of Provo were unaware of the bloody incident that gave the river its name. Provost's contemporaries, however, knew of his skills and nicknamed him "the man of the mountains." Of French Canadian ancestry, Provost was born in 1785 in Chambly, Quebec. Around 1814 he became involved in the St. Louis fur trade, often trapping in what was still Spanish territory. Provost and his companions were twice captured and held prisoner by Spanish authorities. About 1822 he began operating out of Taos in present-day New Mexico. In 1824 he and his partner Francois Leclerc led a company north from Taos into the Great Basin. Some authorities claim that Provost may have been the first white man to see the Great Salt Lake? -- some months before Jim Bridger. In October the party was camped near Utah Lake (then generally known as Timpanogos Lake), probably along the present-named Jordan River. Provost's men encountered a party of Snake (Shoshone) Indians. In his Life in the Rocky Mountains Warren Angus Ferris claims that a Shoshone chief known to the whites as "Bad Gocha" (from mauvais gauche or "bad left-handed one") wanted to smoke the peace pipe with the Taos trappers. Bad Gocha claimed that it was bad luck to have metallic objects nearby, so Provost had his men set their weapons aside. At a signal, the Shoshones then attacked the whites, killing all but Provost and two or three others, who barely managed to fight their way out. The survivors made their way northeast over the Wasatch range. EtEienne Provost The following spring Provost and his party met Peter Skene Ogden and members of his Hudson's Bay Company trapping party on the Weber River, near present-day Mountain Green. Upon hearing the story of Provost's narrow escape, Ogden wrote his superiors that he believed that the ambush may have been caused by the behavior of a Hudson's Bay party of the previous year. Ogden reported that Alexander Ross's company had stolen horses and furs from Shoshones and had killed one Indian. Provost nearly got caught up in another fight, partly on account of Ogden. A party of American trappers encountered Ogden's Englishmen in the Weber Valley, and an argument over trapping rights ensued—part of a much larger dispute about the ownership of the "Oregon country." The American and English trappers each claimed the territory for their respective companies and nations. Author Jack B. Tykal points out that, in reality, only the bystander Provost had a legal right to trap in what was still Mexican territory. Provost met William Ashley's large trapping party soon after and helped to guide Ashley to the site of the first annual mountain man rendezvous at Henry's Fork. Provost continued to work and explore in the American West out of St. Louis, although his active trapping days ended in 1830. He developed a reputation as a tough, resourceful man who also liked to drink and carouse. In 1839 he served as camp conductor for the Jean Nicollet party that mapped the country between the upper Mississippi and Missouri rivers. In 1843 Provost helped guide John James Audubon through the region. Although no photographs of Provost are known to exist, artist Alfred Jacob Miller painted members of the Nicollet expedition. Provost appears short, fat, and round; Miller captioned one picture "Monsieur Proveau, subleader, with a corpus round as a porpoise." In 1849 Mormon pioneers built "Fort Utah" on a Utah Valley stream that had generally been known as the Timpanogos. Mormons dubbed the river flowing between Utah Lake and the Great Salt Lake the Jordan, after the Holy Land river that connected the Sea of Galilee with the Dead Sea. Barney Ward, a mountain man who helped to guide the Utah Valley settlers, apparently told the Mormons that the Timpanogos stream was also called the "Provo." Why the names got switched is unclear, but the October 1849 LDS Conference directed the establishment of the city of "Provo" on the river. The city's namesake, meanwhile, still lived in St. Louis, unaware of the honor. Etienne Provost died there on July 3, 1850.

163

Sources: Leroy R. Hafen, "Etienne Provost, Mountain Man and Utah Pioneer," Utah Historical Quarterly 36 (1968); Jack B. Tykal, Etienne Provost: Man of the Mountains (Liberty, Utah: Eagle's View Publishing Company, 1989). https://historytogo.utah.gov/people/etienneprovost.html

Section 2: THE SPRING CANYON/TRIAL LAKE ROAD At 6.1 miles from the North Fork Trailhead, or 18 miles from Kamas we see on the right a sign to SPRING CANYON. It has never attracted attention from those of us who focus on the Wilderness Area, but might if the sign also stated what the road is called on the National Geographic topographic maps--THE TRIAL LAKE ROAD. Once you turn off to the left or north, we see the sign in the middle below…..a bit more interesting. The road switch-backs up into the high country, you see me doing in the 3rd picture--if you look carefully you can see the road below me on the left, and the switch-back behind me as I drove up this dirt/gravel road. Any car can handle the road, even if it is raining--which would be an advantage eliminating the dust. NOTE: By the way, if you don't have a lot of experience on

dusty roads, you can keep it from finding its way into your car by having the windows closed, and ventilation system--A/C, or heater, turned on bringing fresh air in the front and creating inside pressure that keeps dust from coming in. Of course when a car passes, turn it off until the air clears. Additional Note: The “Duchesne Tunnel” mentioned in the sign on the left, is part of the Central Utah Project, explained in Appendix 11.

The main road, FR-041, is fine, with at least 14 secondary roads taking off from it leading to, or close to, around a dozen fishable lakes. The pictures we see on the following page show

one of these secondary roads, the DWR sometimes call jeep trails, are for 4-wheel drive vehicles as you will note.
