From the fork seen above we proceed northwest past the large meadow to a point where the road turns abruptly west. From there you head northeast on foot 300 yards to Lambert Lake--which is not the one in the panel above which is rather Trident Lake described later. LAMBERT (A-2): Accessed as described above. Lambert is a natural lake in a meadow with floating banks and conifers on its southern shoreline, 9,630 ft. elevation, 2 acres, 8' deep, stocked with brook trout

Now, back to the fork in the road, we proceed on FR-041. ALEXANDER (A-1): Access is 3 miles north on the Spring Canyon Road, or about 1 mile on FR-041, then 1/4 mile southeast on a "Forest Service trail"--I believe is Road 940. The lake is located in heavy timber at 9,360 ft. elevation, 23 acres, 28' deep, stocked with brook trout, with heavy pressure. SPRING CANYON (A-4): No fish life. SPECTACLE (HOURGLASS) (A-44): Access is 4.5 miles north on the Spring Canyon Road to a small roadside pond and then west for 1/4 mile to Spectacle. No trail to the lake. At 9,740 ft. elevation, 9.3 acres, 17' deep with some floating banks164 and islands, stocked with brook trout with moderate pressure.

We then come to a fork in the road, about 5 miles from Highway 150, the direct route to the Trial Lake area is to the right. The longer route is to the left that takes you by Buckeye Lake and on to Blue Lake, both of which I'll describe next.

BUCKEYE LAKE (A-3): Access is 4.75 miles north of Highway 150 on the Spring Canyon Road to the junction, and then 1/4 mile north to the lake. Located at 9,660 ft. elevation, 5 acres, 8' deep, with grass covered floating banks. There is natural reproduction, but due to intensive fishing pressure, it also receives planted brook trout. BLUE (A-5): Access is 1.25 miles past Buckeye Lake on a well marked jeep trail. Located at 9,680 ft. elevation, 8 acres, 26' deep, surrounded by conifers and small meadows, stocked with brook trout, with heavy fishing pressure.

The road then continues northeast and joins the other road, and soon on the right is seen Trident Lake that was pictured in the previous photo panel. TRIDENT (A-41): Located to the east of the Spring Canyon Road, 6-3/8th miles from Highway 150, at 9,400 ft. elevation, 4 acres, 5' deep, with brook trout under heavy fishing pressure. BETH (A-6): Located 6.5 miles north on the Spring Canyon Road, and then 1/4 mile west on a marked jeep road (Rd. #961), again a lake with open shorelines and floating banks, 9,780 ft. elevation, 5.4 acres, 10' deep with a good population of brook trout, under heavy fishing use. HAYSTACK (A-9): This is a beautiful lake surrounded by thick forests interspersed with meadows, access is 1/2 mile west on a jeep road, from about 7 miles north on the Spring Canyon Road, with brook and cutthroat trout with heavy fishing pressure. AZURE (A-11): Is a natural lake in a glacial basin formed by a moraine of large boulders, surrounded by rocky, talus slopes on the western and northern margins of the lake. Located 3/8th mile west of Haystack Lake, and approximately 200 yards north and slightly west of Rock Lake, not horse friendly--it's a backpacker's lake, at 10,140 ft. elevation, 9 acres, 23' deep, in 2008 was stocked with Grayling, use very light. Was stocked in the 1960s and 70s with brook trout, stocked in the 80s with cutthroat trout, again with brook trout in the early 90s; prone to winterkill, stocking discontinued. ROCK (A-10): Located 1/4th mile west of Haystack Lake, at the base of Haystack Mountain, with no clearly defined trails, limited to backpackers, at 10,140 ft. elevation, 8 acres, 14 ' deep, planted with brook trout, with moderate pressure. SHADOW (A-52): Located 1/2 mile south of Washington Reservoir along the major drainage system, at 10,060 ft. elevation, 14 acres, 20' deep, horse friendly, with brook trout and heavy fishing use. TAIL (A-53): Located south of Washington Reservoir--accessed 1/2 mile southwest of the dam in dense forest, at 9,980 ft. elevation, 9.8 acres, 14' deep, with a good population of brook, cutthroat, and rainbow trout, fish migrating from Washington Reservoir during high water, or reproduce naturally. Heavy pressure.

In this northeastern portion of the Spring Canyon Road there are two lakes: SHADOW and SHOESTRING, but listed by the DWR as "not sustaining fish life." As we get into the northern portion of this area we have open up to the north Bald Mountain, Reids Peak, Mt. Watson and others, and then we come to the pavement, 7.4 miles from our launching point on the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway.

It has been obvious in the photographs I've used for this section, they were taken late in the season, actually on September 21st, with all dead and ready for winter, except the conifers. Of course being fall, down along the Scenic Byway, we enjoyed the colors of Autumn

Section 3: THE CRYSTAL LAKE & BALD MT. TRAILHEADS ***************************

PREFACE

THE TRAGIC SURVIVAL STORIES FROM CRYSTAL LAKE TRAILHEADS……WHY & HOW TO AVOID THEM On pages 343-350 we told the story of 58 year old Carole Wetherton, and her daughter, 39 year old Kim, who went on a day hike from the Crystal Lake Trailhead, turned up missing and were never found in spite of a large scale search effort in September 2003. Nine months later their bones were found. In 2004 a 11 year old boy, Garrett Bardesley was lost and never found. In early August, 2017 the following notice was posted at the Crystal Lake Trailhead.

p. 427

Melvin was an experienced hiker in the Uintas and had gone on a day hike, but then disappeared. His family reported him missing and an intensive search ensued. In the notice it says, "It is believed that he is wearing a rust colored……..long sleeve shirt, and blue jeans…." Is that all? If so, could he have survived cold nights? Did he have a day pack with a heavier jacket, with rain gear, a waterproof fire making kit, a headlamp or flashlight, any communication devices, and other emergency equipment? Apparently it isn't known, nor was there any indication in the news reports that he had left specific information with the family exactly what trail he would be taking and his destination. His car was found in the Trailhead parking lot. Search efforts intensified and continued during the week using trained Search & Rescue personnel, dogs and even a helicopter but no trace was found. By the end of the week 150 volunteers showed up at the Trailhead to help, but with no luck. Even trained mountaineers, knowing the areas along all the trails and around the area lakes had been searched, focused their search efforts in the off-trail areas, all with no results, and made the comment: "This area seems to be the Bermuda Triangle of Utah's mountains." 165

Now at the end of the 2018 hiking season in the Uintas the notice about Melvin Heaps has been taken down at the Crystal Lake Trailhead. On seeing this I hoped that it meant he had been found, but a Google search doesn't give any such news, and a call to the Forest Service in Kamas confirms he has not been found. I suspect they'll get the sign back up at the trailhead. ERIC ROBINSON FROM AUSTRALIA In Chapter 2: THE WILDERNESS AREA, Section 1 on the HIGHLINE TRAIL, pages 156159, we also discussed the case or Eric Robinson. He wasn't just a day hiker, but a world-wide experienced backpacker from Australia who went missing, the search eventually was abandoned after turning up nothing--until 5 years later when his remains were found just by chance. I discuss in that article how such a tragedy can be avoided.

Above we see the Crystal Lake Trailhead

RAY HUMPHREYS MISSING IN UINTAS -- A MASSIVE SEARCH MADE During the 2018 season, once again an experienced backpacker in the Uintas, 66 year old Ray Humphreys, who along with his family had left the Crystal Lake Trailhead on the Clyde Lake/Mt. Watson Trail, then past Clyde Lake they had hiked northwest to Hidden 165

https://backcountrypost.com/threads/searching-for-melvin-heaps.7228/

p. 428

Lake where the family has traditionally gone each year. In the evening of Wednesday, July 18th, at about 10:00 PM, Ray left the camp to go 40 yards down to the lake to get some water to put out their fire. Apparently all had gone to their tents and hadn't noticed until the next morning that Ray had never returned to his tent. They searched finding nothing and at 12:30 PM that day--July 19th, advised the Summit County Sheriff. All were puzzled as he couldn't have gone very far off. The search turned up no sign of him.

An even more intensive search continued involving the Summit County Search and Rescue, the Utah Department of Public Safety, Civil Air Patrol and the Great Basin K9 Search & Rescue, and a dive team searched Hidden Lake. By Saturday all efforts were fruitless, and on Sunday, with Ray missing for 4 days, 300 volunteers organized by the Garrett Bardsley Foundation showed up to help in the search. The Foundation is named for Garrett Bardsley, mentioned on page 426, lost in the Uintas in 2004 and never found.166 The Summit County Sheriff told the Deseret News after Ray had been missing for 4 days, "He's definitely someone who has a lot of outdoors experience as we understand from some of the family this is his 29th year being up in that area. You know, it's definitely possible for someone to survive this long especially if they use their natural resources. It was also reported he was dressed for cold weather, possibly wearing a black jacket or a blue hoodie." 167

THE SIXTH DAY On July 24th Matt Canham, from the Salt Lake Tribune, published the news that a search and rescue crew flying a state helicopter spotted Ray's body and led search crews to it near the Middle Fork of the Weber River, about 1.5 miles, and way down into the canyon from where the family had been camped at Hidden Lake. The Summit County Sheriff's Office said his injuries were "consistent with the harsh terrain and environment." 168

It isn't known how he could have got so disoriented to wander so far away from their camp--just 40 yards above the lake, but rather going down 1.5 miles into a rough canyon 166

https://www.parkrecord.com/news/hundreds-of-volunteers-join-search-for-man-missing-in-the-uintas/

167

http://www.missingpersonsofamerica.com/2018/07/23/ray-humpherys-missing-while-camping-in-utah/

168

https://www.sltrib.com/news/2018/07/25/helicopter-crew-finds/

p. 429

in the dark of night. In so doing he certainly could have eventually taken a fall, all complicated by cold temperatures at night. So far I have found no published autopsy reports indicating exactly why he died. When I have inquired I'm just told what the Sherriff said that his "injuries and death were consistent with the harsh terrain and environment."

WHAT CAN WE LEARN TO AVOID SIMILAR TRAGEDIES? This is such a matter of life and death, let me repeat here what was said concerning the mother and daughter: Over the next few months officials learned that a Forest Ranger saw the women near the trailhead on September 8th and told the women they would need heavier clothing in case the weather quickly changed as is frequent in the Uintas. 169 Apparently in the area that same afternoon rain fell and temperatures dropped below freezing, and the next night snow fell in the area. Later it was discovered they did not have rain gear, nor a compass--even though they did have a map, but left it in their vehicle. They had no matches, nor any emergency items like a headlamp, much less any kind of communication devices. They had not left any specific information with anyone of their planned for hike. NOTE: One report says matches were found with their remains, but they didn't use them, likely they were the wrong kind, and got wet and useless! NINE MONTHS LATER - Reported on June 27th: On June 24th, 1 mile northwest of where searchers scoured the area last September, and 1/2 mile from any trail in rocky timbered terrain, bone fragments were found in a crude shelter made of pine boughs in a natural formation of rocks, along with clothing, personal items, a set of car keys, 170 and a camera. "It appeared they were huddled in a small stone, kind of a shelter, and looked like they'd removed some of their clothing to dry," he said. "They probably died by the first night, and 171 definitely by the second." "Hypothermia occurs when the body loses more heat than it generates, and the condition can be fatal. The pair could survive in the dropping temperatures if they could start a fire to stay warm and dry their clothing. But shivering and without means to make a fire, their core body temperatures began dropping, and eventually they sank into a hypothermic state and died." 172

Concerning the advice given in the case of lone backpacker, Eric Robinson, I said:

169

https://www.deseretnews.com/article/510054604/Mother-daughter-still-lost-in-Uintas.html

170 171

172

Remains found in Uintas, https://www.deseretnews.com/article/595073455/Remains-found-in-Uintas.html

Reported on KSL.com on June 27, 2004: https://www.ksl.com/?sid=83779 http://climb-utah.com/Uinta/losthiker.htm

p. 430

WHAT WAS THE MISTAKE….OR THE MISTAKES? None of the things I mention here were done by Eric. I have said repeatedly that no one should go alone, unless they take all the precautions I take, which are:

1.) Leave a detailed itinerary where you're going to be each day, A duplicate set of maps showing itinerary left with family or friend, and/or on the internet. 2.) Have a satellite phone to give notice of changes, or emergency needs--

3.) Have a (PLB) Personal satellite locator device--mine a SPOT TRACKER, and,

4. USE IT DAILY, which sends a reassuring email to 10 friends each time you hit the OK button, with a link that shows exactly where you are each time with Google Earth as seen above. Or, in case of an emergency need, hit the 911 button which shows exactly where you are and immediately triggers Search & Rescue to come for you. One first has to take the responsibility of being in optimum physical shape, and focus carefully on every step--each of which has to be taken with perfection--especially when alone. Robison had a PLB but didn't use it. He had no satellite phone--if he had of, a change in plans would have been known--where he was yesterday to narrow the search today. It might not have saved him, but sure avoided a massive search and 5 years before being found. One shouldn't take excessive risks such as choosing an extremely dangerous alternative route as was done. I ended Section 11 of Chapter 2, pages 251-255, entitled SURVIVAL by saying:

"LET'S NOT DIE STUPIDLY!"

p. 431

Chapter 3: THE WESTERN UINTAS

Section 3:

THE CRYSTAL LAKE & BALD MT. TRAILHEADS HOW TO GET HERE: For Crystal Lake TH about 26 miles from Kamas you come to a big bend in the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway and see this sign, where you leave the highway and follow the paved road northwest to the Crystal Lake Trailhead, a TOTAL of about 26 miles from Kamas, 75 from Provo, and 69 from Salt Lake. The Spring Canyon/Trial Lake Road, comes out at this same junction.

As we can see in the trailhead parking lot, it is a very popular beginning point for hikes and backpacks. Literally thousands of nature lovers use this trailhead each summer, so it's a small percentage that have problems--but that's no excuse to not take seriously the dangers, and ignore the rules--that will make everybody's experience a fun, safe and inspirational one. So before launching ourselves into the Uintas, let's look at the advice given us by the Forest Service at the trailhead. On the next page we'll zoom in on the advice & the rules given us by the Forest Service.

p. 432

(photos / maps — no text on this page)

p. 433

(photos / maps — no text on this page)

p. 434

NOTE: You should have noticed there are some important differences between the above rules, and those for the Wilderness Area, on page 151. Primarily: 1. Groups restricted to 14 persons in the Wilderness rather than 20 in other areas. 2. Camping restricted to 200 feet from other camps, trails or water sources, rather than 100 feet in other Forest areas. 3. No campfires within 1/4 mile of lakes and water sources, according to restricted areas posted at Wilderness trailheads. The use of stoves is suggested. FOUR LAKES SEPARATE FROM THE TRAILHEADS: TRIAL (A-61): Located 1/2 mile west of the Mirror Lake highway on the road to the Crystal Lake Trailhead, at 9,800 ft. elevation, 98 acres, 68' maximum depth, but it is a reservoir/lake and level fluctuates. There is a full-service campground here, and the fishing pressure is heavy for rainbow, albino-rainbow, and brook trout stocked regularly by the DWR. Now also has Tiger trout.

DIAMOND (A-22): This is a productive lake that lies in a meadow at the head of the eastern most tributary to Trial Lake. It can be accessed by following the inlet stream from the northeastern end of the campground near the stream. 9,900 ft. elevation, 3 acres, 7' deep, with a wary population of brook and cutthroat trout, with moderate angling pressure.

STAR (A-42): It is a reservoir/lake located 1 mile northeast of Trial Lake, accessed by following Trial Lake's major inlet stream north to a small pond on a tributary. The reservoir is located at the top of this tributary stream. 9,980 ft. elevation, 16 acres, 35' maximum depth, with a limited population of cutthroat trout with heavy fishing pressure, but also has a population of mountain suckers that unbeknownst the DWR got into the lake. Now also stocked with Tiger trout.

WASHINGTON (A-23): Access is 3.4 mile west of U-150 at the Trial Lake Turnoff, and located 1/4 mile directly south of the Crystal Lake Trailhead, 9,900 ft. elevation, 106 acres, 70' deep, stocked with rainbow trout and has brook, cutthroat and Tiger trout, as well as Grayling, with heavy angling pressure.

NOW LET'S DIG INTO THE DETAILS OF LAKES ACCESSIBLE FROM THE DIFFERENT TRAILS THAT TAKE OFF FROM THE CRYSTAL LAKE TRAILHEAD

CRYSTAL (A-51): It is located 200 yards west of the Crystal Lake Trailhead on the North Fork Trail. 10,020 ft. elevation, 9.8 acres, 7' deep, but is a reservoir and so fluctuates, stocked with brook trout and receives heavy pressure.

LONG (A-37): It is located 2 miles west of the Crystal Lake Trailhead on the Lake Country Trail. 10,100 ft. elevation, 35 acres, 26' deep, horse friendly, has brook and cutthroat trout with heavy fishing pressure.

WEIR (A-50): Access is 2.5 miles west of the Crystal Lake Trailhead on the Lake Country and Weir Lake trails, horse accessible but scarce feed. It is a reservoired lake in the North Fork Drainage directly downstream from Long Reservoir, 9,940 ft. elevation, 7 acres, 13' deep, with cutthroat trout and arctic grayling, with moderate fishing pressure.

p. 435

MARJORIE (A-12): It is a reservoir lake on the ridge 1/8th mile southeast of Weir Lake, 9,980 ft. elevation, 13 acres, 16' deep, with arctic grayling under heavy fishing pressure. HIDDEN (A-15): It is in a small, remote basin and is difficult to locate in rocky, timbered country. Access is 2.25 miles south of Weir Lake on an indistinct segment of the Weir Lake Trail, distance from the Crystal Lake Trailhead is 5 miles. 9,760 ft. elevation, 8.2 acres, 25' deep, not horse friendly, fishing pressure moderate for brook trout. POT (A-8): It is a reservoir/lake located 1.4 mile southwest of Weir Lake on the Weir Lake Cutoff Trail-distance from trailhead, 2.25 miles, horse accessible but feed scarce, 9,940 ft. elevation, 4 acres, 28' deep, under heavy fishing pressure for stocked brook trout. DUCK (A-7): Another reservoir/lake located west of Pot Lake, or 1.25 miles beyond Long Lake on the Lake Country Trail, 3.25 miles from the trailhead, horse friendly, 9,780 ft. elevation, 12.7 acres, 15' deep, with heavy fishing pressure for brook and cutthroat trout sustained naturally. BEAVER (A-17): It is a remote lake surrounded by thick timber located 1/2 mile southwest of Duck, following the outlet stream, not too horse friendly, 9,900 ft. elevation, 3.5 acres, 15' deep, subject to winterkill, but stocked with brook trout every other year. Light pressure. CUTTHROAT (or CLINT) (A-40): It is a meadow lake at the foot of a steep shale ridge located 1 mile west of the Long Lake Dam and within sight north of the Lake Country Trail just before the trail to Duck Lake, horse friendly, 9,940 ft. elevation 3 acres, 10' deep, with brook trout. ISLAND (A-57): Located 3.5 miles west of the Crystal lake Trailhead on the Lake Country Trail. It is a reservoired lake with a shoreline characterized by rocky cliffs, at 10,140 ft. elevation, 28 acres, 40' deep but fluctuates. It is a popular lake with heavy fishing use for wary brook and Cutthroat & Tiger trout. JUNIOR (A-56): Located 1/4 mile southwest of Island Lake at the base of a steep, rocky ridge, with no access trails, but can easily be reached on foot or horseback, 10,200 ft. elevation, 2.8 acres, 11' deep, horse friendly, light fishing pressure for good cutthroat and Tiger trout. FIRE (A-14): Access is 150 yards south of Junior Lake following the outlet stream, 10,200 ft. elevation, 9 acres, 59' deep but fluctuates as it is a reservoired lake. Angling pressure is moderate for cutthroat trout. RAMONA (A-38): It is located on the ridge 1/4 mile northeast of Island Lake with no trail access, but can be reached on horseback, distance from the Crystal Lake Trailhead is 3.75 miles. 10,340 ft. elevation, 4.7 acres, 21' deep, moderate pressure for stocked brook trout.

Now back to the Crystal Lake Trailhead, to explore the Clyde Lake [Watson Clyde] Trail that heads northwest from the Trailhead. CLIFF (A-34): The lake is located 1/2 mile north of the Crystal Lake Trailhead on the Watson Clyde Trail the trail is unmarked but can be located at the northwestern extremity of Upper Lily Lake. 10,230 ft. elevation, 9 acres, 20' deep, horse friendly, has pan-sized cutthroat and Tiger trout and with heavy angler use. PETIT [JUNIOR] (A-26): Located on the ridge north of Cliff Lake, 3/4 mile north of the Crystal Lake Trailhead on the unmarked Watson-Clyde Trail, horse friendly. 10,300 ft. elevation, 2 acres, 3' deep with a small population of wary brook trout, pressure moderate.

WATSON (A-27): Located in thick forest at the base of Mount Watson, one mile north of the Trailhead on the Watson Clyde Trail. 10,420 ft. elevation 6 acres, 10' deep, horse friendly, moderate pressure for brook trout.

CLYDE (A-28): An oblong lake in a rocky basin at the foot of Mount Watson, accessed 1.5 miles north of the Trailhead on the unmarked and indistinct Watson Clyde Trail, 10,420 ft. elevation, 16 acres, 21' deep, fished heavily for brook trout.

p. 436

BOOKER (A-35): Located 200 yards northwest of Clyde Lake, horse friendly, 10,460 ft. elevation, 4.1 acres, 8' deep, has brook trout under heavy fishing pressure.

DIVIDE #1 (A-36): Located in a rugged basin between Watson and Notch mountains--one of three lakes on the divide. Access is 3/8th mile northwest of Clyde Lake on an indistinct trail, horse friendly, 10,460 ft. elevation, 3.5 acres, 5' deep, has brook trout with heavy fishing pressure.

JOHN (A-30): Located on a rocky ridge 1/8th mile northeast of Clyde Lake, 10,500 ft. elevation, 4 acres, 10' deep, horse access difficult, with a good population of brook trout.

LITTLE HIDDEN (W-21): Access is 2.5 miles from the Crystal Lake Trailhead on the Watson-Clyde Trail, then 1/2 mile over the pass from the Divide Lakes into the Middle Fork of the Weber drainage. Direct access trails do not exist, somewhat horse friendly, 10,280 ft. elevation, 8 aces, 28' deep, with a good population of brook trout under moderate pressure.

NOW WHAT IS KNOWN AS THE NOTCH MOUNTAIN TRAIL & LOOP TO THE BALD MT. TRAILHEAD UPPER LILY (A-24): The Lily Lakes lie 200 yards north of the trailhead, on the Notch Mountain Trail, the trail going between the two Lily Lakes. Upper lies west of the trail, at 10,020 ft. elevation 3.2 acres, 12' deep. It is not stocked and has been set aside as a botanical station for Brigham Young University. Stocked experimentally with brook trout in 1988; winterkill suspected--stocking discontinued.

LOWER LILY (A-25): It is located 200 yards north of the trailhead and is the eastern of the two Lily Lakes. At 10,030 ft. elevation, 3.2 acres, 16' deep, with brook trout under heavy fishing pressure.

WALL (A-29): Access to this large reservoir/lake is 1 mile north on the Notch Mountain Trail, found at 10,140 ft. elevation, 80 acres, 97' maximum depth, horse friendly but limited pasture, it has Brook and Tiger trout, as well as Grayling, with heavy angling pressure.

Looking over Wall Lake towards the pass known as "THE NOTCH"

HOPE (A-54): Located on the Notch Mountain Trail on a rock ledge over-looking Faith and Wall lakes. horse friendly, 10,340 ft. elevation, 2 acres, 5' deep, experimentally stocked with brook trout….afterwards winterkill suspected, stocking discontinued

p. 437

LOWER TWIN (A-33): Access is 2.25 miles north of the Crystal Lake Trailhead on the Notch Mountain Trail. Leave the trail at the point where it begins the last incline to Notch Pass and head directly west for 1/8 mile to the Twin Lakes Basin. 10,410 ft. elevation, 3 acres, 14' deep, contains Brook and Tiger trout, heavy day hike use.

UPPER TWIN (A-32): To access follow the instructions for Lower Twin Lake. 10,420 ft. elevation, 9 acres, 13' deep, access on horseback is difficult, with brook trout, heavy fishing pressure.

LOVENIA (W-23): The Notch Mountain Trail has taken us over the Pass ("The Notch"), onto the Weber River drainage, 2.75 miles from the Crystal Lake Trailhead. This is sometimes called the Notch Mountain Loop from the Crystal Lake Trailhead to the Bald Mountain Trailhead. Horse friendly. 10,300 ft. elevation, 2.5 acres, 11' deep, with brook trout under heavy fishing pressure.

The view we see from "The NOTCH" looking down the Weber River drainage over Lovenia Lake

IBANITIK (W-24): It is located 3 miles north of the Crystal Lake Trailhead on the Notch Mountain Trail. can be accessed by horses but no feed is available. 10,100 ft. elevation, 10.2 acres, 28' deep, with a selfsustaining population of brook trout, fished heavily.

MEADOW (W-27): Access is 4 miles north of the Crystal Lake Trailhead, or 4.5 miles northwest of the Bald Mountain Trailhead, on the Notch Mountain Trail Loop, to a junction with a trail leading 1/2 mile to the lake--the trail well used and clearly marked, horse accessible, but no feed, 9,820 ft. elevation, 29 acres, 46' maximum depth but fluctuates 14' as it is a reservoired lake, has a large self-sustaining population of cutthroat trout and now Grayling.

BENCH (W-37): It is an oblong lake along the Notch Mountain Trail, surrounded by dense conifers, 6 miles from the Crystal Lake Trailhead, and 2.6 miles from the Bald Mountain Trailhead, horse friendly but limited feed, 10,260 ft. elevation, 7 acres, 10' deep. In 1999 the DWR stated "does not have suitable fish habitat and is no longer managed for fishing," so recreational use is light.

NOTCH (W-36): Is a lake/reservoir at the base of Notch Mountain, 6.3 miles from the Crystal Lake Trailhead, and 2.2 miles from the Bald Mountain Trailhead and is a popular lake, 10,300 ft. elevation, 20.2 acres, 57' deep but with an annual fluctuation of up to 21 feet, has cutthroat, and predominantly brook trout, with heavy pressure.

REIDS (W-38): Access is 1/4 mile east of the Notch Mountain Trail from the vicinity of Notch Lake that is 6.3 miles from the Crystal Lake Trailhead, 2.2 miles from the Bald Mountain Trailhead with Brook trout. Managed for brook trout, stocked two out of every three years.

p. 438

DEAN (W-35): It is a natural lake surrounded by meadows and open timber at the head of the Main Fork of the Weber drainage, 2 miles southwest of the Bald Mountain Trailhead on the Notch Mountain Trail, horse friendly. 10,060 ft. elevation, 12 acres, 16' deep has brook and cutthroat trout, but subject to sporadic winterkill. Under heavy fishing pressure. Now with Arctic Grayling.

CLEGG (A-47): We have again crossed a divide and are in the Provo River drainage, 1.5 miles from the Bald Mountain Trailhead, horse friendly, 10,460 ft. elevation, 5.1 acres, 12' deep, has planted Brook and Tiger trout, under heavy use.

WE HAVE NOW ARRIVED AT THE BALD MOUNTAIN TRAILHEAD, seen below.

Sunrise from Bald Mountain with Mirror Lake at our feet.

Chapter 3: THE WESTERN UINTAS

Section 4: THE MURDOCK BASIN, FEHR LAKE TRAILHEAD to MIRROR LAKE OUR OBJECTIVE: We are dealing with the east side of the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway beginning down to the southeast from where we took the Spring Canyon Road on the other side of the highway, and will work our way up to the Murdock Basin, all part of the Duchesne River drainage. Then we'll pick up the lakes along the highway part of the Provo River drainage, then up to and past the Mirror Lake area and on to Hayden Pass, all lakes that are part of the Duchesne River drainage. HOW TO GET HERE: For the Murdock Basin Road about 22 miles from Kamas where you leave the highway and follow the paved road 1 mile northwest to the Murdock Basin Trailhead, a TOTAL of about 23 miles from Kamas, 71 from Provo, and 63 from Salt Lake.

But we'll start even further back down the Mirror Lake Highway at the Soapstone Basin road, about 14 miles from Kamas. IRON MINE (D-33): Access is 7.5 miles southeast of U-150 on the Soapstone Basin and Iron Mine Roads to the main iron Mine Fork and then 2.5 miles south 9,580 ft. elevation, 15.2 acres, 21' deep, , but perhaps not worth the drive as it "is subject to frequent winterkill ……" but recently stocked with Brook trout. Managed for brook trout, stocked on a 2 year cycle.

Further north there are a number of lakes, D-34, D-31, D-30, D-40, all listed in the pamphlet as "This [these] lake(s) does not sustain fish life." BROADHEAD (D-40): "Broadhead Lake is situated on a ledge 3/4 mile south of the Little Deer Creek Damsite. Access to the dam site is provided by the Duchesne tunnel road………there are no trails and horse access is difficult. Old timber sale roads in the vicinity have become overgrown and eroded and no longer suitable for vehicles." This perhaps needs updating at the Trailhead as the sign on the road mentions a road

to Broadhead Meadows. 9,960 ft. elevation, 8.8 acres, 16' deep, stocked with brook trout.

We now move up to the Murdock Basin Road, 22 miles from Kamas, or 4 miles from the Spring Canyon Road. It is paved……..for a while.

We'll see on the next page the Trailhead bulletin board and a map of the basin.

p. 441

Map from the Forest Service bulletin board

p. 442

Past the trailhead, or Forest Service bulletin board, the pavement ends, and soon the road divides, one going down into the Duchesne River Canyon. The other one is our road that leads to the lakes we'll detail now. My recollection is that the road gets quite rough, needing a 4-wheel drive vehicle…..but maybe things have improved over the past four years. PYRAMID (Z-14): Access is 5.25 miles northeast on the Murdock Basin Road to the Echo Lake turnoff, then continue north to the first left-hand turn and then west for 3/8 mile. It is a natural lake at 9,700 ft. elevation, 15 acres, 36' deep with a population of brook trout. With heavy fishing pressure.

ECHO (Z-16): It is a beautiful, natural lake at the base of a talus slope, as you see in the following photo I'll insert. Access is 5.25 miles northeast on the Murdock Basin Road to the Echo Lake turnoff, then north for 1/2 mile on a quite rough road. Limited horse feed. 9,740 ft. elevation, 18 acres, 44' deep, has brook and GOLDEN trout, under heavy fishing pressure. See: http://wildlife.utah.gov/blog/2014/theres-gold-in-the-uintas/

The above picture of Echo Lake was taken from the trail that leads to Joan Lake.

JOAN (Z-19): Located 1/4 mile west and above Echo Lake, the pamphlet saying horse access is difficult, but I've seen horses manage trails much worse in the Wilderness Area. 10,050 ft. elevation, 15.2 acres, 20' deep, with a good population of fat brook trout, under moderate pressure. Joan Lake below .

p. 443

BLIZZARD (D-25): Up above Joan Lake in 1999 did not have fish. Marginal habitat, no stocking. GEM (Z-18): It is about 1/4 mile northeast of Joan Lake. 10,070 ft. elevation 3.8 acres, 14' deep. has brook trout with light fishing pressure.

LAKE D-26: Is about ¼ mile north of Echo Lk., 10,060 ft. elevation, 10’ deep, 3 acres. It has Brook trout MARSHALL (Z-11): Accessed according to NG Topographical map about 4 miles north via the Murdock Basin Road, from the takeoff road to Echo Lake. Also accessed from the Fehr Lake Trailhead, near Mirror Lake, where I'll describe the details of this deep natural lake and others from the Murdock Basin.

Now we will return to the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway and continue up the highway describing the lakes accessible from the Byway. TEAPOT (A-60): Found along the highway’s north side 27 miles from Kamas, it is a reservoired lake with a dam on its eastern end., 9,950 ft. elevation, 13 acres, 46' deep maximum, receives heavy use and fishing pressure for stocked rainbow and albino rainbow trout as well as Brook and Tiger trout.

LILLY (A-58): Located 300 yards from Teapot lake along the highway, at 9,800 ft. elevation, 4.1 acres, 13' deep, with heavy fishing pressure for frequently stocked rainbow trout, a few brook and now Tiger trout. There is a full service Forest Service campground there.

LOST (A-59): It is a large reservoir across the highway from Lilly Lake, 9,400 ft. elevation, 62 acres, 22' deep when full. heavy fishing use for stocked rainbow & Tiger trout. Also with an improved campground.

MOOSEHORN (Z-11): This lake, enlarged by a dike across the outlet, sits at the eastern base of Bald Mountain, along U-150, and also has a campground, at 10,400 ft. elevation, 8 acres, 11' deep, under heavy fishing pressure for frequently stocked rainbow, albino and Tiger trout.

EMERALD (D-20): Located between the northeastern base of Bald Mountain and the highway. It has been stocked with brook trout.

MIRROR LAKE (Z-3): It is a picturesque natural lake located 32 miles from Kamas on the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway, 2 miles beyond the Bald Mt. Pass, with a full-service Forest Service Campground, and boat ramp for launching small boats--outboard motors are prohibited. At 10,200 ft. elevation, 42 acres, 37' deep, the lake receives frequent stocking of rainbow and albino trout, and yearly stockings of brook trout fingerlings. Also now has Tiger trout. Is heavily used.

As we have noted, there is a Trailhead here giving access to the Wilderness Area and to the Duchesne River Canyon. BONNIE (Z-6): Is a natural lake located 150 yards south of U-150 at a point past the Steiner Boy Scout Camp turnoff, where there is a turn-out from which a well established trail leads to the lake. It can also be accessed 1 mile on the trail from Mirror Lake to Highline Trail. At 10,100 ft. elevation, 3.6 aces, 7' deep, stocked annually with brook trout, with cutthroat present too. Heavy fishing pressure.

BUD (Z-2): Located 75 yards south of U-150 where there is a turn-out, before getting to Butterfly Lake. 3.7 acres, 13' deep, has stocked brook trout.

p. 444

NOW FOR THE FEHR LAKE TRAILHEAD, between the Bald Mountain Pass and Mirror Lake, where we will pick up also Marshall Lake from the Murdock Basin.

FEHR (Z-7): This is a natural meadow lake in thick timber at the foot of Murdock Mountain, at 10,260 ft. elevation, 5.7 acres, 27' deep, with a large population of brook trout, under heavy pressure as it is a popular lake.

SHEPARD (Z-9): It is a natural lake surrounded by confers, located 1 mile from the Fehr Lake Trailhead, at 9,980 ft. elevation, 14.2 acres, 32' deep, horse feed is restricted, it has a small population of brook, cutthroat and rainbow trout, with heavy fishing pressure.

MABA (Z-8): Located at the head of Murdock Basin, east of Shepard Lake, and 50 yard north of Hoover Lake, 75 yards west of the Murdock Basin Road, is a natural lake at 9,900 ft. elevation, 4.2 acres, 20' deep with a small population of brook trout, with heavy fishing pressure.

HOOVER (Z-10): This natural lake is surrounded by conifers with some open shoreline, 1.5 miles from the Fehr Lake Trailhead, 50 yards south of Maba Lake, 8 miles northeast of U-150 on the Murdock Basin Road to the Hoover Lake turnoff, the lake found 100 yards northwest of this point. Has brook and cutthroat trout with heavy fishing pressure.

MARSHALL (Z-11): Located about 2 miles from the Fehr Lake Trailhead, south of Shepard Lake and southwest of Hoover Lake and a couple of hundred yards west of the Murdock Basin Road. It is a natural lake surrounded by conifers at 9,980 ft. elevation, 18 acres, 36' deep, stocked with brook trout, also with Cutthroat trout, with heavy angling pressure.

PREFACE

THE DEADLY SHOOTOUT AT SCOUT LAKE Back in pioneer times in Utah there arose tales of GOLD in the Uintas–everywhere from “Montezuma’s Treasure” from the Aztecs from 1521, then from about 1540 a series of old Spanish mines, the “Gold of Carre-Shinob,” and of course to the last half of the 19th century, “The Lost Rhoades mine.” People involved in the stories are Montezuma, Hernando Cortes, Isaac Morley, Brigham Young, Ute Chief Walker, Thomas Rhoades, his son, Caleb and his partner from the 1890's, F.M.C. Hathenbruck. For decades to end the 19th century, there were rumors of Caleb making many trips with pack animals into the Uintas and returning, thereafter to show signs of riches, and finally he actually admitted much of this, even though keeping his vow to never reveal the whereabouts of the mines and sacred caves. Eventually from 1906 when Caleb died — until at least 1920 the search was much in the hands of a European immigrant, F.M.C. Hathenbruck who had married a Mormon convert. He was of royal European ancestry, but an illegitimate son who nonetheless could have become Kaiser of Germany, and at another point in his life could have become the “richest

man in the world.” He rather won degrees in Europe as a medical doctor and mineralogist who migrated to the U.S. and via working for the Army--even being the Dr. that signed General Custer's Death Certificate, then having a Medical Clinic & Assay Office in Telluride, Colorado, another in Park City, Utah, and ending up in Provo, Utah with a medical practice and a store. He was an expert in Indian cultures and became a trusted friend of the Utes who would come all the way from the Uintah Basin to be treated by him. He was always a mineral seeker, had a store in Provo–he neglected by seeking for mineral riches, and in 1920 organized a serious, last ditch effort to find the Lost Rhoades mine, but by 1928 was selling sewing machines and life insurance door to door in Provo to survive. NOTE: See pages 365-374 for a

summary of the Gold saga in Utah. Backing up a bit, in about 1894 he became involved with Caleb Rhoades who needed someone the Indians trusted to gain access to Indian Reservation lands in search of the mines mentioned. In those adventures they often needed the protection of “gunfighters,” beginning friendships with Butch Cassidy and his Wild Bunch--that continued with some of the gang up to 1920 when this story I'm telling here took place at Scout Lake up the trail from the Pass Lake Trailhead.

p. 448

In 1920 Hathenbruck organized a team to come into the Uintas from Wyoming to avoid detection. His group of 13, included 11 who were the best gunmen available–at least five of them connected to Butch’s Wild Bunch, plus a cook and an assayer. The leader, Caleb Landreth, was also a self-proclaimed prophet who claimed divine guidance from a deceased Indian Princess. On horseback they followed the Bear River south, and then up Hayden Fork and over the pass arriving at their destination, SCOUT LAKE, and an old cabin from which a well defined trail led up the mountain. NOTE: The Cabin was years later burned down by

the Forest Service

Here I am heading for Scout Lake & the treasure in 2018--well armed to imagine “The Shootout” with a Glock 43 loaded with deadly +P Grizzly bullets!

Now, back to our story: There, Landreth announced a vision revealing that half of what they found would be used to organize a new church--of course with him as prophet. That created murmuring and protests in the group–who were anything but the religious type. Rock M. Pope, from Vernal began plotting to kill some of the group as soon as they found the mine. Matt Warner, who rode with the Wild Bunch, heard about it and made a plan to save them. As they returned to camp after the first day’s search, one apparently having found rich ore, but when asked where, he defiantly told Pope to, “Go to hell!” He was promptly shot by Pope in the head killing him instantly, which began a shootout, Warner shooting Pope, and by the end five of them were dead, and others wounded some never to be seen again. Several efforts were made by survivors to return to the area and find the mine, but with no success. Matt Warner, was later elected Justice of the Peace, town marshal and deputy sheriff at Price. He returned several times to the Scout Lake area prior to his death in 1938, but failed to find the mine. (Information above summarized from the book, THE UTAH GOLD RUSH: The Lost Rhoades Mine and the Hathenbruck Legacy, by Kerry Rose Boren & Lisa Lee Boren). THE “TREASURE” TODAY STRETCHES EAST FROM THE SHORE OF THE LAKE, BEING…….

………..A “SUMMER CAMP FOR THE BOY SCOUTS OF AMERICA”

HOW TO GET HERE: From Kamas, Utah follow the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway over Bald Mountain Pass, and down past Mirror Lake, continuing 1/2 mile down to a big turn as the highway goes up east past the Lake, a total of 32.4 miles from Kamas.

PASS LAKE (Z-5): A popular lake for day fishermen with no campground, but areas are available for what the DWR calls "primitive camping and off-road parking," at 9,940 ft. elevation, 4.5 acres, 10' deep with stocked rainbow, albino, brook and Tiger trout, as well as Grayling.

Now the TRAILHEAD

Below are the trail signs at the trailhead. We will now examine the details for all the lakes that can be accessed from this trailhead beginning with the LOFTY LAKE LOOP, that includes three lakes: SCOUT, LOFTY and KAMAS LAKES, plus one mentioned on the topographical map, but not in the DWR pamphlet, Picturesque Lake.

PICTURESQUE LAKE ….no details in the DWR pamphlet. The topographical map has it just east of the trail as you climb up to Scout Lake. The DWR can find no records of this lake.

p. 450

CASTLE (D-14): Is a small natural lake—1 acre in size, at 10,300 ft. elevation, 3/8 mile west of Butterfly Lake with Cutthroat and now with Tiger trout.

SCOUT (Z-12): It is a natural glacial lake in rocky, timbered terrain northwest of the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway, on the western edge of the BOY SCOUT CAMP STEINER--closed to the public, but the lake can be accessed from the Pass Lake Trailhead just north of Pass Lake on the west side of the highway. The first trail at the trailhead is the beginning of the Lofty Lake Loop, with Scout Lake 1/2 mile up the steep trail. It is part of the Duchesne River drainage, 10,300 ft. elevation, 30 acres, 17' deep, and stocked with rainbow and Tiger trout, under heavy fishing pressure. See a picture of it in the Preface to this section. LOFTY (W-41): It is a beautiful alpine lake near timberline about 1 mile above Scout Lake, horse friendly, at 10,820 ft. elevation, 4 acres, 20' deep, stocked with Cutthroat & Tiger trout, with moderate fishing pressure. KAMAS (W-40): Accessed via the Lofty Lake Loop, 2 miles from the trailhead in steep and rocky terrain with precipitous cliffs and talus slopes, and is a scenic natural lake but with a small dam to increase its capacity, found at 10,500 ft. elevation, 12.1 acres, 42' deep but fluctuates 3'. Has a good population of cutthroat trout with moderate fishing pressure. Now also with Tiger trout. Horse feed not available.

The Lofty Lake Loop from Kamas Lake returns 2 miles to the Trailhead. From the same trailhead we now head for the CUBERANT BASIN, and I'll take you on a swing of all the lakes in that basin. CUBERANT #1 (W-42): The Cuberant Basin is accessed from the Pass Lake Trailhead, the trailhead sign indicating the distance at 3 miles, the DWR pamphlet at 2.5 miles, and my topo measurement at 2.2 to Lake #1. The access trail is in places steep and rocky, so it might feel like the "3 miles," but can be accessed on horseback, but feed scarce. At 10,360 ft. elevation, 3.5 acres, 18' deep, with brook and cutthroat trout with fast fishing under moderate pressure. CUBERANT #4 (W-45): Located at the head of the basin and the largest of the lakes, at 10,420 ft. elevation, 22 acres, 25' deep, and is 1/8th of a mile from Lake #1, distance from the trailhead is 2.5 miles, horse friendly, with aerial stocked Cutthroat and Tiger trout under moderate pressure. CUBERANT #5 (W-46): Accessed in a loop around the basin from #4 by bushwhacking west 0.9 mile, for a total from the trailhead of 3.4 miles, horse access is difficult, no trails. 10,060 ft. elevation, 5 acres, 15' deep, subject to winterkill and in 1999-2018 not managed as a fishery. CUBERANT #3 (W-44): Accessed by going east from #5 over a saddle 0.4 mile, or 150 yards northwest of Cuberant #2 along the connecting stream, at 10,180 ft. elevation, 3.5 acres, 24' deep, has a good population of pan-sized brook trout under moderate pressure. CUBERANT #2 (W-43): Located 150 yards southeast of Lake #3 along the connecting stream, or from the entrance to the basin, 2 miles from the trailhead to the first meadow and 1/4 mile west on an indistinct trail, horse friendly, 10,220 ft. elevation, 3.2 acres, 6' deep, with brook and cutthroat trout under moderate pressure.

The signs at the trailhead indicate distance to two more locations. MEADOW (W-27): It's a 4 mile hike from the Pass Lake Trailhead. I also gave indications about it from the Crystal Lake and Bald Mt. Trailheads--both about 4 miles, but I'll repeat here: It is a reservoired lake at 9,820 ft. elevation, 29 acres, 46' maximum depth fluctuating 14' with a trail well marked and used. It has a large population of self-sustaining cutthroat trout. Cutthroat natural reproduction observed in 1981 survey; stocked experimentally with tiger trout in 2014 and 2018, no follow up yet.

The other trail marker is 7 miles to HOLIDAY PARK, one of the Weber River Trailheads. The topographical mileage is 6.6 miles.

PREFACE THE MILL CREEK GHOST TOWN AT GOLD HILL and THE HILLIARD FLUME In the INTRODUCTION we began learning about the tie hackers I call "the unsung heroes without whom the West might not have been won," and their work 12 months a year making with their broadaxes millions of railroad ties for the Transcontinental Railroad. I showed you pictures of their splash dams behind which they would accumulate the ties during the winter, and with the run-off blow the dam with dynamite, creating a SPLASH that would wash them down into Wyoming to be picked up by the railroad. I went on to tell you about the Hilliard Flume and inserted a picture of the Forest Service display--back when it was still legible, showing the V-shaped flume they used to carry the lumber products from Gold Hill down to Hilliard, Wyoming, and I inserted a map of my discoveries of the remnants of the flume that, as far as I know, is the first time such was documented and published. All of that and much more, like their ghost town described as "the liveliest if not the most wicked town in America," and much more on pages 19-23, 4849, 58-59, 73, 232-233, etc. In our GUIDE CHAPTERS, we are now in the Northwest section where we find GOLD HILL, prominent in the history of the Hilliard Flume and the tie hacks, and I thought it might be interesting for you to see a picture of Gold Hill, where all of that started at what is called the MILL CITY GHOST TOWN. So below you see Gold Hill.

We are looking south, having come up the Whitney Road, then turn south towards Gold Hill, where there was a town with about 500 people, that was on the left, or eastern flank of the Hill. On that eastern side I first noticed way across the creek in the shade of the trees some

p. 453

log ruins, and discovered the first loading platform, and the pathway of the flume you can see below.

I examined and photographed the first loading platform, and the pathway of the flume, and then followed the pathway down and soon discovered a breeched diversion dam, and on one side of the dam the pathway of the flume following a wide v-shaped trench cutting through the hill as the flume had to be maintained with a 15% down incline--so at times they had to cut through areas, but usually had the flume up off the ground on what we could call a scaffold to maintain that constant angle--in some places the flume was as high as 16 feet off the ground. Below is one of several diversion dams, and on the right the pathway going through a trench.

Eventually I returned to the loading platform and followed the pathway up along the creek, discovering several more loading platforms, and then came to a narrowing of the canyon and got back to the road, which in boggy places was a corduroy road to keep their wagons from getting stuck, but then as I got up the canyon the road became the worst road of my earthly experience, and I had to park my car and hoof it.

What I was searching for was the Mill City Ghost town, mentioned in the book I'll insert a picture of below, followed by the only printed description I have been able to find describing

p. 454

the ghost town. It was there where the flume started, and the tie hacks lived, while they logged the area and got their products going down the flume 30 miles to Hilliard, Wyoming.

As I worked my way up the rocky road, I found many rotted stumps from the tie hacker early period--1867-1880, and found some that weren't rotted that had to be from the 1912 to 1936 period. Eventually I came to a large area of two kinds of ruins and artifacts: Some, mostly rotted away from the early period, and then others mixed in with all kinds of artifacts from the 20th century. I didn't find any cabins or buildings that were still intact…..the same also for the flume all the way to Hilliard, Wyoming, as everything was cannibalized, the logs and planks used by ranchers and others for their farm structures. Historical accounts say no remnants of the flume remain, but I have found support structures on one private property further north and reported on them with photos in one of my YouTube videos.

p. 455

Above we see mostly rotted away ruins of cabins, and stumps from the 1867-1880 period

I guess I should also insert a few pictures below of some of the 20th century artifacts, so you can compare with the rotting wood from 1867-80.

There were square nails like the ones on the right, 80 tons of them used to build the Hilliard Flume--they are from the 1867-1880 period. Then I found round galvanized ones like on the left above, from the 1912-1936 period since round nails weren't invented until 1910.

Then there were lots of items like you see above from the 1912-1936 period. It was very much like the Ghost book paragraphs explained-- the original site from the early period with most of it rotted away, then there were items from the modern period too. If you're interested in learning more, below are two sources that helped me a lot, even though mostly dealing with tie hackers from Wyoming: The 1st a DVD, then a book.

JEWELL (BR-38): It is a glacial lake at the foot of a talus rockslide in partially timbered country, located 1/2 mile northwest of Ruth Lake, 10,300 ft. elevation, 2.4 acres, 13' deep, stocked with cutthroat trout with moderate fishing pressure.

Section 7

"THE WEBER?" In 1822 the first expedition to the West by the Rocky Mountain Fur Co., owned by William Ashley and Andrew Henry, had a group who would become famous in the conquering of the West, like Jim Bridger, Jedediah Smith, Thomas Fitzpatrick, Hugh Glass, Daniel T. Potts, Milton Sublette, and an older mountain man and explorer at 43, John Henry Weber. At the mouth of the Yellowstone River, they were divided into two brigades, John Weber in the leadership of one of them. By the summer of 1824 Weber's brigade crossed South Pass and descended the Bear River and on to Bear Lake, then for the winter down to Cache Valley. He and his brigade explored and trapped in southeastern Idaho, and by the summer of 1825 were at the First Rocky Mountain Rendezvous on the Uinta's Henry Fork River. He and his men spent the winter of 1825-26 in the area of the Great Salt Lake Valley, and it was during this period that the northwestern river coming out of the Uintas that flowed into the Great Salt Lake was given his name. Weber participated in the 2nd Rendezvous held in Cache Valley, and thereafter left the fur trade and the west, and eventually lived in Iowa where he died in 1859 when 80 years old. Some historical accounts confuse John Henry Weber with a trapper, John Weber, killed by Indians in the winter of 1828-29.174

THE LOWER SOUTHWESTERN WEBER RIVER DRAINAGE LEDGEFORK TRAILHEAD The DWR pamphlet calls it:

PREFACE

THE WEBER RIVER DRAINAGE LEGENDS OF GOLD "The old Spanish Mine--The Lost Josephine Mine" on Hoyt Peak In the INTRODUCTION, on pages 24, and 25, I introduced the subject of riches in the Uinta Mountains, mentioning "Montezuma's Treasure," hidden there to keep them out of the hands of the Spaniards, and leaving the Utes as "guardians." Then related the stories of Spaniards coming north looking for the treasures, and beginning the legends of Spanish mines on the Uinta's South Slope. In the Preface to Chapter 2, Section 21, I expanded the legends to include "The Lost Rhoades Mine," and 7 Spanish mines, with locations pointing to Rock Creek, the Grandaddies, and up to Scout Lake near the present Boy Scout Steiner Camp near Hayden Pass on the Mirror Lake Scenic Byway, even including participation by some of Butch Cassidy's Wilde Bunch, in a bloody shootout. But, there are more similar legends all around Utah, one of an incredibly rich mine called THE LOST JOSEPHINE MINE, reputedly in the Henry Mountains, or the La Sal Mountains, in southern Utah. However, there's a long history that rather connects it to the Uinta Mountains. Specifically to the slopes of 10,228 ft. high Hoyt Peak175 on the South Fork of the Weber River. The Hoyt Peak claimant seems to have its beginning as a mine worked by Spaniards using slave labor from the mid-eighteenth century to about 1814 when they were attacked by Indians and forced to abandon the mine, but leaving incredible riches deep in the ground.

NOTE: There's a contradiction between the chronology mentioned above and another recounting of seemingly the same event at a later period, by a 103 year old Indian, mentioned further along. I won't swear to the truth of the history I'm recounting, but rather calling them interesting and fascinating "legends." NOW JUMP FORWARD TO 1939

175

https://www.summitpost.org/hoyt-peak/376121

p. 469

Late in the season of that year John Wesley Young was herding cattle with his son, Keith, on Hoyt Peak. A sudden rainstorm forced them to take shelter under a bushy tree at the edge of a limestone ledge. There they found a hole and Keith crawled in finding a large room 2540 feet in diameter with a 10 foot high ceiling. They returned to camp and got a good light and returned, finding a variety of old tools, very old horse manure, and noticed the ceiling covered with soot. From one corner they found a shaft angling down to another level and a tunnel that eventually they found blocked by a large wood door, but were afraid to try and open it as resting on the top was a large slab of rock and feared causing a cave-in. Their first thought was that they had found the Lost Rhoades Mine. Wes later returned with his 17 year old son, Marion. Once again they were afraid of a cave-in, but concluded that first they should remove rubble at the cave's entrance, but winter stopped them from doing so. Other family responsibilities kept them from doing more, then World War II interrupted their lives, the boys joining the military and going off to war.176 Wes visited the area several more times exploring the area hoping to make other finds, and eventually in 1943 he filed a claim on the southeast slope of Hoyt Peak. Fearing interference by unscrupulous giants he was vague in registering the claim, saying

"Near Polsin Basin in Summit County." 177 In 1946, upon Marion's return from the war, he went with his father to check out the mine but determined excavation would be too dangerous, and would require a lot of money they didn't have, and so the claim was abandoned. Thirteen years later Wes renewed the claim. Later he made another trip with Marion, and his 4 boys, and in hiking around the area he showed them where he had found some Indian graves and some spear heads. Later that year, 1959, Wes cultivated a friendship with a John W. McBee who was searching for "an old Spanish mine" on Hoyt Peak, to the west of Wes' claims and eventually learned from McBee that he was aware that Indians knew of an old Spanish mine on Hoyt Peak, and Wes revealed to him what they had found in 1939. That led to McBee bringing an old Indian, Tommy Jewel, from the Uintah Basin reservation, reputed to be 103 years old. Tommy Jewel told them that in about 1870 he was "brought to Hoyt Peak by my father along

with a band of warriors who were sent to kill a small group of Spaniards who were working an old gold mine. The leader known as 'Black Whiskers'…….who had come from California with a group of Mexicans…….working them in this mine [as] slave labor…….and store up a 176

THE UTAH GOLD RUSH by Kerry Ross Boren and Lisa Lee Boren, pages 79-94

177

LA MINA del YUTAS by Stephan Shaffer, page 26

p. 470

large cache of gold and silver bars which they stockpiled behind an old wooden door deep inside the mine." Tommy went on to explain that they killed the Spaniards, and turned the Mexicans loose, but the Mexicans later returned to load as much gold as they could on their animals, but a short distance from the mine, the Indians ambushed them, forcing them to bury the gold, and told them to never return--which they didn't, according to Tommy. Wes later found a wooden cross where the Spaniards were buried but didn't want to desecrate the graves. He and McBee filed claims on that area hoping to find the buried gold, but never did.178 Later Wes met some geology students from the University of Utah and in the conversation they told him they were looking for an old lost mine. Wes asked, "What mine?" They replied "The Lost Josephine Mine." They claimed to have a copy of a journal they had found in archives in Spain, from "the only survivor…..of men who came out here from Spain to

work the mine…..using Indians as slaves…..but Indians massacred them…..and he told of a sixmillion-dollar cache of gold and silver which was hidden in the old mine behind a large wooden door." Wes asked why they thought it might be in the Hoyt Peak area? They replied, "We have the Spaniards story and the maps……We've followed the trail…..and the map led us to Hoyt Peak." Eventually Wes formed partnerships with others and with a D-6 Caterpillar bulldozer built a road to the area and they hired an old miner who lived in Gold Hill (a ghost town at the north end o the Deep Creek Mountains along the Nevada border) to help them. But along the way one of the partners got impatient and attempted to get quickly to the riches with dynamite, but rather collapsed the tunnels making getting to the gold next to impossible. But they persisted with other efforts year in and year out, but then one partner became a cripple in a fall, and then:

"John Wesley Young died on 8 Jane 1981 at the age of 93, none the richer for finding perhaps the richest mine in Utah history, known as the Lost Josephine. He had worked as a rancher all over the West, helped to build Geneva Steel, operated his own candy store, and was an employee of two railroads. The only time he had been confined to the hospital was the last week of his life. The day before he died, he asked the young nurse to marry him, saying, 'I'm just about getting to and I can't do anything anymore, and I need someone to take care of me.' In his final moments he asked to see his sons to 'tell them something important about the mine on Hoyt Peak.' He was buried in the Sterling, Utah, Cemetery next to his wife Irene."179 178

CHAPTER 4: THE EASTERN UINTAS Section 1: THE NORTH SLOPE-- THE SHEEP/CARTER CREEK DRAINAGE ************************

PREFACE The HISTORY OF THE OLD CARTER MILITARY ROAD180 In 1981, the Utah territory still had only a small population, mostly scattered along the Wasatch Front in towns of orderly Mormon design. Heber City was the eastern edge of civilized territorial settlement, and it was a good two-day ride from the Wasatch Front. Almost no whites lived east of Heber City except a few sheepherders and cattlemen who trespassed on the large Ute reservation set aside by President Lincoln and Congress in the early 1860s. Most of the Uinta Basin, Colorado Plateau, and the western half of Colorado were virtually unsettled by whites. This area of rich natural resources adequately supported several bands of Ute Indians. The whites, coveting these resources, began to encroach on the Utes' large range, leading to confrontations that became increasingly hostile. At the White River Agency (now Meeker, Colorado), Ute bands became resentful of Indian Agent Nathan Meeker's attempts to reform them into an agriculturally-based society. Fearing for his life, Meeker sought assistance from the Military in September of 1879. Major Thomas T. Thornburgh and a column of four companies were sent from Ft. Steele, Wyoming, to assist Meeker. Upon entering the reservation the column was attacked by over seven hundred mounted Utes. Sixteen soldiers died, including Thornburgh, and forty-three were wounded. At the same time Meeker and ten other employees were killed at the agency. As a result of these skirmishes, the Ute bands involved and other bands--including Chief Ouray's Uncompaghres from western Colorado--were coerced onto the Utah reservation, joining Chief Tabiona's band from the Uinta Basin. Ashley Valley residents were concerned about their safety after Custer's defeat in 1876, and the recent fighting in western Colorado. In 1881, Fort Thornburgh was established at the mouth of Ashley Canyon, just northwest of Vernal. The army's mission was to keep the Utes on the reservation. The fort's location was uncomfortably remote, given the recent bloodshed. It was several days march from Fort Douglas in Salt Lake City, and more from Denver or other help in Colorado. Only about one hundred white settlers lived in the Ashley Valley, mostly cattlemen attracted to the area by lush grazing lands on the flanks of the Uinta Mountains. JUDGE CARTER'S ROAD At Fort Bridger in southwest Wyoming, the entrepreneurial Judge William A. Carter had made a profitable career out of provisioning the army. Described by former Uintah County Historian Mike Brown as "the very image of the Southern gentleman," Carter had been raised in Virginia and fought Florida Indians in the Seminole War. When he did not receive a commission in the army he resigned and became post trader at Fort Lauderdale. In 1858, when Johnston's army was sent west to quell the "Mormon Rebellion," Carter accompanied the expedition as the civilian supplier. Carter settled at Fort Bridger and quickly amassed a fortune trading with soldiers. emigrants, railroad builders, cattlemen, and Indians. In 1858, he was appointed post trader, post master, and probate judge. He also participated in mining, lumber, and cattle ventures. Carter's business suffered after troops were removed from Fort Bridger in 1878. He used the growing fears of the local white population to lobby in Washington for a return of troops. Carter also hoped to continue and enhance his

180

https://www.fs.usda.gov/detail/ashley/learning/history-culture/?cid=fsm9_002401 ; Jeffrey A. Rust, 435-781-

5156 jarust@fs.fed.us

p. 475

relationship with the army by supplying Fort Thornburgh. Carter was successful in his efforts. Troops returned to Fort Bridger and he was awarded a contract to supply Fort Thornburgh. CONSTRUCTION BEGINS During the summer of 1881, General George Crook inspected the old Lodgepole Trail across the Uinta Mountains that had been used by the Uinta Utes. Crook approved this route over an alternate trail as the supply route to the garrison at Fort Thornburgh. Note: The other route used by the Indians was up Henry's Fork, over Gunsight Pass, and down the Uinta River, which route was never considered as there was no way it could be navigated by wagons (CA). Routes from Park city and Heber City had been considered, but the route across the Uintas was chosen to accommodate Carter, and because it was the shortest, if not the easiest. Minor work on the trail commenced immediately under Carter's direction. Judge Carter died of pneumonia in November, contracted from working on the road in harsh weather. His son, William Jr. (Willie), returned from Cornell University to continue his father's work. In May of 1882, Willie Carter attempted the first freighting across the trail with 11 six-mule teams and wagons. This is one of the markers along the pathway of the trail, with the plaque en-larged to the right. This is at the Beaver Creek Trail-head, on the road down to Browne Lake where we will see a display on the Carter Road--Trail. "It soon became evident that from the character of the past winter at Fort Bridger, we had very erroneous conceptions of what we would encounter in attempting to freight through the mountains so early in the spring. The Dugway between Sand Canyon and Lodgepole was blocked with snow and ice, which had to be removed before we could get our outfit up the mountains. At the head of the dugway the road was almost impassable. Ravines filled with melting snow and water nearly up to the wagon beds; bogs in which both teams and wagons were often mired down at the same time; hills so soft that all the teams we could hook on were required to pull a single wagon to the top; the slopes so sidling that the whole crew, with ropes, were needed to keep a loaded wagon from upsetting; were everyday experiences." "….In one locality, a separate road had to be cut through the timber for each wagon. The ground at this place appeared dry and firm, but each wagon broke through a thin crust into quicksand beneath, making the road impossible for the next team." In the summer of 1882, the army sent up work parties, but the primary commitment of the military to road building came in the summer of 1883. Four companies of troops were sent to develop the road under Major L. De Russey. The Major's detachment worked out of a field camp at Burnt Cabins, and it was this force that did most of the work we can now see. Their work consisted largely of corduroying (laying lodgepole logs across marshy sections), clearing large boulders and constructing dugways (road cuts and fills). The troops also set up a sawmill in Summit Park to supply Fort Thornburgh, and a military telegraph line was strung along the route. De Russey's force worked hard during the summer, and a review of the military records from the National Archive reveals that court martials were carried out almost weekly. Troops were fined several weeks pay for disorderly conduct, drunkenness, desertion and other offenses that indicate the difficulty of the work and lonely social conditions in this remote wilderness. By 1883, it became clear that the route was a poor choice because of the high terrain and short season of travel. In addition, a Denver and Rio Grande Railroad route was completed, linking Salt Lake City and Denver through Price, Utah. Supplies could easily be wagon-freighted to the Ashley Valley from Price. Fort Thornburgh was abandoned in 1884, and most of the durable items were hauled back to Fort Bridger. When Fort Duchesne was established in the summer of 1886, some materials were hauled back over the Carter Road, but most came from the new rail depot at Price. Although, the military utility of the Carter Road ceased, it continued to be important to local inhabitants. The road was used to haul copper, gold, and silver ore from the Dyer Mine area during the last decade of the 1800's. It was the

p. 476

primary north-south wagon route from Daggett County to the Vernal area until the early 1920's, when a passenger car road was constructed along the route of Utah Highway 44. Daggett County historians Dick and Vivian Dunham state that:

"While it [the Carter Road] was treacherous for heavy loads, hardy souls could at least get over to Ashley Valley in a buckboard to pick up honey and apples, then as now that district's specialties, or maybe take a sack or so of grain over to the grist mill to be ground into flour." In 1880, Ashley, (or Vernal, as it was called after 1850 became the main government seat). "So to Ashley or Vernal everybody had to go to file on land, pay taxes, get married, serve or answer a writ, or any other official business. For these trips the old road came in mighty handy. It was used right up until 1924. Some adventurous souls even managed to get their Model T's part way over it."

p. 477

In 1936, Willie Carter commented, "To the traveler who comes upon this road at any part of its course through the Uinta Range, it seems to present an unusual example of wasted effort and money, but like many other of the works of man, it served its purpose, and gave way to changes in the development of the country."

Chapter 4: THE EASTERN UINTAS--North Slope INTRODUCTION: Let's begin orienting ourselves, with the map we used in Chapter 3, to familiarize ourselves now with the Eastern High Uintas--that is basically from the Wilderness Area east to U.S. Highway 191 that begins in Vernal, Utah and takes us north towards Flaming Gorge, then where it turns east, we continue north on U-44 to the Geologic Backway and from there our area continues west encompassing Forest Service lands to the Sheep Creek Drainage.

You'll notice that on our Loop Auto Tour of the Uinta Mountains we traveled the eastern end of the NORTH SLOPE SCENIC BACKWAY, including the Spirit Lake Scenic Backway, ending with the Sheep Creek Geologic marvel. From there we drove south on U-44 and then on US-191 seeing the eastern Trailhead of the Highline Trail, then on to the SOUTH SLOPE SCENIC BACKWAY, the first leg of which was the Red Cloud Scenic Backway. That took us into the heart of the Eastern Uintas at the Leidy Peak Trailhead of the Highline Trail, then down Dry Canyon to Vernal, Utah. We finished seeing the Eastern Uintas exploring the Whiterocks River Drainage, driving up the Elkhorn Loop road and to Chepeta Lake, and then over and down into the Uinta River Canyon where the Wilderness Area begins. One area we didn't include in the Loop Tour was the Dry Fork Drainage, accessed by the Paradise Park Road to Paradise Park Reservoir, and a bit beyond with a large basin between the Red Cloud Loop Backway, and the Whiterocks River Drainage. It has areas like: Johnson Park, Blanchard Park, Lonesome Park, Hell's Kitchen Park , and others with access by several primary trails, like: Deadman's Lake Trail, and others that lead up to the spine of the Uintas and the Highline Trail with many alpine lakes along the way. This area will be explored with details of the many lakes that are part of the Ashley Creek Drainage. You'll notice that the EASTERN UINTAS is an area much larger than the WESTERN UINTAS, but with many roads which likely is the reason why the Wilderness Area wasn't extended further east.
