Section 1:

The North Slope--THE SHEEP/CARTER CREEK DRAINAGE This drainage is the first with alpine lakes west of Flaming Gorge, with peaks over 12,000 feet in elevation. The highest is a no-name peak 12,276 feet high at the head of the glacial basin where Dagget Lake is found, with other prominent peaks like: Mt. Untermann (12.074 ft.), Leidy Peak (12,028 ft.), Marsh Peak (12,240 ft.), plus another couple of no-name 12,000+ peaks, and more than a half dozen at 11,000+. Trails from the North Slope that cross the spine of the Uintas to connect with the Highline Trail on the South Slope, could be called "PASSES" considered among the highest in the Uintas: From the Weyland Lakes Basin, 11,776 feet—let’s name it WEYLAND PASS; from the Lamb Lakes Basin, 11,865 feet LAMB PASS; and the trail from the Browne Lake Trailhead to the Teepee Lakes continues up the ridge to cross the spine at 11,578 feet TEEPEE PASS, west of Leidy Peak. Four lakes in the area are reachable by car, shown in Chapter 1 and the Auto Loop Tour, which are reservoired lakes not described in the DWR pamphlet. They are: Spirit Lake, Sheep Creek Lake, Long Park Reservoir, and Browne Lake. Nice Forest Service campgrounds are found at each. There are 58 other lakes in the Drainage with at least 34 that have game fish, some under experimental management. Additionally there are hundreds of ponds, many of them beaver ponds, and those that are on streams have populations of trout. As I have shown in the Auto Loop Tour in chapter 1, access is mainly from WY-414 at Nila's Store near McKinnon, generally known as the Spirit Lake Scenic Backway that becomes Forest Service Rd. 221, then intersected 8 miles from WY-414 by what I call in this book the North Slope Scenic Backway coming from the west. FR-221 continues on to the east where it intersects with U-44 north of Manila, Utah, and to the south intersects with US-191 that originates in Vernal, Utah. From FR-221, our first access to the Sheep/Carter Drainage is the Spirit Lake Rd. (FR-01) that takes you south 9 miles to SPIRIT LAKE--the most remote resort and trailhead in the Uintas. From there two trailheads give access to the 10 lakes in the Jessen/Tamarack lakes area, and Daggett Lake--which areas receive the heaviest fishing use. Accessed also from Spirit Lake are the 8 lakes in the Weyman Lakes Basin, which receive moderate pressure. The other trail access is at the Beaver Creek Trailhead on the road down to BROWNE LAKE where there are two trailheads that give access to the 5 lakes in the Teepee Lakes area--that also receives fairly heavy pressure, to the 3 lakes in the Potter Lakes area, and to 6 lakes in the Lamb Lakes Basin--which areas receive the least pressure because of greater distances, lack of maintained trails and rough, rocky terrain. Brook trout is the most common trout, along with cutthroat, and rainbow trout is exclusive to Daggett Lake. Tiger trout are being stocked in more and more lakes. Golden trout now stocked in Marsh Lake GR-39.

p. 481

NOW TO THE DETAILS A mile or so after leaving FR-221, you come to the first two trail signs, seen below:

The sign on the left leads to areas in the Wilderness Area. The one on the right is in the Sheep/Carter Creeks area. As you will notice, access to the areas of our interest, are best from the Spirit Lake area. But to give you a complete picture, I'm showing the signs as we come to them, another of which is found 2 miles further along, seen below, that has us in the zone.

About 4 miles further we come to Spirit Lake and as we drive a mile around the eastern side, we come to another trail sign seen below.

Then, after passing the full-service Forest Service campground, we come to the main Trailhead, seeing just a little further along the gate of the Resort--with lodge, restaurant, cabins and boats for rent, but closed with the FOR SALE sign I showed in Chapter 1.

p. 482

Fish Lake, 5 miles distant, is in the Wilderness Area, which we have dealt with already. We'll now go into the details of the lakes accessed from these two trailheads. Quotes & info. as throughout the book, are from the DWR pamphlets, this one: LAKES OF THE HIGH

UINTAS: Sheep Creek, Carter Creek, & Burnt Fork Drainages, Publication No. 96-17 / First printing 1986, Revised Edition, 1996.

FIRST THE JESSEN/TAMARACK LAKES AREA NEAR SPIRIT LAKE: LILY PAD (GR-11): It is the first we come to after leaving the trailhead, about 1/2 mile on the right, but the 1996 DWR pamphlet says "does not support fish life." Too bad to start with a dud…..sorry.

JESSEN (GR-1): The DWR pamphlet spells it as "Jesson," but the topo map and signs do it as listed. It is found 1 mile from the trailhead. It is a natural lake, horse friendly, but sparse feed, located at 10,392 ft. elevation, 25.5 acres, 56' deep, with stocked brook, cutthroats, and Tiger trout, with heavy fishing pressure.

TAMARACK (GR-2): It is the largest lake in the drainage at 79.1 acres, 90' deep, at 10,429 ft. elevation, with best camping sites on the eastern side, horse friendly, with self-sustaining cutthroats, and now with Tiger trout under heavy pressure.

brook trout, some

LOST (GR-4): Accessed 0.3 miles past Lily Pad, turn north off the trail, and go 0.1 miles down the slope, total distance from the TH is 1.1 miles. Also accessed by following the outlet of Tamarack Lake. It is found at 10,300 ft. elevation, 3.2 acres, 7' deep, semi-horse friendly, has a natural population of cutthroat trout, as well as now with Tiger trout, under light pressure.

HIDDEN LAKE (GR-112): It is a natural lake surrounded by heavy timber, accessed from Lost Lake and then north cross-country 0.2 miles, total distance from TH is 1.3 miles. At 10,270 ft. elevation, 4.3 acres, 8' deep, stocked with Brook & Tiger trout, but also has cutthroat trout, with light pressure.

SUMMIT (GR-5): It is a pretty lake at the bottom of a talus slope a mile south of Spirit Lake. Accessed is hiking "due south of Spirit Lake until you hit a line of steep cliffs. Follow the base of the slope to Summit." At 10,460 ft. elevation, 9.9 cares, 7' deep, experiences at times winterkill, so in 1996 stocking was suspended, but Grayling stocked in 2014 and 2017. The DWR pamphlet says: "Even without a fishery, the lake is worth a visit." Hope to get an updating soon.

COLUMBINE (GR-116): Found "on a rocky bench at the base of a talus slope 1.3 miles southwest of Spirit Lake." Accessed by "following the Middle Fork of Sheep Creek upstream from Spirit Lake until the stream goes underground. The lake lies across the boulder fields to the south. Horse access is impossible." At 10,550 ft. elevation, 5.7 acres, 5' deep, but the lake manages to support a population of Brook & Tiger trout with periodic stocking. Light fishing pressure.

GAIL (GR-115): Located at the bottom of a rock slide 1.1 miles southwest of Spirit Lake, by following the Jessen Lake trail, then 0.2 miles south across downed timber and rocky terrain, not horse friendly. At 10,420 ft. elevation, 4.5 acres, 25' deep, with Cutthroat, an occasional Brook & Tiger trout, with very light pressure.

JUDY (GR-25): A rarely visited picturesque pond high on a bench 0.4 miles from the south shore of Tamarack Lake, by scrambling up 400 vertical feet to the top of the bench, then a short distance south at the base of the boulder fields. Not horse friendly. Distance from Spirit Lake is 1.8 miles, at 10,830 ft. elevation, 4.7 acres, 24' deep, with stocked brook and Tiger trout, under light fishing pressure.

p. 483

TOPOGRAPHICAL MAP FOR JESSEN/TAMARACK AREA LAKES

LAKES ACCESSED FROM THE FIRST TRAILHEAD AT SPIRIT LAKE DAGGET (GR-5): It is a very large and popular lake in the Sheep/Carter Creeks area located on a good trail. The sign says 4 miles, the DWR pamphlet says 2.6 miles. Located at 10,462 ft. elevation, 42.6 acres, 29' deep, horse friendly, famous for abundant mosquitoes. Has stocked rainbow trout, and some cutthroat trout, and now Grayling, under heavy pressure.

THE WEYMAN LAKES BASIN: The sign at Spirit Lake says it is 6 miles to the first lake-Lower Anson. It is 6.2 miles from the Beaver Creek Trailhead located where the road goes down to Browne Lake. From its trailhead it is 8.1 miles to Lower Anson. LOWER ANSON (GR-9): The lake is located at 10,575 ft. elevation, 14.5 acres, 20' deep, horse friendly, has brook trout that naturally reproduce. Pressure moderate to heavy. UPPER ANSON (GR-10): It is a natural lake 0.2 miles above Lower Anson, with a faint trail south along the east side of the connecting creek, horse friendly to within 100 yards of the lake, located at 10,660 ft. elevation, 7.7 acres, 58' deep, has a natural population of brook trout, with moderate fishing pressure. PENGUIN (GR-16): It is a small pond located just a few yards west of Upper Anson Lake. total distance from the Spirit Lake TH is 7.1 miles, located at 10,665 ft. elevation, 2.1 acres, 20' deep, has a natural population of brook trout, with light to moderate fishing pressure.

SESAME (GR-15): "Surrounded by boulder fields and talus slopes….0.4 miles west of Upper Anson and Penguin Lakes…..up the rock slide and across some of the roughest boulder fields in the Uintas. Use caution when traversing the rocks. Even 5 ton boulders can sometimes shift when stepped on." Located 7.4 miles from the Spirit Lake TH, 10,780 ft. elevation, 6 acres, 7' deep, not horse friendly, stocked with brook trout, with light fishing pressure.

p. 484

EAST ANSON (GR-13): This natural lake is found on a glacial shelf in a cirque high in the Weyman Lakes Basin, susceptible to strong winds, at timberline in the middle of boulder fields and stunted sub-alpine firs. It can be accessed 0.7 miles west of Anson Lakes up rock slides and across rough builder fields, a total of 7.8 miles from the Spirit Lake TH. Not horse friendly. Located at 10,820 ft. elevation, 9.2 acres, stocked with brook and Tiger trout, with light pressure. This alpine lake is unique with an underground outlet that

is a visible siphon found along the northeastern shore.

LAKE GR-14: Does not support fish life. CLEAR (GR-12): This is another pretty lake in the Weyman Lakes Basin found 0.4 miles west of Lower Anson Lake through rocky timber, with horse access impossible. It is 6.6 miles from the Spirit Lake TH. At 10,780 ft. elevation, 10.2 acres, 25' deep, has cutthroat and Tiger trout with light pressure. HIDDEN (GR-7): It is a natural lake at the bottom of a meadow 0.7 miles northwest of Lower Anson Lake in the Weyman Lakes Basin, or on the outlet stream from Clear Lake. Horses are not recommended as access is cross-country through downed timber and boulder fields, at 10,380 ft. elevation, 8.5 acres, 26' deep, has stocked Brook trout and a few Cutthroat trout, with very light pressure. SANDY (GR-17): Is found in rocky timbered terrain in the northeast corner of the Weyman Lakes Basin. It is 0.2 miles north of Hidden Lake on its outlet stream, not horse friendly, at 10,290 ft. elevation, 5.5 aces, 29' deep. "The lake does not over-winter fish due to poor inlet flows, and stocking has been discontinued…..

The lake may be experimentally planted sometime in the future with arctic grayling which may prove more tolerant of the harsh environment." No recent records of stocking.

TOPOGRAPHIC MAP FOR DAGGET LAKE & THE WEYLAND LAKES BASIN

p. 485

THE BEAVER CREEK & BROWNE LAKE TRAILHEADS The next trailhead we come to is where we turn off from FR-221, on to FR-096 to drive down to Browne Lake and its trailheads. At the turn-off point there is a meadow on our right where we see the following trail sign. We have called this the Beaver Creek Trailhead.

We now drive about 2 miles on FR-096 to Browne Lake where there are two trailheads, one that gives us access to the Weyland Lakes Basin we have already discussed, as is the case also from the Beaver Creek Trailhead--and it's just a little further from here, so we won't mention that hike, but will check out access to the other areas, but first let's look at the trail signs at Brown Lake.

From this trailhead--that is found at the mid-way point at Browne Lake, the Potter Lake and area interests us, but this also leads the hiker to the very important Lamb Lakes Basin--with 6 alpine lakes, the least visited on the North Slope of the Eastern Uintas. Let's see what the other trail sign tells us, but notice above Leidy Peak and its northern flank where up there above timberline the famous Highline Trail comes around the peak--only the 2nd time the trail touches the North Slope--the other being at Deadhorse Lake at the head of the West Fork of Blacks Fork in the Wilderness Area.

p. 486

The above sign, at the far eastern trailhead at Browne Lake, indicates it accesses the other area of our interest--the Teepee Lakes along with a couple of others in the area. Said trail then climbs up the ridge to Leidy Peak. Another trail from this eastern trailhead, was seen along with a display about the Old Carter Military Trail, discussed in the Preface. That trail divides a couple of miles southeast with a trail that also climbs the slopes of Leidy Peak specifically going to Hacking Lake on the eastern flank of the peak, part of the Ashley Creek Drainage on the South Slope.

In this panorama from the Browne Lake Trailhead, we see 12,028 foot high Leidy Peak on the left, then 12,078 foot high Mt. Untermann in the middle right, and on the right an un-named 12,000+ peak.

NOW TO THE LAKES ACCESSED FROM THE MID-BROWNE LAKE TRAILHEAD:

THE POTTER LAKES AREA UPPER POTTER (GR-28): Access is from the middle Browne Lake Trailhead on Trail #17 called THE BROWNE-SPIRIT LAKE TRAIL, which on my topographical maps is the purple trail I call The North Slope Highline Trail. Follow it southwest for 5.2 miles where Trail #18 takes off to the south and climbs the ridge and at about 1.1 miles there is a faint trail that drops down eastwardly to Upper Potter Lake where the trail ends, a total of about 7 miles from the TH. Not too horse friendly. It is found at 10,130 ft. elevation, 21.3 acres, 75' deep, with a self-sustaining population of brook trout, with light fishing pressure.

NOTE: Trail #018 continues up the ridge and crosses the spine of the Uintas at 11,865 ft. elevation to then drop down intersecting the Highline Trail above Deadman Lake. LOWER POTTER (GR-27): It is a small pond a few yards east of Upper Potter lake, at 10,130 ft. elevation, 3.4 acres, 16' deep, not too horse friendly, has a natural population of brook trout, under light pressure.

POLLEN (?): It is shown on the topographical map as a quite large lake and named, and also on the Forest Service Wilderness Map (not named), but is not on the DWR pamphlet map, nor mentioned. On Google Earth it looks like a body of water that fluctuates, completely drying up at the end of the summer.

p. 487

THE LAMB LAKES AREA

For access see instructions for Upper Potter Lake, but continue up the ridge about 0.3 miles to where "a little used trail drops down from the ridge" to Bummer Lake. "Supposedly, horses can get into Lamb Lakes Basin via two little-used trails, one of which drops from the ridge northeast of Bummer Lake, the other drops from the ridge northwest of Ewe Lake. The existence of these trails was not verified during this project. Horse use in Lamb Lakes Basin would be restricted due to the rocky terrain."

The other instructions for getting to the Basin is as follows: "There is no maintained trail for the last 1.5 miles. The most direct access to lakes in this basin is cross-country from the junction of Forest Service trails 018-1 and 017 southwest up the bottom of the basin. The going is rough through rocky timber and across boulder fields. Horse access is impossible by this route and should not be attempted."

BUMMER (GR-22): It is a small lake on the east side of Lamb Lakes Basin about 7 miles from the TH. At 10,350 ft. elevation, 1.9 acres, 6' deep, stocked with brook trout, light pressure.

LAKE GR-20: It is a rocky pond a short distance southwest of Bummer Lake. 10,355 ft. elevation, 5.7 acres, 8' deep, light pressure for stocked brook trout.

LAKE GR-21: Located 200 yards northwest of Bummer Lake, very similar to GR-20, 3.7 acres, 7' deep, susceptible to winterkill, stocked with brook trout.

MUTTON (GR-23): It is a natural lake in the southern corner of the Basin. There is no trail. The easiest way to access it is to follow the inlet stream of Bummer Lake. Located at 10,570 ft. elevation, 3.8 acres, 10' deep, not horse friendly, light pressure for stocked brook trout.

RAM (GR-24): Located about 0.6 miles northwest of Mutton Lake at the foot of a rock slide, 10380 ft. elevation, 7 acres, 27' deep, not horse friendly, has a small population of cutthroat trout and now with Tiger trout with very light fishing pressure.

LAMB (GR-19): Located around the base of the mountain 0.4 miles from Ram Lake, or 0.9 miles southwest from Bummer Lake, at 10540 ft. elevation, 6 acres, 10' deep, surrounded by rocky timber, but with an open shoreline, but a murky lake with marginal fish habitat now with Tiger trout.

EWE (GR-18): It is located at the foot of a talus slope, 0.3 miles across the basin northwest of Lamb Lake, at 10,750 ft. elevation, 3 acres, 10' deep, "Trout stocked in Ewe Lake in the past have not been able to overwinter, and as of 1986 the lake is fishless.” Grayling were stocked in 2013 and 2017.

THE TEEPEE LAKES & OTHERS ACCESSED FROM THE EASTERN TRAILHLEAD AT BROWNE LAKE From the TH take Trail #12 2.8 miles to a junction, then: ONE LAKE (GR-32): Located in heavy timber 0.3 mile NW of the junction on Trail #21, then north across the Sheep Creek Canal, 9,350 ft. elevation, 4.5 acres, 35' deep, light pressure for stocked brook and Tiger trout.

LOST or MYSTERIOUS (GR-101): Follow Trail #21

1.2 miles where it turns south to the lake, 5.1 miles from the TH. Horse friendly but sparse feed, 9,750 ft. elevation, 10.2 acres, 25' deep, with stocked brook trout, and cutthroat trout, light to moderate fishing pressure.

p. 488

LAKE GR-31 It is an on-stream portion of the Sheep Ck. Canal which supplies water for northern Daggett County, so from the junction follow the canal for 1.4 miles to the lake. Horse friendly. 9,270 ft. elevation, 6 acres, 6' deep, light pressure for natural brook trout. LOWER TEEPEE (GR-29): 3 miles from TH, surrounded by heavy timber, 0.2 miles from junction at the head of the Sheep Ck. Canal, horse friendly, 9,410 ft. elevation, 4.3 acres, 6' deep, has stocked brook trout with moderate pressure. UPPER TEEPEE (GR-30): Located 150 yards southeast of Lower Teepee Lake, 9,430 ft. elevation, 6.5 acres, 28' deep, with cutthroat trout under moderate pressure. RED (GR-33): It is located 1.4 miles south of the junction on Trail #20, 5.2 miles from the TH, horse friendly but sparse feed, 9,850 ft. elevation, 20.9 acres, 57' deep, has stocked brook trout under light to moderate pressure.

TOPOGRAPHICAL MAPS FOR THE BROWNE LAKE TRAILHEADS The purple trail crossing the upper portion of the map is what I have called "The North Slope Highline Trail" that ends two miles east at the Ute Mountain Lookout Tower, for a total of 78.3 miles from its beginning in the Bear River Drainage.

We have now completed the review of the lakes of Sheep/Carter Creeks Drainage and the North Slope of the Eastern Uintas

p. 489

Chapter 4: THE EASTERN UINTAS--South Slope

Section 2: THE ASHLEY CREEK DRAINAGE including Three Basins: 1. North Fork of Ashley Creek; 2. South Fork of Ashley Creek; & 3. Dry Fork Creek ******************************** The North Fork of Ashley Creek:183 Hacking Lake

This is the only lake in this drainage managed as a fishery by the DWR. Down the road FR043 east a couple of miles is also found Long Park Reservoir. HOW TO GET HERE: From Vernal, Utah, go to 2500 West and turn north. It becomes the Taylor Mountain Road. 21 miles from Vernal you come to the Red Cloud Loop Road, FR-018, and turn west for 7.3 miles to road FR-043 and continue 8 miles to the road that goes a short distance to Hacking Lake.,,,36,3 miles from Vernal. Continuing up FR-043, you pass by where the Highline Trail continues east 26 miles to its eastern end or beginning.

At 1 mile from the Hacking Lake junction you come to the Leidy Peak Highline Trailhead where the guide books, and even Backpacker Magazine, say erroneously is the eastern end of that important trail. HACKING (GR-40): It is a natural lake found at the base of a rockslide coming off of Leidy Peak. At 10,652 ft. elevation, 7.4 acres, 15' deep, with Brook, Rainbow and Tiger trout, under heavy fishing pressure, especially on weekends. 184 183

ONLY ONE LAKE, BUT THE South Fork of Ashley Creek is great fishing. See pages 104-105 of the Auto Loop Tour.

184

All info. from: LAKES OF THE HIGH UINTAS Ashley Creek Drainage (Revision 1981), Publication No. 81-6, DWR

p. 490

The South Fork of Ashley Creek Drainage

HOW TO GET HERE: From Vernal, Utah, get on 500 North and go west following the signs to DRY FORK CANYON & THE RED CLOUD LOOP. As you drive up into the Uintas, 27 miles from Vernal you will come to a jeep road on your left, FR-027, and drive 5.5 miles to Ashley Twins Reservoir which puts you at the access points to the lakes of the South Fork of Ashley Creek. WARNING: Horses cannot be hauled the

last 3 miles because of the rugged road.

SEE PAGES 105-106 ASHLEY CREEK.

FOR STREAM FISHING ON THE BEAUTIFUL SOUTH FORK OF

ASHLEY TWINS RES. (GR-35): It has a large earthen dam on the east end. At 10,332 ft. elevation, 20.7 to 30.3 acres, 8' to 18' deep. At maximum drawdown, three small lakes are formed (North, South and

East)……has sizable brook trout, and pan-size cutthroat trout. Angling pressure drops off in late summer because of the mucky shoreline resulting from drawdown. MUD (GR-27): In spite of its name, the pamphlet says: This pretty, irregular-shaped lake….with a riprap dam on the north sits at the base of a steep, talus ridge that extends eastward from Marsh Peak……There is no trail, but access is 1/2 mile south up a thick timbered, rocky ridge from Ashley Twins Res. Horse access is difficult 10,582 ft. elevation, 4.2 acres, 11' to 15' deep…..experimentally stocked with cutthroat trout beginning in 1981, light pressure. MARSH (GR-39): A cirque lake mostly surrounded by talus slopes. Head 1 mile from Ashley Twins Res. in a westward direction into the cirque basin on the northwest side of Marsh Peak. There is no trail over this steep, timbered terrain and horses are not recommended. Has brook & now with GOLDEN trout with moderate pressure. See: http://wildlife.utah.gov/blog/2014/theres-gold-in-the-uintas/ GOOSE #2 (GR-43): Access is 1/2 mile north of Ashley Twin Res. via a good Forest Service trail, horse friendly…..Has a dam on the east end. at 10,252 ft. elevation, 19.4 max. acres, 9'-15' deep, with a mucky shoreline caused by drawdown, has cutthroat trout on experimental basis since 1981. Didn’t work. GOOSE #1 (GR-42): Also a reservoired lake, surrounded by marshes and deadfall. To access follow

outlet of Goose Lake #2 125 yards east to Goose #3, then turn south for 20 yards to the lake, horse access slow due to marshy terrain, only with a few trout with little pressure. SANDY (GR-45): It is a natural lake surrounded by conifers. Access is northwest 2/3 mile from Ashley Twins Res on the trail to the inlet of Goose Lake #2, then west and follow the trailess inlet 1/2 mile through thick timber to the lake. Horse access is difficult the last 1/2 mile, 10,500 ft. elevation, 5.6 acres, 10' deep, with slow-growing cutthroat trout, with little pressure.

p. 491

HOOPER (GR-46): Found in a wet meadow, access is 1.25 miles northwest from the Ashley Twins Res on a well-marked Forest Service trail, horse friendly, at 10,305 ft. elevation, 4.5 acres, 4' deep, has an abundant natural population of cutthroat trout, ideal for the fly fisherman. Horseflies are a real nuisance during midsummer.

LAKESHORE (GR-34): It is a picturesque meadow lake in the middle of rolling ridges and scattered timber, accessed by the well-marked Forest Service trail, 4.5 miles from Ashley Twins Reservoir, or southwest by Forest Service trail 5 miles from the trailhead at Hacking Lake. Horse friendly, 10,792 ft. elevation, 11.1 acres, 18' deep, with a natural population of brook and cutthroat trout, pressure moderate. WILDE (GR-36): Found in a small basin at the southwest corner of Leidy Peak, and is the largest in a series of three cirque lakes, at 10,950 ft. elevation, 4.3 acres, 13' deep, accessed by a trail from Ashley Twins

Res. 4 miles into the Lakeshore Basin. Turn north at a small meadow pond (GR-76) and go 1/2 mile past another Lake (GR-77) climbing a steep, talus ledge into Wilde Lake Basin, horse access is impossible the last 1/2 mile, with no fish, but the area is scenic for those seeking solitude.

LITTLE BLUE (GR-48): It is a natural lake above timberline in windswept tundra at 11,215 ft. elevation, 3.2 acres, 6' deep, accessed by a well-marked Forest Service trail 5.5 miles to the end of Lakeshore Basin

from Ashley Twins Res, horse friendly, fishless at the time of the 1979 survey, and later stocked experimentally, and today has Brook trout.

DRY FORK CREEK a tributary of the South Fork of Ashley Creek Accessed from the Paradise Park Reservoir area HOW TO GET HERE: In Vernal, Utah get on 500 North and head west--it turns into County Rd. 121--go 17 miles to LaPoint, but turn north on the first road--the Deep Creek Road and continue north for 26.8 miles. It eventually turns into the Paradise Peak Road and continue north to the Paradise Park Reservoir area, the access point for the lakes of Dry Fork Creek. If you're coming from the west Wasatch Front to Roosevelt is about 128 miles, then continue on U.S-40 9.2 miles to Gusher and there turn north 10 miles to LaPoint and at its eastern edge turn north on the Deep Creek Rd. and continue as explained above, for a total of 47 miles from Roosevelt, from the Wasatch Front, 175 miles..

WE WILL BEGIN ON THE EASTERN SIDE OF THE DRY FORK DRAINAGE CHIMNEY ROCK (GR-63): A pothole lake sits at the southeast base of Marsh Peak in a steep cirque basin. It is best accessed from FR-027 about a mile before getting to the Ashley Twin Res. where the Marsh Peak Trail takes off going west about 1 mile to a point high on the ridge. The pamphlet then says: Follow the Marsh Peak trail 1 mile onto the ridge extending from Marsh Peak. Pick your way down the east side of the cirque basin to the lake over large talus boulders and thick timber. Horse access is impossible. At 10,540 ft elevation, 6.5 acres, 16' deep. Little water exchange and low water levels cause winterkill, making it impossible to support fish. Scenery and solitude are assured for rugged individuals.

BERT (GR-62): This attractive, natural lake sits at the base of some rock slides extending south from Marsh Peak. For access follow the instructions for Chimney Rock Lake, and continue 1 mile south. Horse access is impossible. 10,220 ft. elevation 3.7 acres, 11' deep, stocked with Brook trout, & Grayling, rarely receives visitors.

WE WILL NOW MOVE TO THE PARADISE PARK RESERVOIR AREA & LOOK NORTH One named lake, Mill Pond, is not listed in the DWR pamphlet. The next lake north is Little Elk Lake, but first we’ll describe the reservoir and one nearby lake with fish.

p. 492

PARADISE PARK RESERVOIR (WR-18): It is found 26 miles north of the town of Lapoint on an improved dirt road. Forest Service campgrounds are nearby. Not considered by the Department of Wildlife Resources (DWR) as a high lake for management purposes, but is stocked with Rainbow and Brook trout. Has heavy usage. DEAD (WR-29): Located due north of the Paradise Campground, and 0.2 miles east of the reservoir. At 10,075 elevation, 9.7 acres, 15’ deep, with a history of winterkill, but previously stocked with Brook and Cutthroat trout, and with Grayling in 2014 and 2017. LITTLE ELK (DF-17): Access is by following the inlet stream to Paradise Park Res. 1/3 mile to a small meadow, turn north and go 1 mile up a rugged, timbered mountain , not horse friendly, at 10,550 ft. elevation, 7.4 acres, 10' deep, tends to winterkill but has been stocked with Tiger trout and Grayling.

PAUL (DF-18): It is a natural lake surrounded by rocky, timbered ridges 2.25 miles northwest of Paradise Park Res. Access is by a trail that starts on the north shore of Little Elk 1.4 mile south of Paul. Access is generally rough and trails poorly marked, horse access is very difficult. 10,630 ft. elevation, 11.1 acres, 17' deep, with stocked Brook trout that grow well feeding on freshwater shrimp, with light pressure.

WE WILL NOW GO UP TO THE NORTHEAST INTO HELL'S KITCHEN PARK SOUTH TWIN (GR-49): It is a natural lake surrounded by marshy vegetation, meadows and scattered timber. Access: Follow the Forest Service tail from Paradise Park 6 miles northeast to the lake. Horse access is easy. At 10,300 ft. elevation, 6.2 acres, 8' deep, has pan-size brook and cutthroat trout, with heavy pressure.

NORTH TWIN (GR-50): See access instructions for Southtwin Lake. Northtwin Lake is 150 yards north of Southtwin. Horse friendly. 10,305 ft. elevation, 10.3 acres, 24' deep, with abundant populations of brook and cutthroat trout, with heavy pressure.

FISH (GR-57): It is described as a beautiful lake surrounded by scattered timber and steep, talus slopes. At 10,745 ft. elevation, 17.5 acres, 40' deep, fairly horse friendly. For see access see instructions for Southtwin, then follow a vague Forest Service trail along the east inlet stream towards Marsh Peak for 1.25 miles. Has a natural population of cutthroat trout, with heavy pressure.

SHAW (GR-59): It is a natural lake in a large, wet meadow. For access see directions for Fish Lake. Shaw sits a short distance northwest of Fish. 10,700 ft. elevation, 2.8 acres, 5' deep, horse friendly, has a population of cutthroat trout, has little fishing pressure.

RED BELLY (GR-51): The topographical map shows trails to all these lakes, including to Red Belly, from Northtwin Lake. The pamphlet says: Follow the north inlet stream to North Twin Lake 1/2 mile, then turn

north and follow the stream tributary 1/2 mile to the lake at the base of a rock ledge. Horse access is easy. At 10,540 ft. elevation, 6.3 acres, 8' deep, has a few healthy cutthroat trout that inhabit the lake, with moderate fishing pressure.

LAKE GR-62: It is a small natural lake surrounded by boggy meadows, and conifers on the south, found 600 yards southeast of Red Belly Lake. At 10,515 ft. elevation, 2.1 acres, 4' deep, with a natural population of brook trout, with moderate pressure.

NOW BACK DOWN TO DO THE WESTERN PORTION OF DRY FORK, FIRST, THE KIBAH LAKES

p. 493

ACCESS ACCORDING TO THE DWR PAMPHLET: The five Kibah lakes are accessible via a

jeep road north from Paradise Park Reservoir 3 miles into Blanchett Park. Head crosscountry northwest 1 mile into Kibah Basin: DF-11 is the first lake encountered in the small drainage. There are no trails….and the rough boulder terrain is too rugged for horses. Excellent camping and abundant horse feed are available at Blanchett Park. Fishing pressure is mostly through day hikers. EAST KIBAH (DF-11): A natural lake at 10,495 ft. elevation, 2.9 acres, 12' deep, with stocked brook trout that have good growth, also with a population of rainbow trout, under moderate pressure FINGER KIBAH (DF-12): A long narrow lake located 90 yards southwest of DF-11, at 10,515 ft. elevation, 4.7 acres, 9' deep, with a healthy population of brook trout, with moderate pressure. WEST KIBAH (DF-14): Locate at the base of a talus slope in the far southwest corner of Kibah Basin, at 10,580 elevation, 7.8, 15' deep. Go 1/2 mil southwest from DF-11 over rough, timbered terrain, past DF-12, has stocked brook trout, with moderate fishing pressure. NORTH KIBAH (DF-15): It is a cirque lake in the northwest corner of the basin, 3/4 mile northwest of DF-11, at 10,750 ft. elevation, 4.5 acres, 12' deep, no fish due to winterkill. ISLAND KIBAH (DF-16): It is a natural like surrounded by rocky ridges covered with conifers, found by following the west inlet of DF-11 northwest about 300 yards over rough, boulder terrain to DF-16, R 10,540 ft. elevation, 8 acres, 14' deep, with brook trout with moderate pressure.

WE'LL NOW MOVE NORTH UP TRAIL #075*185 TO THE LONESOME BASIN & TO THE HIGHLINE TRAIL MOAP (DF-2): This is a small cirque lake at the base of a steep talus slope, accessed by going north on the jeep road into Blanchett Park 3 miles north of Paradise Park Res. Then go north 1/2 mile on the Forest Service Trail #075 past Lonesome Park to a large, wet meadow, then turn due east through the timber 1/2 mile into the small cirque basin, horse friendly but no feed, at 10,740 ft. elevation, 2.7 acres, 5' deep, has brook trout with moderate pressure.

BLUE (DF-1): This scenic windswept lake sits at the top of a cirque basin surrounded by arctic tundra. Accessed going north on the jeep road into Blanchett Park 3 miles north of Paradise Park Res . then follow FS Trail #075 2 miles north of Lonesome park to Deadman Lake and the Highline Trail, and then follow it east about 1 mile to a junction and take Trail #132* southeast down 1 mile to the lake. Access also might be possible from Moap Lake following the drainage cross-country 1.5 miles up to the lake. At 11,160 ft. elevation, 6.5 acres, 16' deep, has an abundant population of brook trout, with moderate pressure. DEADMAN (GR-38): It is a natural lake at the very head of the Dry Fork Drainage, accessed by following the directions for Blue Lake. Horse friendly, but sparse feed. At 10,790 ft. elevation, 7 acres, 9' deep, has both brook and cutthroat trout, with heavy pressure, including from Scout groups.

LAKE DF-4: This is a natural cirque lake for anglers who like solitude and ruggedness. Accessed by following the Forest Service trail 2.75 miles above Blanchett Park to Reynolds Creek, which you follow 1 mile to its source, then head due west over boulder terrain to the lake. Horses can be taken up Reynolds Creek only partway because of rough terrain. At 10,830 ft. elevation, 10 acres, 23' deep, with Cutthroat trout.

We have now completed the Ashley Creek Drainage having reviewed 32 lakes

185

Chapter 4: THE EASTERN UINTAS

Section 3: THE WHITEROCKS RIVER DRAINAGE ******************

PREFACE

From a well known eastern backpacker on BYU Radio--

"HE'S A BADASS"

On June 29, 2018 I participated in a panel discussion about backpacking on BYU RADIO, on the JULIE ROSE SHOW, in a segment entitled THE HIKING CULTURE. One of the panelist was Zach Davis, Author of Appalachian Trails: The Psychological and Emotional Guide to Successfully Thru-Hiking The Appalachian Trail, and Owner & Editor-In-Chief of - The Trek, along with, Ciara Hulet, Producer of TOP OF THE MIND, and Creator of Cici Outside YouTube Channel. As the show was coming to an end Julie asked Zach what he thought about me--an 82 year old with my High Uintas Wilderness Project, 2,000 miles of backpacking, exploring and photographing the Uintas, and still backpacking. His reply,

"HE'S A BADASS!" Among outdoors people that is generally understood to be a good thing, so I reported it on my website and sent an email notice to my High Uinta Friends. A couple of quite religious friends reacted a bit negatively saying it was ……crude, vulgar, and inappropriate. I tried to explain that among a certain adventurous group of outdoor lovers this was understood to be a good thing. I even quoted Julie Rose in an email to me, saying:

“Cordell, you deserved the praise. Thanks again for coming on the show!”

p. 498

So Julie, a very well informed radio host, recognized it was a good thing--a word of "praise." NOTE: If you go to the show's website and scroll down through the incredible number of topics she has covered on her show--just this year, you'll be amazed how well informed she has to be. 186 That still didn't satisfy the objectors--who likely will never accept such, but it led me to doing a little investigation on the subject, and in the process had drop into my internet lap a sort of QUIZ about whether one was a BADASS or not. Here it is along with the questions and qualifications:

1st Question: "Live out of a van?" I think my funky little 7'x 11' travel trailer I call home

qualifies! 2nd Question: "Eats mostly out of titanium mugs?" I do have a titanium pot for

backpacking and eat out of it. 186

https://www.byuradio.org/show/e9a84fc9-4bb1-476f-bd5d-0e907b754af8/top-of-mind-with-julie-rose

p. 499

3rd Question: "Befriended a squirrel named Jerry (probably)?" I don't have a pet squirrel or

any kind of pet--and certainly don't need a "comfort pet" for "emotional support," which maybe qualifies me as a BADASS. I have taken some awfully cute photographs of squirrels in the Uintas, as well as chipmunks, one of which at Jackson Park got inside my tent and I had one heck of a time freeing him--his name could have been "Jerry," but I forgot to ask. 4th Question: "Climbed, hiked places most people don't even know about?" I have climbed and hiked to many places most people don't think are important, neither know they exist. 5th Question: "Never lost…just exploring?" I have gone astray twice when I didn't check my topographical map and compass carefully--and am confessing it here for the first time, but they were both wonderful "exploring" experiences, and on realizing my navigational error, I knew exactly where I was--so I WASN'T LOST! 6th Question: "A professional wanderer?" I do wander all over in my funky little home, and f I can finally make some money from this book I'll be able to say "I’m a professional!" So, hey, all you friends out there, help me get out of the amateur class and become professional BADASS! 7th Question: "Pavement freaks you out?" All Winter and off-season I train on the pavement every day with a pack on my back and am mistaken for an old homeless guy-which is kind of fun, but I do prefer rocky trails that I try and get to at least once a week for training. 8th Question: "Bears come to your camp to bring you food?" I've failed with BEARS. Haven't seen one yet in all my years exploring the Uintas, but I did have a Charolais bull and also a mama moose come after me--but not to bring me food, rather to grind me into the meadow mud. My Colt .45 Defender was used to protect me--which qualifies me. 9th Question: "Mosquitoes, poison ivy pass on you?" Mosquitoes love me! Not a good thing, rather BAD(ASS)! When young I was just about killed by poison oak, but that immunized me so I became the one to go into a camp spot and clear it out so the guys would be safe. I did alright with some of the questions, not so good with others, but NO BODY IS A PERFECT BADASS! You be the judge….and let me know. In the meantime I'm grateful for Zach, Julie & Ciara, and will even in my 84th year (2019) do my darndest to not let anyone down. If you're interested in the radio show, here is the link--you'll notice that the HIKING CULTURE segment is the second half of the show: Top of Mind https://www.byuradio.org/episode/e7b87e9c-1bb7-4f4d-8d8a-c9908bcd3f0d/top-ofmind-with-julie-rose-the-making-of-a-psychiatrist-hiking-culture-panelon BYUradio

BY THE WAY….THERE'S ANOTHER DEFINITION OF "BADASS," in addition to: distinctively tough or powerful; exceptional, maybe what Zach meant; The other definition is: (of a person) difficult to deal with; mean-tempered; touchy,187 I'll have to admit there is a

group of influential people who believe that's me, but they don't even want to know me, chat with me, much less go hiking with me in the High Uintas, so I don't worry about them.

187

https://www.dictionary.com/browse/badass

p. 500

Chapter 4: THE EASTERN UINTAS--The South Slope

Section 3: THE WHITEROCKS RIVER DRAINAGE HOW TO GET HERE: From downtown Vernal we get on 500 North and go west, it soon becomes State Road UT-121. It will continue west until the turn-off to Whiterocks--on the "Whiterocks Highway" taking you through the community (25.5 miles)--on the Ute Reservation, and continue north on this Hwy….It becomes the Farm Creek Road that turns north, then back to the east, then north to the Elkhorn Guard Station, where you will see a sign turning left onto a well graded dirt/gravel road, which is the ELKHORN LOOP RD. This road is Forest Road FR-117 that takes you up into the Whiterocks River Drainage of the Uinta Mountains. See maps on pages 110 & 111.

THE WHITEROCKS DRAINAGE This is one of the largest drainages in the Uintas, just east of the Uinta River Drainage, and is the only drainage on the South Slope where a passenger car can get within two miles of the spine of the Uintas at Chepeta Lake. Forty-five of the 70 natural lakes and ponds have trout populations managed by the DWR. Along the road up to Chepeta Lake there are several established trailheads, and there are others where just a sign becomes a trailhead with trails leading to the many lakes. I will insert below a Google Earth view of the drainage.

©2018 Google LLC, used with permission. Google and the Google logo are registered trademarks of Google LLC. Highlights, extra routes and labels by author

p. 501

The first lakes we come to is in the Pole Lake area where there is a full-service Forest Service Campground. At 14.2 miles from leaving the pavement we come to a sign pointing to Pole Creek Lake and campground which is 0.7 mile from the junction following the Elkhorn Loop Rd. we did on the Auto Loop Tour. POLE CREEK (WR-13): It is a fairly large lake, about 30 acres in size. The DWR pamphlet says: This large water is not technically considered to be a high lake for management purposes……is stocked on an annual basis with catchable-size rainbow trout. Recreational use is very heavy. Elevation is about 10,160 feet.

LOWER ROCK (WR-17): This natural lake is surrounded by rocks and conifers with little open shoreline. It is found 1.4 miles north of Pole Creek Lake. The pamphlet describes access: The easiest is to

follow the inlet of Pole Creek Lake upstream to a large meadow, 0.05 mile north of the road. Skirt the south side of the meadow and follow the outlet of Lower Rock Lake through heavy timber to the lake. You'll notice on the topographical map I take the high point on the road and go cross-country north to the meadow mentioned and then follow the stream to the lake measuring the distance at 1.2 miles. 10,550 ft. elevation, 18.7 acres, 39' deep, stocked with Brook and Tiger trout with light to moderate pressure. MIDDLE ROCK (WR-16): This lake is similar to Lower Rock Lake in that there is little open shoreline, but it is the smallest of the lakes found 200 yards north of Lower Rock Lake, not too horse friendly, at 10,580 ft. elevation, 7.3 acres, 10' deep, stocked with brook trout under light to moderate fishing pressure. UPPER ROCK (WR-15): The lake is surrounded by boulders and rock slides, located 0.3 mile north of Middle Rock Lake crossing boulder fields, impossible for horses, at 10,592 ft. elevation, 33.4 acres, 33' deep, with a level that fluctuates and has been known to winterkill, the pamphlet says: Upper Rock Lake provides a rather inhospitable environment for both fish and people. Stocked with cutthroat trout, light pressure. LARVAE (WR-12): A small lake found 0.3 mile east of the junction of the Chepeta Lake Rd. and the road to Pole Ck. Lake, 10,030 ft. elevation, 5.8 acres, 29' deep, with stocked brook trout, pressure moderate.

TOPOGRAPHICAL MAPS FOR THE POLE CREEK LAKE AREA

Above, the Pole Creek Lake, Larvae Lake & the Rock Lakes501

p. 502

We now return to FR-117 and continue up the canyon about 3 miles and at the sign--WEST FORK TRAILHEAD--turn to the left and drive about 0.6 mile to the trailhead we see below.

From this very nice trailhead--by far the best in the drainage, complete with everything you need including corals for horses and more. From here we can access at least 15 lakes, but I'm recalling that I promised to tell you about one of my adventures when we got to this area. I joke about it as my:

It was in 2016 when I came here with the specific intention of completing my record of climbing all of the 22 passes in the Wilderness Area. From here I wanted to bag 11,360 ft. Fox-Queant Pass, and 12,226 foot North Pole Pass. It was actually my first experience backpacking in the Eastern Uintas, as over the years I had focused mainly on the High Uintas Wilderness Area. I first noticed what seemed like more use of horses. Second, almost everybody was armed with pistols and revolvers, one with a powerful .454 Casull Taurus Raging Bull revolver. His concern wasn't bears as was the case with most, but rather with cougars. I haven't heard of such attacks, so I'm not sure how justified they were, but who knows? I guess carrying makes us all feel like badasses! At Cleveland Lake I had some good fishing, and got a shot or two of bull moose feeding in the lake.

p. 503

Then the weather began closing in on me, but I pushed myself up the rocky trail--and the variety of the rocks--as always, fascinated me and I got a new collection, like the one below on the left.

At times it was hard to distinguish just where the trail was, as we can see in the middle photo--the trail actually going right up the middle of the picture. I was wondering how on earth horses could ever make it, and then I noticed dried spots of blood and then a horseshoe, indicating it wasn't easy for man or beast.

I finally made it to Fox-Queant Pass and the Wilderness Boundary and once again felt the effects of high altitude, and so with that and the strong winds and storm clouds closing in on me, I headed back down, rather than do as planned--swinging down into the Uinta River Drainage, and then up over North Pole Pass to bring me back down to the West Fork and the trailhead. I made it back to Cleveland Lake in the middle of a rain storm, and quickly set up my tent and slithered inside. It rained all night, but I had water and food that didn't need cooking so I was alright. By morning the rain had stopped but the sky was stormy so I decided to hurry down the trail before the rain started again. I got about half-way to the trailhead when the first drops began falling and I stopped to get on my rain gear, and while working on that J.C. Batty and his buddy, Graham, on horseback came by.

p. 504

I probably didn't look all that tough at the moment (not much of a BADASS!), so J.C. said they'd continue down to the trailhead with their pack animal and then he'd come back for me with Graham's horse. I would keep moving in that direction in the meantime. An hour later K.C. made it back and took my pack, and told me to mount up. Have to admit it took some doing to get my stiff old leg--with titanium knee, up over the saddle, but soon we were on our way in a light drizzle of cold rain. As we moved down the trail I told K.C. the story of when I was a Boy Scout in California and accompanied my friend, Dick

Johnson, to get his Merit Badge in Horsemanship. The counselor asked Dick if we were both there to get the badge, and before I could say, no, Dick, said, "Yes." and motioned for me to just play along. When I could answer some question, I spoke up quickly, but it was rare because I didn't know anything. For Dick's replies I quickly gave my authoritative nod. Then it was time to go into the ring and show our horsemanship skills, on horseback. Dick did fine riding at different gaits, etc. Then it was my turn, and I literally prayed for some kind of miracle to save me. Dick was tall and long legged, and of course I was Little Andy, so the stirrups were way too long for me, and we were about to take time to adjust, when the counselor stepped in and said, "I have an appointment, so let's not waste time. BOTH OF YOU PASSED!" My real test came 65 years later on the Fox-Queant Pass Trail, and I actually made it to the trailhead without falling off…..and so have always joked about it being:

“MY JOHN WAYNE LOOK-ALIKE HIGH UINTAS ‘BADASS’ ADVENTURE!”

Hope you notice the resemblance between me and "The Duke"--the tilt of the hat?

************************ NOW, LET'S CHECK OUT THE LAKES AS WE GO UP THE TRAIL188 R.C. No. 1 (WR-2): Located on the north side of the West Fork….drainage, 2.6 miles from the TH. The topographic map indicates that a short spur trail leads from the West Fork Trail directly to the R.C. lakes, however, the existence of this spur trail couldn't be verified during our survey. Access is, nonetheless, relatively easy. The outlet stream of the R.C. lakes crosses the West fork Trail at a point 1.6 miles from the trailhead, where the trail breaks out of the trees into a large meadow. Follow the outlet up through a rocky, tree-lined draw to the lakes. 10,630 ft. elevation, 10.2 acres, 16' deep, horse friendly but sparse feed, stocked with Cutthroat trout under light pressure.

188

Information from: LAKES OF THE HIGH UINTAS--Whiterocks River Drainage, 1987, DWR Publication No. 87-6

p. 505

R.C. No. 2 (WR-3): Not noted on the topographical map, it is a small pond west of R.C. No. 1, 1.7 acres, 7' deep, stocked with cutthroat trout and gets also migrating trout from R.C. No.1. QUEANT (WR-4): It is a large popular lake in the West Fork drainage, 4 miles from the TH, horse friendly, at 10,652 ft. elevation, 57 acres, 44' deep, stocked with brook trout under heavy fishing pressure.

NOTE: From Queant Lake one can also access Denise and Taylor Lakes, hiking about 2 miles on the trail that goes northeast of Queant. Above Taylor Lake the trail intersects with the Highline Trail that comes down a couple of miles from North Pole Pass, and continues on to the Chepeta Lake Trailhead. For your convenience I'll describe here Denise & Taylor Lakes. DENISE (WR-9): Located above timberline about 2 miles northeast of Queant Lake, 5.9 miles from the West Fork Trailhead, horse friendly. 11,160 ft. elevation, 3 acres, 9' deep, stocked with brook trout under light pressure. TAYLOR (WR-8): Is a large lake above timberline at 11,220 ft. elevation, 2.2 miles northwest of Queant Lake, 6.3 miles from the West Fork Trailhead, and 4 miles from the Chepeta Lake Trailhead. Is 22.4 acres, 53' deep, open shoreline, no horse feed, stocked with brook trout under moderate fishing pressure.

NOW BACK TO THE FOX-QUEANT PASS TRAIL: CLEVELAND (WR-7): A shallow lake along the trail leading to Fox-Queant Pass, 4.5 miles from the TH, horse friendly, at 10,640 ft. elevation, 23.9 acres, 6' deep, with an open shoreline, stocked with brook trout, but also has cutthroat trout, with moderate pressure. OGDEN (WR-5): It is a natural lake found at the bottom of a steep cliff, 0.6 mile from the trail, 5.2 miles from the TH. The pamphlet suggests: ….stay on the West Fork Trail until it crosses to the south

bank, a short distance from Cleveland Lake. Continue on the north side of the stream and turn north through a series of small meadows. You will eventually wind up at the outlet of Ogden Lake, at 10,900 ft. elevation, 13.9 acres, 21' deep, horse friendly, stocked with cutthroat trout, pressure light to moderate. ROBB (WR-1): It is a shallow cirque lake along the rocky trail below the Fox-Queant Pass, 5.7 miles from the TH, above timberline at 11,060 ft. elevation, 4.2 acres, 5' deep, stocked with brook trout with light pressure. May winterkill from time to time.

Robb Lake as seen from near Fox-Queant Pass, showing the West Fork of Whietrocks Drainage.

NOW LET'S GO BACK DOWN TO THE TRAILHEAD AND CHECK THE LAKES SOUTHWEST OF THE TRAIL ON THE OTHER SIDE OF WEST FORK RIVER ANGEL (WR-19): It is a natural lake at the bottom of a cirque 0.7 mile southwest of the West Fork Trailhead, accessed up a rocky, timbered slope, so horse access is difficult. Located at 10,407 ft. elevation, 10.4 acres, 17' deep, stocked with cutthroat trout, under light pressure, rarely visited, winterkills on occasion.

p. 506

LAKE WR-37: Found 1 mile east of the West fork Trailhead, has historically winterkilled. RASMUSSEN 1 (WR-35): Found in a rocky, timbered basin 1.8 miles west of the West Fork Trailhead. There is no trail to the lake, and access is cross-country from the trailhead up a steep, rocky slope covered with thick stands of pine. You might also follow the main drainage stream of Rasmussen Lake Basin and follow the outlet of Rasmussen 2 to that lake. Rasmussen 1 lies a few hundred yards to the northwest through a brushy swale, not too horse friendly. At 10,473 ft. elevation, 17 acres, 5' deep, stocked with brook trout under light pressure.

RASMUSSEN 2 (WR-36): Found a short distance from Rasmussen 1, 1.6 miles northwest of the West Fork Trailhead, 10,620 ft. elevation, not horse friendly, 15.6 acres, 8' deep, stocked with brook trout, with light pressure. CIRQUE (WR-33): Lies in a cirque 0.4 mile southwest of Rasmussen Lakes, 2.1 miles due west of the West Fork Trailhead, located at the foot of a massive rock glacier with turbid water known to winterkill. Has Brook trout & Grayling were stocked in 2013 and 2017, inaccessible by horses, light fishing pressure.

ERIC (WR-76): …….located on the main drainage stream of Rasmussen Lakes Basin, 3.7 miles west of the West Fork Trailhead. The most direct access is to follow the West Fork upstream 0.8 miles to its confluence with Eric Lake's outlet. The West Fork Trail on the north side of the creek takes you close to this point, but you're then forced to cross to the south bank of the West Fork. Although there is no trail, staying on the south side of the West fork until you reach the confluence may keep your boots dry. Follow the outlet up the slope through downed timber until you break out of the trees. Eric Lake lies at the head of a series of narrow, brushy meadows which line the bottom of Rasmussen Lakes Basin. At 10,610 ft. elevation, horse friendly, the series of ponds lead to the main pond, 4.2 acres, 6' deep, with natural populations of brook and cutthroat trout, under light pressure. BECKY (WR-14): Located on a high, rocky bench overlooking the Rasmussen Lakes Basin, directly south of Eric Lake, 1.5 miles west of Rasmussen Lakes, horse access not recommended, at 10,960 ft. elevation, 6.5 acres, 24' deep, stocked with brook trout under very light pressure. POINT (WR-6): It lies on a high, rocky bench below the tip of the mountain which separates Rasmussen

Lakes Basin from the Cleveland Lake area. There is no trail to the lake. Access is fairly straight forward if you follow the West fork Trail to the confluence of the West Fork and the outlet of Point Lake, and follow the outlet up a rocky slope to the lake, 3.2 miles from the West Fork Trailhead, 10,720 ft. elevation, horse access difficult due to the rocky, rough terrain, 16.1 acres, 21' deep, has stocked brook trout, with light to moderate pressure. KATY (WR-34): It is a natural a cold remote glacial lake located in a high rocky cirque, 1 mile northwest of Point Lake, 4.8 miles from the West Fork Trailhead. A deep and steep, boulder-strewn cleft extends from near Point Lake along the base of the talus slope, eventually terminating at Katy Lake , not horse friendly, 11,200 ft. elevation, 9 acres, 45' deep, has stocked cutthroat trout, rarely visited. NELLIE (WR-75): This is a small on-stream pond near the head of the Rasmussen Lakes Basin, 0.4 mile upstream from Eric Lake, 3.7 miles from the TH--see directions for Eric Lake. 10,691 ft. elevation, 2.7 acres, 8' deep, semi-horse friendly, stocked with cutthroat trout, under light pressure. ANN (WR-74): Located at the head of the Rasmussen Lakes Basin, about 0.25 mile due north of Nellie Lake, 0.5 mile northwest of Eric Lake, and 4 miles from the West Fork TH. See directions for Eric Lake. There are no trails and horse access is difficult. At 10,910 ft. elevation, 3.4 acres, 14' deep, winterkills regularly but will be stocked with cutthroat on an experimental basis. Has Cutthroat trout in 2018. TAMARA (WR-73): Tamara is a picturesque, remote lake which sits at the very head of the Rasmussen Lakes Basin in the West Fork of the Whiterocks Drainage. See Eric Lake for access. Continue up the bottom of the basin, past Nellie Lake, a steep, rocky slope through downed timber, 4.2 miles from the TH all cross-country. Horse use is not recommended. Found at 10,960 ft. elevation, 6.9 acres, 18' deep, stocked with cutthroat trout, with very light fishing pressure.

p. 507

TOPOGRAPHICAL MAPS FOR THE WEST FORK OF WHITEFOCKS AREA

Above is the enlarged extension of the upper West Fork trails and lakes.

Above on the right lower is the TRAILHEAD, with the trail going northwest. Of great importance are the lakes on the southwest side of the West Fork with no trails.

p. 508

NOW, BACK ON FR-110 WE CONTINUE NORTH TOWARDS CHEPETA LAKE About 3.4 miles up the road north, Trail No. 048 crosses the road, I'll insert the sign below as seen coming down the canyon.

This trail will take us to the next lake on the west side of the road described next. HIDDEN (WR-63): The lake is located 400 yards west of the road found by following Trail #048, which trail bypasses the lake, but a sign points to its general location. At 10,350 ft. elevation, 13.2 acres, 45' deep, surrounded by heavy timber making fly fishing difficult, horse feed scarce, with stocked brook trout with light angling pressure.

We continue up FR-110, and a couple of miles north we come to a large meadow and there find the sign we see below.

Trail #133 takes you northwest about 2 miles to the Highline Trail at a point about mid-way between the Chepeta Trailhead, and the trail junction near Taylor Lake. This is apparently what some call the Reader Creek Trailhead. We'll wait to describe all the lakes in that area as accessed from Chepeta Lake. The next trail marker a mile or so up the road is where the Highline Trail crosses the road and heads east. A littler further along on the western side of the road is the Trailhead.

The lakes accessed from this trailhead will be described beginning up the trail with the first.

p. 509

CHEPETA LAKE seen below, Fox-Queant Pass on the left of the big mountain, North Pole Pass on the right.

CHEPETA (WR-64): This lake, made larger by a dike and drainage system to help keep alive the Uintah Basin down below, is located 24 miles from the Elkhorn Guard Station on a good quality dirt road that ends here at the lake, found at 10,560 ft. elevation, 135+ acres, 55' deep, horse friendly, stocked with brook trout, but also with a natural population of cutthroat trout with heavy fishing pressure.

At the Chepeta Lake parking lot we find a trail sign introducing the first lakes we will describe on trails that head north from here.

MOCCASIN (WR-53): This is another of what they call "impounded" found 0.7 mile east of Chepeta Lake, at 10,620 ft. elevation, 11.1 acres, 27' deep, with a self-reproducing population of brook trout, with moderate pressure. PAPOOSE (WR-52): Another impounded or reservoired lake, with no trail to the lake (in 1987), but with the sign indicating it is 1.5 to the lake, I assume there is now a trail. It is located on a bench 500 yards north of Chepeta Lake. The pamphlet states: Access is quite easy if you follow the lake's outlet from where it flows into the northeastern arm of Chepeta Lake. At 10,635 ft. elevation, 14.9 acres, 21' deep, with an open shoreline, and a natural population of brook trout, and some cutthroat trout. Moderate pressure. WIGWAM (WR-54): Another impounded lake located at the bottom of a talus slope 150 yards northwest of Moccasin Lake. 10,607 ft. elevation, 13.5 acres, 11' deep, horse feed scarce, stocked with brook trout, also with some cutthroat trout, moderate pressure. WALK-UP (WR-55): The pamphlet states: Walk-up Lake is a classic example of a glacially-formed,

cirque lake…..sits in a deep bowl with surrounding cliffs towering a thousand feet above…..the lake. The striking lake can be reached by horseback from Papoose Lake through steep, rocky meadows. A rocky cleft also leads from Figure-Eight Lake due north to Walk-Up. Some steep climbing is involved, and you should be in half-decent shape before attempting it. Follow the base of the mountain northwest to the lake. Horse

p. 510

feed is scarce. At 11,114 ft. elevation, 18.4 acres, 55' deep, being above timberline it has an open shoreline. stocked with brook trout, with light pressure. FIGURE-EIGHT (WR-56): As described above, it is accessible from Walk-Up Lake, but from lower country, it is located on a rocky bench a few hundred yards northwest of Chepeta Lake, at 10,660 ft. elevation, 3.6 acres, 5' deep, horse access difficult, with a natural population of cutthroat trout, with light pressure.

WE'LL NOW MOVE EAST FROM CHEPETA LAKE and/or THE CHEPETA TRAILHEAD ELBOW (WR-58): Described as a picturesque lake, located at the base of a steep cliff west of Chepeta Lake. On the topographical map I roughed in a cross-country a 0.8 mile route from the Highline Trail. The pamphlet says: A no less arduous but more certain route is to follow the west shore of Chepeta Lake to the

lake's northwest corner, where Elbow Lake's outlet enters Chepeta. Traveling up the outlet is still rough going, but the odds of becoming disoriented are lessened. Found at 10,910 ft. elevation, not too horse friendly, 26 acres, 27' deep, stocked with brook trout with moderate pressure. SHARLEE (WR-57): It is located 1.9 miles from Chepeta along the trail, surrounded by meadows with open shorelines, horse friendly, at 10,740 ft. elevation, 9.4 acres, 4' deep, has a natural population of both brook and cutthroat trout, with moderate pressure. HORSESHOE (WR-67): This lake is 3 miles from Chepeta Lake at the bottom of a rocky bluff in the Reader Lakes Basin. It is 2.6 miles from the trailhead at Reader Creek. At 10,860 ft. elevation, 12 acres, 14' deep, horse friendly, stocked with cutthroat trout, with some brook trout, light to moderate pressure. READER (WR-66): Located at the head of the Reader Lakes Basin, 4.2 miles from Chepeta, and 3.8 miles from the Reader Creek Trailhead, horse friendly, at 10,960 ft. elevation, 10 acres, 10'deep, it has winterkilled in the past and not managed as a fishery, but does have trout that migrate from Reader Creek, with light pressure.

TAYLOR (WR-8): Located 6.3 miles from Chepeta, 6.7 miles from the West Fork Trailhead. See details in the West Fork Trailhead pages. DENISE (WR-9): Located 6.9 miles from Chepeta, 6.4 miles from the West Fork Trailhead. See details in the West Fork Trailhead pages.

NOW WE'LL START DOWN THE CANYON and DESCRIBE THE LAKES FOUND ON THE EAST SIDE OF THE WHITEROCKS DRAINAGE A GREAT LOOP SUGGESTION: We'll start from the Chepeta Trailhead, head again south and then east on the Highline Trail, and at about 1 mile come to a junction with Trail #049, and take it for two miles southeast to intersect with Trail #124. From there we'll go just a little south to visit first two lakes off-trail to the east, then work our way north describing 4 more lakes before getting back to the Highline Trail, and then work our way north to Whiterocks Lake, and on the way west back to the Chepeta Trailhead, visit Pearl Lake, completing our exploration of 8 lakes.. WORKMAN (WR-50): Access is described above and on the topographical map with a roughed in 0fftrail route from the trail to the lake, but the best way might be as described in the pamphlet: Once you

reach the junction ….. turn south 0.2 mile. An old jeep trail cuts off the main trail, tending upslope and southeast. Continue along this trail 0.6 miles until you cross Wolley Lake's outlet, a short distance downstream from the lake itself. Distance is about 4.1 miles from the Chepeta Trailhead, from Paradise Park

p. 511

it is 13 miles. Horse friendly. Lake at 10,460 ft. elevation, 16.3 acres, 12' deep, has natural populations of brook and cutthroat trout, pressure light to moderate.

WOOLEY (WR-40): This is a pretty lake at the head of a rough, rocky, heavily timbered basin in the East fork of the Whiterocks drainage. It is accessed cross-country 0.9 mile east of Workman Lake, 5 miles from the Chepeta Trailhead. Found at 10,680 ft. elevation, 20.5 acres, 42' deep, with a natural population of brook trout, pressure very light.

NOW WE'LL RETURN TO TRAIL #124 and to the junction with Trail #049.. TEDS (WR-44): Lies just east of Trail #124, 0.4 mile north of the junction. It is a popular lake with moderate to heavy pressure, horse friendly, found at 10,336 ft. elevation, 13.9 acres, 20' deep, stocked with brook trout, also with cutthroat trout.

SAUCER (WR-41): It is a small pond located in heavy timber at the point of the southernmost rocky ridge coming off the mountain, 0.4 mile east of Ted's Lake, following the first in a series of meadows above Ted's then up through timber to Saucer, located at 10,500 ft. elevation, 4.5 acres, 4.5' deep, may winterkill, but stocked with brook trout, with light pressure.

SAND (WR-42): It is a very shallow lake at the bottom of a talus slope 0.4 mile east of Saucer. As you come down from Saucer you come to a large meadow at the head of which is Sand Lake, 10,435 ft. elevation, horse friendly, 4.9 acres, 4.5' deep, with open meadow shorelines, with a natural population of brook trout, under light pressure. DOLLAR (WR-43): It is located 0.4 mile north of Sand Lake, accessed hiking cross-country north along the base of the rocky ridge, not too horse friendly due to rocky, timbered terrain, at 10,500 ft. elevation, 7.3 acres, 15' deep, with self-sustaining populations of brook and cutthroat trout, with light to moderate pressure.

WHITEROCKS (WR-48): Is found at the head of the drainage, 3.5 miles east of the Chepeta Trailhead on the Highline Trail. It is 5 miles by following Trail #049--that heads south one mile along the Highline Trail, that connects with Trail #124 that heads north to visit Teds, Saucer, Sand. Dollar, then to Whiterocks Lakes. It is a reservoired lake experiencing severe drawdown during the summer having the lake vary in size from 30 to 67 acres, so stocking was discontinued due the inability of the lake to overwinter fish, but the lake does have trout that migrate from the streams. So fishing pressure is light.

PEARL (WR-45):

This lake is found at the head of the Whiterocks Drainage, accessed from the Whiterocks Lake following the Highline Trail west about 1 mile, then northeast cross-country through a series of long, narrow meadows up to the lake, at 10,700 ft. elevation, 7.9 acres, 15' deep, horse friendly, stocked with cutthroat trout, and has a natural population of brook trout, under very light fishing pressure.

Back to the Highline Trail, we follow it west 3 miles to the Chepeta Trailhead. TO FINISH THIS LOOP, FOLLOW THE HIGHLINE TRAIL WEST 3 MILES TO THE CHEPETA TRAILHEAD. This would be a wonderful loop backpack of from 20-25 miles. NOW LET'S MOVE DOWN FR-110 A FEW MILES

p. 512

We soon come to our last trail marker--one we've seen already when we came up and from the sign went to the west to Hidden Lake. Now we'll go to the east, looking for Cliff Lake.

CLIFF (WR-49):

This is another impounded lake which lies at the base of a talus slope in the southeastern portion of the Whiterocks River drainage, accessed by Trail #048 as seen above, but vehicle

access is possible from the Paradise Park Campground. Follow the dirt road west past the guard station (U.S.F.S. Road #104)……..the road continues (above Johnson Creek) down the slope, eventually connecting with the jeep road along Johnson Creek (#140). The jeep road circles the west side of the bare mountain to the north and terminates at Cliff Lake, a total distance of 11.5 miles from Paradise Park. Although access by vehicle is possible, it is not recommended……the road…..extremely rough. You've got to hate your truck for this one. At 10,348 ft. elevation, 68 acres at full pool, 55' deep, horse friendly, has stocked brook, cutthroats, and Tiger trout. Fishing pressure is light. WATKINS (WR-48): This lake is found 100 yards southeast of Cliff Lake, at 10,390 ft. elevation, 18.4 acres, 36' deep, horse fee scarce, has stocked brook trout with light pressure.

JOHNSON (WR-30): Does not sustain fish life. ROCKS OF THE HIGH UINTA MOUNTAINS: The insert from Little East Fork of Blacks Fk--Squaw Pass: Rocks from there, and Henrys & Whiterocks Drainages

PREFACE

WHY WE EXPLORE

There's a biblical verse that says, "without vision the people perish." In the context of our subject, I interpret it to mean that………

Through EXPLORATION: We are taken out of the darkness of ignorance into having a greater VISION --or understanding--of the unknown, giving humanity life---a more fulfilling life. This kind of awakening through exploration is at the very heart of being human. Obviously some have this urge with greater intensity than others, for which all of us have to be grateful--as it is this impulse to EXPLORE--TAKING RISKS--ADVENTURING INTO THE UNKNOWN, that has pushed the frontiers of mankind. Of such EXPLORERS, we each have pop into our minds brave souls--who were CURIOUS about the unknown who have made a gigantic difference in our world. Christopher Columbus is one whose courage opened up new worlds for the benefit of humanity, as likewise did Louis Pasteur who dealt with an unknown world--a microscopic unseen one, opening up a new vision resulting in vastly better health and longevity for humanity. Both

p. 517

were sort of "laughed to scorn," by the supposed experts among their own people. That descriptive terminology was used with another explorer, or pioneer, who anciently was criticized by his own people for forging his way into a dangerous, mysterious area that needed spiritual discovery and development—his name was Ammon,190 another of my heroes. President Theodore Roosevelt in 1899 described such adventurous souls pushed with the impulse to explore, saying:191

In my case as a young kid, as mentioned in the PREFACE, I was impressed by the early mountain men who explored the unknown frontiers of North America-- Jedediah Smith, becoming another of my heroes.192

MY LIFE AS AN EXPLORER BEGINS Soon, Jed's life inspired me with one of my FIRST ADVENTURES as a young teenager in 1950. Along with my friend Dick Johnson, mentioned in my tongue-in-cheek JOHN WAYNE LOOKALIKE ADVENTURE. His family had a small property in the hills east of Berkeley, California, where they had a couple of horses. We would ride our bicycles the 10 miles up over the hills to the east and rode the horses some, but I was interested in exploring. So, I wandered off down along a creek that crossed the property, and noticed animal tracks concluding they were from raccoons. I was taking a correspondence course in taxidermy and needed to practice with an animal, so on another trip I had a steel jaw-trap and a can of tuna fish for bait. I was excited to follow my mountain man/trapper hero. I carefully did as I had learned from my reading, and set the trap attaching the chain to a stake I pounded deep into the ground with a rock. The next day, as we cycled back up into the hills, I started thinking, "What will I do if I have caught something?" I at least needed my dad's Browning .22 rifle, but only had my pocket knife, finally concluding I'd have to use a club. I was excited approaching the creek, and immediately noticed the terrain all messed up--and the stake had been pulled up--the trap was gone. I soon noticed the tracks of what I had caught and had escaped with my trap. IT WAS A COUGAR! 193

190

See the "The Adventure of Ammon," another of my heroes, BOOK OF MORMON, Mosiah 27,28; and Alma 17-

26 191

See President Roosevelt's complete statement at the end of this article, the above taken from a plaque in Worland, Wyoming. 192

About Jedediah Smith, see pages 2, 19, 28 and 74 of this writing.

p. 518

I felt sorry for the cougar with a trap on one paw, but yet grateful that it had escaped, as

WHAT THE HECK WOULD I HAVE DONE TO CONFRONT MY FIRST TRAPPED ANIMAL-A COUGAR? That would have been HIGH ADVENTURE, but, the point is, I had become-sort of--an EXPLORER--A MOUNTAIN MAN--JUST LIKE MY HERO, "DIAH!" In the opening photograph of this chapter from 2016, with 2,000 plus miles of backpacking/exploring the High Uintas under my belt, you see me as an 81 year old backpacker on my 3rd attempt to get to a remote lake, the highest in the state of Utah, at 12,302 feet that had been given my name, LITTLE ANDY LAKE. By the time I got to it, the weather was closing in on me, with high winds and snowflakes falling, so I didn't hang around long enough to really check it out, but decided it best to get back down to my camp before the steep, rocky terrain became wet and slippery. It looks better from up on South Kings Peak, as seen in the picture on pages 11, 76, 242 & 258, but this is the picture I took before getting out of there ahead of the storm. It doesn't appear to be much more than a puddle--but it was MY PUDDLE!

South Kings Peak, 13,512 ft. high on the left. Kings Peak, at 13,528 ft., Utah's highest on the right.

Some in the family had tried to convince me not to do that exploration in my 81st year, just as others had attempted to talk me out of doing my 27 day expedition alone in my 68th year, 13 years before. But, the powerful urge to EXPLORE and attempt to get to every nook and cranny of the High Uinta Wilderness' remote areas, and be able to share with the world, was the same kind of inclination that has made our world what it is today--even though in my case on a pretty tame level--unless considering my age. Yet my 2,000+ miles of exploring, since 2003 in the Uintas, do qualify as ADVENTURE, as they have involved elements of discomfort and even danger--although done in such a way as to be ENJOYABLE, INSPIRING and SAFE--for which I'm most grateful. That is the point of this chapter for all of my friends and readers--ENJOY SAFELY and BE INSPIRED BY THE WILDERNESS. In January 2013 the National Geographic Magazine, for its 125th Year Anniversary issue, had the theme: WHY WE EXPLORE with articles like: Heading Off to the Stars, The Wildest Place on Earth, Surviving Antarctica, and The Secret World of Microbes.

p. 519

It states that EXPLORING "……is a defining part of human identity and success," and then tells the story of Captain James Cook, British explorer who in 1769 made his first voyage crossing the Pacific and met Polynesian Priest Tupaia, who had in his head a map of all the major islands of the Pacific. His people had colonized this vast area in 300 B.C. and, without any navigational instruments, had explored and mapped the South Pacific, and Tupaia took Cook to many far off islands. Ten years later Cook was killed by Hawaiian natives and some historians at that time said, "……it brought to a close the age of exploration." Well……. NOT EXACTLY!--as the articles in the magazine describe most vividly the persistent RESTLESSNESS and CURIOSITY of man, and then examines WHAT CREATES THIS

"MADNESS?" The article goes on to explain that there are studies indicating the existence of the mutation and variant of a gene called "DRD4-7R, carried roughly by 20% of all humans that drive

curiosity and restlessness. The 7R makes people more likely to take risks; explore new places, ideas, foods, relationships, drugs or sexual opportunities and generally embrace movement, change, and adventure." In the conclusion, the writer quoted Svante Paabo, evolutionary geneticist, who said: "NO OTHER MAMMAL MOVES AROUND LIKE WE DO. THERE'S A KIND OF MADNESS TO IT." 194

I conclude my--madman--simple thoughts with President Teddy Roosevelt's speech, THE MAN IN THE ARENA, given in Paris, France on April 23, 1910.195 The Background picture is from 12,150 ft. East Fork Pass with 13,219 ft. Mt Lovenia--mountain named by famous pioneer artist/photographer & explorer, George Beard, honoring his beloved wife.

Chapter 5:

LIGHTWEIGHT, JOYFULL & SAFE BACKPACKING INTRODUCTION: Below you see me in one of the most remote and wonderful spots--up a talus slope way above the High Uinta Wilderness' deepest lake--147 feet deep CRATER LAKE found in a glacial cirque in the northern shadow of 12,708 foot high Explorer Peak. You can't get here in your All-Wheel drive SUV, nor in your ATV, or mountain bike, neither on your horse………

…….YOUR ONLY OPTION IS TO SHOULDER A BACKPACK, HIKE ABOUT 20 MILES, THEN CLIMB CAREFULLY & BE REWARDED WITH

THE GLORIOUS MAGIC OF THE MOUNTAINS Could there be ……. A GLITCH IN THIS WONDROUS MAGIC? Another memory pops into my mind, when on my 2003--27 day Expedition. I was moving east along the Highline Trail when a large group of Boy Scouts came towards me. I courteously stepped off the trail, greeting them, and began observing the unforgettable scene. The boy breaking trail was excitedly bounding up the trail with a warm smile as he said, "Hi!" Others similarly excited about their outdoor experience followed, and then there were increasingly larger gaps between the 14 backpackers as some were struggling--the smiles degenerating into serious grimaces, then down to nasty scowls, with their adult leader patiently bringing up the rear--riding herd on the stragglers. I'll never forget the last boy--a little chubby, with a bulky disarrayed looking backpack as though hoping to lose some of his load. No hint of a smile, nor with enough energy to say hello. He seemed to be muttering naughty words under his breath describing his misery,

and swearing his determination--if he made it to civilization, to never go backpacking again! As I continued east for 206 miles--I swore that part of my objective in my HIGH UINTAS WILDERNESS PROJECT would be to help change for many that misery to….

"man is that he might have JOY!"

p. 521

But, not to be misleading, if ADVENTURE is what we are after, we must remember that an experience to qualify is most likely going to involve elements of DANGER, DISCOMFORT

& PAIN. To put up with that we have to be able to COMPENSATE by also WAKING UP and NOTICING details around us that give us the JOY of DISCOVERY, and ACCOMPLISHMENT, and awakens in us a spirit of APPRECIATION and INSPIRATION--that far outweigh the danger, discomfort and pain. We have to focus on the positive--be it the blessing of life and being on the trail--knowing that if we persist we will become stronger, reducing the discomfort and pain, and let in the exhilaration of discovery, plus the inspiration of seeing at every turn the beauties of the Creator: The incredible variety of rocks, wildflowers, mushrooms, lichens, wildlife, and even the fantastic--beyond belief--coloration of dead trees and much more that I have called the VISIONS OF NATURE a few examples of the thousands we see below.

TURNING THE PAIN & DISCOMFORT >> INTO PLEASURE & INSPIRATION On my website I created a number of posts that I called photo/essays to help turn the misery into enjoyment, like: HOW I DO A THREE DAY BACKPACK,196 WHERE DO I GET SO MUCH ENERGY,197 and combining those two into one--simply entitled, 2018 198 GEAR/SUPPLEMENTS. Then a detailed article, THE ANTI-AGING CHALLENGE.199 196
