In 2017, near the conclusion of my Project, I launched myself into the Grandaddy Basin to explore and photograph two named lakes that had escaped me, Range & Jeff. On the first leg of my exploration I was resting on Hades Pass when a father, and his daughter stopped and asked if I would do them the favor of taking their picture, which I happily did, you see below, that turned gratefully into another of those coincidental experiences that are the spice

of life!

As I approached them, all of a sudden Terry recognized me and surprised me, saying,

"You're Cordell Andersen! Thanks for your ANTI-AGING CHALLENGE, article. My father downloaded all 26 pages of it and it has helped make possible us hiking together again!" Doug Coats, elaborated on what his daughter had said, and two more High Uinta Friends were added to my long and cherished list. Hearing that my efforts were producing results--even if just for only a father and his daughter, energized me and had me bouncing down the trail…...well, at least as much as could be expected from an 81 year old explorer. On my way back from the successful exploration--as I was climbing back up to Hades Pass, all of a sudden a couple stopped me, saying,

"Hey, you're Cordell Andersen. Thanks a million for your website, and your guidance about HOW TO DO A 3 DAY BACKPACK. Because of your simple suggestions, we are on our very first backpack!" It was Clay Barrett and his wife, you see below--and importantly, they were both smiling.

p. 523

As I was saying goodbye to the Barretts, and about to head up the trail, I was stopped again hearing, "Hey, Cordell, we appreciate your website and all your updates," and another conversation ensued with brothers, Brent and Jeff Benson, seen below.

As I have become a backpacker/explorer, increasingly more mature--I don't want to admit being "old" yet—but, I have to admit it is getting just a tiny bit harder, and it's great to meet on the trail such people who I have helped a little--to experience the MAGIC OF THE

MOUNTAINS.

TRYING HARD TO HELP OTHERS FOR SIXTY YEARS In my youth, before going off in 1967 to do what I could to help the Mayans in Guatemala for 35 years, I worked with Explorer Scouts along with buddy, Ted Packard. We did our best to teach our group of 23 how to enjoyably backpack, and even worked with them during the winter to make some of their gear, like backpacks. Then in the summers we took them on two weeks of high adventure in the Uintas. After Ted left to continue his higher education, I continued for a while making myself available to Boy Scout groups learn how to backpack enjoyably and economically. I would show up at the invitations dressed for the mountains--shouldering my backpack--as though ready to head for the high country. I would then carefully unpack and show them exactly what I would use for a backpack, including the food. It was very satisfying to know I was helping a few, if not many. This chapter will likewise--SHOW HOW I DO IT.

NOW BACK TO THE PRESENT & THE CULMINATION OF SUCH DESIRES. In my 2018 GEAR/SUPPLEMENT photo/essay, I show a couple of the well known books on the subject, I'll insert below.

p. 524

So, if you really need and want to get into all the nitty-gritty details, these books and others will give you great information, but in my opinion, it really doesn't have to be that complicated. The very description of what we are after--LIGHT WEIGHT BACKPACKING, indicates to me that we have to SIMPLIFY and reduce it all down to the MINIMUM. I'll do it mainly with photographs--A PHOTO/ESSAY--which is my entire book, that we can all easily understand--with a minimum of effort--each photograph WORTH A THOUSAND WORDS!

MAYBE A GOOD PLACE TO START……IS EMPHASIZING SOME OF THE DUMB THINGS I HAVE DONE IN MY LEARNING PROCESS On a Family Backpack in 2005, my boys, Jesse, Lito & Rich had fun showing me they had learned from my writings about my first backpack in 1952 when me and buddies stupidly struggled up Hades Canyon in the dark carrying a watermelon, quarts of Hires Root Beer in glass bottles, and cans of Pork & Beans--described in the PREFACE. Next up: A GIANT SLEEPING BAG! -- Below is a 1952 picture of Ted and me at the cross trail junction at the head of Yellowstone Canyon, on our 14 day backpack traversing the entire High Uintas Primitive Area. The insert on the left is the famous sleeping bag.

I did the best I could under my financial circumstances, using World War II used gear that saw action fighting against the Japanese in the Pacific. First, a heavy rucksack--that at least pulled back on my shoulders keeping me from being a hunchback, but required extra energy and weighed too much, as well as having me perilously unbalanced in dangerous mountaineering situations. The Army surplus sleeping bag--shown inserted on the left,

weighed a whopping 9 lbs., and was used in my first backpack in 1952, but later I carefully saved enough to get a down sleeping bag for the backpack in the picture. With the 9 lb. bag I wouldn't have had enough space in my rucksack for food! I was also wearing a heavy, leather jacket that had to weigh 4-5 lbs. and then, to look like an outdoorsman, I had on my waist the traditional sheath knife. If you are thinking all of that sounds fine, keep all of that

p. 525

in mind as we explore light weight, minimalist alternatives--which has me now smiling a lot at how mentally challenged I was in my early attempts to appear to be an outdoor BADASS!

LIGHTWEIGHT BACKPACKING SHOULD BE REALLY SIMPLE. Everything I suggest here is based totally on my own experience over many years, and has application to backpacking almost anywhere. THIS WILL BE A LOT SIMPLER THAN HAVING TO GO THROUGH ENTIRE THICK BOOKS THAT HAVE NO COLOR PHOTOS!

You'll notice I cut something out of the above title….which we will get to as item #3-Gear/Supplements, in the THREE STEPS, when I'll insert the complete title.

So, let's get started and learn how to get to the high country in a way that is ENJOYABLE and INSPIRING -- having an experience we will want to do again many times.

THE LOGICAL ORDER OF PREPARATION Let's try and put the process in a logical order that can help us from becoming:

[The] "…. chubby [Boy Scout], with a bulky disarrayed looking backpack ……….[with] No hint of a smile, nor with enough energy to say hello, [who] seemed to be muttering naughty words under his breath describing his misery, and swearing his determination--if he made it to civilization, to never go backpacking again!"

THREE STEPS My first impulse was to launch myself into describing the EQUIPMENT/GEAR needed, and quite frankly in this writing, I already did that with about 27 pages created, including describing some of my experience to show graphically the life and death importance of a few items, but the other two steps are critical for us to do something about--FIRST. They are: 1. AVOID BEING THE "CHUBBY…BACKPACKER…MUTTERING NAUGHTY WORDS" -ACCOMPLISHED BY BEING IN GOOD PHYSICAL SHAPE and, 2. RESEARCH WHERE YOU'RE GOING, PLOT YOUR COURSE & HAVE TOPOGRAPHICAL MAPS FOR YOUR TRIP. Then will come item #3 3. EQUIPMENT & GEAR

p. 526

THE FIRST POINT…..YOU'VE GOT TO START WORKING ON NOW! 1. "……[NOT] BEING THE "CHUBBY…BACKPACKER…MUTTERING NAUGHTY WORDS" --

DONE BY BEING IN GOOD PHYSICAL SHAPE & MAINTAIN IT FOREVER

NOTE: I realize we are all individuals and vary a lot in what each has to do to GET & KEEP IN SHAPE. For example, even though I was supposedly the athleteon the football team, etc., my original--and still--backpacking buddies, Ted Packard and Charlie Peterson, were always better backpackers than I was. Now, all in our eighties, I have to work-out every day to feel good, be able to put my socks on, and not feel like my body is freezing up. But, Ted is too busy professionally to do that, and still beats me--except maybe in pushups and situps. Others, might have to do a lot more than I do to just keep from being a couch potato, as most my age are. So, glean from my experience whatever you have to so as to NEVER GIVE IN…..EASILY!

AN EXAMPLE: MY 27 DAY, NO RE-SUPPLY, EXPEDITION My preparation began many years before leaving the Highline Trailhead and heading east. During my 35 years of working in Guatemala I once in a while remembered the vow I had made back in my first years in the Uintas--that, before leaving this life I would:

"Explore, photograph, and report on all of the High Uintas Primitive Area." During those years in Guatemala I envisioned that to do that I would make one gigantic effort of exploration with a backpack of three or four weeks. To do so I would need to be very strong. INSERTED BELOW IS A PICTURE OF WHEN THAT EXPEDITION STARTED IN 2003

You see me with 81 pounds of load: A backpack, plus camera waist pack, and an additional waist pack for my .45 Colt Defender, with a special pocket for my satellite phone. Down the trail a mile or so from the Highline Trailhead I added 2 lbs. of water, my total load then weighed 83 lbs. as I headed east. How the heck did I ever manage that? Read below what I did to be ready to do it.

p. 527

NOTE: Later, after accomplishing my challenge, at an REI lecture in Salt Lake City I was criticized and made fun of by a famous through/marathon backpacker--for my heavy load, but I pointed out to him that my expedition was "no re-supply," not as backpackers like he did. They carefully plan their trips to be able to drop by a town every 3 or 4 days, where a package awaits them with clean clothes, and another 3 or 4 days of food--and then in that box mail back their dirty clothes to be washed and sent to them in a town up ahead somewhere, along with more food.

On the other hand on my back and around my waist I had everything needed for almost any emergency, including 27 days of food you'll see a picture of in the EQUIPMENT SECTION of this chapter. I also had the SUPPLEMENTS I needed, including 5 lbs. of a powdered RECOVERY supplement to be able to do the equivalent of a half marathon or more every day--this is no exaggeration when considering carrying a heavy load, at elevations over 10,500 ft. I had to RECOVER to do it the next day, and the next, etc. I of course also had my professional photo equipment, including 35 roles of color transparency film, etc. Later I will confess how I could have reduced my load by at least 10-20 lbs. or more. NOTE: Pay attention to what I did….and still do--GETTING & KEEPING IN SHAPE-- to be able to backpack enjoyably, even with heavy loads. and not be the "Chubby….…..muttering kid." To do so takes time, so needs to be worked on months--and even years in advance of actually rounding up your equipment and heading for the trailhead. I RETELL BRIEFLY MY EXPERIENCE--because whether you are young or old--SOME ASPECT OF MY EXPERIENCE WILL LIKELY HAVE APPLICATION SOMETIME DURING YOUR LIFE. In Guatemala my gym was the great outdoors as I always loved to work, and so I kept real busy working alongside my Mayan brothers and sisters, helping to load and unload 100 lb. bags of feed, fertilizer, etc. Additionally my mom had given me her "green thumb," so I always insisted on working every day along with my kids in our vegetable and fruit gardens-and that wasn't just a few months a year, but we would plant, harvest and then repeat it during the 12 month growing season--with never ending harvests and work.

NOTE: The Foundation mentioned in the book that eventually helped us with altruistic projects, paid no wages, nor living allowance, to any of us--I was literally a "true believer" and volunteer for 50 years--so we all worked and supported ourselves with our sweat--and loved it! BUT, THE FIRST OF MANY GLITCHES began messing up the plan when about 10 years into my Guatemalan adventure I had all my workers trained, and my role was reduced to office work, complicated by some puzzlingly depressing opposition and family setbacks that were converting me into a kind of chubby guy with heart and other health problems. Embarrassingly an elderly visitor commented how out of breath I was when just going up a few stairs or a tiny hill! I was only around 40 years old! I started checking on my heart and noticed it would actually STOP BEATING for 3 or 4 seconds a few times every minute.

I WOKE UP!

p. 528

I exchanged a regular sized plate for a small pie plate, not piling on the food, nor filling it twice, and started jogging for the first time in my life--just 1/2 mile the first day--WHICH ALMOST KILLED ME! I also renewed my admiration for my youthful hero, Jedediah Smith, and another, an "ancient American," whose example I was trying to follow in my Guatemalan adventure--whose name was Ammon.

MY HEROES JUST DIDN'T GIVE UP, and I COULDN'T EITHER! So, I persisted, increasing the jogging distance a little every day, losing some weight, and became the inventor of an exercise program--copied (tongue-in-cheek) by Sylvester Stallone a few years later in his movie, ROCKY IV! With my chain saw I'd cut down a large pine tree, and saw it up into 18" lengths, then using a heavy sledge hammer/ax and wedge, chop firewood every day for 30 minutes. By two weeks I'd lost some weight, my jog was getting longer, we had mountains of great firewood, and……my irregular heart beat had gone away. I wasn't depressed anymore either and I was raring to go on ALL FRONTS! Those suckers who opposed a good work I was doing now had me more determined than ever in every aspect of my somewhat controversial and dangerous life. Sorry about using the perhaps disrespectful term, suckers , to describe an actually quite educated and sophisticated opposition. One definition of that sort of slang word is "people who are easily deceived ," which was happening. Maybe there’s a more respectful word in the Thesaurus--I found one that is softer: innocent. They had been misinformed, believed what they were told, and just didn't know fully what they were doing, putting too much trust in information passed on to them and were clearly not clairvoyant.

Eventually, when 58, I started participating in an International Half-Marathon in our remote Coban area that became very popular with Guatemalans, Kenyans, and people from all over the world.

Eventually, by 2005, on the front of my T-shirt I had the Guatemalan Foundation's logo, and on the back me, representing the High Uintas Wilderness Project, stating,

"Fighting to Become a Cancer & Heart Attack Survivor."

p. 529

By the time I started my High Uintas Wilderness Project in 2003, I had done that race 10 consecutive times. Afterwards, on annual supervisory trips to Guatemala for the Guatemalan Foundation, I continued doing the race for a total of 14 times--until the financial disaster in 2008-09 stopped my trips to Guatemala. BACK TO MY GUATEMALAN PREPARATION FOR THE UINTAS, as explained previously in the PREFACE--with more detail--on pages 8-10, during my last years in Guatemala I began hiking around the rolling hills of our farm with a 100 lb. bag of fertilizer on my shoulders, gradually working up to doing 4 miles two or three times a week. Also during that period I began researching supplements that hopefully would help me overcome some of my problems, slow down some the aging process, give me the energy I needed, and make possible quick recovery after long workouts, races, and of critical importance back in Utah--recover every day on my expedition and long backpacks, as the next day I had to do another 10+ miles. So when the expedition came in 2003, when I was 67 years old, I was able to handle the 83 lbs. of load.

KNOW YOURSELF, KEEP IN SHAPE & MEET THE ………

Prior to that expedition, some of my children, especially two of my daughters--Registered Nurses, insisted on me getting a "complete physical" which I had never had. But--surprise, I was stubborn, and believed that with years of preparation, it was enough for me to do several experimental backpacks to see how I did, how I felt, and make my own decision.

NOTE: The truth was, I suspected that any reputable physician, worth his salt who examined me--knowing what I was going to attempt, would recommend me not doing it. So, I didn't risk that, and went forward, which to be honest I wouldn't recommend for anybody else--unless willing to follow my example getting in shape, and then take all the precautions I take, explained in Survival articles like that of Eric Robinson on pages 156-159, repeated on pages 343-350, and explained in detail in this chapter. So, in July 2003 I went up the South Fork of Rock Creek, and bushwhacked my way up past Arta and Survey lakes to the East Grandadday Mountain saddle. My curiosity in this spot was aroused on reading Jeffrey and Brad Probst's book, HIGH UINTAS BACKCOUNTRY, where it was simply said about the saddle, "WHAT A VIEW." That was an understatement as you should have noticed pictures from up there of Grandaddy Lake have been used repeated times in this book, like on page 1, etc. Thanks, Jeff and Brad, for arousing my

curiosity about that most inspiring spot in the Uintas, and for that being my amazing first exploration in the new millennium, and of this Project.

p. 530

I did two more exploratory trips into the Grandaddies--one from the Rock Creek Trailhead, and another from the Grandview Trailhead, and became convinced I was physically and mentally ready for the expedition. On that long backpack I carried what I would need for any emergency, and fulfilled my objective. THEN……..….I WENT IN FOR THE COMPLETE PHYSICAL. That began my history of many glitches that had to be solved over the next 15 years--almost always during the winters: Two cancer surgeries, two radiation treatments, chemotherapy several times for skin cancer, then………

……..7 more surgeries to repair, reconstruct, and/or to remove body parts that were holding me back, along with solving myself metatarsalitis on the balls of my feet (diagnosed in 1994

by a rheumatologist in Guatemala who advised me not to do half-marathons or backpack anymore), and peripheral neuropathy of my feet. And, with the problem of High Altitude Sickness--I have coped with since 2003, I finally learned how to manage it. Now, in 2018 with worsening complications—that come with the aging process, which story I'll tell in Appendix 4 and 5. All of that in addition to miraculously being saved from a heart attack, and overcoming another kind of irregular heart beat--a stuttering one--gone after a few years of my HIGH UINTAS WILDERNESS PROJECT. NOTE: I believe it went away after being

miraculously saved from a heart attack, told on pages 250-255.

After one of the surgeries--to reconstruct my "football ankle" with a tendon transplant, plus 3 titanium screws to hold it together, the kids came home to find me on the floor and were about to call 911 and the Mortuary, but then noticed me softly snoring, so got out the camera for a great photo shoot--thanks Jesse!

The above event happened the day I came home from my ankle surgery. For pain I was prescribed Percocet (oxycodone), an opioid (narcotic) pain reliever, and to help me sleep,

p. 531

Ambien. For whatever reasons I fainted. The combination of these two medications created some funny events and others, not so funny.

The hilarious one was that night, a Thursday, when at 11:00 PM, my kids came in my room, like to--see if I was still alive and say goodnight, but found me attempting to put my suit pants on over the cast, which of course was impossible. But I was determined and had somehow ripped open the pant leg to get it over the cast. Then seeing that the kids weren't dressed and ready to go to Sunday morning Church with me, I got very upset. They had an impossible time trying to convince me it was Thursday night, rather than Sunday morning! During my recovery I became addicted to the opioid, and the Ambien, and to make it worse I became very sick--like with the flu, and it went on for months with nothing giving me relief. Eventually I got on my computer and discovered on the internet that sometimes the combination of those two drugs created a secondary effect in a few people "like flu." I was already only taking the two at night, but immediately began cutting back and soon went cold turkey, resulting in me going through a week of hell, unable to sleep.

NOTE: My recovery that year, in 2007, to be able to backpack required intensive effort, but I gratefully made 9 backpacks that summer: Notch Pass, Grandaddies, Salamander Lake, Middle Fk. of Blacks Fork, East Grandaddy Saddle, Red Castle, and the Family Backpack to the Grandaddies, plus climbing Bald Mountain and bivouacking right on the peak for a great moon photo shoot.

On subsequent surgeries I never let that addiction happen again.

2. RESEARCH WHERE YOU'RE GOING, PLOT YOUR COURSE & HAVE TOPOGRAPHICAL MAPS FOR YOUR TRIP. You have to do a little research, PRIMARILY from this book, but also from DWR publications, other books, the internet and using the National Geographic CD/Rom collection for topographical maps. Every adventurer should have this for areas of interest. For most purposes the topo maps in this book should suffice, just print the one you need, or you can do your own with this NG set. You can also get topographical maps at the Forest Service offices in Kamas, Duchesne, Vernal, Evanston and Mt. View, Wyo. See the Appendix for contact info. CONCERNING AVAILABILITY: NGS doesn’t list it anymore, and AMAZON says: “Currently unavailable. We don't know when or if this item will be back in stock”

I noticed used ones available on E-Bay

p. 536

Do your homework and research the area you're going to explore, in this book--that hopefully will be sufficient, but check others out too--including a Google search of your target area. The basic map, a must, is the National Geographic HIGH UINTAS WILDERNESS MAP, you can get at outdoor outlets, or on Amazon. Another option is the Forest Service Wilderness Map--very good, BUT HUGE. Then print the topographical maps you'll need plotting your route--and leave copies with family and/or friends (or online like I do) so it will be clear where you're going and your schedule. Sometimes it's good also to go to Google Earth and zero in on your area and even print if you feel you might need it--especially if going off-trail to remote areas. Some of the DWR pamphlets are still available, but now expensive--like collector's items, but hopefully soon all will be updated. NOTE: I had to pay $15.99 to get the one on the Ashley Creek

area, acquired through Amazon, but coming from someone in Texas. There was a time when I had a large printer doing 13" x 19" maps that I would waterproof with Clear Covering, then roll up and take with in varnished paper towel rolls like you see below. The point is have good maps and know about the area you're going into.

p. 537

Next we will study #3 --EQUIPMENT & GEAR But first let's just see a picture emphasizing how important backpacking can be for you and your loved ones.

A GREAT FAMILY ACTIVITY -- A SPORT

In 2007 I was back on the Grandaddy Trail and just after leaving the Trailhead met this wonderful family --THE PHILLIPS, and soon in the conversation learned they had visited in Guatemala, and even named their daughter, in the middle of the three, Eva QUETZAL, the quetzal being Guatemala's National Bird…..seen inserted in a typical embroidered textile. They represent well the many such families I have met on the trail--all part of the great group of HIGH UINTA FRIENDS. In 2005 I started my annual FAMLY BACKPACK, with just a small group, that I put on the cover of our Family Calender for 2006.

Below another of our Family Backpacks, with three families represented, me taking them into the Grandaddies.

Once I get the book finished, I'll do my best to get back to this great activity. But for the book, let's now get into the nitty-gritty of LIGHTWEIGHT BACKPACKING. *********************************

p. 539

(photos / maps — no text on this page)

p. 540

Of course we also need food, and here it is--but needs to be compacted--minimalized. You should notice that nearly everything is inexpensive, bought at the supermarket. Missing from this picture: A gallon of dehydrated eggs I use a lot of, also available in most supermarkets.

NOW, LET'S GET INTO THE SPECIFIC SIMPLIFICATION OF ALL OF THIS It takes a little time, but I get highly organized before leaving for the trailhead, putting breakfasts, lunches, and dinners in individual meal-sized bags. Breakfasts and lunches require no cooking, just add water in shaker bottles. The main course for dinner will require cooking, plus an instant pudding, eggnog, and recovery drinks, just add water and shake. IMPORTANTLY….I DON'T GO TO THE MOUNTAINS TO COOK & DO DIRTY DISHES

Above we see all of my food for a 6 day backpack. Might as well insert next a photo of all the food for my 27 day expedition, mentioned in the Preface & Introduction. Included are spices, sauces and salt used in some dinners, and for fish I cook using aluminum foil.

p. 541

I had an additional 7 -8 lbs. of supplements & recovery items. Below is a view of food preparation using my one pot, and what I call shaker bottles. The pot has a macaroni meal with bacon bits added, next on the right, a chocolate instant pudding, then a calcium/magnesium/HGH stimulator drink taken just before going to sleep, then a couple of recovery drinks; Below on the left: Eggnog, and then my breakfast for the next morning put to soak. Before getting all of this ready to add water, I put my GravityWorks water filter/purification system working, and will now add water to everything & shake. The prime recovery drink will be drank immediately. The macaroni dinner will be left to soak to require less cooking, and I'll now set up my shelter, and then go fishing!

p. 542

NOW WE'LL DEAL WITH WHAT BACKPACKERS CALL:

THE BASIC PACK

Those experts include pack, pad, bag & shelter, as though they don't need anything else. I heard of one who didn't need anything for cooking but did his entire Thru Backpacking Trip eating Snickers chocolate bars. Hope you're not disappointed with me, but I'm not that dedicated to the "sport," and rather need a few other creature comforts and so I call it

BASIC EQUIPMENT #1

p. 543

THE BACKPACK: A few pages back we saw a family backpacking--the Phillips family, the 3 girls have exterior frame backpacks: An aluminum frame with a bag for gear attached, and usually a space below to tie on a tent or whatever. They are usually inexpensive, and large versions are capable of carrying heavy loads. The Phillips parents, rather have interior frame backpacks which are the most popular now days. Mine, pictured above is an interior

frame backpack. If you've followed my efforts since 2003, you'll have noticed that I began with an REI Morning Star interior frame backpack, but over the 16 years have tried others in an effort to find more efficient, and lighter weight backpacks. I've tried some very light ones, 1 pound or so, but with the relatively heavy loads I carry for long backpacks, the suspension systems--for very light packs, were uncomfortable and just didn't work. Then, back in 2015 OSPREY-which packs were usually heavier than others, came out with a revolutionary suspension system that just wrapped around your body and became like a part of you to the point of not even feeling it was there. So, in spite of it weighing about the same as my heavier than normal Morning Star, I went for it and am so pleased that all the new, improved packs developed every year since, don't interest me at all--so, like for the duration, my choice is the OSPREY ATMOS 65 liter AG backpack. I'll insert some photos of it below. The female model is called AURA. By the way "AG" means "anti'gravity." There are also other colors. As it hugs your back, total ventilation is given, and there are no pressure points, so you pretty well don’t feel anything. It includes a rain cover, and that and the top lid—with its two large pockets, can be removed for shorter backpacks, and reduce the weight by more than 1 lb. Since, other models have been developed. For most backpacks of 3-6 days, loads will be quite light and can be handled adequately with very light weight, inexpensive backpacks like the exterior frame ones. SLEEPING BAG….or QUILT: For many years I have used my mummy sleeping bag as a quilt, laying down on the pad or mattress, and just putting my feet in the end of the bag, and spreading it over me without using the zipper. For me it is much more comfortable. A few years ago I actually bought a Golite Quilt good down to 20 degrees, and only weighing 15 oz. You see me using it below.

p. 544

I have used it for 4 years. It's good down to 20 degrees and called: Golite UltraLite 3Season Quilt that weighs 15 oz. You see it covering me in the above photo. Note: When

cold I use a stocking cap as I can’t stand covering my head as most do with mummy bags. Golite doesn’t exist anymore but now several companies offer Quilts, one being ENLIGHTENED EQUIPMENT/Revelation weighing 19 oz. with a variety of options for size, length, color and temperature. I’ll insert a photo below, of the down version. As mentioned you lay down on your sleeping pad or air mattress….with no need of anything else to insulate you from the ground, then put your feet in the bottom and spread it over you. I'll insert below a picture of one of the sleeping quilts available.

The QUILT is laid over the top of you, with feet in the closed end. BELOW IS SEEN THE EVOLUTION OF MY SLEEPING SYSTEM STARTING BACK IN 1952

First, from 1952 the 9 lb. World War II bag used for a year;

then, After the World War II bag, I finally woke up and got a down sleeping bag I don't have a picture of; 2nd, from 2003 a NORTH FACE Blue Kazoo down bag weighing 3 lbs; 3rd, an REI Sub-Kilo Down sleeping bag weighing 2 lbs., and last, my Golite UltraLite 3-Season Quilt that weighs 15 oz. The three are all in compression sacks reducing the bulk.

p. 545

THE SLEEPING PAD: (or air mattress) Whether you use a mummy sleeping bag, or a sleeping quilt, you will need for your comfort and warmth some good insulation under you. Below you can see the packed up sleeping pads I have used since 2003.

All of these pads are from Therm-A-Rest. From the left the maroon and orange ones are especially for minimalist backpackers, measuring 20″x 48″. Thickness is 3/4″ and 1.5″. The 3/4" pad is for the real believers, but after ’03 I went to 1.5″ thick for greater comfort. The 48" length means you have to use your pack or something to insulate your legs from the cold ground. By 2005 I decided I needed greater comfort so the flaming pink one, 66″ long, my exact length, and 1.5" thick became necessary as I began using my bag laid over me like a quilt, laying directly on the pad. Most of us, as we grow older, have more difficulty sleeping, and so need more in a sleeping pad rather than less. NOTE: In addition to the thicker pad, I also needed from the

beginning--since I sleep on my side--digging a hip hole (that I dutifully fill in afterwards to “Leave No Trace.”). The young gun “marathon backpackers” can perhaps sleep soundly on a rock, or a very thin, short pad, but NOT ME. To go with their gear I would also need a sackfull of Ambien tablets! The TINY YELLOW one on the far right is the one I have used since 2011. It is a Therm-aRest NeoAir Air Mattress that is 20″x 72″x2.5″ thick–just what I need for greater comfort. As you can see it is also very compact, and only weighs 12 oz. compared to 22 oz. for the pink one. It is pricy, but for me well worth it. It can be punctured as happened one miserable night on the Garfield Basin Trail when I had to survive on the cold ground. Luckily my repair kit had what I needed to repair it the next day. Over these 8 years it did go flat on me one other time, and I went to work at 1:00 AM to find the problem, inflating it a lot, and then as I put pressure on it running my hand over it I luckily found the leak and fixed it. A repair kit is an essential, so don't forget to get one-that is worth its weight in gold.

p. 546

NOW FOR THE SHELTER For a couple of years I used an REI tent for 2 people, as I liked to have inside with me all my gear, but I eventually went for a lighter tent, always one with a floor, and mosquito netting. The one I've used in recent years is the one pictured with my BASIC EQUIPMENT #1 graphic: A BIG AGNES Fly Creek UL 1, that weighs 2 lbs. 3 oz.. It is very narrow, actually a sort of glorified bivy bag, except that you can sit up in it, get dressed, have some needed gear along each side, and a vestibule large enough for your pack to be protected. Even as short as I am it is hard to turn around inside, so you have to back into it. The basic tent with just netting is free standing, seen below on the left. Then the rain canopy is installed using stakes, seen on the right.

Being free standing, you can position it prior to installing the rain canopy and putting in the stakes. On taking it down, in the free standing state, you can shake out any debris it might have, and even hang it up to dry if needed. Once packed up it makes a small package seen on the right to fit into your pack. I'm not trying to promote this tent, just explain my experience. I must say that the model that opens to the side, would be much better. There are many good tents available, the good ones quite pricey, but I'm rather moving to a more minimalist position, as I'll explain next. Big Agnes just came out with a new 2 man tent only weighing 1 lbs.-7oz. but it costs around $849. A one man version weighs 1 lb. 5 oz. and costs $799. For me ridiculous prices.

ANOTHER OPTION FOR A SHELTER A lean-to, using your rain poncho. I put grommets all around the edge making possible flexibility. Then use my lightweight bivy bag.

My rain poncho is used (which you take anyway--so its weight is not included in the shelter category), along with a waterproof bivy bag--mine with mosquito netting–it weighs 14 oz.

p. 547

saving nearly one lb. in weight compared to my tent. Best to take along a few aluminum stakes, and a bunch of nylon rope as seen in the pictures, included in the bivy weight. The poncho pictured is Golite, but now I have an REI poncho. As mentioned, I install grommets all around the edges so I can set it up in a variety of ways, such as seen below.

If my present COMEBACK works, all my backpacking during the 2019 season--in my 84th year will be done with this as my shelter.

NOTE: To be effective you should use the semi-protection of trees or boulders/rocks from wind and weather. You have to be careful as wind can turn it into a sail and you're in trouble. Mosquitoes are not a problem with me as insect repellants are very effective, and usually the cool to cold nights have the mosquitoes go away anyway.

p. 548

ANOTHER POINT: I have many times during the nights heard some animal moving outside my tent, but had no way of knowing what it was, but with this shelter you can see what's around you—at least on three sides. IMPORTANTLY: Pepper spray for bears could be effective with this system, but….. From inside a tent? The spray would hurt YOU, not the bear.

PONCHO, WATERPROOF WINDBREAKER & PANTS We've already dealt with the poncho, except to say that you need one long in the back so it will cover your backpack--unless you have a waterproof cover for your backpack, like you see me with below. A picture of the packed up waterproof pants is inserted, below.

The above picture is on my successful exploration of Little Andy Lake in late August, 2016. As I was crossing the Painter Basin moving towards Gunsight Pass, the weather began closing in on me. I stopped quickly, put on my waterproof pants, warm jacket with

p. 549

waterproof rain parka on top, put my photo waist pack inside my backpack, and covered the pack with its rain cover--not needing my poncho--although if the rain was intense the poncho might also have been a good idea. The waterproof pants: Mine weigh a bit more than normal--10 oz., because they have heavy duty zippered legs to be able to put them on without taking off your footgear, and also have pockets--a very worthwhile feature. Early and late in the season I usually take them in case of extra cool weather, and greater possibility of rain or snow. Of course lighter weight and more compactable versions are available. Back to the exploration: Dressed for cold, wet/snowy weather, and, with my waterproof down gloves on, I continued my hike as rain and snow fell, and made it fine up over the pass and down to the first water in the Henry's Fork Basin, and easily set up my tent and snuggled in. I wasn't able to cook dinner, but I had meals that didn't require cooking and so got through the night in great shape, awakened at 6:00 AM in freezing temperatures and made my satellite phone call report to KSL OUTDOORS RADIO, and a bit later was welcomed by a warm sun.

NOW THE CRITICAL ITEM OF WATER Below you see me having hiked a hundred yards from my camp to get water using my Platypus bucket. I have on my waterproof rain parka and windbreaker, mentioned above.

I'll take the water back to my camp and there do the necessary treatment.

p. 550

We now find a WARNING everywhere GIARDIA200

BACK IN THE OLD DAYS we had never heard about Giardia, and didn't seem to know about danger from drinking water from the springs, streams and lakes of the Uintas, and I don't recall getting this intestinal infection--even though the incubation period is at least 15 days, so if we got sick, we didn't blame it on the Uintas, but rather because of getting back to civilization. THE 2003 EXPEDITION Once back from my 35 years working in Guatemala in 2002, I began preparing for my High Uintas Wilderness Project and backpacking during the summer of 2003. I reconnected with REI--Recreation Equipment Incorporated, where I had many years before become a member of the cooperative when it was just in Seattle, Washington. In my visits to their store in Salt Lake City, I began learning about all the new equipment, and heard the word giardia--the beaver fever, and became aware of water purification systems--pumps/filters and purification tablets. But, my backpacks were going to be in the high country, above 10,000 feet, and beavers were only found in lower country along the streams leading to where I would be. So, I didn't worry about it, yet heard from Fish & Game people (sorry, I mean DWR: Division of Wildlife Resources), that we had to worry about giardia all over the Uintas. So, I at least bought a bunch of purification tablets. Once on the trail I tried the two systems recommended: Purification tablets, and boiling for 20 minutes. But, I hated the taste of chlorine from the tablets, and likewise hated the taste

200

https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/giardia-infection/symptoms-causes/syc20372786?utm_source=Google&utm_medium=abstract&utm_content=Giardiasis&utm_campaign=Knowledgepanel

p. 551

of smoky tasting water. Besides I figured I would need about two gallons of water a day, and to boil that much with my single quart sized titanium pot would be impossible. So, from the second day of my expedition, I just chose carefully the best water sources available filling all my containers, and continued doing that for the entire expedition and never got sick during, or after the backpack. Yet, during the off season preparing for the 2004 season, researching the DWR pamphlets and Jeff and Brad Probst's book, HIGH UINTAS BACKCOUNTRY of Utah, I kept reading about the dangers of giardia, and decided I'd best get what was popular at the time: A PURIFICATION/FILTER PUMP.

I tried one for a few years, and then tried another, hoping for better, easier efficiency, but quite frankly I didn't like either, and hoped someone would come up with something better. Someone then came up with another system which sounded good:

THE SQUEEZE SYSTEM

I used this system for 2013, even trying to make it work easily by sitting on it--which sounded pretty easy, but I ended up not liking it either--and WAITED FOR THE ULTIMATE! *********************************************

p. 552

THE ULTMATE….FINALLY

THE GRAVITY-WORKS SYSTEM So, for 2014 I had the new GRAVITY SYSTEM and,,,,, WOW! So I picture below my use of it from 2014 to the present. You've already seen me fetching water to take back to my camp using a Platypus bucket, but with the new system I also fill the “Dirty Water” bucket that comes with the system, giving me enough water for the afternoon, morning, and getting on the trail. The bucket hanging in the tree is the DIRTY WATER BUCKET, then connected to the FILTER, the out-let tube is connected to your clean water containers. Adapters for a wide variety of containers come with the system. The approximate gallon of dirty water drains by gravity down through the filter, usually in about 2 minutes. No pumping, no squeezing, nor sitting on it. Just go about pouring your recovery powders into their containers, your instant pudding in its, your dinner in the pot, your powdered eggnog in its bottle, etc. then go get your water and fill the containers. The whole system is seen below.

You’ll notice in 2019 that all the producers of water purification systems now all have gravity systems too, including the Life Straw I explain next.

p. 553

I’m also experimenting with another simple system….tried out on my hikes up the canyons of the Wasatch Front. It’s the LIFE STRAW you see me using below. I have taken it with me into the High Uintas and it was useful once, when rain was coming and I had to set up my tent quickly and get inside for the oncoming night. I didn't have time to look for a good water source, and resorted to filling a container with swampy water, and jumping into the refuge of my tent quick. I at least had drinking water for the night with the Life Straw.

Before we move on to examine other items in EQUIPMENT #2, it might be best to provide some good detail about giardia, which you can read in APPENDIX 6. Now, let's get back to our equipment with the graphic to remind us.

p. 554

BELOW IS A CLOSER LOOK AT FOOD PREPARATION items

The 1 quart pot I have used since 2005 is Titanium. You can see a large selection of titanium cookware at the outdoor outlets, but you can also save a bunch of money checking at your local supermarket, or Wal-Mart's, where you can find much less expensive cookware. Just remember "lightweight" is what we always have to keep in mind. For what I call shaker bottles you can get them for nothing using containers you get with your chocolate milk, jam, peanut butter, vitamins and supplements in etc. It's always best to stick to clear plastic, with smooth insides for easier cleaning, and wide openings to facilitate filling with your powders, and dehydrated items They will cost nothing and be a lot lighter than the containers sold at the outdoor outlets, and if you keep your eyes open you'll find some that are very tough and leak proof. Just remove the labels, and with a solvent clean off the sticky residue. The aluminum foil seen is used to cook my fish. Just add salt, lemon pepper, or whatever you prefer, and learn to not overcook--usually about 10 minutes is enough, then open up and you can usually grab the end of the backbone and remove all the bones and have filets of pure delight. To eat a fish daily will greatly reduce the amount of food you carry, but realize that fish alone is not a diet that will give you the energy and endurance you need to enjoyably backpack. Maybe best relate one of my experiences that taught me that lesson.

p. 555

A SURVIVAL EXPERIENCE TEACHING IMPORTANT LESSONS

In the late spring of 1981, a death threat from the guerrillas in Guatemala, had me bringing my family back to Provo, Utah. That started a 10 yearlong effort to keep the family going in Utah, while also managing the agro-business in Guatemala that supported us, along with supervising the altruistic projects among the Mayans. That had me making 5-6 trips a year spending 2 months in Utah, and then 2 in Guatemala, and accumulating around 1/2 million miles of travel. On one of those trips to Utah, I made a quick backpack into the Red Castle area of the High Uintas., that I called a SURVIVAL BACKPACK. I used a day-pack, with a small down sleeping bag, a sleeping pad you see rolled up on the outside, plus a poncho as my rain protection and shelter. I carried no food, only a salt shaker, some aluminum foil, and my light-weight spinning equipment. I recall my pack weight at 22 lbs., and if you're wondering why so much, it was because I also had a fairly heavy Mamiya Twin-lens Reflex camera using 2-1/4" x 2-1/4" transparency film, and a tiny tripod--used to take the above picture. I was to live on fish. I was 45 years old and not into vitamin/mineral supplements yet--that started 4 years later when arthritis began making me a cripple, solved by the Cod Father, Dale Alexander, story told in my ANTI-AGING CHALLENGE article.201 Also in Appendix 5. I recall getting to the Broadbent Meadows area, maybe 5 miles from the China Meadows Trailhead, when hunger hit me. I stopped for lunch--caught out of the East Fork of Smiths Fork. Wasn't much, just 4-5 tiny pan-sized brook trout. I wrapped them in foil and cooked them in my small campfire, and was then on my way. I made it up to Lower Red Castle Lake and set up my simple camp. Hunger had me again go fishing, but I had no luck whatsoever, and went to sleep that night hungry. The next day I tried the fishing again, but I don't ever recall having any luck in Lower Red Castle and didn't that day. It is one beautiful scene--I'll insert a picture of it below. 201

http://www.guatemalanfoundation.org/p/anti-aging-challenge.html

p. 556

By the 3rd day I was getting just a bit worried.. I took a few casts but was so pessimistic, my heart wasn't in it. But, up to the right of the mountain, where you see quite a bit of snow, was Red Castle Lake, at 11,295 ft. elevation and even higher at 11,600 ft. was Upper Red Castle where in 1962 I had caught my biggest cutthroat, estimated at 8 pounds. I knew I could catch fish up there. My strength was waning, but I had no choice but head for Red Castle Lake. A few hours later, along the talus slopes coming down into the western shore of the lake, I soon caught a couple of 16" cutthroats, and went to work cleaning and filleting. There was no wood of any kind around so I just salted down the fillets and started eating raw fish. I likely didn't know about sushi back at that time, nor have I tried it since. In January 2019 I was just invited to a Sushi dinner—it was pretty good! I just didn’t have any Japanese chefs/spices/sauces along at Red Castle. I guess I should have also brought along a little Ketchup or Thousand Island, as it wasn't really that good. To be honest, I apparently wasn't as hungry as I thought I was. I soon headed back to my camp on Lower Red Castle, taking a nice trout along, which I soon was eating baked in aluminum foil. But, as evening came on I began noticing something different. Unless hiking, or huddled close to the campfire, or in my sleeping bag, I trembled with cold. My diet of just fish wasn't fueling my body with what was required to keep me warm.

p. 557

Somehow I kept the experiment going until the 5th day, and then late in the afternoon I decided I had accomplished the purposes of the backpack, and so packed up and headed down the trail, determined to do the 10-12 miles and get to my pickup by dark. I would jog for 45 minutes, then take my pack off and lay flat out on the ground for 15 minutes, then repeat. I'm not sure how many cycles I got through but just as it was almost too dark to see the trail I made it to the Trailhead and my pickup, then headed for Mt. View, Wyoming and the convenience store. But, once I cooled off from all the exercise, I again began trembling with cold. I turned the heater on high, and it still didn't seem to be enough. I desperately needed something to eat. I sorted through an old tackle box I had in my pickup used for toiletries, medicines, and such, and found a box of PeptoBismol tablets, and as I sped towards Mt. View, I chewed on one after another until gone! At the convenience store (I don't think Maverick existed yet), I bought a bunch of great food: Doritos, yogurt, a box of donuts, and of course 32 oz. of Mt. Dew--did it exist back in 1981? If not it was Pepsi. And headed for Utah listening to KSL radio, and interestingly heard a commercial promoting Sam Wellers book store in Salt Lake that had just got in the first book written about the personal/intimate life of Thomas Jefferson, by Fawn Brodie. Part of this whole saga was a dream I had that involved Thomas Jefferson and his famous home, Monticello--but which I saw in ruins. I had the impression it signified some aspect of his personal life that had been a disaster--which I had to learn about. Hearing on the radio that there was a book that perhaps would give me the understanding I needed, was more than coincidental. I got to Salt Lake and slept in the pickup to be able to get the book the next day. NOTE: Thomas Jefferson was meticulous--almost, in keeping records, but also secretive. He developed an apparatus with which, as he wrote a letter, a copy was made, and he kept in his file around 23,000 copies of his letters, along with almost an equal number of letters received, but they were not made public, and on his orders the family kept them hidden from the world for like 150 years. Then they were made available to historians like, Fawn Brodie, who was one of the first to go through them and write her book. At the same time, all such letters and records of his relationship with his first wife, were burned by him after her death and so to this day his relationship with her is a mystery--except that on her death bed she made him promise to never marry again.

All in all this experience I call a SURVIVAL EXPERIENCE, really did teach me some important lessons that have been very important over these many years. Mainly, for our purposes here, we should understand that while fish, high in protein, is good food, it isn't enough by itself to sustain one doing heavy duty backpacking--unless we do like a coyote would do, eat everything--head, eyes, intestines, skin, tail, bones, and of course the flesh.

FIREMAKING KIT This is a critical part of your equipment. You should recall the SURVIVAL story of the

mother and her daughter who went missing in the Uintas on a day hike. You can refresh your memory of this sad story on pages 343-350. Their remains were found 9 months later. They did about everything wrong to be able to survive, but one thing could have perhaps saved them from hypothermia--MATCHES, and the ability to make a fire and keep warm. They actually had matches, but the regular kind and with everything wet, they were useless.

p. 558

For years I used the strike anywhere matches, protected in a plastic container, along with a couple of those magic candles you can't blow out that give a good flame, even with a bit of wind, to get my fire started. Coupled with them I got at Sportsman's Warehouse Montana Campfire starter--seen below on the right, and with just a squirt on the twigs I'd have the fire going quickly. Then in one experience when everything was totally soaked I couldn't find a dry rock or anything for my strike anywhere matches to work. What finally did the trick was using the tiny file on my Squirt Leatherman tool to strike the matches.

ITEMS IN MY TINY FIREMAKING KIT

You'll notice that strike-anywhere matches aren't part of the kit anymore, as I then discovered, or someone invented at that time, STORMPROOF MATCHES.

NOTE: For the STORMPROOF MATCHES, you have to have the little abrasive strip that comes with the matches. You can also get them in a small waterproof plastic container, seen on the right. I can't find the Montana Campfire stuff anymore, but Fire Paste is readily available. I just fill a little squirt bottle about half full with the paste, then add diesel fuel or kerosene to semi-liquefy it to squirt onto my twigs and have instant fire. For difficult situations, I always have some pine pitch, as seen on the left in the previous montage, which you can find in the mountains. It burns long and hot--enough to dry out your twigs and firewood. This little FIREMAKING bag should always go with you on a day hike, or backpack.

THESE TWO ITEMS ALONE WOULD SAVE THE LIVES OF MANY LOST EACH YEAR!

p. 559

A REVOLUTIONARY CHANGE–A BUTANE STOVE I have always said “I LOVE MY CAMPFIRE” and

“IT WILL ONLY BE TAKEN AWAY FROM MY COLD DEAD HANDS!” But, not only are campfires prohibited in high traffic areas, where we like to be–NEAR TO THE LAKES & STREAMS–but a camp with a cooking fire has to be a quarter of a mile distant. We can have a camp 200 feet away from the lakes, streams and trails….BUT NO CAMPFIRE.

A tiny stove for my one cooked meal a day makes possible being close to water, fishing and beauty. So I finally had to give in and add this to my light backpack.

Oh, by the way, I completely understand why these rules have to exist and have done my best to comply as there are many high traffic areas where all the dead wood, and even twigs, have disappeared due to the scrounging of dead wood for campfires, and the consequences aren’t good for the wildlife–some areas are almost like a desert or a well manicured park! I'll insert below a picture of one such area--at the north end of Pinto Lake. We see no dead branches on any tree, nor the usual downed timber with dry branches, not even twigs that are usually common-place.

EVEN WITH STRICT RULES, SAID AREAS WILL NEVER RECOVER DURING OUR LIFE-TIME! Of course I will love even more the remote areas I usually seek--where I will be able to warm myself in the evening cozied up to my small campfire! But, let's keep them small.

p. 560

NOW FOR THE LAST CATEGORY OF EQUIPMENT #2

We eliminate the usual heavy flashlight and large Leatherman type tool, for tiny alternatives. Below I’ll show the evolution of my thinking about a knife. I loved my Browning folding knife I use for deer hunting, and the Leatherman tool is great to have in a drawer in your kitchen, or in your car's glove box. Likewise the Swiss Army knife, but they are all too heavy and bulky for lightweight backpacking. The Leatherman Squirt is my solution.

The large Leatherman tool weighs 6 oz., but my tiny Squirt Leatherman tool weighs less than 2 oz. and is all I need–not just in the mountains, but it’s in my pocket always, even in Church! The blade is small, but sufficient to gut a fish, the pliers always come in handy– like to unhook a fish, make a repair, and the tiny file once helped save me from hypothermia as mentioned a few paragraphs back.

p. 561

Likewise the leather punch has served me well on my backpacks as I shed unwanted weight and need to punch a new hole in my belt.

A sheaf knife, like I had on my belt in the 1954 backpack traversing the High Uintas Primitive Area, isn't needed in lightweight backpacking…….. ……unless you really need it psychologically to feel like an outdoor badass!

FOR YOUR FIREWOOD? -- (where permitted or needed) On my 27 day expedition I found between Rosalie & Gladys lakes up above timberline in the far reaches of Rock Creek a--like new--hatchet . I’m a scavenger by nature, so had to pick it up, but by the time I got to Helen Lake I realized how ridiculous it was to carry such a heavy, useless, and un-needed tool…… ….so left it on the post that once had the Helen Lake sign.

I had my elk skin gloves, as I always do, and all I needed to do was gather up dead wood, break it up in campfire lengths over a rock, and you’re ready to cook dinner. The gloves also come in handy to handle a hot pot. NOTE: You might notice that the pot in the photo

is not titanium. My first pot in 2003 was bought at the supermarket for comparably nothing and served me well for several years. Elk skin gloves have the advantage of not becoming stiff after being wet. The point is, no need of a hatchet or axe or big knife.

p. 562

LET THERE BE LIGHT You might have noticed that in 2003 to begin the HIGH UINTAS WILDERNESS PROJECT, I was working at bringing myself up-to-date on how lightweight backpacking had developed during my years of absence. In addition to all the things mentioned, I next needed some kind of effective light--of course thinking flashlight. Once again at REI I looked for the Flashlight Section, and found a few, but mostly I found a whole lineup of HEADLAMPS……

….. and was impressed that you just didn't turn one on, then off. Rather you could choose a spotlight mode, or a broader choice, like for setting up your camp, or reading along with the ability to tilt it. Not only that, but choose 3 different levels of intensity--the least, enough to read something would have your 3 AAA batteries lasting for 150 hours! The brighter mode perhaps used if you have to hike in the dark. Then there was the blinking emergency mode. WOW…..I was impressed, and bought one that cost $29 that lasted me for 13 years! Now replaced by an inexpensive ENERGIZER headlamp bought at Walmart's for like $15.95.

In this photo you see me with my headlamp making possible a little reading of National Geographic magazine on my “expedition”. ******************************************

p. 563

A SURVIVAL EXPERIENCE saved by the HEADLAMP & CALMNESS A few years ago while recovering from almost becoming a cripple--again, and unable to backpack in 2012, I dedicated myself to becoming a sort of expert--or the only human who cared--about PIONEER TIMBER SLIDES that in 1853 had been built down the front of the Wasatch Mountains to bring needed timber for the building of Provo and Springville, Utah. I reported my explorations into the mountains east of Provo with a number of photo/essays, and then a YouTube video202 that summed up the efforts of exploration and discovery, which were a first. From years ago I had noticed the three pathways of of these slides and on doing a little research found mention in an old newspaper article about "timber slides." A Google search at that time showed literally NOTHING! So, I went to the top of the mountains to find the launching sites, and thought I'd found one of them. On that day-hike I was determined to follow the pathway from the top down to the bottom. I had with me my tiny day-pack with the critical items: poncho, water, food, my Fire Making kit, my headlamp and cell phone. And, just in case I had my Colt .45 Defender. On that first attempt to follow the pathway down the very steep mountain, I made a navigational mistake or two and got off course, and began having a very difficult time. Several times I had to backtrack to get around cliffs, that, along with fighting the scrub oak--that was worse than any jungle I had experienced in Guatemala, had me losing more time. But, with the errors and lost time, the day came to an end and it became pitch black--except for the flickering lights of Utah Valley communities below me-- which valley was first named in 1776 by Catholic Priests/Explorers, Escalante and Dominguez, who called it:

THE VALLEY OF OUR LADY OF MERCY OF TIMPANOGOS

"The most pleasing, beautiful and fertile site in New Spain"

202

PIONEER TIMBER SLIDES: THE MAKING OF PROVO, UTAH https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qo7P8kCZtHA&feature=youtu.be

p. 564

But for me, it became pitch black and I was only half-way down the mountain.

I was fatigued, my leg muscles trembling, so I sat down, took a rest, had a bite to eat and got out my HEADLAMP. Before leaving home I had installed 3 new AAA batteries just to be safe. A little word of prayer helped. It was clear that if I was careful, all would be fine, but if for any reason it got real dangerous, I could easily get a fire going to keep warm, and spend the night on the mountain. With the cell phone I could call the family to assure them I was okay--the High Uintas equivalent would be the satellite phone that always goes with me.

THE CRUCIAL LESSON: Since I had all the emergency equipment I needed, NO NEED TO PANIC, which happens to many in-experienced who don't go prepared. Panic leads to making mistakes, often deadly ones. I got up and carefully went down the mountain, always remembering the advise I give to all in such dangerous mountainous situations--TO ALWAYS LEAN INTO THE MOUNTAIN--as to fall the other way would be sure death. This had me often sliding on my rearend, and I made it fine--except for my pants, that gratefully were tough/cheap ones from Deseret Industries …..you see below.

And you can see I had my trusty RED BANDANNA, that I'm never without. When we get to CLOTHING needed for backpacking I'll explain why the red bandanna is ALSO A MUST!

p. 565

NOTE: In the YouTube video referenced on the previous page, you'll see I finally found the launch site and made it all the way down the path of the timber slide to the foothills east of Provo. 203

*******************************

Last--in EQUIPMENT #2 comes the all important COMPASS –to orient your map--north & south, and navigate safely in the high country, as seen below being taught to a group of Explorer/Boy Scouts in the Four Lakes Basin.

You don’t have to spend much money. Mine, inserted in the photo, probably cost $2.95 and it can be slipped in your pocket without even noticing it--yet, along with a good topographical map, it can keep you from going astray and get you safely to that remote lake maybe never seen by a human before!

WE WILL NOW GO ON TO OUR NEXT CATEGORY OF EQUIPMENT--FOR EMERGENCIES & DISASTER PREVENTION

The MOSQUITOES REPELLANT is for everyone. The other three, PERSONAL SATELLITE TRACKER, SATELLITE PHONE, & OXIMETER and BLOOD PRESSURE/PULSE CUFF, are for groups, like Boy Scouts, and possibly for the solo backpacker, as I have been. See recommendations below. 203

Ibid. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qo7P8kCZtHA&feature=youtu.be

p. 566

MOSQUITOES:

You'll notice one beginning to suck my blood. Early in the season in the Uintas--June and maybe early July, they aren't a problem so it's a good time to hike or backpack in the mountains, but then they begin, usually at first sort of weak still. But soon they gather strength with clouds of them that begin to do their darndest to drive the human invaders CRAZY! This discomfort has to be compensated for by things you love in the mountains, overcoming any discouragement, but you've got to be prepared to survive the little demons. This plague and its intensity and life span depend on how the season is developing, whether wet, or warm, also influenced by the altitude and consequent temperatures. Then, as the season moves on into August the intensity begins to weaken, the tiny critters getting to the end of their life-span, plus cooler weather, and eventually frosts in the higher elevations, and they gradually are gone, usually making our forays into the mountains in late August quite pleasant--always depending on the elevation, and how the ever changing climate develops from year to year.

THE POINT HERE IS: GO PREPARED TO SURVIVE & ENJOY THE MAGIC OF THE MOUNTAINS. INSECT REPELLANT is a must, and it should contain DEET, and my advice is to always choose 98-100%. Two popular brands are shown above. I like the transparent one as you can see clearly how much you have left. For those afraid of toxins, my way of looking at it is: I'd prefer to risk a little poison in my system for a day or two, rather

than to be driven crazy while being eaten alive by mosquitoes. The repellants are very effective. Don't spray from the container onto your skin, rather squirt a couple of times into your palm, rub the two together, and then lightly apply to your head, face--careful always to avoid the eyes--neck, arms, legs, and also to your Tshirt--and before I even get out of my tent I do the application, including taking off my shirt and lightly applying to the shirt's back--because the mosquitoes will get you penetrating your shirt, which they can't do with the pants I use. Usually the repellants say they will last "8 hours," or "12 hours," but I apply during the day as many times as needed. At rest stops for added protection I usually put on my wind-shirt, windbreaker, or rain parka, and have an enjoyable rest--mosquito free.

p. 567

THE NEXT THREE ITEMS ARE FOR LONE BACKPACKERS204 and FOR GROUPS--LIKE BOY SCOUTS & EXPLORERS

A Personal Locater Beacon--PLB, of one type or another is a must. I'll insert an article about them in APPENDIX 7,205 but what I use is the SPOT PERSONAL SATELLITE TRACKER, seen above. and, on the following pages I'll show exactly what it does. The tragic story of Eric Robinson is a case in point, having turned up lost hiking the Highline Trail, triggering a massive fruitless search. Five years later his remains were just by chance found. He had a PLB, but didn't use it--the instructions for his device state, "A Personal Locator Beacon should be activated only in situations of grave and imminent danger, and only as a last resort when all means of self-rescue have been exhausted."

His device apparently was just for a life and death emergency, but likely not used as a sudden fall that took his life didn't give him the opportunity to turn it on and punch the emergency button. Let me explain what the SPOT Tracker does and why and how I use it. 1. Prior to your trip you go on your computer to the SPOT website, and set up a Trip, with an OK message to be sent to 10 individuals, whose emails are chosen by you and programmed, with the purpose of advising family and friends that you are OK, with a message like the one I'll insert on the next page.

204

See the end of the article about Eric Robinson, explaining the precautions necessary to go alone, pages 156-159, and repeated--AS IT IS SO CRUCIAL--on pages 343-350. 205

How to Choose PLBs and Satellite Messengers, in Appendix 7

p. 568

You need to set your SPOT Tracker in a place looking skyward with an unobstructed view of the sky, then hit the OK button, and wait until the light above the OK button pauses. Best to let it continue for 20 minutes as it will send the signal two more times to make sure it is sent. The message will be sent to your list of 10 with a message like seen below.

Those on your pre-programmed list will know that you are OK, and then they can click on the link at the end of the email, and they will be taken to the SPOT website and a Google Earth view showing exactly where you are, like in the sequence below--zoomed in.

NOTE: On my trips I always check in every day once arriving at the spot where I would camp that night. You can do it as often as you want during each day, but at least do it at the end of every day, so that if they don't hear from you the next day, they will at least know where to start looking for you, rather than have no idea whatsoever, like in the case of Eric Robinson who never used his device and was never found….until 5 years later by chance. You can also get a link for your trip, and make it available on a website, or through emails to a large list, with which link anyone can be led to the SPOT website and see where you are from day to day. I'll insert below the instructions for this point from the SPOT instructions:

p. 569

Check-in / OK: This feature allows you to let your friends and family know that all is OK with a pre-programmed message along with your GPS location. With a push of a button a message is sent via email or SMS to up to 10 predetermined contacts and your waypoint is stored in your SPOT account for later reference. Your stored waypoints can be easily integrated into a SPOT Shared Page or SPOT Adventure account. Read more

Track Progress: Start/stop tracking at any time using your SPOT device. You can also mark a Reference Point or send Check-in/OK messages from specific locations while in Track Progress mode. Read more

2. You can also pre=program a HELP message of some kind, to be sent to one or two specified individuals, indicating possible difficulties you might have. The SPOT instructions say:

Help: In the event of a non-life threatening emergency, you can use this function to notify your personal contacts that you need assistance. Additional SPOT S.O.V. (Save Our Vehicle) can be purchased and programmed to your Help button as well. When activating SPOT S.O.V., the Help button will notify professional roadside services. SPOT has partnered with Nation Safe Drivers (NSD) to provide a vehicle assistance program like no other. Read more

3. Then comes the real EMERGENCY 911 button, the instructions saying:

SOS / 911: Use this function In the event of a life threatening or other critical emergency to notify emergency services of your GPS location and that you need assistance. The GEOS International Emergency Response Center alerts the appropriate agencies worldwide – for example contacting 9-1-1 responders in North America and 1-1-2 responders in Europe. Read more

SPOT S.O.V. (Save Our Vehicle): SPOT S.O.V. is a 24/7 roadside vehicle assistance program that gets help for you and your car, SUV, ATV, RV, trailer or motorcycle with the simple push of a button. It doesn't matter how far off the grid you go, you can always count on SPOT S.O.V. to get you out of a jam. (Additional service required). SPOT S.O.V.
