3. BEING ABLE TO SAY "HAPPY BIRTHDAY," TO SPECIAL PEOPLE on SPECIAL DATES.

or "I lOVE YOU,"

4. BEING ABLE TO SHARE YOUR INSPIRING EXPERIENCE WITH OTHERS , such as I did over the years with Russ Smith and Tim Hughes on KSL OUTDOOR RADIO every Saturday morning as seen below:

p. 573

MORE EMERGENCY ITEMS

The OXIMETER, that will measure the oxygen in your blood--important to detect High Altitude Sickness, and the BLOOD PRESSURE/PULSE Cuff, are two items I didn't have until I began having trouble. Now, in my mature years, I won't go without them, and with the examples I give on pages 208-215 of my problem, that of the young man who lost his life, and of the Best Backpacker I Have Ever Known, I'm about at the point of saying it's almost criminal for a group of Boy Scouts to go into the Mountains, without

the leader having one, and knowing how to recognize and manage High Altitude Sickness. So, quoting from those pages mentioned above: I now take with me an OXIMETER--seen above, which on Amazon only costs around $25, and as I ascend into the mountains I check myself at rest stops. At home (elevation 4,500 ft.) the oxygen count in my blood is 96. When in the mountains I climb slowly, and if the count drops below 90 I rest just a little longer and it usually normalizes at least to 90. At higher elevations, some people might need to rest longer, even for a day, to have your body normalize. But, in the end of it doesn't adjust and you get worse, the only solution is GO DOWN! With the Blood Pressure Cuff, since I have had a little problem with high blood pressure, it goes with me too, along with extra blood pressure medication--just in case. So far I haven't had to use it, but it would be fascinating for me to know what was happening with my blood pressure, and pulse when I had a heart attack--described on pages 250-255.

MEDICAL HELPED ADVISED For groups, such as Boy Scouts and Explorers, it would be worthwhile, during the winter months, to have a medical doctor talk to your group about possible emergencies: High Altitude Sickness, Hypothermia, Heart Attack, etc. and how to detect them with these two instruments, and what to do for an emergency.

p. 574

CLOTHES & FOOTGEAR Sounds like a pretty personal category, but a few suggestions might help. WE'LL BEGIN FROM THE GROUND UP --Your feet you will depend on. From time to time I’ve heard stories from even experienced outdoorsmen, mountain runners, and marathoners that tell horror stories about how blisters have had them go through hell, and even stopped them. There was a time when I was part of that scene, needing Moleskin, and such as part of my emergency kit. Then I discovered CoolMesh WrightSocks or blister preventing socks you put on first to protect your feet from getting blisters. I'll insert a picture of one brand below.

To make sure you focus on the right thing, I've blocked out one of the brands I use on top of the "blister preventing socks"-- that are available also in medium, and short versions.

They have two thin layers that eliminate rubbing on your skin and causing blisters. SINCE I HAVE USED THEM HIKING/ BACKPACKING, and RUNNING, I'VE NEVER AGAIN HAD A BLISTER.

ANOTHER INTERESTING THING TO CONSIDER KNOW YOUR FEET & ADJUST ACORDINGLY, demonstrated by the picture below when I took my shoes and socks off to put on my wadding slippers to ford a stream.

Notice that there are two socks for my left foot, and an extra one for my right, because my right foot is smaller than my left. An extra running sock for my right is the equalizer.

p. 575

One more thing for another foot emergency, is a TOE BANDAGE, as pictured to the right. On the Lake Atwood Trail I once had a very painful toe problem with two toes rubbing painfully together. I solved it with some tape from my emergency bag, but since added to that bag a TOE BANDAGE, I found at Walgreens that has been useful several times over the last 2,000 miles.

NOW A WORD ABOUT FOOTGEAR MY 25 YEAR EVOLUTION OF EXPERIENCE MIGHT HELP: From the beginning of my HIGH UINTAS WILDERNESS PROJECT, at least from when I began reporting on the explorations, I mentioned frequently my "football ankle," that, from a football injury in 1953, had me limping some all my life.209 That was complicated, after a lot of training and then running my first International Half Marathon in 1994, by having terrible pain on the balls of my feet--like as though stepping on a rock. I went to a rheumatologist in Guatemala City. He called my condition metatarsalitis and advised me not to do half-

marathons anymore, nor dream about backpacking. Of course I persisted finding a way to eliminate the pain with running shoe modifications, and inserts to keep pressure off the balls of my feet, and kept running and then preparing for the High Uintas. For hiking boots, I believed I needed ankle support--so at least 8" boots were researched. I also needed to remember lightweight and waterproof. I found a pretty good boot made with kangaroo leather--by nature waterproof. I needed to have a combination of inserts, so had to buy boots two sizes larger than normal. You see below the boot and the combination of inserts I had to use.

After my ankle reconstruction, with a tendon transplant, and 3 titanium screws holding it together, I still felt I needed ankle support for a year. I had worn out my kangaroo skin boots, and found a very lightweight boot at Cabelas I used for a year--you see above on the right, and then evolved to lighter weight footgear, that most of you should start with. 209

If interested in that injury and its aftermath, see my CHECKERED FAITH & WORK JOURNEY at: http://www.guatemalanfoundation.org/p/the-checkered-faith-work.html

p. 576

Forget those famous, bulky, heavy, tough, badass looking hiking boots. As you will notice, lightweight mountain running shoes do just fine in the Uintas, which further evolution of footgear is seen below. This occurred as I gradually solved my metatarsalitis problem, finally to this day with only one extra insert with a cut-out, and thick socks. First a Salomon very lightweight hiking boot on the left--pair weight at 2 lbs., used for a year--and still used like for my Pioneer Timber Slide adventures. I then shaved off another 6 ounces with the Salomon Hiking shoe--called years ago Heavy Duty Trail Running Shoe, seen to the right of the boot. I then cut another 8 ounces with a pair of Light Weight Trail Running Shoes, weight 1 lb. 2 ounces, on the right.

For whatever it's worth, my last major exploration in the Uintas--a 6 day backpack to Little Andy Lake--going through some pretty tough country, was made using the lightest weight mountain running shoe on the right, and all was perfect.

IMPORTANT NOTE: You might not think shaving off 8 ounces, or 1 pound of weight is important, but think of it this way: In a half-marathon (13.1 miles), I take approximately 26,000 steps. An extra pound means you lifted 26,000 extra pounds during that day's hike. To cut down your total load by 10 pounds, would mean avoiding lifting 260,000 lbs. every day. How much better would each day be by avoiding lifting every day 1/4 million pounds of weight?

TREKKING POLES Some might ask, “Why haven’t you mentioned trekking poles?” Simply because I don’t use them. I have better things to use my hands for, like: Camera in hand for that once in a life time shot; or, my fishing rod to cast into streams and lakes as I hike; or, a bag of munchies, etc. I can’t afford to expend extra energy on something I don’t need. I HOPE & PRAY THAT MY EXPERIENCE AND SUGGESTIONS ABOUT FOOTGEAR-SOCKS TO SHOES, WILL HELP MAKE YOUR EXPERIENCE IN THE MOUNTAINS MORE JOYOUS & INSPIRING.

NOW MOVE UP TO A SUGGESTION FOR PANTS I've already mentioned my suggestion for waterproof pants, that by the way--my preference is the Marmot brand, with zippered legs and pockets. now to…….

p. 577

………PANTS, my preference being the lightweight, convertible ones I'll picture below, which have zippers to make possible removing the bottom portion without taking off your shoes (if you have light weight mountain running shoes--with heavy boots you might have to take them off). During warm days that permits you to comfortably hike in short pants. Also go for synthetic material, as it is lightweight, a windbreaker, and mosquitoes can’t go through it. But you do have to be careful around your campfire, as embers will melt/burn holes in them. My current pants--not the ones pictured on the right, are a little heavier duty, with a blend of synthetic and cotton. I usually don't recommend cotton for reasons I'll explain when talking about shirts, but these pants are more resistant to fire embers. They are the North Face brand--I got them at REI.

SHIRTS You should use polyester fabric T-shirts. They are more expensive, but last forever, even when humid retain some insulation value, and dry quickly. Below I’ll insert a couple that I use always–focusing on bright colors for better photographs.

First my Lance Armstrong cycling jersey that helps me psychologically be STRONG!

And my bright orange Golite T-shirt I perhaps use too much…..just another example, but best to have one or two long sleeved ones too.

p. 578

Another option is what some call a WINDSHIRT which you see me using below. It is a Golite product which only weighs 3 oz. and can be stuffed in a back pocket. It is a windbreaker, not waterproof, so in a good rain, get your rain parka or poncho on too or you’ll be in trouble! I have mine handy when I stop to rest to protect me from mosquitoes, and also to avoid cooling off as I’m usually sweaty and have to avoid chilling.

Golite doesn’t exist anymore so you’ll have to look around and see what’s available. Usually your rain jacket will suffice.

NOW FOR A WARM, LIGHTWEIGHT JACKET For my expedition, and more I just depended on the layering system when encountering cool to cold weather. I'd put on two or three T-shirts, with at least one being long sleeved, and on top put on my rain parka. Then on renewing my backpacking with original backpack buddy, Ted Packard, I tried his Patagonia lightweight jacket, and….WOW! I was hooked and when back in civilization bought a lightweight Mountain Hardware Primaloft jacket you see me wearing below, along with Ted. I'm not talking about a really expensive heavy duty down winter jacket, rather a quite lightweight, compressible jacket with synthetic insulation. Mine weighs 12 ounces.

p. 579

Note, also in the above photo, my FISHERMEN’S GLOVES — very useful with finger tips out to zip up or down something, operate a camera, read at night in your tent, and of course tie a fishing knot, etc. They do make a difference.

ELK SKIN GLOVES They have been mentioned already, and they certainly are not an essential, but I love to take mine, seen in a previous photograph, used when gathering firewood, breaking it over a rock, moving rocks around, handling a hot pot, rolling up my tent--keeping hands clean, etc. They only weigh 3 oz. Remember Elk skin is better than deer or cowhide as it remains soft and pliable after drying.

DON’T FORGET YOUR HAT–High Country radiation is more intense.

For the last couple of years I have been using a waterproof hat you see above, which is the Outdoor Research Seattle Sombrero hat. I just suggest that you use one that is waterproof. The one you see also has some insulation keeping my head warm in cool weather. In my tent at night I unload my pockets into my hat for safekeeping.

ALMOST FORGOT "THE ESSENTIAL"

It is traditionally "YE OLD RED BANDANNA," but it can be the color of your choice, but it is the most useful, and varied piece of your equipment. FOR WHAT? Of course for the nose thing, then tied around your neck to prevent sunburn, or on your head if you forgot your hat, or you lost your hat in a high wind. Then for other emergencies, like seen above, as a bandage, or a tourniquet, or an arm sling. Maybe to grab a hot pot, or for a towel, etc. We're not talking about a little hanky!

p. 580

THE ALL IMPORTANT (for me) FISHING GEAR

Basically I use a combination rod–spinning/fly fishing, so I have both types of reels, plus an assortment of the lures and flies I have found most effective. Total weight = 2 lbs. For just 2 or 3 days I often reduce my fishing equipment down a little with a few select lures, and swivels, like seen below, stuffed in a Zip-lock bag, along with rod and reel.

AN ESSENTIAL ITEM (for me) — A CAMERA I can’t imagine not being able to record and bring home with me the incredible VISIONS OF NATURE & beauty I experience in the High Country–memories I will have with me as long as I live, and be able to share with loved ones. Of course I’ve kind of gone off the deep end with it as you see on the next page, even my wide angle lens weighing more than my tent, and camera, lenses & tripod weighing more than my BASIC PACK! My photo equipment, for a lightweight backpack, was getting up to at least 12 lbs. It was more back in the first years with a film camera and 35 roles of slide film for my

expedition--15 lbs.

p. 581

I often leave my tripod at home and save 2 lbs. in weight–with all you good photographers SCREAMING, NO, NO, NO! Most professionals say they never take a photograph without their tripod–and they have BIG ONES, but I’ll have to confess that with fast shutter speeds and my impatience, I rarely use mine, and for self-portraits when I feel a human should be in a photograph--like me, a SOLID ROCK or LOG usually is used, with my red bandanna used to level the camera (another use of the bandanna). The above wide-angle zoom lens is now also left at home as my original 28mm. to 300 mm. zoom lens finally died and replaced with a better one 18mm. to 400 mm. zoom lens you see below that is incredible--heavier than the original, but the heavy wide angle seen above, that weighs 2 lbs., is left at home with total weight reduced.

Plus a small fish-eye lens, now all carried in a very light-weight waist pack contrasted with the previous bulky photographers waist pack. Likely most of you are thinking that your SMART CELL PHONE will do just fine, and you’re probably right as they are incredible and getting better every year–but, however you do it….MAKE SURE AND BRING BACK THE WONDERFUL MEMORIES! ******************************

p. 582

ANOTHER OPTION--KEEP IN TOUCH WITH THE WORLD ON YOUR BACKPACK WITH A small AM/FM/SW RADIO For you purists this must sound like heresy—polluting the silence of the mountains, but it helped a lot on my long expedition maintain my sanity--being able to listen to the news, the weather report, and OF COURSE KSL OUTDOORS RADIO each Saturday morning from 6:00-8:00 to make sure Tim, and Russ are ready for my call from the High Uintas. Below is seen the small GRUNDIG radio used in recent years, weighing a couple of oz.

One last item I feel is a necessity: READING MATERIAL As seen below, for me it often includes one National Geographic Magazine, and a handful of special articles I'm interested in I rip out of magazines, plus my tiny Military version of the scriptures--in keeping with Jedediah Smith's tradition of always having the BIBLE and reading from it daily.

p. 583

TOILETRIES & MEDICAL/HEALTH EMERGENCIES At one time in my 2,000 miles of backpacking since 2003, I carried in a big bag the vast array of stuff seen on the right which I thought I needed for nearly any emergency for an old guy …..and there was even more in the Emergency repair bag. I was getting a bit paranoid, and needed to simplify, so followed the advice of my older brother, Marlo. He suggested after a trip,

separate from all the equipment, a pile of things never used and eliminate them. I got rid of a lot of stuff, retaining only those things that were really used, plus a few items a

now 80+ year old explorer would need for the most probable emergencies. Ingenuity and prayer would have to cover the rest. THE MINIMIZED VERSION -- Weight = 1 lb. Including the Emergency repair kit underneath all of what you see in my KIT. I'll insert its picture below, with an explanation. But, first I'll insert with it a zoomed in picture of 5 emergency items, some of which aren't in the picture with all the vast array of stuff above, but which have become critical for me.

They are: 1. An EMERGENCY ANTI-BIOTIC called a Z-Pack; 2. ACETAZOLAMIDE or DIAMOX, to aid in acclimatization to higher altitudes; 3. MEDICATION FOR LEG CRAMPS; 4. Another for IRRITABLE LEG SYNDROME; & 5. Anti-Diarrhea - LOPERAMIDE, to aid Redmond Clay with gamboo issues (that sometimes are problems for a few days in getting used to a different diet than used in civilization).

p. 584

I'll admit that perhaps younger people, like most everyone reading this, might not have as much need of these items than is my case, but I mention them just in case it might help one or two. In recent years, after a long and hard day--backpacking or running a half-marathon, my legs would cramp up at night. The Leg Cramp medication, solves that problem. Also, due to the intense physical effort, I have had difficulty sleeping due to my legs being very restless and tense, sometimes called irritable leg syndrome--the medication solving quickly that problem too. They can be purchased at Walgreens or Walmarts.

Diamox is mentioned in the articles about High Altitude Sickness, on pages 332-336, and helps speed up acclimatization to higher altitudes and helps one to sleep better ( it is a prescription item, so you'll have to talk to a Dr., as is the case also with the anti-biotic). Twice the anti-biotic helped save me by beginning to take effect after 2 days, making possible carefully getting back to civilization. See pages 250-255.

REDMOND CLAY -- a dark gray colored bottle in the lower left hand corner of what I'm calling the vast array of stuff picture on the previous page. It is a fine powdered clay called bentonite. When your digestive system feels out-of-whack, which I sometimes call gamboo, this product solves the problem. Since I was introduced to it years ago it goes everywhere with me, taking the place of anti-acids, Pepto-Bismol, and such. Fill a small bottle half full of the powder and add water and shake vigorously. Then open and add more water and shake. It should be permitted an hour or so to totally absorb, then take a big spoon full, swallow and drink a full glass of water. Repeat as needed, and it will do the job, but in difficult cases--to not lose time, the Anti-Diarrhea medication might be used too.

NOW THE TINY EMERGENCY REPAIR KIT I'll insert a panel of three pictures: One, the kit with repair items for your air mattress, your tent, poncho, your jacket, your water bladder, etc. and with the Plastic Surgery cement--I never go backpacking without, proven by me to be much more effective than any other glue.

The Plastic Surgery cement can be purchased on Amazon. In the middle picture it is seen with a crown that fell out during a backpack. I cleaned, disinfected, dried and glued it back with the Plastic Surgery--it lasted for an entire year. With it I have repaired my air mattress, my glasses, my water bladder--that no other cement would do, etc. The 3rd picture is something you don't want to forget….what us outdoor guys call BUM FODDER or tissue paper. I'll admit forgetting it once, and—imagine this—I had to use snow!

p. 585

That could reduce the 68 lbs. to perhaps 62 lbs. approaching the maximum I have hiked with for long backpacks in recent years, and which might be required for me doing the entire Highline Trail FOR SUPPLEMENTS, you'll have to go to APPENDIX 5, p. 616, and read the ANTIAGING CHALLENGE article which has been updated from the original, with photographs added. ***************************

LET'S END LEARNING FROM MY “MOST DIFFICULT EXPEDITION DAY” I was about to leave Lambert Meadows when a quick rain storm hit. In time I set up my tent and took refuge. An hour later the sun was out, so I packed up and headed east for Porcupine Pass, crossing the arctic tundra of Oweep Basin. An hour later the only really serious rain storm of my expedition, hit like a whirlwind. I headed down desperately looking for some protection. I found a clump of alpine firs and literally kicked out a herd of elk. It was too late and almost dark--best always to stop earlier in the day. In a heavy downpour I did a poor job of setting up my tent, and dove inside. About everything was wet-except my sleeping bag compressed in its bag. The wetness seemed to prime drips everywhere and I went through a miserable night. Somehow the next day had to be a good one to dry out everything--or it would almost be difficult to continue. Luckily the sun was out and for half a day I had my gear spread all over drying out. I was soon packed up and ready to climb Porcupine Pass, where you see me on the right looking back at the Oweep Basin and Porcupine Lake. It's best to stop earlier, set up your camp and prepare better for bad weather.

210

If a sure need, .45 highly preferred. 9mm. will go thru one side of a cement block, while the .45 demolishes the entire block. To be accurate, the 9mm. bullet only penetrating half of the block was not +P Grizzly ammo. Got to repeat that test.

p. 586

EPILOGUE In 2007 I was coming down the GRANDADDY TRAIL, on my first backpack, after my "football ankle" reconstruction, and met coming up the trail a great family--the MOSSINGERS, from Ogden, Utah.

You'll notice the huge backpacks of the parents, helping their younger children, but it is mostly what I call "fluff," and not really as heavy as it looks. Their son, gave me the quote that has pushed me to do my best and NOT STOP BACKPACKING. He said,

"You don't grow old and stop backpacking, rather....if you stop backpacking you will grow old!" I'll admit it is getting harder, but, I persist stubbornly, at least doing a little backpacking in 2018, and come 2019 backpacking season—in my 84th year--HOPE TO MEET YOU ON THE TRAIL…AND NOT BE OLD……YET!-586

p. 587

THE FIRST and THE LAST

In the beginning of the Project, on August 5, 2003, I left the Highline Trailhead, and headed east on my expedition. About a mile or so down the trail I met the first High Uinta Friend on the trail--another of those consequential coincidences. He was 68 year old Phillip Fradkin on a day hike as part of his research to publish an update of his 1989 book, SAGEBRUSH COUNTRY--basically a water conservation/environmentalist book about the Uinta Mountains that are surrounded by "sabebrush." 211

'

I later jotted down in my notebook:

"He said he hadn't backpacked for 18 years, and thanked me for my example that was encouraging to him. He encouraged me to stick with my 'UINTA PROJECT.' As I continued up the trail I could hear him recording his meeting with me. It will be interesting to see if he mentions me in his revised edition." His revised book was published in 2004, beginning with Words of Praise for the author, the first from a fellow author, saying, "Phillip Fradkin is simply one of the best journalists writing in America. He tells taut, incisive stories about vivid, embattled places and people…." 211

SAGEBRUSH COUNTRY: Land and the American West, by Phillip Fradkin, 2004 by Johnson Books, Boulder

p. 588

In his EPILOGUE, page 274, he says:

He congratulated me for what I was working hard to do, and was always encouraging over the next few years. He passed on 9 years later when 77 years old. The "book" he mentioned I was intending to write is now finished. Strangely, our unique Uinta Mountains have never been featured in the National Geographic magazine…..yet. That hope is still alive.

p. 589

APPENDIX 4 From CHAPTER 5: LIGHTWEIGHT, JOYFULL & SAFE BACKPACKING ****************************

1. AVOID BEING THE "CHUBBY…BACKPACKER…MUTTERING NAUGHTY WORDS" -- DONE BY BEING IN GOOD PHYSICAL SHAPE

DETAILS OF MY ONGOING STRUGGLE TO SOLVE GLITCHES and meet…..

THE FIRST CHALLENGE ON THE DAY ONE OF MY EXPEDITION The heavy 83 lb. load put incredible pressure on what I have called my "motorcycle knee," injured in a motorcycle accident in Guatemala City in 1976. On 6th Avenue and 18th Street a girl darted across the street in my path and I braked violently, then sacrificed myself swerving and going onto the pavement just nicking her, skidding to the pavement to avoid a direct hit. All the weight of my mud bike went onto my right knee. The girl vanished into the crowd leaving me in bad shape in the middle of the intersection. Eventually an apparent temporary fix was attempted in a surgery back in Utah on a Fall trip, making possible walking, jogging and later backpacking, but coupled with my "football

p. 601

ankle," also on my right leg, had my limp become a bit more pronounced, always with a bit of pain from both injuries. With a late morning start, and my 83 lb. load, I only made 6 miles that first day on the Highline Trail and set up my camp in the vicinity of Carolyn Lake. As I cooled off, my knee began to give me a lot of pain, and sleep became impossible. So I got out the book I had brought along to read on the trail……and pretty well ended up reading all night.

I was mesmerized reading the incredible story of Lance beating a 2% chance of being saved from cancer, and making a comeback in the Tour de France. It matters not what happened later in his cycling career--he was added to my list of heroes motivating me to NEVER GIVE IN nor GIVE UP! I had to find a way to go on all across the High Uintas Wilderness. Excedrin during the day, and Ibuprofen at night wasn't enough. During the day the pain was bearable, but sleeping at night was the problem. I soon learned that cold on the knee gave me the relief I needed at night to sleep some. My tiny 1 quart pot became my salvation.

I found that by filling it with cold water, then contorting myself like a pretzel on my knees in my tent with the knee in the tiny pot for 10 minutes gave me pain relief making possible 1 hour of sleep. I would then repeat all night, and persisted with that during the entire expedition, except for one night at Deadhorse Lake when a heavy hail made possible using ice.

p. 602

--NEVER ENDING GLITCHES-PHYSICAL THERAPY & RECOVERY FROM EACH SURGERY/TREATMENT Two surgeries were for thyroid and skin cancer; one for my "football ankle"--injured in 1953; two surgeries for my "motorcycle knee"--injured in 1976 in Guatemala; another for terminate reduction on internal nose." Next, in 2012, another surgery to fuse the two lower vertebrae's of my back to solve pinched nerves that were making me a cripple. Then in 2013 problems arose and after trying several solutions, concluded I had to mask the problem and fake not being a cripple with a new way of walking! But, then the trouble was discovered--bone on bone on my left hip, resulting in the easiest surgery to recover from: hip replacement-which had me "not feeling pain for the first time in 30 years." But, by 2017 another pinched nerve made again being a cripple a real possibility, but before giving up I went under the scalpel again on my back--fusing the last two vertebraes, with the problem persisting some today--November 2018--making difficult heavy duty physical activity, but seemingly solved by doubling and tripling my intake of cod liver oil. During the early years of my Project, I solved gradually the metatarsilitis with shoe modifications, explained on pages 575-576, plus from 2003 to the present, undergoing several radiation and chemotherapy treatments--in some respects more difficult than the surgeries--one chemotherapy treatment I'm going through as I put this book together in late Fall 2018 in an effort to burn out of my respiratory system chronic bronchitis that has complicated my oxygen intake--I'll mention in a moment.. Each required a lot of work, pain and determination--for months and months each year leading to the next backpacking season, but the other option was a grim one that didn't interest me in the least. I had to be able to finish what I started.

None of it was easy, and required true commitment to my goals, and I will admit that several times over the years I had what I call my FOREST GUMP MOMENT, pictured below, coupled with some Kenny Roger's wisdom I resorted to in 2015 on my second attempt to get to Little Andy Lake, when High Altitude Sickness had me "fold" and "walk away" down the trail to be able to make another attempt later.

p. 603

That kept me alive for another failed try in 2016 resulting in that great coincidence of meeting Teresa as I was coming down the trail, when she recognized me and SHOUTED:

NO, YOU'RE DEAD! 212 Those three failures forced me to finally learn to manage the altitude problem--which I should have done years before, and led to finally getting to my lake. If some of you aren't familiar with The Forest Gump Moment, let me explain. He had been traumatized by--wouldn't you know it--a woman thing, and so he started jogging around the country and it went on for more than three years, during which time he had attracted a little group of hippy-like followers who ran behind him. Then out in the middle of the Arizona dessert he all of a sudden stopped and turned towards them. One of them shouted, "Quiet, he's going to say something!" They expected some kind of prophetic utterance, but he rather said….I'M PRETTY TIRED…..I THINK I'LL GO HOME NOW! I have had over the last portion of my 16 year Project, several such moments, when it was just getting too hard, and no fun anymore. Yet, after thinking about it, resting up a bit, my stubborn streak clicked in resulting each time as indicated below.

THE COMEBACK THEME with four Youtube videos 213

212

Story told on pages 71-72 of this book.

ONE OF THE PROBLEMS & THE SOLUTION Backing up just a little, in 2009 I concluded that one of my serious problems was keeping in shape during the winter. As I was getting older, I found that I would lose very quickly my strength and conditioning during the off season, and once lost, getting it back was increasingly more difficult. I needed something to keep me in shape during the off-season. My solution was applying for a job at nearby REAMS SUPER MARKET in Springville, Utah. The manager, Lori, was a little puzzled why a graduate of BYU with exceptional grades, a strong minor in Business Management, and a history of more than 35 years owning and managing my own agro-business with around 40 employees, would want to work at REAMS, specifically requesting a job as what I had fun calling "a shopping cart herder," a "bagger technician," a "sign hanging engineer," and a "toilet sanitation scientist." I explained my High Uintas Wilderness Project, up to then with over 1,500 miles of backpacking/exploring, and my need of a fairly hard physical job that would keep me in shape during the off-season. She gave me a try. I had been told that it was "the worst job in the world," and that I "would hate it," but I guaranteed that person I would find a way to love the job…….and I did, soon jogging all over the place to attend to the customers, taking on every task nobody else wanted….or wasn't being done properly.

Soon women were thanking me for finally having the restrooms smelling good, a few elderly ladies falling in love with me, one applying wonderful pressure to marry her--bringing me complete meals, inviting me to her immaculate apartment to fix her computer, and chasing me all over trying to get a kiss--which on reflection I probably should have accepted. But I had to keep my options open, and a new rule was established for me at REAMS, prohibiting

me from being embraced, or embracing any lady unless 90 or over …… and there were a few who loved to do it with the manager watching!

p. 605

I was even the first man to be invited by a group of elderly ladies to go with them on their annual bus trip to Wendover to gamble! But of more importance I was put in charge of training new youth and a new program of public relations. I used one of those gadgets to measure distances and concluded I was doing about 8 miles a day hustling all over in one of the best jobs I have ever had, and soon did as requested, by men and women, doing a special photo/essay WHERE DO I GET SO MUCH ENERGY. 214 But in early 2012 all of a sudden I began having pain in my good leg--the left, and I was no longer able to jog out to help a customer load groceries, or jog down to the other end of the parking lot to get a stray shopping cart. I was near admitting again being a cripple, but learned at the Sports Medicine Clinic that I had a pinched nerve and needed back surgery, so had to quit Reams that resulted in no backpacking during the 2012 season, and had me seriously doing a whole bunch of things explained in the COMEBACK videos mentioned a page or so ago.

My "motorcycle knee" had previously been replaced by titanium, partnering with the 3 titanium screws holding my "football ankle" together on the same leg.

My winters always included working out at home while watching TV, but intensified with special therapy after surgeries. Then once able I moved outside hiking the hills around Springville carrying a backpack with 30 lbs. and increasing 5 lbs./month until backpacking season.

214

https://cordellmandersen.com/where-do-you-get-so-much-energy/

p. 606

These hikes revealed, as seen in some of the YouTube videos, that I had a hitch in my walking, as though my leg was on the verge of collapsing, and I determined that I had to learn a new way to walk and hike. The back surgeries helped solve that problem. During especially intense winter weather I would drive to Provo and the BYU Smith Fieldhouse where I would jog on the straight-aways--with a beautiful young lady doing her

darndest to catch me!

When I would come to the eastern curve I would go up the stairs and do a criss-crossing up and down of the benches and then down to the track for another lap--all to get me ready for mountain climbing and to help me with balance and agility. A year after the first back surgery I began having some trouble again and went through a treatment that didn't work. Of course I was stubborn and got an appointment with Dr. College who had done the failed treatment, and started joking about him about giving me a refund, which conversation led me to tell him my history and he remarked, "I think I know what the trouble is. Let's take an x-ray!" He came back and put the x-ray on his monitor, and pointing to my left ["good"] hip said, "I don't know how you're walking. You're bone on bone and need hip replacement

surgery!" Compare in the image on the left, the photo's left side--clearly defined ball joint, with the right side--all sort of blended together--no cartilage left with bone on bone. Don't be

embarrassed seeing me naked--MY ZIPPER IS UP!

To install the titanium joint, Dr. Jackson had to cut off the ball end of my femur, and I asked him to save it for me to mount on a piece of wood--like for a trophy. Afterward I asked him for it, and he said, "I don't think you would have wanted it, as we found your bones the

hardest we have ever seen, and sawing it off wouldn't work. We had to take it off in four pieces with a hammer and chisel!"

p. 607

That I couldn't quite imagine, and the truth is that the four pieces would have made even a greater trophy. But, IMPORTANTLY, my taking for years of a calcium/magnesium supplement, plus other supplements, is a TESTIMONY OF THE EFFECTIVNESS of what I explain in my ANTI-AGING CHALLENGE ARTICLE, found in Appendix 5. That surgery in 2013 was the quickest to recover from, and had me for a couple of years

"without pain anywhere for the first time in 30 years!"

MY COMEBACK EFFORTS: BECOMING THE EXPERT IN PIONEER TIMBER SLIDES After my first back surgery, and then my hip replacement surgery, I needed physical therapy and so did it on Y and Maple Mountains, in Rock and Slate Canyons, and went to work exploring something nobody had ever done before, much less reported on. I had been observing the evidence--pathways, of these timber slides on the mountains east of Provo for years, and then doing some research noticed mention in an old newspaper article, and then some details in the history books about Provo by Richard Carter. 215 So I had double purpose in what I launched myself into. Eight adventurous exploratory trips of discovery were made into the mountains east of Provo and Springville, that you can learn about through a YouTube video. 216

215

FROM FORT TO VILLAGE Provo, Utah 1850-1854, by D. Robert Carter, 2008

216

Friend, Ken Kartchener, accompanied me on one of those hikes, which for me resulted in a great Survival experience related on pages 564-565 when I discuss the importance of having a good headlamp & the key attitude of remaining calm rather than panicking and doing something deadly stupid in a survival situation. As you can notice, it was a bloody experience for me---because of being "thin skinned." A quick glance Goggling "pioneer timber slides" at that time revealed that I was seemingly the only one interested and knowledgeable about such an important theme that was critical for the making of Provo and Springville. The only other thing that showed up on page 1 was Pioneer Play Apparatuses, that placed me in good company. I'll insert the whole page next so you can see what I mean. NOTE: Today, in 2018, Google has added other items, but I'm

still there, and was the first.

p. 609

Then came 2017 and a flare-up of left-leg problems related again to my back, resulting in a second back surgery--fusing the last two vertebrae, and installing more titanium hardware to try and hold everything lined up properly. Then followed constant RECOVERY-COMEBACK efforts, including scaling one of the last of the mountains I hadn't climbed near Provo. Below on the left showing one of the titanium gadget placed in my spine, and the successful effort to climb Squaw Peak we see in the 2nd photo overlooking Rock Canyon Park.

Along with jogging, I do a hike around town every day with a pack on my back with 35 lbs. of load--good or bad weather, as seen below. Also to solve one of the problems of getting older with loss of good balance--literally a matter of life and death in the mountains, I do as I did when I was 8 years old returning from my newspaper route walking the rails--1 mile each way--when I learned to go for the entire mile without falling, and even was eventually able to jump from one side to the other and keep my balance.

Now, walking the rails is a real test for me, and crucial to maintain good balance and agility in the mountains when following a narrow trail, with a drop-off of sometimes hundreds of feet on one side, when a misstep would be sure death.

p. 610

Making it more fun, I have all kinds of great people stop and offer me a ride, or try and give me money, assuming I'm a poor old homeless guy, but I tell them,

"Thanks, but I'm rather an eccentric millionaire out getting my life-giving exercise." Then I give them my card and tell them what I'm doing and add new HIGH UINTA FRIENDS to my list. The experience is interesting to say the least, usually only with young and middle age people stopping. The older people, like my age, on seeing me just shake their heads in disgust and proudly drive on, in spite of me not having a cardboard sign, nor asking for anything. One actually stopped to offer me something confessing he did so imagining that maybe I was one of the "three Nephites." (A Mormon thing).

The last such experience was on November 22, 2018, a sort of dreary cold day. All of a sudden a beautiful pickup truck pulled across the street onto the wrong side--my side and stopped. A nice looking couple were saying something--which I didn't hear clearly as my hearing system is sort of fading away—and had on earphones listening to the radio, so I was beginning to have my fun about not being "an old homeless guy, rather an eccentric millionaire……." but then recognized a word they were saying, "CROW BASIN!" That had me remove my earphones and come alive listening more carefully, and I met Shane and Leann Jackson full of smiles as they explained that, due to my website reports on Crow Basin and Jonathan Jausi's stunning aerial photos, they had made it into the remote box canyon following my "Yee-Haw trail," and caught and released like 130 beautiful native cutthroat trout.217 Leann went on to explain how her husband feasted on many of my 217

See pages 308-314 of this writing.

p. 611

YouTube videos for hours at a time. Two new wonderful High Uinta Friends were added to my list. WINTERS have sometimes complicated the effort to keep in shape, especially for jogging, so I usually visit every day the wonderful AMERCAN FORK FITNESS CENTER, just a mile from my 7'x 11' travel trailer/millionaire mansion home. NOTE: Being 80+ the Fitness Center costs

me nothing, one of the great perks of being OLD.!

If I was close to Provo I would still include the Fieldhouse as part of the "fitness program." Wherever, you the reader might live, you likely can find equivalent places close-by, but the point is: You likely have noticed that as I have grown older with my Project, I have had to add something to my quote from Winston Churchill……..EASILY!

We human beings have to learn to adapt to "new normal's," which I'm trying to have fun with for as long as possible.

A CRIPPLE AGAIN……MAYBE! A serious GLITCH hit me from January to March 2018, when a bad case of bronchitis hit me. I struggled with my Wellness Formula, other supplements, eating dandelions every day, and getting my vaccinations to prevent it from turning into flu and/or pneumonia, and accomplished that, but was totally out of action for 3 months, and after extensive testing at the hospital, was told that I suffered what was likely a permanent reduction of my respiratory capacity to absorb oxygen--with serious reduction in energy and likely in the Uintas, increased problems with High Altitude Sickness.

p. 612

The 2018 backpacking season came and symptoms persisted, diagnosed as chronic bronchitis, and, as reported on my website, I did some experimentation spending a couple of nights in the Bald Mt./Mirror Lake area, and did hike………

………. up to Scout Lake as I wanted to see the spot of the 1920 SHOOTOUT when a team of tough guys--all but two being gunslingers--half of whom had rode with Butch Cassidy and his Wild Bunch, were sent by F.M.C. Hathenbruck to search for the Lost Rhoades Mine. 218 I didn't feel normal on that trip and hike. Something had changed. Then I decided to try a backpack and went with Ted Packard and son Mike to the Grandview Trailhead, but let them go ahead up the trail to the Grandaddy Basin, as I had to be careful with my experimentation.

I had to do it my way, alone….as best I could, and told them,

“Not to worry if you don’t ever see me again!” That wasn't worded very well, sounding a little fatalistic, so I quickly added…..

"…..until you come back down the trail on the last day of the backpack!” As I ascended in elevation I would easily get out of breath, rested often and checked the oxygen content in my blood with my Oximeter --it usually dropping into the 80's, so I had to rest each time until it normalized.

218

See pages 447-448 of this writing.

p. 613

I only made it to Hades Pass, then backtracked to where there was water, camping out up on the hill. The next day I headed down the trail, but with the jolt of every step down--there was a stabbing pain in my lower back, so I had to move very slowly as I returned to the Trailhead and set up a camp waiting for Ted and Mike.

It rained some each night but I was alright with my shelter using my poncho set up in the protection of the conifers. As I waited for Ted and Mike I had a great time exploring the area near the trailhead, and got some good photos of the fauna and flora of the area. I even had a couple of handfuls of wild strawberries for lunch.

As reported on my website, I became convinced that what I had to do was concentrate more on writing the book--which I have done with over 500 pages completed as I write this today, on Thanksgiving, November 22, 2018.

RESIGNED TO WORK OUT & GET STRONG Yet, too much of me worked too good to throw in the towel, so I carefully set up a program to strengthen myself. Every day I begin with flexibility exercises, then do 40-50 complete pushups, rather than the 100 phony fast ones I used to do, and feel that the complete ones make a big difference, muscle tone improving, my strength increasing, with biceps and chest

p. 614

muscles noticeably growing (doesn't have to be much to be noticeable with an old guy). Then to strengthen my back I carefully do 100 sit-ups with an 8 lb. barbell in each hand. In the summer I did every day what I call my hike with the backpack as already explained and shown with a few photos. But, towards the end of the summer I was making my bed, twisting and turning a little to tuck in the sheets when, all of a sudden I felt a sharp pain. SOMETHING GOT SCREWED UP IN MY LOWER BACK AND LEFT BUTTOCK! It was bad and for two days I couldn't hardly walk. The step down out of my trailer was very close to being impossible. I WAS A CRIPPLE, with no way to fake not being one. I called the clinic to get an appointment, but the earliest opening was 10 days off. Telling them it was an emergency, had them tell me GO TO THE EMERGENCY AT THE HOSPITAL! So, I had to get by on my own for 10 days. That night I said a prayer a bit more fervent than usual, and had come to mind I had to double and even triple my normal dose of two cod liver oil gel caps--taken for 33 years that saved me from arthritis. In addition to the two I take every morning, that night I took three along with a couple of Ibuprofen. In 10 minutes all the pain was gone and I slept peacefully. It had worked the same as when fighting bronchitis when a dull pain in my upper back wouldn't let me sleep-solved also by taking 2-3 gel caps of cod liver oil just before retiring. The anti-inflammatory power of the oil was dramatic (along with my prayer). By the time my Dr. appointment came I had no pain, so when I filled out the form where I had to indicate the level of my pain, I circled 2 so they wouldn't kick me out, but the truth was 0. I explained to the Dr. why I was there and how things had developed. He sent me for X-rays, that showed all was fine. Since, I have had to be careful, and when doing my hike with backpack, or going to the Fitness Center, take an extra couple of gel caps, and I have hope that another COMEBACK is possible. The big question remaining: Getting through the winter avoiding a flare-up of chronic bronchitis, and getting it out of my system to have the energy and the high altitude problems solved. Near the same time my son, Lito (Cordel Ammon), introduced me to something he had heard of, THE ONE MINUTE CURE,219 and I was willing to try anything to hopefully burn the bronchitis and wheezing out of my chest, and restore its normal function. I started with a TRIPLE WHAMMY treatment: Using food grade Hyrodgen Peroxide -Ingested, inhaled, and topical (for skin cancer). Within two days the phlegm was loosening up in my chest for the first time since last winter. Now, with about two months of the

treatment behind me, some progress has been accomplished--up to November 22nd when I met Shane and Leanne.220 I had carefully persisted with my hikes around town with backpack with gradually increasing cold weather that should have strengthened me in every way--as long as I was careful and avoided getting sick. My walking/jogging at the Fitness Center was gradually being increased, which should have helped my respiratory function as well as my overall strength, and I had hopes of being strong enough to keep well during the winter, and have the vision of yet being able to make another COMEBACK! My hike with backpack on November 22nd--a cold dreary day, then jog at the Fitness Center on November 23rd, were not extreme, yet that night I didn't feel well, and by the next day an attack of bronchitis hit me quite hard and I’m struggling to overcome it--so far with some success in that I have achieved not having a fever, nor having it slide down to flu or pneumonia. Today, December 10th, I'm beginning the extreme version of the treatment with hyrodgen peroxide and feel it's helping. Persisting so far has not been……EASY. As I write and recall the EPILOGUE, where I pictured the Mossinger family, and quoted the son who said: "You don't grow old and stop backpacking, rather if you stop backpacking you will grow old!" UPDATING – April 12, 2019 The extreme treatment—like chemotherapy, helped some, made possible avoiding flu and pneumonia, and permitted working out every day carefully—unlike 2018 when I was out of action for 3 months. Now using my Wellness Formula treatment explained in my Anti-Aging Challenge article in Appendix 5. I am now cautiously working out daily at the Fitness Center, increasing daily very carefully the repetitions and intensity—today doing 20 laps walking with backpack, and finish by jogging a couple of laps. All to gradually increase carefully and now beginning to go outside. So, I didn’t completely get rid of the chronic bronchitis, but am convinced I can learn to manage it, like I have learned to do with High Altitude Sickness, and am excited about being able to do much more exploring/backpacking during the 2019 season than even I would have guessed possible a couple of months ago—and much more than in 2018.
